questions.officialText: A 40-year-old patient presents with a palpable pulsation on the left side of her chest. Upon examination, it is found that the pulsation is localized to the left fifth intercostal space 9cm lateral to the sternum. a) What is the term used to describe this pulsation. b) Name the chamber of heart which causes this palpable pulsation c) Explain the external features and internal features of this chamber of heart d) Describe the blood supply of this chamber of heart (1+1+4+4)

note.title: Apex Beat and Left Ventricle of Heart
note.content:
##### a) Term Used to Describe This Pulsation * **Apex Beat** (or *point of maximal impulse* [PMI]): The outermost and lowermost thrust of cardiac pulsation felt over the precordium, produced by the impact of the apex of the left ventricle against the chest wall during early ventricular systole. * **Normal Location:** Left 5th intercostal space, approximately 9 cm (or $3\frac{1}{2}$ inches) lateral to the midsternal line, just medial to the midclavicular line. ##### b) Chamber of Heart Forming This Pulsation * **Left Ventricle:** Forms the entirety of the apex of the heart. ``` ANTERIOR / STERNOCOSTAL VIEW Superior Vena Cava | / Aorta | / / Pulmonary Trunk +------+--+-+--+ | RA | | \ Left Auricle | Right | \ | Ventricle | \ LEFT VENTRICLE +---------------+ \ \ \ \_____\ <--- APEX (5th ICS, 9 cm from midline) ``` ##### c) External and Internal Features of the Left Ventricle * **External Features:** * **Shape:** Conical; wall thickness is 3 times thicker (8–12 mm) than that of the right ventricle to generate high systemic pressures. * **Surfaces Contributed:** * *Apex:* Formed entirely by the left ventricle. * *Sternocostal surface:* Contributes a small lateral strip (one-third). * *Diaphragmatic (inferior) surface:* Contributes the left two-thirds. * *Left (pulmonary) surface:* Contributes almost the entire surface. * **Grooves:** Separated from the right ventricle anteriorly by the *anterior interventricular groove* and inferiorly by the *posterior interventricular groove*. Separated from the left atrium by the posterior part of the *atrioventricular (coronary) sulcus*. * **Internal Features:** * The cavity is circular in transverse cross-section (in contrast to the crescentic right ventricle). * **Inflowing Part (Rough part):** * *Trabeculae Carneae:* Muscular ridges, bridges, and pillars lining the muscular wall. They are finer, denser, and more numerous than in the right ventricle. * *Papillary Muscles:* Two large, well-developed muscles—**Anterolateral papillary muscle** and **Posteromedial papillary muscle**. * *Chordae Tendineae:* Fibrous cords arising from the apices of both papillary muscles; attach to the free margins and ventricular surfaces of the anterior and posterior cusps of the bicuspid (mitral) valve. * **Outflowing Part (Smooth part / Aortic Vestibule):** * Smooth-walled upper anteromedial part situated immediately below the aortic orifice. * Fibrous walls allow smooth laminar ejection of blood into the ascending aorta. * **Orifices:** * *Bicuspid (Mitral) Orifice:* Guarded by the mitral valve, located postero-inferiorly; possesses 2 cusps (anterior/aortic cusp and posterior cusp). * *Aortic Orifice:* Guarded by the aortic valve (consisting of 3 semilunar cusps: anterior, left posterior, right posterior), directing blood into the ascending aorta. * **Interventricular Septum:** Divides left and right ventricles; comprises a lower thick muscular part and an upper thin membranous part (site of ventricular septal defect). ##### d) Blood Supply of the Left Ventricle The left ventricle has a high metabolic demand and is supplied by branches of both coronary arteries: | Artery | Origin & Course | Territories Supplied in Left Ventricle | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Left Anterior Descending (LAD)** (*Anterior Interventricular Artery*) | Branch of Left Coronary Artery; runs down anterior interventricular groove to the apex. | • Anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum
• Anterior and apical wall of the left ventricle
• Anterolateral papillary muscle | | **Left Circumflex Artery (LCx)** | Branch of Left Coronary Artery; runs in the left anterior/posterior atrioventricular groove. | • Lateral free wall of left ventricle
• Posterior wall via obtuse marginal branches | | **Posterior Interventricular Artery (PDA)** | Branch of Right Coronary Artery (in 85–90% right-dominant hearts) or LCx (left-dominant). | • Posterior one-third of the interventricular septum
• Diaphragmatic (inferior) wall of left ventricle
• Posteromedial papillary muscle | * **Venous Drainage:** * *Great Cardiac Vein:* Ascends in the anterior interventricular groove alongside LAD, drains into the coronary sinus. * *Middle Cardiac Vein:* Runs in the posterior interventricular groove with the PDA. * *Posterior Vein of the Left Ventricle:* Drains directly into the coronary sinus. * **Clinical Diagram Reference:** [Human Heart Anatomy (Wikimedia Commons)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Diagram_of_the_human_heart_%28cropped%29.svg/1280px-Diagram_of_the_human_heart_%28cropped%29.svg.png) ---

questions.officialText: Describe the derivatives of Intraembryonic mesoderm.

note.title: Derivatives of Intraembryonic Mesoderm
note.content:
During the 3rd week of intrauterine development, gastrulation converts the bilaminar embryonic disc into a trilaminar disc. The intraembryonic mesoderm differentiates mediolaterally into three primary regions:

```
        Neural Tube / Notochord (Midline)
                     |
       [Paraxial Mesoderm] (Somites)
                     |
    [Intermediate Mesoderm] (Nephrotome)
                     |
    [Lateral Plate Mesoderm]
       /                   \
Somatic Mesoderm       Splanchnic Mesoderm
(Parietal layer)       (Visceral layer)
```

##### 1. Paraxial Mesoderm
Organized into longitudinal columns alongside the notochord; segments into **somites** (42–44 pairs), each dividing into:
* **Sclerotome:** Forms vertebrae, intervertebral discs (annulus fibrosus), and ribs.
* **Myotome:**
  * *Epimere:* Extensor muscles of the vertebral column (deep back muscles).
  * *Hypomere:* Flexor and lateral muscles of the trunk wall and all limb musculature.
* **Dermatome:** Dermis and subcutaneous tissue of the back, neck, and anterolateral trunk.

##### 2. Intermediate Mesoderm
Connects paraxial and lateral plate mesoderm:
* **Urogenital System:**
  * Pronephros, mesonephros, metanephros (kidneys and ureters) [112001:Q01].
  * Trigone of the urinary bladder.
  * Gonads (testes, ovaries) and duct systems (mesonephric/Wolffian ducts) [112001:Q01, 112001:Q13].
  * Internal genital ducts (cortex of suprarenal gland).

##### 3. Lateral Plate Mesoderm
Cleaves by the formation of the intraembryonic coelom into two layers:
* **Somatic (Parietal) Mesoderm:**
  * Covers the intraembryonic body cavity externally.
  * Forms the parietal layer of serous membranes (pleura, pericardium, peritoneum).
  * Skeletal components of limbs (bones, ligaments, joints, limb dermis).
* **Splanchnic (Visceral) Mesoderm:**
  * Coats the primitive gut tube internally.
  * Forms the visceral layer of serous membranes (visceral pleura, pericardium, peritoneum).
  * Smooth muscle, lamina propria, submucosa, and connective tissue coats of the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts.
  * Heart, cardiac muscle, pericardial cavity, blood vessels, and blood cells (hemangioblasts).

##### 4. Cardiogenic Mesoderm & Septum Transversum
* Arises cranial to the buccopharyngeal membrane; gives rise to the heart tube and central tendon of the diaphragm [112001:Q17].

---

questions.officialText: Lymphatic drainage of mammary gland and its clinical significance.

note.title: Lymphatic Drainage of Mammary Gland and Its Clinical Significance
note.content:
##### Lymphatic Drainage Pathways
The breast drains lymph via superficial (cutaneous) and deep (parenchymal) plexuses (Plexus of Sappey):

```
                                MAMMARY GLAND
                                      |
         +----------------------------+----------------------------+
         | (75%)                      | (20%)                      | (5%)
         v                            v                            v
   Axillary Nodes            Internal Mammary Nodes         Posterior Intercostal
   (Pectoral/Anterior,       (Parasternal Nodes along       Nodes (along posterior
    Lateral, Posterior,       internal thoracic vessels)    intercostal vessels)
    Central, Apical)                  |
         |                            v
         v                    Mediastinal Nodes
   Supraclavicular Nodes      / Subdiaphragmatic
         |                    & Hepatic Connections
         v
  Subclavian Lymph Trunk
```

1. **Axillary Lymph Nodes (approx. 75%):**
   * *Anterior (Pectoral) Group:* Primary recipient; lies along the lower border of pectoralis minor near the lateral thoracic vessels.
   * *Posterior (Subscapular) Group:* Along the lower margin of the posterior axillary fold.
   * *Lateral Group:* Along the upper axillary vein.
   * *Central Group:* Embedded in axillary fat.
   * *Apical (Infraclavicular) Group:* Lies at the apex of axilla; drains into the supraclavicular nodes and the subclavian lymph trunk.
2. **Internal Mammary (Parasternal) Nodes (approx. 20%):**
   * Drains lymph predominantly from the medial quadrants. Crosses across the sternum to the opposite breast, providing a pathway for bilateral metastasis.
3. **Posterior Intercostal Nodes (approx. 5%):**
   * Accompanies posterior intercostal arteries to drain into thoracic duct or posterior mediastinal nodes.

##### Clinical Significance
* **Carcinoma Breast Metastasis:** Axillary nodes are the primary site of sentinel lymph node spread. Fixed, hard, matted lymph nodes are a cardinal diagnostic sign.
* **Peau d'orange:** Tumor emboli block dermal lymphatics, resulting in localized dermal edema. Tethering of hair follicles and sweat glands produces an appearance resembling orange peel [111001:Q01].
* **Nipple Retraction:** Infiltration of the lactiferous ducts and *suspensory ligaments of Cooper* causes mechanical shortening and inverted/retracted nipples.
* **Trans-coelomic Spread (Krukenberg Tumor):** Lymphatic communications through the rectus sheath and falciform ligament allow metastases from medial quadrants to seed subdiaphragmatic and ovarian tissues.
* **Diagram Reference:** [Lymph Nodes of Breast (Wikimedia Commons)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Illu_breast_anatomy.jpg/800px-Illu_breast_anatomy.jpg)

---

note.title: Internal Thoracic Artery
note.content:
##### Origin, Course, and Termination
* **Origin:** Arises from the inferior border of the 1st part of the subclavian artery in the root of the neck, opposite the origin of the thyrocervical trunk.
* **Course:**
  * Descends vertically behind the sternoclavicular joint, deep to the clavicle, subclavius, and internal jugular vein.
  * Enters the thorax behind the costal cartilages of the upper six ribs, running roughly $1.25\text{ cm}$ ($0.5\text{ inch}$) lateral to the lateral sternal edge.
  * Crosses anterior to the pleura and transversus thoracis muscle.
* **Termination:** At the level of the 6th intercostal space by dividing into two terminal branches:
  1. *Superior epigastric artery*
  2. *Musculophrenic artery*

```
Subclavian Artery (1st part)
        |
        v
Internal Thoracic Artery (ITA)
        |---> Pericardiacophrenic Artery (with phrenic nerve)
        |---> Anterior Intercostal Arteries (Upper 6 spaces; 2 per space)
        |---> Perforating Branches (2nd, 3rd, 4th supply breast)
        |---> Sternal & Mediastinal Branches
        |
        +-----> [6th Intercostal Space]
        |
        +---> Superior Epigastric Artery (enters rectus sheath)
        +---> Musculophrenic Artery (runs along costal margin, 7th-9th spaces)
```

##### Branches and Distribution
1. **Pericardiacophrenic Artery:** Accompanies the phrenic nerve between the pleura and pericardium to supply both structures and the diaphragm.
2. **Anterior Intercostal Arteries:** Two in each of the upper six intercostal spaces; anastomose with the posterior intercostal arteries.
3. **Perforating Arteries:** Pierce the intercostal spaces alongside anterior cutaneous nerves; branches in the 2nd–4th spaces form major arterial feeders to the female breast.
4. **Superior Epigastric Artery:** Enters the rectus sheath via the space between the sternal and costal slips of the diaphragm (Larrey's space) to anastomose with the inferior epigastric artery (providing collateral circulation in coarctation of aorta).
5. **Musculophrenic Artery:** Pierces the diaphragm, giving off two anterior intercostal arteries for the 7th, 8th, and 9th spaces.

##### Clinical Anatomy
* **CABG (Coronary Artery Bypass Graft):** The left internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery (LITA/LIMA) is the gold standard conduit for bypass grafting to the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery due to high long-term patency rates [112001:Q22].

---

note.title: Autosomal Dominant Inheritance
note.content:
* **Definition:** A mode of Mendelian inheritance where a phenotype or disease is expressed in heterozygous individuals carrying a single copy of a mutated allele on an autosome (non-sex chromosome).
* **Key Characteristics:**
  * **Vertical Transmission:** Manifests in every generation without skipping; affected individuals typically have an affected parent.
  * **Transmission Risk:** An affected heterozygote ($Aa$) and an unaffected individual ($aa$) produce offpsring with a 50% ($1 \text{ in } 2$) probability of inheriting the disorder, irrespective of sex.
  * **Equal Sex Distribution:** Males and females are affected with equal frequency and transmit the gene equally.
  * **Father-to-son transmission:** Observed (rules out X-linked conditions).
* **Important Genetic Phenomena:**
  * *Incomplete Penetrance:* Some individuals carrying the dominant gene do not express the phenotype.
  * *Variable Expressivity:* Variation in clinical severity among individuals with identical genotypes.
  * *Pleiotropy:* A single mutated gene produces multiple distinct, seemingly unrelated organ manifestations (e.g., Marfan syndrome).
* **Clinical Examples:**
  * Achondroplasia (FGFR3 mutation)
  * Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation)
  * Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1 mutation)
  * Huntington disease (CAG trinucleotide repeats)
  * Familial hypercholesterolemia (LDLR mutation)

note.title: Classification of Synovial Joints with Examples
note.content:
Synovial joints are characterized by a synovial cavity, articular cartilage, a fibrous capsule lined by synovial membrane, and variable intra-articular structures. They are classified based on the shape of their articular surfaces and the axes of movement: | Type | Structural Feature | Axes of Movement | Examples | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Plane (Gliding)** | Opposing surfaces are flat or nearly flat | Non-axial; simple gliding movements | • Intercarpal and intertarsal joints
• Acromioclavicular joint
• Zygapophyseal (facet) joints of spine | | **Hinge (Ginglymus)** | Pulley-shaped spool fitted into a concave surface | Uniaxial; flexion and extension in sagittal plane | • Elbow joint (humeroulnar)
• Ankle (talocrural) joint
• Interphalangeal joints of hand/foot | | **Pivot (Trochoid)** | Central bony pivot surrounded by an osteoligamentous ring | Uniaxial; rotation around vertical axis | • Median atlantoaxial joint
• Superior and inferior radioulnar joints | | **Condylar (Bicondylar)** | Two distinct convex condyles articulate with concave surfaces | Modified multiaxial; predominantly flexion/extension with limited rotation | • Knee joint (tibiofemoral)
• Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) | | **Ellipsoid** | Oval convex surface fits into an elliptical concave socket | Biaxial; flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, circumduction (no axial rotation) | • Radiocarpal (wrist) joint
• Metacarpophalangeal joints | | **Saddle (Sellar)** | Opposing surfaces are concavo-convex reciprocal surfaces | Biaxial with axial conjunct rotation | • 1st carpometacarpal joint (base of thumb)
• Sternoclavicular joint

questions.officialText: Nerve supply and action of Gluteus Medius.

note.title: Nerve Supply and Action of Gluteus Medius
note.content:
* **Nerve Supply:**
  * **Superior Gluteal Nerve:** Arises from the sacral plexus with root value **L4, L5, S1**. It enters the gluteal region through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis muscle.
* **Actions:**
  * **Abduction of the Hip Joint:** The primary abductor of the thigh at the hip joint along with gluteus minimus.
  * **Medial Rotation of the Hip:** The anterior horizontal fibers act as powerful internal/medial rotators.
  * **Stabilization of the Pelvis (Trendelenburg Function):** During unipedal weight-bearing (the stance phase of walking), it contracts to prevent the opposite, unsupported pelvis from dropping.
* **Clinical Significance:**
  * *Trendelenburg Sign:* Damage to the superior gluteal nerve causes gluteus medius paralysis; during standing on the affected side, the pelvis tilts downwards toward the normal, unsupported side [112001:Q01].

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.officialText: Microscopic structure of Transverse section of compact bone.

note.title: Microscopic Structure of Transverse Section of Compact Bone
note.content:
* **Structural Functional Unit:** The **Osteon** or **Haversian System**.

```
    +-----------------------------------------------+
    |            CONCENTRIC LAMELLAE                |
    |         . - ~ ~ ~ - .                         |
    |     . '     Lacuna    ' .                     |
    |   /   (with Osteocyte)    \                   |
    |  /      \       /          \                  |
    | |        Canaliculi         |                 |
    | |             o             |                 |
    | |     HAVERSIAN CANAL       |                 |
    | |    (Vessel & Nerve)       |                 |
    |  \                         /                  |
    |   \                       /                   |
    |     . '                 ' .                   |
    |         ' - ~ ~ ~ - '                         |
    |               CEMENT LINE                     |
    +-----------------------------------------------+
```

* **Microscopic Features:**
  1. **Haversian (Central) Canal:** Longitudinal central channels running parallel to the long axis of the bone; transmit neurovascular bundles (arteriole, venule, capillary, unmyelinated nerve fiber) and lymphatic channels.
  2. **Concentric Lamellae:** 4 to 20 rings of calcified collagenous bone matrix arranged concentrically around each Haversian canal. Collagen fibers run in opposite spiral directions in adjacent lamellae to provide torsional strength.
  3. **Lacunae:** Small, lenticular spaces located between adjacent lamellae, each occupied by the cell body of a single **osteocyte**.
  4. **Canaliculi:** Tiny radiating canalicular tunnels penetrating the lamellae; contain filopodial cytoplasmic processes of osteocytes connected via gap junctions for nutrient, metabolic, and signaling exchange.
  5. **Volkmann’s (Perforating) Canals:** Oblique or transverse canals running perpendicular to Haversian canals; connect Haversian canals with the periosteum and endosteum, carrying communicating blood vessels without concentric lamellae.
  6. **Interstitial Lamellae:** Irregular angular matrix areas occupying spaces between intact circular Haversian systems; represent remnants of remodeled older osteons.
  7. **Circumferential Lamellae:** *Outer circumferential lamellae* situated immediately deep to the periosteum; *inner circumferential lamellae* lining the medullary cavity adjacent to the endosteum.
  8. **Cement Line:** Outer mineralized limiting border of an osteon deficient in collagen fibers.

---

note.title: Bronchopulmonary Segments of Right Lung
note.content:
* **Definition:** Anatomical, functional, and surgically resectable structural units of lung tissue aerated by a tertiary (segmental) bronchus accompanied by a branch of the pulmonary artery.

```
       RIGHT MAIN BRONCHUS
          |
          +---> Superior Lobe Bronchus (Eparterial)
          |        1. Apical
          |        2. Posterior
          |        3. Anterior
          |
          +---> Middle Lobe Bronchus
          |        4. Lateral
          |        5. Medial
          |
          +---> Inferior Lobe Bronchus (Hyparterial)
                   6. Superior (Apical of lower lobe)
                   7. Medial Basal (Cardiac)
                   8. Anterior Basal
                   9. Lateral Basal
                  10. Posterior Basal
```

* **Enumeration (10 Segments):**
  * **Superior Lobe (3 segments):**
    1. Apical segment (B1)
    2. Posterior segment (B2)
    3. Anterior segment (B3)
  * **Middle Lobe (2 segments):**
    4. Lateral segment (B4)
    5. Medial segment (B5)
  * **Inferior Lobe (5 segments):**
    6. Superior (Apical of inferior lobe) segment (B6)
    7. Medial basal (Cardiac) segment (B7)
    8. Anterior basal segment (B8)
    9. Lateral basal segment (B9)
    10. Posterior basal segment (B10)
* **Structural Characteristics:** Each segment is pyramidal with its apex pointing to the lung root; pulmonary veins run *intersegmentally* in the connective tissue septa (act as surgical guide planes during segmentectomy).

---

note.title: Boundaries of Cubital Fossa
note.content:
* **Definition:** A triangular subfascial depression situated on the anterior aspect of the elbow joint.
* **Boundaries:**
  * **Superior (Base):** Imaginary horizontal line joining the medial and lateral epicondyles of the humerus.
  * **Medial:** Lateral border of the **Pronator Teres** muscle.
  * **Lateral:** Medial border of the **Brachioradialis** muscle.
  * **Apex:** Directed downward; formed where the brachioradialis muscle crosses the pronator teres.
  * **Roof:** Skin, superficial fascia (containing median cubital vein, lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm, medial cutaneous nerve of forearm), deep fascia, and reinforced by the **bicipital aponeurosis**.
  * **Floor:** Formed proximally by the **Brachialis** and distally by the **Supinator** muscle.

---

note.title: Branches of Posterior Cord of Brachial Plexus

* **Mnemonic:** **ULTRA**
  1. **U** – **Upper Subscapular nerve** (C5, C6): Supplies Subscapularis.
  2. **L** – **Lower Subscapular nerve** (C5, C6): Supplies Subscapularis and Teres major.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.officialText: A 62 -year-old male patient presents with jaundice, dark urine and pain in the right hypochondriac region. Ultrasound abdomen reveals enlargement of the organ present in right hypochondrium, extending to epigastric and left hypochondrium. Clinical investigation revealed elevated enzymes and altered function from this organ. a) Name the parts and peritoneal folds of the organ likely to be affected in the patient. b) Describe the relations of posterior and inferior surface of this organ. c) Describe the blood supply and microscopic structure of the organ affected. (2+4+4)

note.title: Liver Anatomy, Relations, Blood Supply, and Histology
note.content:
##### a) Parts and Peritoneal Folds of the Liver
* **Anatomical Parts / Lobes:**
  * **Right Lobe:** Large, accounts for $\approx \frac{5}{6}$ of the liver mass.
  * **Left Lobe:** Smaller, flattened; separated from the right lobe anteriorly by the *falciform ligament*, and on the visceral surface by the *fissure for ligamentum venosum* and *fissure for ligamentum teres*.
  * **Caudate Lobe:** Located on the posterior surface; bounded by the IVC groove on the right, fissure for ligamentum venosum on the left, and porta hepatis inferiorly.
  * **Quadrate Lobe:** Located on the inferior/visceral surface; bounded by the gallbladder fossa on the right, fissure for ligamentum teres on the left, and porta hepatis posteriorly.
* **Peritoneal Folds:**
  * **Falciform Ligament:** Sickle-shaped double fold connecting the diaphragmatic surface to the anterior abdominal wall and inferior surface of the diaphragm. Free border houses the *ligamentum teres hepatis* (obliterated left umbilical vein).
  * **Coronary Ligament:** Formed by the reflection of peritoneum from the diaphragm to the liver:
    * *Upper layer:* Diverges along the upper border of the bare area.
    * *Lower layer:* Reflected along the lower margin of the bare area.
  * **Right and Left Triangular Ligaments:** Formed at the right and left acute lateral extremities where the layers of the coronary ligament approximate.
  * **Lesser Omentum:** Connects the porta hepatis and fissure for ligamentum venosum to the lesser curvature of the stomach and 1st part of the duodenum.
  * **Bare Area of Liver:** Non-peritoneal triangular area on the posterosuperior surface of the right lobe attached directly to the diaphragm by loose connective tissue.

##### b) Relations of Posterior and Inferior Surfaces
* **Posterior Surface:**
  1. *Bare Area:* Direct contact with the diaphragm (contains right suprarenal impression inferomedially).
  2. *Groove for Inferior Vena Cava:* Deep vertical sulcus lodging the retrohepatic IVC, receiving the three main hepatic veins.
  3. *Caudate Lobe:* Lies in the superior recess of the lesser sac; faces the crus of diaphragm and T10–T11 vertebrae.
  4. *Fissure for Ligamentum Venosum:* Houses the obliterated ductus venosus; runs vertically between caudate and left lobes.
  5. *Esophageal Impression:* Located on the left lobe, lodging the abdominal part of the esophagus.

```
           VISCERAL / INFERIOR SURFACE OF THE LIVER
               +-----------------------------+
               |      CAUDATE LOBE (Post)     |
               |  (Fissure for   |    (Groove |
               |   Lig. Venosum) |    for IVC)|
               +-----------------+------------+
               |         PORTA HEPATIS        |
               +-----------------+------------+
               |  Gastric Impr.  | Quadrate   |   Renal
               |   (Left Lobe)   | Lobe       |   Impression
               |                 |------------|   (Right Lobe)
               |                 | Gallbladder|
               |                 |   Fossa    |   Colic Impr.
               +-----------------+------------+
```

* **Inferior (Visceral) Surface:**
  1. *Gastric Impression:* Large concave hollow on the left lobe related to the anterosuperior surface of the fundus and body of stomach.
  2. *Tuber Omentale:* Smooth elevation on the left lobe abutting the lesser omentum.
  3. *Quadrate Lobe:* Related to the pylorus, 1st part of duodenum, and transverse colon.
  4. *Fossa for Gallbladder:* Devoid of peritoneum, lodges the gallbladder.
  5. *Duodenal Impression:* Located to the right of the gallbladder fossa; relates to the 2nd part of the duodenum.
  6. *Renal Impression:* Deep hollow lodging the anterior surface of the upper pole of the right kidney.
  7. *Colic Impression:* Located anteriorly on the right lobe; relates to the right colic (hepatic) flexure.

##### c) Blood Supply and Microscopic Structure
* **Blood Supply:** Dual afferent vascular supply:
  * **Portal Vein (75–80% of volume):** Carries partially oxygenated, nutrient-dense blood from the GI tract and spleen.
  * **Hepatic Artery (Proper Hepatic Artery) (20–25% of volume):** Delivers highly oxygenated systemic blood; branches at the porta hepatis into right and left hepatic arteries.
  * Both mix within the **hepatic sinusoids** and drain via the **central veins** $\rightarrow$ **sublobular veins** $\rightarrow$ **hepatic veins (right, middle, left)** $\rightarrow$ **inferior vena cava**.

* **Microscopic Structure:**
  * **Classic Hepatic Lobule:** Hexagonal prism centered around a **Central Vein** [112001:Q01]. At the peripheral corners lie the **Portal Triads** (or portal canals) embedded in Glisson’s capsule.
  * **Components of the Portal Triad:**
    1. Branch of Portal Vein (interlobular venule)
    2. Branch of Hepatic Artery (interlobular arteriole)
    3. Interlobular Bile Ductule (lined by simple cuboidal epithelium)
    4. Lymphatic vessel and sympathetic nerves
  * **Hepatocyte Plates:** Unicellular branching plates of polyhedral hepatocytes radiating from the central vein to the periphery. Hepatocytes contain central spherical vesicular nuclei (often binucleate) with acidophilic cytoplasm rich in glycogen, peroxisomes, and mitochondria.
  * **Hepatic Sinusoids:** Fenestrated, discontinuous capillaries lining plates; lined by endothelial cells and phagocytic **Kupffer cells** (hepatic macrophages).
  * **Space of Disse (Perisinusoidal space):** Subendothelial space between hepatocytes and sinusoidal endothelial cells; site of nutrient exchange and houses **Ito cells (hepatic stellate cells)** that store vitamin A and synthesize collagen when activated [112001:Q01].
  * **Bile Canaliculi:** Dilated intercellular grooves between adjacent hepatocytes draining bile centrifugally (opposite to blood flow) toward the portal triad.
* **Reference Diagram:** [Porta Hepatis and Liver Anatomy (Wikimedia Commons)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Gray1086-liver.PNG/330px-Gray1086-liver.PNG)

---

questions.officialText: Extraocular muscles of eyeball- Attachments, nerve supply, action.

note.title: Extraocular Muscles of the Eyeball
note.content:
The extraocular muscles comprise 4 recti, 2 obliques, and levator palpebrae superioris.

| Muscle | Origin | Insertion | Nerve Supply | Primary Action | Secondary Actions |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Superior Rectus (SR)** | Common tendinous ring (Annulus of Zinn) | Sclera $7.5\text{ mm}$ posterior to superior limbus | Superior division of Oculomotor (CN III) | **Elevation** | Adduction, Intorsion |
| **Inferior Rectus (IR)** | Common tendinous ring | Sclera $6.5\text{ mm}$ posterior to inferior limbus | Inferior division of Oculomotor (CN III) | **Depression** | Adduction, Extorsion |
| **Medial Rectus (MR)** | Common tendinous ring | Sclera $5.5\text{ mm}$ posterior to medial limbus | Inferior division of Oculomotor (CN III) | **Adduction** | None |
| **Lateral Rectus (LR)** | Common tendinous ring | Sclera $6.9\text{ mm}$ posterior to lateral limbus | Abducens (CN VI) | **Abduction** | None |
| **Superior Oblique (SO)**| Body of sphenoid superomedial to optic canal | Passes through cartilaginous pulley (trochlea), inserts onto posterolateral upper quadrant of sclera | Trochlear (CN IV) | **Intorsion** | Depression (maximal when adducted), Abduction |
| **Inferior Oblique (IO)**| Anteromedial orbital floor (orbital surface of maxilla) | Passes posterolaterally deep to lateral rectus into posterolateral sclera | Inferior division of Oculomotor (CN III) | **Extorsion** | Elevation (maximal when adducted), Abduction |
| **Levator Palpebrae Superioris** | Lesser wing of sphenoid above optic canal | Skin of upper eyelid, anterior superior tarsal plate | Superior division of Oculomotor (CN III) | **Elevates upper eyelid** | Maintains palpebral fissure |

* **Mnemonic for Innervation:** **$(LR_6 SO_4)_3$** — Lateral Rectus by CN VI, Superior Oblique by CN IV, all remaining muscles by CN III.
* **H-Pattern Clinical Testing:**
  * To test SO: Direct patient to look medially and then down.
  * To test IO: Direct patient to look medially and then up.

---

note.title: Supports of the Uterus
note.content:
The supports prevent uterine prolapse and are classified into mechanical (primary) and peritoneal/fascial (secondary) supports:

##### 1. Primary (Mechanical / Dynamic & Fibromuscular) Supports
* **Active / Dynamic Support:**
  * **Pelvic Diaphragm:** Consists of the **Levator Ani** (specifically the pubococcygeus and puborectalis forming a U-shaped sling around the vagina) and **Coccygeus** muscles. The principal dynamic support.
  * **Perineal Body:** Central tendon of the perineum located between the anal canal and vagina; provides structural integrity to the lower end of the vaginal canal.
* **Passive / Mechanical (Ligamentous / Endopelvic Fascia) Supports:**
  * **Transverse Cervical (Mackenrodt's / Cardinal) Ligaments:** Dense condensations of endopelvic fascia extending bilaterally from the supravaginal cervix and vaginal vaults to the lateral pelvic wall. The **most critical mechanical ligament**.
  * **Uterosacral Ligaments:** Run from the posterior cervicovaginal junction, curve around the rectum, and insert into the periosteum of the 2nd and 3rd sacral vertebrae. Hold the cervix back in its normal posterior position.
  * **Pubocervical Ligaments:** Extend forward from the cervix to the posterior surface of the pubis, supporting the bladder base and anterior vaginal wall.
  * **Normal Angles of the Uterus:**
    * *Angle of Anteversion ($90^\circ$):* Long axis of the cervix forward on the long axis of the vagina.
    * *Angle of Anteflexion ($125^\circ$–$170^\circ$):* Long axis of the uterine body bent forward on the cervix. This forward tilt ensures increased intra-abdominal pressure pushes the uterus against the bladder and pubic bones rather than through the vaginal introitus.

##### 2. Secondary (Peritoneal) Supports
* **Broad Ligament:** Bilayered peritoneal fold extending from the lateral uterine margins to the pelvic walls (subdivided into mesometrium, mesosalpinx, and mesovarium). Offers no mechanical barrier to prolapse.
* **Round Ligament of Uterus:** Fibromuscular cords extending from the uterine horn (anterior to uterine tube), traversing the inguinal canal to terminate in the labia majora; helps maintain anteversion during pregnancy [112001:Q01].

---

note.title: Arterial Supply of Cerebrum
note.content:
The cerebral arterial supply is derived from two internal carotid arteries and two vertebral arteries forming the **Circle of Willis (Circulus Arteriosus)** at the base of the brain around the interpeduncular fossa.

```
                   Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA)
                              \       /
                      AComA --- [ O ] --- AComA (Anterior Communicating)
                               |     |
                 Internal -----+     +----- Internal
                 Carotid                   Carotid
                    \                         /
                     PComA               PComA (Posterior Communicating)
                       \                 /
                        +---------------+
                        | Posterior     |
                        | Cerebral (PCA)|
                        +---------------+
                                |
                           Basilar Artery
                                |
                        Vertebral Arteries
```

##### 1. Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA)
* **Terminal Branch:** Internal carotid artery.
* **Cortical Distribution:**
  * Medial surface of cerebral hemisphere up to the parieto-occipital sulcus.
  * An upper $1\text{ inch}$ ($2.5\text{ cm}$) strip of the superolateral surface.
  * Supplies the **motor and sensory homunculus of the lower limb and perineum** (micturition and defecation cortical centers).

##### 2. Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA)
* **Terminal Branch:** Direct continuation of the internal carotid artery; courses through the lateral sulcus.
* **Cortical Distribution:**
  * Almost the entire superolateral surface of the hemisphere (except the superior $1\text{ inch}$ strip supplied by ACA and the occipital pole/inferior temporal gyri supplied by PCA).
  * Supplies the **motor and sensory cortex of the upper limb, trunk, head, face, Broca’s motor speech area (areas 44, 45), and Wernicke’s sensory speech area (area 22)** [111001:Q01].
  * *Striate branches (Charcot's artery of cerebral hemorrhage):* Supply the internal capsule.

##### 3. Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA)
* **Terminal Branch:** Bifurcation of the basilar artery.
* **Cortical Distribution:**
  * Tentorial (inferior) surface of the hemisphere.
  * Occipital pole and medial surface of the occipital lobe around the calcarine sulcus (**primary visual cortex, Brodmann area 17**).

---

note.title: Interior of Anal Canal
note.content:
The anal canal (length: $3.8\text{ cm}$) is divided into three zones based on mucosal architecture and embryological origin:

```
    Upper 15 mm  |   Anal Columns of Morgagni (6-10 vertical folds)
                 |   Anal Valves & Anal Sinuses (crypts)
  --- PECTINATE LINE ------------------------------------------------
    Middle 15 mm |   Pecten (Transitional Zone lined by stratified squam.)
  --- HILTON'S WHITE LINE (Intersphincteric groove) ------------------
    Lower 8 mm   |   Cutaneous Zone (True perianal skin with hairs/sweat)
```

1. **Upper Zone (Mucosal / Endodermal, Upper 15 mm):**
   * Lined by simple columnar epithelium.
   * **Anal Columns (of Morgagni):** 6 to 10 longitudinal vertical mucosal folds.
   * **Anal Valves:** Semilunar transverse crescentic mucosal folds uniting lower ends of columns.
   * **Anal Sinuses (Crypts):** Small pocket-like depressions behind the anal valves into which tubular anal glands open (site of cryptitis and perianal abscesses).
2. **Pectinate (Dentate) Line:**
   * Horizontal zigzag line formed by the free margins of the anal valves.
   * Represents the site of junction between the **endoderm of the hindgut** and **ectoderm of the proctodeum**.
   * Critical boundary for arterial, venous, lymphatic, and sensory nerve supply [112001:Q01].
3. **Middle Zone (Pecten, 15 mm):**
   * Pale, smooth non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium; terminates inferiorly at **Hilton’s White Line** (intersphincteric groove between internal and external anal sphincters).
4. **Lower Zone (Cutaneous Zone, Lower 8 mm):**
   * True skin lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium; contains hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and circumanal sweat glands.

---

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.officialText: Extent and external features of spinal cord.

note.title: Extent and External Features of Spinal Cord
note.content:
* **Extent:**
  * **Superior:** Continuous with the lower border of the medulla oblongata at the level of the upper border of the atlas vertebra (or midway between foramen magnum and atlas).
  * **Inferior:**
    * In adults: Tapers to terminate at the lower border of **L1 vertebra** (or L1–L2 intervertebral disc).
    * In neonates: Extends down to the upper border of **L3 vertebra**.
* **Length & Weight:** Approximately $45\text{ cm}$ in males ($43\text{ cm}$ in females); weighs about $30\text{ g}$.
* **Enlargements:**
  * *Cervical Enlargement (C4 to T1):* Corresponds to the origin of the brachial plexus for the upper limbs.
  * *Lumbar (Lumbosacral) Enlargement (L2 to S3):* Corresponds to the origins of the lumbar and sacral plexuses supplying the lower limbs.
* **External Grooves & Terminations:**
  * **Anterior Median Fissure:** Deep midline longitudinal groove containing anterior spinal vessels.
  * **Posterior Median Sulcus:** Shallow groove attached to the posterior median glial septum.
  * **Anterolateral & Posterolateral Sulci:** Mark the exit of ventral (motor) and entry of dorsal (sensory) nerve rootlets.
  * **Conus Medullaris:** The conical, tapered caudal termination of the cord at L1.
  * **Filum Terminale:** Non-neural silvery fibrous prolongation of pia mater extending from the tip of the conus medullaris to attach to the dorsum of the 1st coccygeal segment (upper $15\text{ cm}$ *filum terminale internum* inside the dural sac; lower $5\text{ cm}$ *filum terminale externum* blended with dura).
  * **Cauda Equina:** Bundle of lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal nerve roots descending within the lumbar cistern surrounding the filum terminale.

---

note.title: Nasopharynx
note.content:
* **Location and Extent:** The upper respiratory compartment of the pharynx situated behind the nasal cavities above the soft palate. Extends from the base of the skull (basilar part of occipital bone and sphenoid body) down to the lower margin of the soft palate (pharyngeal isthmus).
* **Walls and Features:**
  * **Anterior Wall:** Deficient; communicates directly with the nasal cavities via the bilateral **choanae** (posterior nasal apertures).
  * **Roof and Posterior Wall:** Forms a continuous sloping surface.
    * *Pharyngeal Tonsil (Adenoids):* Subepithelial collection of lymphoid tissue located at the junction of the roof and posterior wall; hypertrophy can obstruct nasal breathing and eustachian tube.
  * **Lateral Wall:**
    * *Pharyngeal Orifice of Auditory (Eustachian) Tube:* Located $1\text{ to }1.25\text{ cm}$ posterior to the inferior nasal concha.
    * *Tubal Elevation (Torus Tubarius):* Firm hood-like prominence bounding the tube posterosuperiorly, formed by the cartilaginous end of the auditory tube.
    * *Salpingopharyngeal Fold:* Mucosal fold running downward from the elevation containing the salpingopharyngeus muscle.
    * *Pharyngeal Recess (Fossa of Rosenmüller):* Deep slit-like depression situated behind the tubal elevation; common site for hidden nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
* **Epithelium & Nerve Supply:** Lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium; sensory supply is by the pharyngeal branch of the maxillary nerve (V2 via pterygopalatine ganglion).

---

note.title: Structures Passing Through Superior Orbital Fissure
note.content:
The superior orbital fissure connects the middle cranial fossa with the orbit. It is cleft between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid, crossed by the common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn) which divides it into three compartments:

```
  Lateral to Ring           Inside Ring (Central)        Medial to Ring
  ----------------          ---------------------        --------------
  • Lacrimal nerve (V1)     • Superior division of CN III • Recurrent Meningeal
  • Frontal nerve (V1)      • Nasociliary nerve (V1)        branch of Lacrimal Artery
  • Trochlear nerve (CN IV) • Inferior division of CN III
  • Superior Ophthalmic     • Abducens nerve (CN VI)
    vein                    • Sympathetic root to ciliary
  • Meningeal branch of       ganglion
    middle meningeal a.
```

* **Structures Lateral to Ring:**
  1. Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
  2. Frontal nerve (branch of ophthalmic, V1)
  3. Lacrimal nerve (branch of ophthalmic, V1)
  4. Superior ophthalmic vein
* **Structures Passing Through Common Tendinous Ring (Oculomotor Foramen):**
  1. Superior division of Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
  2. Nasociliary nerve (branch of ophthalmic, V1)
  3. Inferior division of Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
  4. Abducens nerve (CN VI; passes between the two heads of lateral rectus)
* **Structures Passing Medial/Inferior to Ring:**
  1. Inferior ophthalmic vein (or branches passing down to pterygoid plexus).

note.title: Contents of Superficial Perineal Pouch
note.content:
* **Boundaries:** Located in the urogenital triangle; bounded inferiorly by the **perineal membrane** (inferior fascia of urogenital diaphragm) and superiorly/superficially by the membranous layer of superficial perineal fascia (**Colles' fascia**) [112001:Q25].
* **Contents in Male:**
  1. **Root of Penis:**
     * *Bulb of Penis:* Midline erectile mass attached to the perineal membrane.
     * *Crura of Penis (two):* Erectile tissues attached to the ischiopubic rami.
  2. **Superficial Perineal Muscles:**
     * *Bulbospongiosus:* Covers the bulb of the penis.
     * *Ischiocavernosus (paired):* Covers each crus of the penis.
     * *Superficial Transverse Perinei (paired):* Runs from the ischial tuberosity to the perineal body.
  3. **Vessels and Nerves:**
     * Posterior scrotal nerves (branches of the pudendal nerve).
     * Posterior scrotal vessels (branches of internal pudendal vessels).
     * Perineal branch of the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve.
* **Contents in Female:**
  1. *Crura of Clitoris* and *Bulbs of the Vestibule*.
  2. *Greater Vestibular (Bartholin’s) Glands*.
  3. Ischiocavernosus, Bulbospongiosus, and Superficial transverse perinei muscles.
  4. Posterior labial nerves and vessels.

note.title: Development of Tongue
note.content:
* **Anterior Two-Thirds (Oral part):**
  * Develops during the 4th week from the mandibular processes (**1st Pharyngeal Arch**) via two lateral lingual swellings and one median swelling (*tuberculum impar*). Overgrown by lateral lingual swellings.
  * *Nerve Supply:* General sensations via the **lingual nerve** (nerve of 1st arch); taste sensations via the **chorda tympani** (pre-trematic branch of 7th arch nerve) [111001:Q02].
* **Posterior One-Third (Pharyngeal part):**
  * Develops from the **hypobranchial eminence** (cranial part, primarily representing the **3rd Pharyngeal Arch**, which overgrows the 2nd arch).
  * *Nerve Supply:* General and taste sensations via the **glossopharyngeal nerve** (nerve of 3rd arch) [111001:Q02].
* **Posterior-most Part (Vallecula / Epiglottis):**
  * Develops from the caudal part of the hypobranchial eminence (**4th Pharyngeal Arch**).
  * *Nerve Supply:* **Internal laryngeal nerve** (vagus).
* **Tongue Muscles:** Develop from migrated **occipital myotomes**; hence supplied by the **Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)** (except palatoglossus, supplied by cranial accessory nerve via pharyngeal plexus) [112001:Q01].

---

note.title: Histology of Duodenum
note.content:
* **Distinguishing Diagnostic Feature:** Presence of **Brunner's (Duodenal) Glands** in the **submucosa**.
* **Layers from Internal to External:**
  1. **Mucosa:**
     * *Villi:* Broad, leaf-like projections lined by simple columnar epithelium with brush border (microvilli) and interspersed goblet cells.
     * *Crypts of Lieberkühn:* Simple tubular mucosal glands containing Paneth cells (acidophilic granules releasing lysozyme) and enteroendocrine cells at the base.
     * *Lamina propria:* Highly cellular loose lymphoid connective tissue.
     * *Muscularis mucosae:* Thin inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer.
  2. **Submucosa:** Packed with branched coiled tubuloalveolar **Brunner’s Glands** that secrete alkaline, bicarbonate-rich mucus (pH 8.0–9.5) to neutralize gastric chyme and protect duodenal mucosa.
  3. **Muscularis Externa:** Inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle layers with intervening Myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus.
  4. **Adventitia / Serosa:** Retroperitoneal (adventitia posteriorly; serosa covering anterior surface only).

---

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.officialText: A 55 year old female came to the surgery OPD with complaints of few small swellings in her right axilla. On clinical examination, there was a palpable swelling in her right breast and retraction of right nipple a) What is the reason for swellings in her axilla b) Name the structures forming the mammary bed c) Describe the lymphatic drainage of breast d) Add a note on development of breast (1+2+5+2)

note.title: Breast Carcinoma, Bed, Lymphatics, and Development
note.content:
##### a) Reason for Swellings in Her Axilla
* **Metastatic Lymphadenopathy:** The axillary lymph nodes receive $\approx 75\%$ of the total lymphatic drainage of the breast. Carcinoma cells from the primary malignant tumor of the breast invade the rich subareolar and parenchymal lymphatic plexuses (Plexus of Sappey) and travel via centrifugal drainage to get arrested in the **anterior (pectoral) group** of axillary lymph nodes, followed by central and apical nodes, causing firm, non-tender, fixed axillary nodal enlargements.

##### b) Structures Forming the Mammary Bed
The mammary bed is the musculoskeletal surface upon which the deep, non-capsulated posterior surface of the breast rests, separated from it by the loose areolar **retromammary space of bursa**:
1. **Pectoralis major muscle** and its covering deep pectoral fascia (forms medial two-thirds).
2. **Serratus anterior muscle** (anterolateral portion).
3. **External oblique abdominis muscle** (inferolateral portion).
4. Upper part of the **rectus sheath** (inferomedial margin).

##### c) Lymphatic Drainage of the Breast
* **REFER TO:** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:101001:Q03]]` under *Anatomy — Paper I — 2026_JANUARY* for full lymphatic mapping, groups of axillary nodes, internal mammary chains, and anatomical basis of peau d’orange and nipple retraction.

##### d) Development of the Breast
* **Ectodermal Mammary Crest / Ridge (Milk Line of Brent):** Develops during the 4th–5th week as a pair of bilateral ectodermal band-like thickenings extending along the ventrolateral body wall from the axilla to the inguinal region.
* **Involution & Primary Bud:** In humans, the ridge disappears except for a small thoracic segment where it proliferates into the underlying mesenchyme as a primary mammary bud.
* **Secondary Buds & Canalization:** The primary bud gives off 15–20 secondary solid epithelial cords. During late fetal life (7th–8th month), these cords canalize to form **lactiferous ducts** and terminal secretory alveoli.
* **Nipple Formation:** The pit into which the lactiferous ducts open is pushed outward after birth by proliferating subcutaneous mesenchyme to form the **nipple**.
* **Developmental Anomalies:**
  * *Polymastia:* Accessory breasts along the embryonic milk line.
  * *Polythelia:* Accessory nipples.
  * *Gynecomastia:* Hypertrophy of male breast tissue.
  * *Inverted Nipple:* Failure of the primary pit to evert.

---

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.officialText: What is primitive streak. Describe the formation of trilaminar germ disc

note.title: Primitive Streak and Formation of Trilaminar Germ Disc
note.content:
##### Primitive Streak
* **Origin and Structure:** At the beginning of the 3rd week of gestation, an elongated linear cellular band appears on the caudal dorsal midline of the epiblast of the bilaminar germ disc.
* **Cranial Landmark:** The cranial end expands to form the **primitive node (Hensen’s node)**, surrounding an indentation called the **primitive pit**. A shallow **primitive groove** extends caudally from the pit.

```
                  CRANIAL
                     |
               [Epiblast Layer]
                     |
           ( Primitive Node / Pit )
                     |
             Primitive Groove
                     |
            [ Primitive Streak ]
                     |
                  CAUDAL
```

##### Formation of the Trilaminar Germ Disc (Gastrulation)
1. **Invagination:** Cells of the epiblast migrate toward the primitive streak, detach, change shape (bottle/flask cells), and invaginate inward beneath the epiblast layer:
   * **Definitive Endoderm:** The first wave of invaginating epiblast cells displaces the underlying hypoblast to establish the embryonic endoderm.
   * **Intraembryonic Mesoderm:** Subsequent migrating epiblast cells disperse into the potential space between the epiblast and newly formed endoderm, forming the middle intraembryonic mesoderm [101001:Q02].
   * **Ectoderm:** The remaining cells on the dorsal surface of the epiblast differentiate into the definitive ectoderm.
2. **Notochord Formation:** Cells invaginating through the primitive pit migrate cranially in the midline toward the prechordal plate, forming the solid cellular rod called the **notochord** [111001:Q01].
3. **Fate:** Once gastrulation is complete, the primitive streak regresses and normally degenerates by the end of the 4th week. Persistence of remnants at the sacrococcygeal region gives rise to a **Sacrococcygeal Teratoma**.

---

note.title: Common Peroneal Nerve
note.content:
##### Origin, Course, and Relations
* **Origin:** Smaller terminal divergence branch of the **Sciatic Nerve** (arising from the posterior divisions of ventral rami **L4, L5, S1, S2**).
* **Course in Popliteal Fossa:**
  * Enters the fossa at its superior angle; descends obliquely along the medial border of the **biceps femoris** tendon.
  * Crosses the lateral head of gastrocnemius, exiting through the lateral angle of the fossa.
* **Course at Fibular Neck:**
  * Winds around the posterolateral aspect of the **neck of the fibula**, passing deep to the peroneus longus muscle [112001:Q01].
  * Here it is subcutaneous and palpable directly against bone, making it the most frequently injured nerve in the lower extremity.
* **Termination:** Divides within the substance of the peroneus longus into two terminal branches:
  1. **Superficial Peroneal (Fibular) Nerve**
  2. **Deep Peroneal (Fibular) Nerve**

##### Branches and Distribution
1. **Cutaneous Branches:**
   * *Lateral sural cutaneous nerve:* Supplies the skin of the upper posterolateral leg.
   * *Sural communicating branch:* Unites with the medial sural nerve to form the sural nerve.
2. **Superficial Peroneal Nerve:**
   * *Muscular:* Supplies muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg (**Peroneus longus, Peroneus brevis**; primary foot evertors) [112001:Q01].
   * *Cutaneous:* Supplies the lower two-thirds of the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot (except the first web space).
3. **Deep Peroneal Nerve (Anterior Tibial Nerve):**
   * Accompanies the anterior tibial artery into the anterior compartment.
   * *Muscular:* Supplies **Tibialis anterior, Extensor hallucis longus, Extensor digitorum longus, Peroneus tertius**, and **Extensor digitorum brevis** (foot and toe dorsiflexors).
   * *Cutaneous:* Supplies the cleft and adjacent skin between the 1st and 2nd toes (first interdigital web space).

##### Clinical Anatomy
* **Foot Drop:** Fracture of the neck of the fibula or tight plaster cast compresses the common peroneal nerve, causing paralysis of all dorsiflexors (deep peroneal) and evertors (superficial peroneal).
* **Presentation:** Unopposed plantarflexion and inversion, leading to **Equinovarus deformity** and a **high-stepping gait**.

---

note.title: Turner's Syndrome
note.content:
* **Karyotype:** **45, XO** (monosomy of X chromosome due to paternal meiotic nondisjunction in 70–80% of cases).
* **Incidence:** $\approx 1 \text{ in } 2500$ live female births.
* **Salient Clinical Features:**
  * **Phenotype:** Phenotypic female.
  * **Short Stature:** Height typically $<5\text{ feet}$ due to loss of the *SHOX* gene.
  * **Ovarian Dysgenesis:** Fibrous "streak ovaries", lack of primordial follicles, resulting in primary amenorrhea, infertility, and absent secondary sexual characteristics.
  * **Craniofacial/Neck Features:** Webbed neck (*cystic hygroma colli*), low posterior hairline, high-arched palate, and low-set ears.
  * **Skeletal Anomalies:** Shield-like chest with widely spaced hypoplastic nipples, increased carrying angle (**cubitus valgus**), short 4th metacarpals.
  * **Cardiovascular & Renal:** **Coarctation of the aorta** (most characteristic cardiovascular lesion), bicuspid aortic valve, and horseshoe kidney.
  * **Barr Body Status:** Negative (0 Barr bodies).

---

note.title: Laws of Ossification
note.content:
* **Law of Ossification (General Rule):**
  1. In long bones possessing an epiphysis at both ends, the center of ossification that appears **first** is the **last** to fuse with the diaphysis.
  2. The center that appears last is the first to fuse.
  3. *Exception:* The **Fibula violates this law**—the primary secondary center appears first at its distal end, yet this distal end fuses first with the diaphysis [111001:Q01].
* **Growing End of a Long Bone:**
  * The growing end is the end of the long bone where the secondary center appears first and fuses last, contributing maximum longitudinal growth.
  * **Direction of Nutrient Artery:** Points away from the growing end:
    * *"To the elbow I go, from the knee I flee."*
    * Upper limb growing ends: Shoulder (upper humerus) and Wrist (lower radius and ulna).
    * Lower limb growing ends: Knee (lower femur and upper tibia).

---

note.title: Extracapsular Ligaments of Knee Joint
note.content:
The knee joint is fortified externally by sturdy extracapsular (or capsular) ligaments:

1. **Ligamentum Patellae (Patellar Ligament):**
   * Heavy fibrous band representing the continuation of the central tendon of the Quadriceps Femoris.
   * Extends from the apex and inferior border of the patella to the upper smooth part of the **tibial tuberosity**. Separated from the synovial membrane by the infrapatellar fat pad.
2. **Tibial Collateral (Medial Collateral) Ligament:**
   * Broad, flat, ribbon-like ligament attached proximally to the medial epicondyle of the femur and distally to the medial condyle and upper medial surface of the tibial shaft.
   * *Firmly attached to the medial meniscus* (making medial meniscal tears frequent in valgus stress).
3. **Fibular Collateral (Lateral Collateral) Ligament:**
   * Cord-like, rounded ligament attached from the lateral epicondyle of the femur to the head of the fibula.
   * Separated from the lateral meniscus by the **popliteus tendon** and inferior lateral genicular vessels; hence completely independent of the lateral meniscus.
4. **Oblique Popliteal Ligament:**
   * An expansion derived from the tendon of the **Semimembranosus** muscle; passes upward and laterally to blend with the posterior fibrous capsule, reinforcing the intercondylar region.
5. **Arcuate Popliteal Ligament:**
   * Y-shaped thickening arching over the popliteus tendon from the posterior fibular head to the intercondylar area of the tibia.

---

note.title: Gluteus Maximus Muscle
note.content:
* **Origin:**
  * Gluteal surface of ilium behind the posterior gluteal line.
  * Posterior surface of the lower sacrum and coccyx.
  * Sacrotuberous ligament and thoracolumbar fascia.
* **Insertion:**
  * Superficial three-fourths: Inserts into the **iliotibial tract**.
  * Deep lower one-fourth: Inserts into the **gluteal tuberosity** of the femur.
* **Nerve Supply:** **Inferior Gluteal Nerve** (root value **L5, S1, S2**).
* **Actions:**
  * Chief extensor of the hip joint when rising from a sitting or stooping posture, climbing stairs, and running.
  * Lateral rotator of the thigh.
  * Maintains knee extension via its tension on the iliotibial tract.

---

note.title: Interatrial Septum – Features and Development
note.content:
* **Anatomical Features (Right Atrial Aspect):**
  * **Fossa Ovalis:** Shallow, smooth oval depression occupying the lower part of the septum; represents the embryonic **septum primum** [112001:Q15].
  * **Limbus Fossa Ovalis (Annulus Ovalis):** Prominent raised muscular crescentic margin bounding the fossa ovalis superiorly and laterally; represents the lower free edge of the embryonic **septum secundum** [112001:Q15].
* **Embryological Development:**
  1. **Septum Primum:** Thin sickle-shaped crescent grows down from the roof of the common atrium toward the endocardial cushions. The disappearing aperture below its free edge is the **foramen primum**.
  2. Perforations form in the upper part of the septum primum, coalescing into the **foramen secundum**.
  3. **Septum Secundum:** A second thick, muscular fold grows down from the roof immediately to the right of the septum primum. It leaves an oval opening called the **foramen ovale**.
  4. The persistent flap-like remnant of the septum primum acts as a one-way valve covering the foramen ovale, allowing right-to-left shunting of oxygenated blood in utero.
  5. Closure at birth: Functional closure occurs due to increased left atrial pressure from pulmonary venous return, converting it into the anatomical fossa ovalis [112001:Q23].

---

note.title: Pronation and Supination
note.content:
* **Definitions:**
  * **Supination:** Movement of the forearm that rotates the radius laterally around the ulna, turning the palm anteriorly (anatomical position) or facing upward.
  * **Pronation:** Movement that rotates the radius medially around the ulna, crossing the radius obliquely over the anterior aspect of the ulna to turn the palm backward or facing downward.
* **Axis of Movement:** An oblique vertical axis passing through the center of the head of the radius proximally to the base of the styloid process of the ulna distally.
* **Muscles Causing the Movements:**
  * *Supinators:* **Biceps brachii** (the most powerful supinator, especially when the elbow is flexed) and **Supinator**.
  * *Pronators:* **Pronator teres** and **Pronator quadratus**.

---

note.title: Microscopic Structure of Thick Skin
note.content:
* **Location:** Palms of the hands and soles of the feet (glabrous skin lacking hair follicles and sebaceous glands).
* **Epidermal Layers (Stratified Squamous Keratinized Epithelium):**
  1. **Stratum Basale (Germinativum):** Single layer of cuboidal to columnar stem cells resting on the basal lamina; displays active mitotic figures and contains melanocytes and Merkel cells.
  2. **Stratum Spinosum:** 4–8 layers of polyhedral cells characterized by prominent tonofibrils and spine-like cytoplasmic processes anchored by desmosomes. Contains Langerhans cells.
  3. **Stratum Granulosum:** 3–5 layers of flattened cells containing coarse, basophilic **keratohyalin granules**.
  4. **Stratum Lucidum:** Clear, translucent, homogeneous eosinophilic band of dead flattened cells filled with **eleidin** (found exclusively in thick skin).
  5. **Stratum Corneum:** Very thick superficial layer of enucleated, flattened, tightly packed, highly keratinized dead squames.
* **Dermis:** Features prominent dermal papillae interlocking with epidermal rete pegs and numerous eccrine sweat glands.

---

note.title: Adductor Canal (Hunter’s Canal)
note.content:
* **Location and Extent:** An aponeurotic intermuscular tunnel situated in the middle third of the medial compartment of the thigh, extending from the apex of the femoral triangle to the adductor hiatus in the adductor magnus.
* **Boundaries:**
  * **Anteromedial (Roof):** Aponeurotic sheet deep to the **Sartorius** muscle and the subsartorial plexus of nerves.
  * **Anterolateral:** **Vastus Medialis** muscle.
  * **Posterior (Floor):** Upper part formed by **Adductor Longus**, lower part by **Adductor Magnus**.
* **Contents:**
  1. Femoral artery
  2. Femoral vein (lies posterolateral to the artery proximally, then posterior)
  3. Saphenous nerve (crosses anterior to the femoral artery from lateral to medial)
  4. Nerve to vastus medialis

---

questions.officialText: A 70-year-old man presented with recurrent episodes of diarrhea and abdominal pain. On examination there is inflammation and ulceration in the rectum. Describe the extent, relations, interior and blood supply of Rectum (1+2+5+2)

note.title: Rectum Anatomy
note.content:
##### a) Extent
* The rectum is the terminal fixed continuation of the sigmoid colon.
* **Begins:** At the rectosigmoid junction in front of the **S3 vertebra** (at the level of the lower border of the third sacral piece).
* **Ends:** At the anorectal junction, $2\text{ to }3\text{ cm}$ below and in front of the tip of the coccyx, where it pierces the pelvic diaphragm to continue as the anal canal [112001:Q09].
* **Length:** Approximately $12\text{ cm}$ ($5\text{ inches}$).

##### b) Relations
* **Peritoneal Relations:**
  * *Upper third:* Covered by peritoneum anteriorly and on both lateral aspects.
  * *Middle third:* Covered by peritoneum on its anterior surface only.
  * *Lower third:* Completely retroperitoneal (subperitoneal); no peritoneal covering.
  * Anterior peritoneal reflection forms the **rectovesical pouch** in males and **rectouterine pouch (Pouch of Douglas)** in females [112001:Q01].
* **Visceral Relations in Male:**
  * *Anteriorly:* Base of urinary bladder, terminal coils of ileum, ampullae of ductus deferentes, seminal vesicles, terminal ureters, and prostate (separated by the *fascia of Denonvilliers* / rectovesical septum).
* **Visceral Relations in Female:**
  * *Anteriorly:* Posterior wall of vagina and cervix (separated by the rectovaginal septum and pouch of Douglas).
* **Posterior Relations (Common to both sexes):**
  * Sacrum (lower 3 pieces), coccyx, and anococcygeal body.
  * Piriformis, Coccygeus, and Levator Ani muscles.
  * Superior rectal vessels, median sacral vessels, and sympathetic trunks with the ganglion impar.

##### c) Interior of Rectum
* **Temporary Folds:** Longitudinal folds seen in the lower relaxed part which flatten out upon distension.
* **Permanent Transverse Folds (Valves of Houston):** Horizontal crescentic shelves projecting into the lumen:
  1. *Upper fold:* Lies near the rectosigmoid junction, projects from the left or right wall.
  2. *Middle fold (Kohlrausch's fold):* The largest and most constant fold; projects from the right anterior wall $\approx 7.5\text{ cm}$ above the anus (corresponds to the anterior peritoneal reflection).
  3. *Lower fold:* Projects from the left wall $\approx 5\text{ cm}$ above the anus.
* **Ampulla of Rectum:** The dilated terminal reservoir occupying the region directly above the pelvic diaphragm.

##### d) Blood Supply of Rectum
* **Arterial Supply:**
  1. **Superior Rectal Artery:** Direct continuation of the Inferior Mesenteric Artery; primary arterial feeder to the rectum, supplying the mucosa down to the anal valves.
  2. **Middle Rectal Arteries (paired):** Branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery; supply the muscular wall of the lower rectum [112001:Q08].
  3. **Inferior Rectal Arteries (paired):** Branches of internal pudendal arteries; supply the anorectal junction [112001:Q09, 112001:Q12].
  4. **Median Sacral Artery:** Tiny terminal twig from the aortic bifurcation.
* **Venous Drainage:**
  * *Superior rectal vein* drains into the inferior mesenteric vein (Portal system) [112001:Q01].
  * *Middle and inferior rectal veins* drain into the internal iliac and internal pudendal veins respectively (Systemic / Caval system) [112001:Q01].
  * Forms a major site of **Portosystemic Anastomosis**.

---

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.officialText: Describe the carotid sheath and its contents

note.title: Carotid Sheath and Its Contents
note.content:
* **Definition:** A tubular condensation of deep cervical fascia extending from the base of the skull down to the thoracic inlet (blending with the adventitia of the aortic arch).
* **Fascial Contributions:** Formed anteriorly by the **investing** and **pretracheal layers**, and posteriorly by the **prevertebral layer** of deep cervical fascia. It is thicker over the arteries and thinner over the internal jugular vein.

```
                    ANTERIOR (Ansa Cervicalis embedded)
                    +---------------------------------+
                    |         CAROTID SHEATH          |
                    |                                 |
                    |     INTERNAL     INTERNAL       |
                    |     JUGULAR      CAROTID        |
                    |       VEIN       ARTERY         |
                    |     (Lateral)    (Medial)       |
                    |                                 |
                    |              VAGUS              |
                    |              NERVE (CN X)       |
                    |           (Posteromedial)       |
                    +---------------------------------+
                    POSTERIOR (Sympathetic Trunk behind)
```

* **Contents:**
  1. **Arteries (Medial):**
     * Common Carotid Artery (inferiorly).
     * Internal Carotid Artery (superiorly).
  2. **Vein (Lateral):**
     * Internal Jugular Vein (overlaps the carotid artery anterolaterally).
  3. **Nerve (Posterior):**
     * **Vagus Nerve (CN X):** Lies posteromedially in the groove between the artery and vein.
  4. **Deep Cervical Lymph Nodes:** Embedded within and along the outer wall of the sheath.
* **Relations Outside the Sheath:**
  * *Anteriorly:* **Ansa cervicalis** is embedded in the anterior wall of the sheath.
  * *Posteriorly:* The **Cervical Sympathetic Trunk** lies vertically directly behind the carotid sheath, embedded in the prevertebral fascia.

---

questions.officialText: Supports and blood supply of uterus

note.title: Supports and Blood Supply of Uterus
note.content:
* **Supports of Uterus:**
  * **REFER TO:** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:102001:Q03]]` under *Anatomy — Paper II — 2026_JANUARY* for full discussion of primary dynamic/muscular supports (levator ani, perineal body), primary mechanical ligaments (Mackenrodt's cardinal ligaments, uterosacral ligaments), and angles of anteversion/anteflexion.
* **Blood Supply of Uterus:**
  * **Arterial Supply:**
    * **Uterine Artery:** Major source; branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery. Courses medially in the base of the broad ligament, crossing **anterior and superior to the ureter** ("water under the bridge") $1.5\text{ to }2\text{ cm}$ lateral to the cervix. Ascends tortuously along the lateral uterine border, terminating by anastomosing with the ovarian artery.
    * **Ovarian Artery:** Branch of abdominal aorta; supplies the uterine fundus via anastomoses.
  * **Venous Drainage:**
    * Forms a uterine venous plexus on each side, draining via **uterine veins** into the internal iliac veins.

note.title: Interior of Larynx
note.content:
The cavity of the larynx extends from the **laryngeal inlet** down to the lower border of the **cricoid cartilage** (continuous with the trachea). It is divided into three compartments by two pairs of mucosal folds:

```
                      LARYNGEAL INLET
                             |
                   +-------------------+
                   |   VESTIBULE       |  (Supraglottic space)
                   +-------------------+
             ================================= VESTIBULAR (FALSE) CORDS
                   |  LARYNGEAL SINUS  |  (Ventricle & Saccule)
             ================================= VOCAL (TRUE) CORDS
                   +-------------------+
                   | INFRAGLOTTIC PART |  (Subglottic space)
                   +-------------------+
                             |
                     TRACHEAL LUMEN
```

1. **Vestibule (Supraglottic Space):**
   * Extends from the laryngeal inlet to the **vestibular folds** (false vocal cords).
   * Bounded anteriorly by the posterior surface of the epiglottis, laterally by the aryepiglottic folds.
2. **Sinus of Larynx (Ventricle) & Middle Compartment:**
   * Recess between the upper vestibular fold and the lower vocal fold on each side.
   * **Laryngeal Saccule:** A conical pouch extending upward from the anterior part of the sinus between the vestibular fold and thyroid cartilage. Contains mucosal glands ("oil can of the larynx") that lubricate the vocal cords.
3. **Vestibular Folds (False Vocal Cords):**
   * Pinkish mucosal folds enclosing the vestibular ligament; protective/sphincteric in function.
4. **Vocal Folds (True Vocal Cords):**
   * Pearly white, avascular mucosal folds lacking submucosa; enclose the **vocal ligament** (upper thickened edge of the cricovocal membrane) and the **vocalis muscle** [111001:Q01].
   * Function in phonation and airway closure.
5. **Rima Glottidis:**
   * The narrowest fissure-like aperture of the laryngeal cavity; bounded anteriorly by intermembranous true vocal cords, posteriorly by intercartilaginous arytenoid vocal processes.
6. **Infraglottic Compartment:**
   * Extends from the true vocal cords down to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage; widened and continuous with the lumen of the trachea.

---

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.officialText: Describe the bones taking part, ligaments and movements occurring at atlanto -occipital joint

note.title: Atlanto-Occipital Joint
note.content:
* **Type of Joint:** Synovial joint of the **Ellipsoid (Condylar)** variety (paired right and left joints).
* **Articulating Bones / Surfaces:**
  * Superior: Convex **Occipital Condyles** located on the sides of the foramen magnum.
  * Inferior: Concave **Superior Articular Facets** of the lateral masses of the **Atlas (C1)**.
* **Ligaments:**
  1. *Articular Capsule:* Encloses each joint.
  2. *Anterior Atlanto-Occipital Membrane:* Broad fibrous sheet extending from the anterior margin of the foramen magnum to the upper border of the anterior arch of the atlas.
  3. *Posterior Atlanto-Occipital Membrane:* Broad thin membrane connecting the posterior margin of the foramen magnum to the posterior arch of the atlas (pierced by the vertebral artery and C1 suboccipital nerve).
* **Movements:**
  * **Flexion and Extension:** The nodding movement ("YES" movement).
  * Slight lateral tilt.

---

note.title: Lateral Ventricle of Brain
note.content:
* **Definition:** Paired, C-shaped cavities within the cerebral hemispheres communicating with the third ventricle via the **Interventricular Foramen of Monro**.
* **Parts:**
  1. **Central Part (Body):** Located within the parietal lobe; roof formed by the corpus callosum; floor formed by the dorsal surface of the thalamus and caudate nucleus; medial wall formed by the septum pellucidum.
  2. **Anterior Horn:** Extends into the frontal lobe; roof by the corpus callosum, anterior wall by the genu, lateral wall by the prominent bulge of the head of the caudate nucleus.
  3. **Posterior Horn:** Extends into the occipital lobe; features the **bulbs of posterior horn** (formed by forceps major) and **calcar avis** (formed by the calcarine sulcus) [111001:Q01, 111001:Q09].
  4. **Inferior Horn:** Extends forward and downward into the temporal lobe; floor contains the **hippocampus** and alveus; roof contains the tail of the caudate nucleus and stria terminalis [111001:Q01, 111001:Q09].
* **Choroid Plexus:** Projects through the choroid fissure into the body and inferior horn; synthesizes cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) [111001:Q01].

---

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.officialText: Extent and structures crossed by root of mesentry

note.title: Extent and Structures Crossed by Root of Mesentery
note.content:
* **Extent:**
  * Narrow parietal attachment of the fan-shaped fold of peritoneum that suspends the jejunum and ileum.
  * Measures $\approx 15\text{ cm}$ ($6\text{ inches}$) in length.
  * Extends obliquely from the **Duodenojejunal Flexure** (on the left side of the L2 vertebra) downwards to the **Ileocecal Junction** (anterior to the right sacroiliac joint).
* **Structures Crossed (from Cranial to Caudal):**
  1. Third (horizontal) part of the Duodenum.
  2. Abdominal Aorta.
  3. Inferior Vena Cava (IVC).
  4. Right Psoas Major muscle.
  5. Right Ureter.
  6. Right Genitofemoral nerve.
  7. Right Gonadal (Testicular/Ovarian) vessels.

note.title: Sites of Portosystemic Anastomosis
note.content:
Portosystemic (portacaval) anastomoses connect the portal venous system with the systemic caval system. In portal hypertension, these collateral pathways dilate and form clinical varices:

| Site | Portal Venous Channel | Systemic Venous Channel | Clinical Manifestation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Lower End of Esophagus** | Esophageal tributaries of **Left Gastric Vein** | Esophageal branches of **Azygos / Hemiazygos Veins** | **Esophageal Varices** (prone to rupture and life-threatening hematemesis) |
| **Anal Canal (Upper vs Lower)** | **Superior Rectal Vein** (drains to IMV $\rightarrow$ Portal Vein) [112001:Q01] | **Middle & Inferior Rectal Veins** (drain to Internal Iliac $\rightarrow$ IVC) [112001:Q01] | **Internal Anorectal Varices** (painless bleeding per rectum) [112001:Q09] |
| **Umbilicus (Anterior Abdominal Wall)** | **Paraumbilical Veins** (run in falciform ligament to Portal Vein) | Superficial epigastric, thoracoepigastric, inferior epigastric veins | **Caput Medusae** (radiating engorged periumbilical tortuous veins) |
| **Retroperitoneum (Organs of Retzius)** | Colic veins, splenic veins | Renal, lumbar, subcostal, phrenic veins | Asymptomatic retroperitoneal collateralization |
| **Bare Area of Liver** | Hepatic portal parenchymal venules | Inferior phrenic and intercostal veins | Asymptomatic |

---

note.title: Development of Pancreas
note.content:
* **Embryological Buds:** Originates during the 5th week from the **endodermal lining of the duodenum** as two outgrowths:
  1. **Ventral Pancreatic Bud:** Develops from the hepatic diverticulum; develops into the **inferior part of head** and the **uncinate process** [112001:Q01].
  2. **Dorsal Pancreatic Bud:** Larger bud developing from the dorsal duodenal wall; forms the **upper part of the head, neck, body, and tail** of the pancreas [112001:Q01].
* **Rotation and Fusion:** When the duodenum rotates to the right, the ventral bud rotates dorsally behind the duodenum to fuse with the inferior aspect of the dorsal bud.
* **Duct System Formation:**
  * *Main Pancreatic Duct (of Wirsung):* Formed by the duct of the ventral bud anastomosing with the distal part of the dorsal duct.
  * *Accessory Pancreatic Duct (of Santorini):* Formed by the proximal part of the dorsal pancreatic duct; opens into the minor duodenal papilla.
* **Anomalies:** **Annular pancreas** occurs when the bifid ventral bud encircles the second part of the duodenum, causing duodenal stenosis [112001:Q01].

---

note.title: Branches of Abdominal Aorta
note.content:
* **Ventral (Visceral Unpaired) Branches (3):**
  1. Celiac Trunk (T12) [112001:Q01]
  2. Superior Mesenteric Artery (L1) [112001:Q01]
  3. Inferior Mesenteric Artery (L3)
* **Lateral (Visceral Paired) Branches (3):**
  1. Middle Suprarenal Arteries (L1)
  2. Renal Arteries (L1–L2)
  3. Gonadal (Testicular/Ovarian) Arteries (L2)
* **Parietal Paired Branches:**
  1. Inferior Phrenic Arteries (T12)
  2. Lumbar Arteries (four pairs, L1–L4)
* **Terminal Branches (at L4):**
  1. Right and Left Common Iliac Arteries
  2. Median Sacral Artery (unpaired parietal)

---

note.title: Histology of Prostate
note.content:
* **Fibromuscular Stroma:** Highly distinctive; constitutes one-third of the total prostatic volume, consisting of a rich network of smooth muscle cells intermingled with dense fibroelastic collagenous tissue.
* **Glandular Architecture:**
  * Contains 30–50 tubuloalveolar glands arranged in three concentric zones (mucosal, submucosal, and main external peripheral glands).
  * Lined by **simple columnar** or **pseudostratified columnar epithelium** with variable height based on hormonal activity.
* **Corpora Amylacea (Amyloid bodies):** Pathognomonic spherical, laminated, calcified eosinophilic secretions found within the alveolar lumina; increase in number and size with advancing age [112001:Q01].

---

note.title: Transverse Section of Spinal Cord Showing Ascending and Descending Tracts
note.content:
```
                          POSTERIOR (Dorsal)
               Fasciculus Gracilis | Fasciculus Cuneatus
                           \       |       /
                 Posterior  \      |      /  Posterior 
                 Horn        \     |     /   Horn
                             +-----+-----+
         Lateral             |           |      Lateral
    Corticospinal Tract ---- | (Central) | ---- Spinothalamic Tract
                             |  (Canal)  |
       Rubrospinal Tract --- |           | ---- Anterior
                             +-----+-----+      Spinocerebellar Tract
                 Anterior    /     |     \
```
