questions.officialText: Describe parts and layers of eye ball

note.title: Parts and Layers of the Eyeball
note.content:
*Reference Image Link:* [Human Eyeball Cross-Section (Wikimedia Commons)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/15/1413_Structure_of_the_Eye.jpg)

#### a) Three Concentric Tunics (Layers)
1.  **Outer Fibrous Tunic:**
    *   *Cornea:* Transparent anterior one-sixth; major refracting surface (+43 D).
    *   *Sclera:* Opaque, tough, protective posterior five-sixths.
    *   *Limbus:* Corneoscleral transition zone containing trabecular meshwork and limbal stem cells.
2.  **Middle Vascular Tunic (Uveal Tract):**
    *   *Iris:* Anterior diaphragm regulating pupillary aperture.
    *   *Ciliary Body:* Pars plicata (produces aqueous) and Pars plana (smooth posterior zone).
    *   *Choroid:* Highly vascular posterior coat nourishing outer retinal layers.
3.  **Inner Nervous Tunic (Retina):**
    *   Consists of outer Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE) and inner 9 layers of neurosensory retina terminating anteriorly at the ora serrata.

#### b) Compartments and Refractive Media
*   *Anterior Segment:*
    *   **Anterior Chamber:** Between cornea and iris ($0.25\text{ mL}$ aqueous).
    *   **Posterior Chamber:** Triangular space between posterior iris and lens ($0.06\text{ mL}$ aqueous).
*   *Posterior Segment:*
    *   **Vitreous Cavity:** Large cavity behind lens filled with vitreous gel ($4.0\text{ mL}$).
*   *Refractive Media:* Cornea $\rightarrow$ Aqueous humor $\rightarrow$ Crystalline lens $\rightarrow$ Vitreous humor.

---

note.title: Lasers in Ophthalmology
note.content:
1.  **Photocoagulation (Thermal Lasers — Argon, Diode 810 nm, Frequency-Doubled Nd:YAG 532 nm):**
    *   Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) in proliferative diabetic retinopathy and ischemic CRVO.
    *   Focal/Grid laser for macular edema.
    *   Barrier laser around retinal tears to prevent rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
    *   Laser trabeculoplasty (ALT / SLT) for open-angle glaucoma.
2.  **Photodisruption (Neodymium:YAG Laser 1064 nm):**
    *   Nd:YAG Posterior Capsulotomy for Posterior Capsular Opacification (After-Cataract).
    *   Nd:YAG Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) for angle-closure glaucoma.
    *   Vitreolysis of vitreous strands.
3.  **Photoablation (Excimer Laser 193 nm):**
    *   Refractive surgery: LASIK, PRK for myopia, hypermetropia, and astigmatism.
    *   Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK) for superficial corneal dystrophies and scars.
4.  **Femtosecond Laser (1053 nm Infrared):**
    *   Femtosecond Laser-Assisted Cataract Surgery (FLACS): Precision capsulotomy, nuclear fragmentation, clear corneal incisions.
    *   Flap creation in Femto-LASIK; lenticule extraction in SMILE.
5.  **Photodynamic Therapy (PDT - 689 nm Diode):**
    *   Activated Verteporfin dye for subfoveal choroidal neovascular membranes (CNVM) and central serous chorioretinopathy.

---

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.officialText: A 50 year old lady came with complaints of frequent decrease in near vision and change of glasses to improve the same. She also complained of clouding of peripheral vision in both eyes at times. She has no other comorbid problems. Answer the following questions: a) What other history will you elicit from her b) What is the probable diagnosis c) What differential diagnosis can you offer d) What investigations you would request e) How will you plan your treatment (1+1+3+3+2)

note.title: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma Case
note.content:
#### a) Additional History to Elicit
*   Family history of glaucoma or irreversible blindness in parents/siblings.
*   History of systemic comorbidities: Diabetes mellitus, systemic hypertension, peripheral vasospasm (migraine, Raynaud's phenomenon).
*   History of long-term use of systemic or topical corticosteroids.
*   History of high myopia.
*   History of transient blackouts, difficulty with night vision (dark adaptation), or bumping into side objects (tunnel vision).

#### b) Probable Diagnosis
**Bilateral Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG).**
*(Frequent change of presbyopic glasses due to accommodative failure + progressive peripheral visual field clouding).*

#### c) Differential Diagnosis
1.  *Normal Tension Glaucoma (NTG):* Glaucomatous disc and field damage with IOP consistently $\le 21\text{ mm Hg}$.
2.  *Ocular Hypertension:* Consistently elevated IOP $>21\text{ mm Hg}$ with normal discs and normal visual fields.
3.  *Chronic Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma:* Closed angle on gonioscopy with PAS.
4.  *Pseudoexfoliative / Pigmentary Glaucoma:* Secondary open-angle glaucomas with characteristic biomicroscopic flakes or pigment dispersion.

#### d) Investigations to Request
*   *Tonometry:* Baseline diurnal IOP phasing using Goldmann Applanation Tonometer (GAT).
*   *Central Corneal Thickness (CCT):* Pachymetry (thin cornea $<555\text{ µm}$ underestimates true IOP).
*   *Gonioscopy:* Confirms wide open angles (Shaffer Grade 3–4) and excludes secondary blockages.
*   *Optic Nerve Head Imaging:* Stereoscopic fundus photography, Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) of peripapillary Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL).
*   *Automated Perimetry:* Humphrey Visual Field Analyzer (HFA central 24-2 or 30-2 SITA-Standard protocol) to map paracentral, arcuate, or nasal step defects.

#### e) Treatment Plan
*   **Establish Target IOP:** Lower baseline IOP by at least 25%–30% (target $<15\text{ mm Hg}$).
*   **Medical Monotherapy (First Line):** Topical **Latanoprost 0.005%** at bedtime or **Timolol maleate 0.5% BD**.
*   **Combination Therapy:** Add Brimonidine 0.2% or Dorzolamide 2% if target IOP is not achieved.
*   **Laser Therapy:** Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT) to improve trabecular outflow.
*   **Surgical Intervention:** **Trabeculectomy with Mitomycin-C (0.02%)** if target IOP is not achieved despite maximal medical/laser therapy or if visual field loss progresses.

note.title: Eye Signs of Thyroid Orbitopathy
note.content:
1.  **Dalrymple’s Sign:** Pathognomonic retraction of the upper eyelid in primary gaze, revealing white sclera above the superior limbus.
2.  **Von Graefe’s Sign:** Dynamic lid lag of the upper eyelid on slow downward gaze.
3.  **Stellwag’s Sign:** Infrequent, incomplete, and sluggish blinking.
4.  **Mobius’ Sign:** Impaired convergence on attempted near focus.
5.  **Joffroy’s Sign:** Absence of normal forehead wrinkling on looking upward.
6.  **Enroth’s Sign:** Puffy, non-inflammatory fullness and edema of the eyelids.

*   **Class:** Direct-acting parasympathomimetic (cholinergic) agonist.
*   **Ocular Actions:**
    1.  *Miosis:* Stimulates muscarinic ($M_3$) receptors of pupillary sphincter.
    2.  *Lowers IOP:* Ciliary muscle contraction pulls the scleral spur posteriorly, opening trabecular meshwork pores.
    3.  *Accommodative Spasm:* Causes transient myopia in young patients.
*   **Preparations & Dosing:** Pilocarpine nitrate/hydrochloride 1%, 2%, 4% eye drops instilled TDS/QID; 4% gel at bedtime.
*   **Clinical Uses:** Acute angle-closure glaucoma (after IOP drops $<30\text{ mm Hg}$), primary open-angle glaucoma, reversal of mydriasis.
*   **Adverse Effects:** Ciliary spasm with browache/headache, blurred vision in dim light, visual field constriction, retinal detachment in high myopes.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.officialText: Causes of secondary glaucoma in the eye

note.title: Causes of Secondary Glaucoma in the Eye
note.content:
1.  **Lens-Induced (Phacogenic):** Phacomorphic, phacolytic, lens particle, phacoantigenic.
2.  **Inflammatory (Uveitic):** Trabecular clogging by inflammatory cells/fibrin, trabeculitis, pupil block via seclusio pupillae (iris bombé), peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS).
3.  **Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG):** Retinal ischemia (PDR, CRVO) stimulating pre-trabecular fibrovascular membrane formation.
4.  **Traumatic:** Angle recession, traumatic hyphema (red cell/ghost cell glaucoma), lens subluxation.
5.  **Pigmentary & Pseudoexfoliative:** Mechanical shedding of pigment or fibrillar pseudoexfoliation material obstructing the intertrabecular spaces.
6.  **Steroid-Induced:** Glycosaminoglycan accumulation in the trabecular meshwork due to prolonged corticosteroid therapy.
7.  **Intraocular Tumors:** Trabecular infiltration or forward displacement of the iris-lens diaphragm by retinoblastoma or melanoma.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.officialText: Late post-operative complications of cataract surgery

note.title: Late Post-Operative Complications of Cataract Surgery
note.content:
1.  **Posterior Capsular Opacification (PCO / After-Cataract):** Most common late complication; proliferation of residual lens epithelial cells (Elschnig pearls, Soemmering ring); treated by Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy.
2.  **Cystoid Macular Edema (CME / Irvine-Gass Syndrome):** Perifoveal capillary leakage peaking at 6–8 weeks postoperatively.
3.  **Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy (PBK):** Progressive corneal endothelial decompensation leading to irreversible corneal edema.
4.  **Delayed Chronic Endophthalmitis:** Low-grade intraocular infection (*Propionibacterium acnes*, fungi) presenting months later with capsular plaque.
5.  **Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RRD):** Higher risk following intraoperative posterior capsular rupture or vitreous loss.
6.  **IOL Malpositioning / Subluxation:** Sunset or sunrise syndrome due to asymmetric haptic placement or zonular dehiscence.

note.title: Vitreous Opacities
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Any non-transparent endogenous or exogenous material within the clear vitreous body that casts shadows on the retina, perceived as "floaters" (muscae volitantes).
*   **Common Causes:**
    1.  *Physiological (Muscae Volitantes):* Remnants of embryonic hyaloid vascular system.
    2.  *Vitreous Condensation & Liquefaction (Synchysis/Syneresis):* Degenerative age-related change or high myopia.
    3.  *Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD):* Characterized by a circular fibrous floaters (**Weiss ring**).
    4.  *Vitreous Hemorrhage:* Extravasated red blood cells secondary to PDR, retinal tears, or retinal vein occlusion.
    5.  *Inflammatory Vitritis:* Inflammatory cell aggregates and exudates (**snowballs / snowbanking**) in intermediate uveitis or endophthalmitis.
    6.  *Degenerative Suspensions:* **Asteroid hyalosis** (calcium-lipid soaps) and **Synchysis scintillans** (refractile cholesterol crystals).
    7.  *Amyloidosis:* Glass-wool appearance.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.officialText: A 70-year-old female patient presents with pain, redness and diminution of vision in the right eye since 10 days. She gives history of having undergone cataract surgery in the left eye 2 years back. On examination, there is circumcorneal congestion, hazy cornea due to corneal edema, shallow anterior chamber and the lens is cataractous and intumescent. Intraocular pressure is high in the right eye. a) What is the probable diagnosis b) What is the immediate medical management c) What is the definitive treatment d) What are the complications if not treated e) What are the differential diagnosis f) What are the surgical complications g) What are the preoperative advice to this patient (1+2+2+3+3+2+2)

note.title: Phacomorphic Glaucoma
note.content:
#### a) Probable Diagnosis
**Right Eye Phacomorphic Glaucoma (Secondary Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma induced by an Intumescent Senile Cataract).**
*Clinical pointers:* 70-year-old female, acute pain, redness, blurred vision, circumcorneal congestion, steamy corneal edema, shallow anterior chamber, swollen intumescent cataractous lens, elevated IOP, with history of pseudophakia in the fellow eye.

#### b) Immediate Medical Management
*   **Intravenous Hyperosmotic:** IV Mannitol 20% (1.5–2.0 g/kg body weight infused over 30 minutes) to rapidly dehydrate the vitreous humor and lower IOP.
*   **Systemic Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitor:** Acetazolamide 500 mg IV stat, followed by 250 mg orally TDS.
*   **Topical Beta-Blocker:** Timolol maleate 0.5% eye drops BD.
*   **Topical Alpha-2 Agonist:** Brimonidine 0.2% eye drops BD.
*   **Topical Steroid:** Prednisolone acetate 1% drops QID to reduce secondary uveal inflammation.
*   *Note:* Strong miotics (Pilocarpine) should be avoided initially as they may exacerbate pupillary block by increasing lens-iris contact and allowing the lens to shift forward.

#### c) Definitive Treatment
*   **Cataract Extraction with Posterior Chamber Intraocular Lens (PCIOL) Implantation:**
    *   Performed once IOP is normalized and corneal edema clears.
    *   *Techniques:* Manual Small Incision Cataract Surgery (SICS) or Phacoemulsification.
    *   *Key steps:* Puncture of anterior capsule with a 26G needle to aspirate milky cortical fluid, decompressing the swollen lens; followed by continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis (CCC), nuclear delivery, and in-the-bag PCIOL placement.

#### d) Complications if Left Untreated
1.  Permanent peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) formation and intractable secondary chronic angle-closure glaucoma.
2.  Glaucomatous optic atrophy resulting in permanent blindness.
3.  Endothelial cell loss causing bullous keratopathy.
4.  Ciliary staphyloma and phthisis bulbi.

#### e) Differential Diagnosis
1.  *Acute Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (PACG):* Fellow eye shows a shallow anterior chamber and narrow occludable angle (in phacomorphic glaucoma, the fellow eye is often pseudophakic or has a normal open angle).
2.  *Phacolytic Glaucoma:* Lens is hypermature (Morgagnian); anterior chamber is deep (not shallow); white protein flakes present in AC.
3.  *Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG):* Rubeosis iridis visible at pupillary border and angle; history of CRVO or PDR.

#### f) Surgical Complications
1.  *Runaway Capsulorhexis:* Due to high intralenticular pressure and tense capsule.
2.  *Posterior Capsular Rupture (PCR):* Due to zonular laxity in mature cataracts.
3.  *Zonular Dialysis:* Fragile zonules stressed by the swollen lens mass.
4.  *Endothelial Damage:* Due to proximity of the anteriorly displaced lens to the cornea during manipulation.
5.  *Expulsive Choroidal Hemorrhage:* Triggered by sudden intraocular decompression in an eye with pre-existing high IOP.

#### g) Preoperative Advice
*   Strict compliance with IOP-lowering medications prior to surgery.
*   Avoid coughing, sneezing, bending forward, or straining.
*   Counseling on guarded visual prognosis, explaining that final vision depends on the health of the optic nerve and macula behind the dense cataract.

---

note.title: Corneal Edema
note.content:
*   **Definition & Pathophysiology:** Abnormal accumulation of fluid within the corneal epithelium and/or stroma, increasing corneal thickness ($>540\text{ µm}$) and causing loss of transparency. Occurs when fluid inflow exceeds the endothelial dehydrating capacity (endothelial cell count $<500–700\text{ cells/mm}^2$) or when intraocular pressure exceeds stromal swelling pressure.
*   **Causes:**
    1.  *Endothelial Pump Failure:* Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy, pseudophakic/aphakic bullous keratopathy (PBK), surgical trauma during phacoemulsification.
    2.  *Acute Severe IOP Elevation:* Acute angle-closure glaucoma, neovascular glaucoma.
    3.  *Inflammatory Endotheliitis:* Acute iridocyclitis, herpes simplex disciform keratitis, corneal graft rejection.
    4.  *Mechanical / Traumatic:* Tears in Descemet's membrane (birth trauma, keratoconus acute hydrops).
*   **Clinical Features:** Hazy, ground-glass appearance; Descemet's folds; microcystic epithelial edema; coalesce into subepithelial bullae (bullous keratopathy) which rupture, causing severe pain, foreign body sensation, and photophobia.
*   **Management:**
    *   *Topical Hypertonic Agents:* Sodium chloride 5% eye drops or ointment to draw fluid osmotically from the epithelium.
    *   *Lowering IOP:* Topical beta-blockers, CAIs.
    *   *Therapeutic Bandage Contact Lens (BCL):* Provides pain relief by shielding exposed nerve endings from ruptured bullae.
    *   *Endothelial Keratoplasty (Definitive):* Descemet Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSAEK) or Descemet Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty (DMEK).

---

note.title: Bitot Spots
note.content:
*   **Definition & Staging:** Stage **X1B** of the WHO classification of xerophthalmia; pathognomonic ocular sign of Vitamin A deficiency.
*   **Morphology:** Raised, dry, silvery-grey, triangular or oval, foamy plaques situated on the bulbar conjunctiva in the interpalpebral fissure, typically temporal to the limbus with its base toward the limbus.
*   **Histopathology:** Keratinizing squamous metaplasia of the conjunctival epithelium with loss of goblet cells and accumulation of keratin debris gasified by *Corynebacterium xerosis*.
*   **Treatment:** High-dose systemic Vitamin A supplementation as per the WHO protocol (200,000 IU orally on Days 1, 2, and 14).

---

note.title: Retinitis Pigmentosa
note.content:
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:301001:Q07]]` (Paper 6 / Diagrams & Notes) & `[[KUHS-QUESTION:314001:Q06]]` (Paper 7):
    *   *Definition:* Hereditary rod-cone dystrophy characterized by progressive apoptosis of rod photoreceptors followed by cone loss.
    *   *Triad of Symptoms:* Night blindness (nyctalopia), progressive visual field constriction (ring scotoma $\rightarrow$ tubular vision), and late central visual decline.
    *   *Classic Fundus Triad:*
        1.  **Bone-spicule pigment deposits** in the mid-peripheral retina (perivascular cuffing).
        2.  **Attenuated, waxy, thread-like retinal arterioles**.
        3.  **Waxy pallor of the optic disc** (consecutive optic atrophy).

---

note.title: Horner-Trantas Spots
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Transient, discrete, chalky-white or gelatinous, elevated peri-limbal spots pathognomonic of the bulbar or limbal form of **Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC)**.
*   **Composition:** Clumps of degenerated eosinophils and shed, necrotic epithelial debris lodged within limbal crypts.
*   **Clinical Significance:** Resolves rapidly with topical anti-inflammatory therapy (mast cell stabilizers/topical steroids).

---

note.title: Rubeosis Iridis
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Pathological neovascularization of the iris surface and the filtration angle of the anterior chamber.
*   **Etiology:** Triggered by widespread, severe retinal ischemia leading to intraocular release of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF):
    1.  Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR).
    2.  Ischemic Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO / 100-day glaucoma).
    3.  Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (severe carotid artery stenosis).
*   **Clinical Course:** New vessels first appear at the pupillary margin as fine, tortuous capillary tufts $\rightarrow$ extend across iris stroma into the trabecular meshwork $\rightarrow$ pre-trabecular fibrovascular membrane forms $\rightarrow$ contraction causes "zipper-like" synechial angle closure $\rightarrow$ **Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG)**.
*   **Management:** Intravitreal Anti-VEGF injections (Ranibizumab, Bevacizumab) to cause rapid vessel regression; urgent Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP); Glaucoma Drainage Device (Ahmed Valve) or cyclodestruction for intractable NVG.

---

note.title: Fungal Corneal Ulcer (Keratomycosis) Case
note.content:
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:301001:Q01]]` (Paper 1):
    *   *a) Probable Diagnosis:* Right Eye Fungal Corneal Ulcer (Keratomycosis) with Hypopyon.
    *   *b) Supporting Features:* History of trauma with sugarcane stick, dry-looking greyish-white central lesion with feathery edges, satellite microinfiltrates, thick non-sterile hypopyon.
    *   *c) Management:* Topical Natamycin 5% suspension 1-hourly; oral Voriconazole/Fluconazole; Atropine 1% TDS; mechanical debridement; Therapeutic Penetrating Keratoplasty (TPK) if progressive.
    *   *d) Topical Drug to be Avoided:* **Topical Corticosteroids** (aggravate fungal proliferation, induce rapid perforation).
    *   *e) Complications:* Corneal perforation, secondary fungal endophthalmitis, secondary glaucoma, dense leucoma, phthisis bulbi.
    *   *f) Differential Diagnosis:* Bacterial keratitis, *Acanthamoeba* keratitis, Herpetic stromal keratitis.
    *   *g) Preventive Measures:* Protective goggles for agricultural workers during harvesting; immediate medical care for ocular abrasions; avoidance of topical steroids for minor trauma.

questions.officialText: Discuss the etiology, clinical features, management and complications of lens induced glaucomas

note.title: Lens-Induced Glaucomas
note.content:
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:314001:Q01]]` (Paper 12) & General notes:
    1.  **Phacomorphic Glaucoma:** Swollen intumescent lens pushes the peripheral iris forward, causing secondary acute angle closure. Treated with systemic hyperosmotics, acetazolamide, topical beta-blockers, followed by cataract extraction with PCIOL.
    2.  **Phacolytic Glaucoma:** Microscopic leakage of high-molecular-weight lens proteins across an intact capsule of a hypermature (Morgagnian) cataract $\rightarrow$ heavy-molecular proteins and engorged macrophages obstruct the trabecular meshwork $\rightarrow$ secondary open-angle glaucoma. Deep AC, milky fluid with pseudohypopyon. Treated with medical pressure reduction followed by urgent cataract extraction.
    3.  **Lens Particle Glaucoma:** Free cortical lens fragments following trauma or incomplete ECCE mechanically block trabecular spaces. Managed by AC washout and cortex aspiration.
    4.  **Phacoantigenic (Phacoanaphylactic) Glaucoma:** Autoimmune granulomatous reaction to exposed lens proteins after trauma or capsular disruption. Treated with intensive steroids, cycloplegics, and surgical clearance of residual lens matter.
    5.  **Ectopia Lentis (Phacotopic Glaucoma):** Anterior subluxation/dislocation of the crystalline lens into the anterior chamber causing direct pupillary block.

note.title: Ocular Manifestations of Diabetes Mellitus
note.content:
1.  **Eyelids:** Recurrent styes, blepharitis, xanthelasma.
2.  **Cornea:** Diabetic keratopathy (reduced corneal sensitivity, delayed epithelial wound healing, recurrent erosions).
3.  **Iris:** Rubeosis iridis (neovascularization of iris), ectropion uveae.
4.  **Lens:**
    *   *True Diabetic Cataract:* "Snowflake" subcapsular opacities in juvenile diabetics.
    *   *Senile Cataract:* Earlier onset, rapid maturation of nuclear/cortical cataracts.
    *   *Refractive Changes:* Transient myopic shift during acute hyperglycemia; hyperopic shift during sudden reduction of blood sugar.
5.  **Glaucoma:** Primary open-angle glaucoma (higher prevalence) and Neovascular Glaucoma.
6.  **Retina:** **Diabetic Retinopathy** (NPDR, PDR, Diabetic Macular Edema) and central retinal vein occlusion.
7.  **Neuro-Ophthalmology:** Diabetic cranial mononeuropathies: Isolated, pupil-sparing $3^{\text{rd}}$ nerve palsy (microvascular infarction sparing superficial pupillary fibers), $6^{\text{th}}$ nerve palsy, diabetic papillopathy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.officialText: A 70-year-old man came with sudden painless loss of vision. He described the visual loss as a curtain coming down in front of his left eye. He maintained normal vision in his right eye. He is a known hypertensive since 7 years and diabetic since 2 years. His further examination showed a cherry red spot in the left eye. Answer the following questions: a) What is the probable diagnosis b) What other signs you will look for c) Four differential diagnosis of sudden visual loss in an elderly patient. d) What is the plan of management e) What complications can occur (1+2+2+3+2)

note.title: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) Case
note.content:
#### a) Probable Diagnosis
**Left Eye Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO).**

#### b) Other Signs to Look For
*   *Visual Acuity:* Profound loss of vision, typically reduced to Counting Fingers close to face or Light Perception only.
*   *Pupil:* Dilated, fixed, with an **amaurotic pupillary response** (absent direct light reflex in left eye, absent consensual reflex in right eye; normal left consensual reflex when right eye is illuminated; positive Marcus Gunn RAPD).
*   *Fundus Signs:*
    *   **Milky-White Retinal Edema:** Opacification of the posterior pole due to ischemia of ganglion cells and nerve fiber layers.
    *   **Cherry Red Spot at Macula:** The fovea centralis lacks inner retinal layers; the underlying vascular choroid and choriocapillaris shine through the thin foveola, contrasting sharply against the surrounding pale, milky-white edematous retina.
    *   **Severe Arteriolar Narrowing:** Retinal arteries appear thread-like; veins show segmentation of the blood column (**"cattle-trucking"** or "box-carring").
    *   *Emboli:* Hollenhorst plaques (cholesterol) or calcific emboli at arterial bifurcations.
    *   *Sparing:* Retinal area supplied by a patent **cilioretinal artery** (present in 15–20% of population) remains clear and pink.

#### c) Four Differential Diagnoses of Sudden Painless Visual Loss in an Elderly Patient
1.  *Ischemic Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO)* (splashed-tomato fundus with massive hemorrhages).
2.  *Non-Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (NAION)* (pale disc edema, altitudinal visual field defect).
3.  *Arteritic AION secondary to Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA)* (tender temporal artery, elevated ESR/CRP).
4.  *Massive Vitreous Hemorrhage* (e.g., secondary to proliferative diabetic retinopathy).

#### d) Plan of Management
*   *True Ophthalmic Emergency:* Retinal survival time is approximately **90–100 minutes**; treatment must be initiated immediately:
    1.  **Immediate Ocular Massage:** Digital massage applied intermittently through closed lids (press firmly for 10 seconds, release for 5 seconds) to lower IOP, induce retinal vasodilation, and dislodge the embolus into a more peripheral branch.
    2.  **Immediate Reduction of Intraocular Pressure:**
        *   **Anterior Chamber Paracentesis:** Aspiration of 0.1–0.2 mL of aqueous using a 30G needle under topical anesthesia to produce immediate profound ocular decompression.
        *   **IV Acetazolamide 500 mg stat** + **IV Mannitol 20% (200 mL)**.
        *   Topical Timolol 0.5% and Brimonidine 0.2%.
    3.  **Vasodilation Therapy:**
        *   Inhalation of a carbogen mixture (**95% oxygen + 5% carbon dioxide**) or breathing into a paper bag to induce hypercapnic retinal arteriolar dilation and enhance oxygenation.
        *   Sublingual Isosorbide dinitrate.
    4.  **Systemic Workup & Secondary Prevention:**
        *   Rule out Giant Cell Arteritis: Urgent ESR, C-reactive protein, and temporal artery biopsy if elevated; start high-dose IV methylprednisolone if suspected.
        *   Carotid Doppler ultrasonography to detect carotid artery stenosis/atheromatous plaques.
        *   Echocardiography to rule out cardiac valvular vegetations or mural thrombi.
        *   Daily oral Aspirin (antiplatelet therapy) to prevent impending stroke/myocardial infarction.

#### e) Complications
*   Permanent, irreversible optic atrophy (consecutive/ischemic).
*   Neovascular Glaucoma (develops in 2%–5% of CRAO cases).
*   Cerebrovascular stroke and myocardial infarction (high systemic mortality).

---

note.title: Signs of Herpes Simplex Keratitis
note.content:
1.  **Punctate Epithelial Keratitis:** Multiple tiny, coarse, raised epithelial vesicles.
2.  **Dendritic Ulcer (Pathognomonic):** Irregular, branching, arborizing linear ulcer with terminal buds or knobs; stains brilliantly with fluorescein (bed) and rose bengal (virus-laden devitalized margins).
3.  **Geographical (Amoeboid) Ulcer:** Large epithelial defect with scalloped margins resulting from enlargement and coalescence of dendrites (frequently induced by misuse of topical steroids).
4.  **Marked Reduction of Corneal Sensations.**
5.  **Disciform Keratitis:** Focal, central, disc-shaped stromal edema without necrosis, accompanied by folds in Descemet's membrane and keratic precipitates.

note.title: Berlin’s Edema (Commotio Retinae)
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Transient, milky-grey/white opacification of the outer sensory retina, typically involving the posterior pole and macula, occurring secondary to blunt ocular contusion.
*   **Pathophysiology:** Mechanical shock waves cause disruption, fragmentation, and damage to the photoreceptor outer segments and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) with intracellular edema (not extracellular fluid extravasation).
*   **Clinical Features:** Sudden reduction in visual acuity following blunt trauma; ophthalmoscopy demonstrates a well-circumscribed, milky-white retinal haze at the macula with an apparent **pseudo-cherry red spot** at the foveola (due to normal choroidal transmission through the thin foveola).
*   **Prognosis & Treatment:** Self-limiting condition; usually resolves completely within 1–2 weeks without residual deficit. In severe trauma, permanent visual loss may ensue secondary to pigmentary macular degeneration or traumatic macular hole formation. No specific treatment is required.

note.title: Sub-Conjunctival Haemorrhage
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Extravasation of blood into the potential space between the bulbar conjunctiva and the underlying episclera.
*   **Etiology:**
    1.  *Trauma:* Direct ocular contusion, rubbing of eyes, foreign body, fracture of base of skull (no posterior limit visible).
    2.  *Sudden Venous Congestion (Valsalva):* Severe coughing (whooping cough), sneezing, straining, vomiting, strangulation.
    3.  *Systemic Vascular Diseases:* Systemic hypertension, arteriosclerosis, diabetes mellitus.
    4.  *Hematological & Bleeding Disorders:* Purpura, hemophilia, leukemia, anticoagulant therapy.
    5.  *Infections:* Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis (Enterovirus 70, Coxsackie A24), Pneumococcal conjunctivitis.
*   **Clinical Features:** Bright red, flat, homogenous, well-circumscribed patch on the bulbar conjunctiva; asymptomatic aside from cosmesis.
*   **Treatment:** Self-limiting; absorbs completely within 1–3 weeks, changing color from bright red to orange and yellow. Cold compresses initially, followed by warm compresses.

note.title: Ophthalmia Neonatorum
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Any acute conjunctival inflammation with discharge occurring in an infant during the first **28 days (4 weeks) of life**.
*   **Etiology and Incubation Periods:**
    1.  *Chemical (Silver nitrate / antiseptic prophylaxis):* Within **6–24 hours**; self-limiting.
    2.  *Neisseria gonorrhoeae:* **2–5 days**; hyperacute, copious, thick purulent discharge; can penetrate intact corneal epithelium leading to rapid perforation.
    3.  *Chlamydia trachomatis (Inclusion blennorrhea, commonest infectious):* **5–14 days**; mucopurulent discharge, papillary conjunctivitis (infant conjunctiva cannot form follicles until 3 months).
    4.  *Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-2):* **6–14 days**; vesicular lid lesions, epithelial dendrites.
    5.  *Other bacteria (Staphylococci, Streptococci):* **5–8 days**.
*   **Prophylaxis (Credé’s Method & Modern Equivalents):**
    *   Antenatal screening and treatment of maternal genital infections.
    *   Aseptic delivery; immediate cleansing of the newborn's eyelids.
    *   Postnatal instillation of **Povidone-Iodine 2.5% solution** (preferred) or Erythromycin 0.5% / Tetracycline 1% ointment.
*   **Management:**
    *   *Gonococcal:* Urgent hospitalization. Systemic **Ceftriaxone (25–50 mg/kg IV/IM single dose up to 125 mg)** + frequent hourly saline irrigation of eyes + topical Bacitracin/Ciprofloxacin.
    *   *Chlamydial:* Oral **Erythromycin syrup (50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 14 days)** to clear systemic colonization (prevents chlamydial interstitial pneumonitis) + topical Erythromycin ointment. Both parents must be treated.

note.title: Presbyopia
note.content:
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:301001:Q02]]` (Paper 8 / General notes):
    *   *Definition:* Physiological age-related decline in accommodative amplitude causing progressive recession of the near point of accommodation ($>25–33\text{ cm}$) beyond normal reading distance, typically manifesting after 40 years of age.
    *   *Causes:* Age-related sclerosis and loss of elasticity of the crystalline lens substance; weakening of ciliary muscle power.
    *   *Clinical Features:* Asthenopia, difficulty reading small print in dim light, holding reading materials at arm's length.
    *   *Treatment:* Prescribe convex spherical reading additions over distance optical correction (+1.0 D at 40 years, +1.5 D at 45, +2.0 D at 50, +2.5 D at 55–60 years). Available as unifocal, bifocal, or progressive addition lenses (PALs).

note.title: Staphylomas
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Localized bulging or ectasia of the weak, thinned outer fibrous coat of the eyeball (cornea or sclera), lined internally by uveal tissue which shows through as a slate-blue or black discoloration.
*   **Types:**
    1.  **Anterior Staphyloma:** Ectasia of pseudocornea lined by incarcerated iris tissue following total sloughing and perforation of a corneal ulcer.
    2.  **Intercalary Staphyloma:** Localized bulge at the limbus (up to 2 mm behind limbus) lined by the root of the iris.
    3.  **Ciliary Staphyloma:** Bulge in the sclera 2–8 mm behind the limbus, lined by the ciliary body. Causes: Trauma, scleritis, absolute glaucoma.
    4.  **Equatorial Staphyloma:** Bulge at the equator of the eyeball (14 mm behind limbus) in the region of the vortex veins, lined by the choroid.
    5.  **Posterior Staphyloma:** Bulge posterior to the equator, commonly around the optic nerve head and macula, lined by atrophic choroid. Pathognomonic of **pathological high myopia**.

---

note.title: Atropine
note.content:
*   **Class:** Naturally occurring belladonna alkaloid; non-selective muscarinic antagonist (parasympatholytic agent).
*   **Ocular Actions:**
    *   *Mydriasis:* Paralyzes the pupillary sphincter muscle (onset 30–40 min, lasts 10–14 days).
    *   *Cycloplegia:* Paralyzes the ciliary muscle, abolishing accommodation (onset 1–2 hours, lasts 7–12 days).
*   **Preparations:** Atropine sulphate 1% eye ointment and 1% eye drops.
*   **Indications:**
    1.  Cycloplegic refraction in children $<5$ years of age.
    2.  Acute anterior uveitis (relieves ciliary spasm, prevents/breaks posterior synechiae).
    3.  Corneal ulcers (relieves reflex ciliary spasm and pain).
    4.  Malignant (ciliary-block) glaucoma (relaxes ciliary ring).
    5.  Amblyopia penalization therapy.

note.title: Non-Healing Corneal Ulcer
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Corneal ulcer showing no signs of regression or healing despite 7–10 days of intensive antimicrobial therapy.
*   **Causes:**
    *   *Local Factors:* Inaccurate etiological diagnosis (e.g., fungal, *Acanthamoeba*, or atypical mycobacterial keratitis treated with antibacterial drops); chronic dacryocystitis; persistent trichiasis; lagophthalmos; raised IOP; topical drug toxicity (preservatives).
    *   *Systemic Factors:* Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, severe malnutrition, immunosuppression (systemic steroid use, HIV).
*   **Management:** Re-scrape for repeated cultures and KOH mount; stop all toxic medications for 24 hours; treat associated dacryocystitis; perform corneal debridement; application of tissue adhesive (cyanoacrylate) with BCL for deep ulcers; **Therapeutic Penetrating Keratoplasty (TPK)**.

note.title: Hypertensive Retinopathy
note.content:
*   **Pathogenesis:** Vasospasm (acute vasoconstriction) $\rightarrow$ Sclerosis (arteriosclerotic thickening) $\rightarrow$ Exudation (blood-retinal barrier breakdown).
*   **Keith-Wagener-Barker Classification:**
    *   *Grade I:* Mild, generalized arteriolar attenuation, broadening of arteriolar light reflex.
    *   *Grade II:* Marked generalized and focal arteriolar narrowing; **A-V crossing changes (Salus’ sign [deflection], Gunn’s sign [tapering], Bonnet’s sign [banking])**.
    *   *Grade III:* "Copper-wiring" of arterioles; flame-shaped intraretinal hemorrhages; cotton-wool spots; hard exudates in a **macular star** pattern.
    *   *Grade IV (Malignant Hypertension):* All features of Grade III + **"Silver-wiring" of arterioles** + **Papilledema (bilateral disc edema)**.
*   **Management:** Stepwise, controlled systemic antihypertensive therapy (avoid sudden reduction of BP to prevent optic nerve head infarction).

note.title: After-Cataract (Posterior Capsular Opacification - PCO)
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Opacification of the posterior lens capsule occurring weeks, months, or years after extracapsular cataract extraction or phacoemulsification. Most common late complication.
*   **Pathogenesis:** Proliferation, migration, and metaplasia of residual equatorial lens epithelial cells (LECs) across the posterior capsule.
*   **Morphological Forms:**
    1.  *Elschnig’s Pearls:* Swollen, balloon-like, vacuolated epithelial cells clustered like "soap bubbles" on the visual axis.
    2.  *Fibrous PCO:* Myofibroblastic transdifferentiation causing wrinkling and fibrous sheet opacification.
    3.  *Soemmering’s Ring:* Annular ring of dense regenerative cortex sandwiched between anterior and posterior capsular remnants.
*   **Treatment:** **Nd:YAG Laser Posterior Capsulotomy** (1064 nm Q-switched laser creates a 3–4 mm clear central optical opening in the posterior capsule).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.officialText: A 70 year old male, diabetic and hypertensive, came with painless progressive diminution of vision in both eyes since about six months. His vision is counting fingers close to face in both eyes, not improving further with any glasses. There is a while reflex in the pupil in both the eyes and the fundus cannot be visualized.  What is the most probable diagnosis  What are the investigations you need to perform before operating on him  What are the types of surgeries which can be planned for him  Discuss the possible early post-operative complications of the surgery (1+3+3+3)

note.title: Bilateral Mature Senile Cataract Case
note.content:
#### a) Most Probable Diagnosis
**Bilateral Mature Senile Cataract (MSC) in a Diabetic and Hypertensive Patient.**

#### b) Preoperative Investigations
1.  *Systemic Workup:* Strict glycemic profiling (Fasting, Postprandial Blood Sugar, HbA1c $<7\%$), blood pressure control, ECG, cardiology clearance, urine analysis (r/o sugar/albumin).
2.  *Ocular Surface & Sepsis Screening:* Regurgitation test and lacrimal syringing to rule out chronic dacryocystitis; rule out blepharitis and conjunctival discharge.
3.  *Biometry:* Keratometry + A-Scan ultrasound to determine axial length and calculate IOL power (SRK/T formula).
4.  *Posterior Segment Evaluation:* B-Scan ultrasonography (since fundus view is completely obscured by dense cataract) to exclude posterior staphyloma, vitreous hemorrhage, or retinal detachment.
5.  *Macular Function Testing:* Two-light discrimination, color perception, projection of rays (PR) in all four quadrants.

#### c) Types of Surgeries Planned
1.  **Phacoemulsification with Foldable Posterior Chamber IOL (PCIOL):** Modern standard technique.
2.  **Manual Small Incision Cataract Surgery (SICS) with Rigid PMMA PCIOL:** Extremely safe and cost-effective, especially advantageous for mature hard brown nuclei.
3.  **Conventional Extracapsular Cataract Extraction (ECCE):** Large incision, indicated only if SICS/Phaco facilities are unavailable.

#### d) Early Postoperative Complications
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:314001:Q09]]` (Paper 2): Wound leak, iris prolapse, striate keratopathy, hyphaema, acute post-op endophthalmitis, TASS, and secondary IOP spikes.

---

note.title: Visual Acuity Testing
note.content:
*   **Distance Visual Acuity:** Snellen’s chart tested at 6 meters (rays are parallel, minimal accommodation). Principle: Subtends $5\text{ minutes}$ of arc at the nodal point, constituent lines subtend $1\text{ minute}$. Recorded as $d/D$. Landolt’s C and Tumbling E charts for illiterates; LogMAR charts for standardized research.
*   **Near Visual Acuity:** Jaeger’s chart or Roman test types (N5 to N48) tested at $33–35\text{ cm}$ in adequate illumination.

note.title: Sturm’s Conoid
note.content:
*Reference Image Link:* [Sturm's Conoid Diagram (Wikimedia Commons)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/15/1413_Structure_of_the_Eye.jpg)

```
        Toric Refracting Surface
             (Vertical > Horizontal Curvature)
                 |
  Parallel Rays  |             A             B (First Focus)       C             D                     E     F (Second Focus)  G
  -------------->|            ( )           ---                 ( )           ( O )                  ( )          |          ( )
  -------------->|        Horizontal    Horizontal Focal    Horizontal     Circle of Least       Vertical    Vertical Focal  Vertical
  -------------->|           Oval             Line             Oval           Diffusion            Oval          Line           Oval
                 |
                 |<------------------ Focal Interval of Sturm ------------------------>|
```
*Key Elements to Label:*
1. Toric refracting surface.
2. Vertical rays converge faster $\rightarrow$ First focal line (B, horizontal).
3. Horizontal rays converge slower $\rightarrow$ Second focal line (F, vertical).
4. Focal Interval of Sturm (distance between first and second focal lines).
5. Circle of Least Diffusion (D, dioptric midpoint where visual confusion is minimized).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.officialText: Describe the development of the lens

note.title: Development of the Lens
note.content:
*   **Embryological Origin:** Surface ectoderm.
*   **Key Milestones:**
    1.  *Day 22–27:* Optic vesicle contacts overlying surface ectoderm, inducing it to thicken and form the **Lens Placode**.
    2.  *Day 27–30:* Lens placode invaginates to form the **Lens Pit**, which pinches off by Day 33 as a hollow **Lens Vesicle** lined by a single layer of cells enclosed in a basement membrane (capsule).
    3.  *Primary Lens Fibers (Embryonic Nucleus):* Cells of the posterior wall of the lens vesicle elongate anteriorly, obliterate the central cavity, and form primary lens fibers (completed by 3rd month).
    4.  *Secondary Lens Fibers (Fetal & Adult Nuclei):* Anterior epithelial cells migrate to the equator, multiply, and elongate to form concentric secondary fibers meeting at the Y-sutures throughout life.

note.title: WHO Classification of Xerophthalmia
note.content:
*   **XN:** Night blindness (Nyctalopia).
*   **X1A:** Conjunctival xerosis (dry, non-wettable, lustreless patches).
*   **X1B:** Bitot's spots (silvery foamy triangular patches in temporal interpalpebral conjunctiva).
*   **X2:** Corneal xerosis (hazy, pebbly, dull cornea).
*   **X3A:** Corneal ulceration / Keratomalacia involving $<1/3$ of the corneal surface.
*   **X3B:** Corneal ulceration / Keratomalacia involving $\ge 1/3$ of the corneal surface (blinding).
*   **XS:** Corneal scars secondary to healed xerophthalmia.
*   **XF:** Xerophthalmic fundus (white seed-like retinal deposits).

questions.officialText: A man was hit on his right eye by cricket ball while playing. On examination his vision was 6/6 both eyes. He had binocular diplopia and periorbital ecchymosis with crepitus in right eye. Answer the following questions:  What type of ocular trauma he encountered  Two causes of diplopia probable in this patient  Two other clinical signs likely in this patient  Four causes of decreased vision following blunt trauma to eye  How will you manage this patient (1+2+2+2+3)

note.title: Blunt Ocular Trauma Case (Cricket Ball)
note.content:
#### a) Type of Ocular Trauma
**Closed-Globe Contusional Ocular Trauma** with an **Orbital Blow-Out Fracture (Floor/Medial Wall)** of the Right Orbit.

#### b) Two Causes of Diplopia Probable in this Patient
1.  **Mechanical Entrapment:** Incarceration of the inferior rectus muscle and surrounding orbital fibrofatty tissue within the fractured bony orbital floor.
2.  **Neuromuscular Injury:** Contusion or neuropraxia of the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve ($3^{\text{rd}}$ CN) or intramuscular hematoma.

#### c) Two Other Clinical Signs Likely in this Patient
1.  **Infraorbital Nerve Hypoesthesia:** Numbness over the right cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of nose due to infraorbital canal fracture.
2.  **Enophthalmos:** Sunken appearance of the right eyeball occurring as edema resolves, due to herniation of orbital fat into the maxillary antrum.

#### d) Four Causes of Decreased Vision Following Blunt Trauma
1.  *Hyphema:* Bleeding in the anterior chamber blocking the visual axis.
2.  *Commotio Retinae (Berlin's Edema):* Photoreceptor disruption at the fovea.
3.  *Traumatic Cataract / Lens Subluxation:* Rupture of lens capsule or zonules.
4.  *Vitreous Hemorrhage / Retinal Detachment (Dialysis at Ora Serrata).*

#### e) Management of this Patient
*   *Conservative Medical Phase (Initial 10–14 days):*
    *   Instruct patient strictly **not to blow the nose** (prevents orbital emphysema and orbital cellulitis).
    *   Broad-spectrum oral prophylactic antibiotics (Amoxicillin-Clavulanate) to prevent secondary infection from the maxillary sinus.
    *   Systemic corticosteroids (oral Prednisolone) to reduce peri-orbital soft-tissue edema.
    *   Cold dry compresses for 48 hours.
*   *Diagnostic Investigations:* Non-contrast CT scan of the orbit (coronal and axial cuts, 1.5 mm slices) to confirm floor fracture, detect the **"tear-drop sign"** (herniated soft tissue in maxillary sinus), and identify muscle entrapment.
*   *Surgical Management (Orbital Floor Repair):* Indicated at 10–14 days if:
    *   Persistent disabling vertical diplopia in primary/downgaze with positive Forced Duction Test (FDT).
    *   Significant enophthalmos ($>2–3\text{ mm}$).
    *   Large floor fracture defect ($>50\%$ of floor area).
    *   *Procedure:* Transconjunctival or subciliary incision, release of entrapped muscle, and reconstruction of orbital floor using porous polyethylene (Medpor), titanium mesh, or autologous bone graft.

---

note.title: Mooren’s Ulcer
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Severe, progressive, painful, chronic idiopathic ulcerative keratitis that begins in the corneal periphery and spreads circumferentially and centripetally. Autoimmune basis (antibodies against corneal-associated antigens).
*   **Clinical Features:**
    *   Starts as marginal greyish-white infiltrate near the limbus with intense pain and photophobia.
    *   Breaks down into a progressive furrow/gutter with a characteristic **overhanging, undermined, vascularized leading edge**.
    *   Spreads centripetally to involve the entire cornea; sclera is characteristically spared; no systemic collagen vascular disease present.
*   **Types:**
    1.  *Unilateral / Benign:* Elderly patients, slow progression, responds well to therapy.
    2.  *Bilateral / Atypical (Virulent):* Young patients, rapidly progressive, resistant to treatment.
*   **Treatment:** Topical corticosteroids, topical Cyclosporine A (1%), systemic immunosuppressants (Methotrexate), conjunctival resection (peritomy) adjacent to the ulcer, and tectonic lamellar keratoplasty.

note.title: Pseudorosettes
note.content:
*   *Note:* The term **Pseudorosettes** (Homer-Wright rosettes) represents neuroblastic tumor cells arranged radially around an irregular central meshwork of neural cytoplasmic processes without a true central lumen (seen in Retinoblastoma, Neuroblastoma, Medulloblastoma).
    *(In contrast, true **Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes** surround a distinct, empty central lumen lined by a terminal bar membrane).*

```
      [ HOMER-WRIGHT PSEUDOROSETTE ]          [ FLEXNER-WINTERSTEINER ROSETTE ]
                 ( * )                                    ( * )
               /   |   \                                /   |   \
             ( * ) | ( * )                            ( * )=== ( * )
            --- [Dense] ---                          --- [LUMEN] ---
             ( * ) | ( * )                            ( * )=== ( * )
               \   |   /                                \   |   /
                 ( * )                                    ( * )
        (Central tangle of fibers)                (True empty central lumen)
```

note.title: Glaukomflecken
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Multiple, small, greyish-white, subcapsular/anterior cortical lenticular opacities pathognomonic of a prior acute attack of angle-closure glaucoma.
*   **Pathogenesis:** High intraocular pressure ($>50–60\text{ mm Hg}$) during an acute congestive attack causes focal ischemic necrosis of the anterior lens epithelial cells.
*   **Significance:** Diagnostic hallmark indicating an old resolved episode of acute angle closure (part of Vogt’s triad along with iris sector atrophy and a dilated pupil).

---

note.title: Cycloplegia
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Pharmacological paralysis of the ciliary muscle, abolishing the eye's power of accommodation; accompanied by pupillary dilatation (mydriasis) due to muscarinic receptor blockade.
*   **Drugs:** Atropine (lasts 7–14 days), Homatropine (48–72 hours), Cyclopentolate (6–24 hours).
*   **Indications:** Accurate refraction in children (unmasks latent hypermetropia), treatment of iridocyclitis and corneal ulcers.

---

note.title: Nuclear Cataract
note.content:
*   **Pathophysiology:** Intensification of physiological age-related nuclear sclerosis; compaction and dehydration of the central nucleus with accumulation of insoluble protein aggregates and brown/yellow urochrome pigments.
*   **Clinical Features:** Gradual painless visual loss for distance; **Index Myopia** produces temporary improvement in near vision without reading glasses (**"second sight"**); poor color discrimination (blue-blindness). Lens appears amber, brown (*cataracta brunescens*), or black (*cataracta nigra*).

---

note.title: Ectopia Lentis
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Displacement or malposition of the crystalline lens from its normal anatomical seat in the patellar fossa due to partial or complete disruption of ciliary zonules.
*   **Forms:**
    1.  *Subluxation (Incomplete displacement):* Lens remains partially within the pupillary space.
    2.  *Luxation / Dislocation (Complete displacement):* Lens entirely displaced into anterior chamber, vitreous, or subretinal space.
*   **Causes:**
    *   *Heritable (Systemic):* **Marfan syndrome** (bilateral, symmetrical, superotemporal subluxation), **Homocystinuria** (inferonasal subluxation), **Weill-Marchesani syndrome** (microspherophakia with anterior subluxation).
    *   *Traumatic:* Blunt contusion (commonest overall cause).
    *   *Consecutive / Spontaneous:* Hypermature cataract, buphthalmos, high myopia, pseudoexfoliation.

questions.officialText: Patient presents with a history of gradual painless progressive loss of vision in both eyes with a vision of counting fingers 2½ meter s. Lens appears grayish white in colour with iris shadow. Answer the following:  What is your more probable diagnosis  How do you classify  What are the clinical features of the condition  Mention differential diagnosis.  How will you manage the case (1+2+2+2+3)

note.title: Case of Immature Senile Cataract
note.content:
#### a) Most Probable Diagnosis
**Bilateral Immature Senile Cataract (ISC) - Cortical Type.**
*(Gradual painless progressive visual decline, counting fingers 2.5 meters, greyish-white lens with positive iris shadow).*

#### b) Classification of Cataract
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:314001:Q09]]` (Paper 2) for complete etiological and morphological classifications.

#### c) Clinical Features
*   *Symptoms:* Painless, progressive reduction of visual acuity; monocular polyopia/diplopia; glare and halos around light sources; distortion of images.
*   *Signs:*
    *   Visual acuity reduced to counting fingers or decimal fractions.
    *   Greyish-white opacity within the cortex with clear zones between opacity and pupillary border.
    *   **Positive Iris Shadow Test:** Oblique illumination casts a crescentic shadow of the pupillary margin of the iris onto the underlying greyish lens opacity because clear cortex separates the two.
    *   Distant direct ophthalmoscopy demonstrates dark spokes/opacities moving against the red fundus glow.

#### d) Differential Diagnosis
1.  *Nuclear Sclerosis:* Refraction shows progressive myopic shift ("second sight"); iris shadow is negative; central golden-yellow haze without distinct cortical water clefts.
2.  *Open-Angle Glaucoma:* Elevated IOP, glaucomatous cupping, arcuate scotomas.
3.  *Age-Related Macular Degeneration (Dry ARMD):* Distorted central vision (metamorphopsia) with drusen at the macula.

#### e) Management of the Case
*   *Preoperative Evaluation:* Full systemic screening (BP, blood sugar), lacrimal sac syringing (rules out dacryocystitis), keratometry, and A-scan ultrasound biometry to calculate intraocular lens power (SRK/T formula).
*   *Surgical Intervention (Definitive Cure):*
    *   **Phacoemulsification with Foldable Posterior Chamber IOL (PCIOL):** Sutureless, clear corneal 2.2 mm incision, continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis, ultrasonic phacoemulsification, in-the-bag foldable IOL placement.
    *   *Alternative:* **Manual Small Incision Cataract Surgery (MSICS)** with rigid PMMA IOL.
*   *Postoperative Care:* Topical antibiotic-steroid eye drops (e.g., Moxifloxacin 0.5% + Prednisolone acetate 1%) tapered over 4–6 weeks; final refractive spectacle prescription at 4–6 weeks.

note.title: Keratoconus
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Non-inflammatory, progressive, bilateral, asymmetrical ectatic corneal dystrophy characterized by central and paracentral stromal thinning, protrusion, and irregular myopic astigmatism.
*   **Pathophysiology:** Fragmentation of Bowman's layer, loss of stromal collagen fibril architecture, and keratocyte apoptosis.
*   **Clinical Features:**
    *   *Symptoms:* Progressive diminution of vision, frequent changes in spectacle prescriptions, visual distortion, monocular diplopia, glare.
    *   *Signs:*
        *   Window reflex / Placido disc rings show irregular, distorted, egg-shaped reflection.
        *   Retinoscopy demonstrates **"scissor reflex"**.
        *   Distant direct ophthalmoscopy shows an **"oil-droplet reflex"**.
        *   **Munson’s Sign:** V-shaped protrusion of the lower eyelid margin in extreme downgaze.
        *   **Fleischer’s Ring:** Golden-brown iron pigment ring in basal epithelium at the base of the cone.
        *   **Vogt’s Striae:** Fine, parallel, vertical stress lines in the deep stroma/Descemet's that disappear with gentle digital pressure on the globe.
        *   *Acute Hydrops:* Sudden, painful corneal clouding caused by spontaneous rupture of Descemet's membrane with acute aqueous influx.
*   **Management:**
    1.  *Early Stage:* Spectacle correction; Rigid Gas-Permeable (RGP) contact lenses, Rose-K lenses, or Scleral lenses.
    2.  *Halt Progression:* **Corneal Collagen Cross-Linking with Riboflavin (CXL / C3R):** Epithelial debridement + Riboflavin 0.1% drops + UVA light (365 nm) creates covalent bonds between collagen lamellae, stabilizing corneal biomechanics.
    3.  *Intracorneal Ring Segments (ICRS / Intacs):* Flatten the central cone.
    4.  *Advanced Scarred Stage:* Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) or Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP).

---

note.title: Heterochromia
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Asymmetry or difference in coloration of the iris.
*   **Types:**
    1.  *Heterochromia Iridum:* Color of one iris differs entirely from that of the fellow eye.
    2.  *Heterochromia Iridis:* Sectors of different colors within the same iris.
*   **Etiological Causes:**
    *   *Hypochromic (Lighter Iris):* Congenital Horner syndrome, Fuchs’ heterochromic iridocyclitis, Waardenburg syndrome, iris atrophy following uveitis or acute angle closure.
    *   *Hyperchromic (Darker Iris):* Ocular melanosis, Nevus of Ota, Siderosis bulbi (retained iron IOFB), diffuse iris melanoma, chronic topical prostaglandin analogue therapy (Latanoprost).

---

note.title: Munson Sign
note.content:
*   **Definition & Significance:** A characteristic clinical sign of advanced **Keratoconus**, characterized by a **V-shaped angular protrusion and indentation of the lower eyelid margin** when the patient is instructed to look downward. Produced by the mechanical pushing force of the sharply protruding ectatic conical cornea against the lower lid.

---

note.title: Phlyctenular Conjunctivitis
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Cell-mediated, nodular allergic keratoconjunctivitis occurring as a **Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction** to endogenous microbial proteins (most commonly *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, or *Chlamydia*). Peak age: 3–15 years, females, undernourished children.
*   **Clinical Features:**
    *   Symptoms: Mild irritation, foreign body sensation, lacrimation.
    *   Signs: Solitary or multiple, small (1–3 mm), pinkish-white, elevated hard nodules situated on the bulbar conjunctiva at or near the limbus, surrounded by a localized triangular wedge of intense conjunctival hyperemia.
    *   Course: Nodule undergoes apex necrosis, ulcerates, and resolves within 8–10 days without leaving a scar.
*   **Treatment:** Short course of topical corticosteroid drops (Fluorometholone/Dexamethasone) + broad-spectrum antibiotic drops. Treat underlying systemic focus: Mantoux test, Chest X-ray, antitubercular therapy if positive; improve general nutrition (high-protein diet, Vitamins A and D).

questions.officialText: Patient presents with a history of watering with mucopurulent discharge for the last six months in the right eye. Regurgitation test positive. Answer the following:  What is your more probable diagnosis  Describe the anatomy  How do you confirm the diagnosis  What are the complications  How will you manage the condition (1+2+2+2+3)

note.title: Case of Chronic Dacryocystitis
note.content:
#### a) Most Probable Diagnosis
**Right Eye Chronic Dacryocystitis with Lacrimal Mucocele.**

#### b) Anatomy of the Lacrimal Drainage Apparatus
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:314001:Q12]]` (Paper 13 / Diagram) & `[[KUHS-QUESTION:314001:Q21]]` (Paper 3 / Notes): Puncta $\rightarrow$ Canaliculi (vertical 2 mm, horizontal 6–8 mm) $\rightarrow$ Common canaliculus $\rightarrow$ Lacrimal sac (in lacrimal fossa) $\rightarrow$ Nasolacrimal duct (12–18 mm, opens into inferior meatus).

#### c) Confirmation of Diagnosis
1.  *Positive Regurgitation Test:* Manual pressure over the lacrimal sac elicits copious regurgitation of mucopurulent/gelatinous fluid through the puncta.
2.  *Lacrimal Syringing Test:* Complete obstruction in the NLD; saline refluxes completely through the upper/lower punctum with none entering the throat.
3.  *Dacryocystography (DCG):* Contrast radiography demonstrates dilated lacrimal sac with non-passage of dye into the nose.

#### d) Complications
*   Acute exacerbation into acute dacryocystitis / lacrimal abscess.
*   Spontaneous external lacrimal fistula formation.
*   Chronic intractable purulent conjunctivitis.
*   Corneal ulceration following minor abrasions.
*   High risk of postoperative acute endophthalmitis if intraocular surgery is performed without treating dacryocystitis.

#### e) Management
*   **Surgery of Choice:** **Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR)** (External or Endoscopic Endonasal approach). Creates a surgical anastomosis between the lacrimal sac mucosa and nasal mucosa of the middle meatus, bypassing the blocked NLD.
*   *Alternative:* **Dacryocystectomy (DCT)** (complete excision of sac) indicated if DCR is contraindicated (marked atrophic rhinitis, tuberculosis, elderly debilitated patients).

note.title: Phthisis Bulbi
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Final, irreversible, end-stage clinical state of a disorganized, atrophic, shrunken, soft, non-functioning blind eye resulting from severe intraocular destruction (trauma, endophthalmitis, chronic uveitis, absolute glaucoma).
*   **Pathophysiology:** Ciliary body destruction and detachment causes cessation of aqueous production $\rightarrow$ profound hypotony ($IOP \approx 0–4\text{ mm Hg}$) $\rightarrow$ architectural collapse of the scleral shell $\rightarrow$ fibrosis, intraocular calcification, and bone metaplasia.
*   **Clinical Features:** Marked enophthalmos, small square-shaped globe (due to recti traction on soft sclera), thickened opaque vascularized cornea, collapsed anterior chamber, hypotony, total blindness (no light perception).
*   **Treatment:** Enucleation or evisceration with an orbital implant for cosmesis if chronically painful.

note.title: Occlusio Pupillae
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Complete occlusion and closure of the pupillary aperture by an organized inflammatory, fibro-cellular pseudomembrane following severe plastic anterior uveitis.
*   **Consequences:** Blocks passage of light into the eye (severe visual loss) and obstructs physiological aqueous flow from posterior to anterior chamber, leading to iris bombé and secondary angle-closure glaucoma.
*   **Treatment:** Nd:YAG laser membranectomy or surgical optical iridectomy / pupilloplasty.

note.title: Preservation Methods of Donor Cornea
note.content:
1.  *Short-Term Storage (24–48 hours):* Moist chamber method at $4^\circ\text{C}$ (whole globe storage).
2.  *Intermediate-Term Storage (4–14 days):* Corneoscleral rim stored in enriched liquid nutrient media at $4^\circ\text{C}$:
    *   **McCarey-Kaufman (MK) Medium:** TC-199 + Dextran (up to 4 days).
    *   **Optisol-GS / Cornisol:** Chondroitin sulfate + Dextran + Gentamicin/Streptomycin (up to 14 days; gold standard).
3.  *Long-Term Storage (Up to 30 days):* Organ culture method at $31–37^\circ\text{C}$.
4.  *Very Long-Term Storage (Years):* Cryopreservation at $-196^\circ\text{C}$ in liquid nitrogen.

note.title: Absolute Glaucoma
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Final, irreversible, painful terminal stage of untreated glaucoma (angle-closure or open-angle) resulting in total, permanent blindness (No Light Perception).
*   **Clinical Features:**
    *   Painful, irritable, stony-hard eye ($IOP > 50–70\text{ mm Hg}$).
    *   Circumcorneal perilimbal dark-reddish flush and dilated, tortuous anterior ciliary veins (**caput medusae**).
    *   Cornea is hazy, insensitive, with epithelial bullae (**bullous keratopathy**).
    *   Anterior chamber is very shallow or flat.
    *   Iris is atrophic with ectropion uveae and rubeosis iridis.
    *   Pupil is wide, fixed, non-reactive, showing a greenish-blue reflex.
    *   Deep, total glaucomatous optic atrophy (bean-pot cupping).
*   **Treatment:** Aims to relieve intractable pain:
    *   Retrobulbar alcohol injection (1–2 mL of 80% alcohol) to destroy the ciliary ganglion.
    *   Cyclocryotherapy / Cyclodiode photocoagulation to destroy ciliary processes.
    *   Enucleation or evisceration of the painful blind eye.

note.title: Membranous Conjunctivitis
note.content:
*   **Etiology:** Acute conjunctival infection characterized by a true fibrinous membrane firmly adherent to the palpebral conjunctiva; caused classical by **Corynebacterium diphtheriae** or virulent **Streptococcus pyogenes**.
*   **Pathology:** Coagulative necrosis of epithelium; dense fibrinous exudate deeply invades the substantia propria.
*   **Clinical Features:** Severe lid swelling with woody brawny induration, dirty-grey membrane covering palpebral conjunctiva; **peeling the membrane leaves a raw, actively bleeding surface** (distinguishing it from pseudomembrane).
*   **Treatment:** Isolation; systemic and topical anti-diphtheritic serum (ADS); topical and systemic Penicillin G; sweeping fornices with glass rod to prevent symblepharon.

---

note.title: Evisceration
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Surgical removal of all intraocular contents (uvea, retina, vitreous, lens) through a corneal/limbal incision, leaving behind the intact outer scleral shell, extraocular muscle insertions, and optic nerve.
*   **Indications:** Panophthalmitis (preferred over enucleation to avoid opening subarachnoid space and transmitting intracranial meningitis), anterior staphyloma, bleeding unsalvageable trauma.
*   **Contraindication:** Intraocular malignant tumors (Retinoblastoma, Choroidal Melanoma).

---

note.title: Band Keratopathy
note.content:
*   **Definition:** A degenerative corneal condition characterized by the horizontal, band-like deposition of calcium salts (**hydroxyapatite**) in the basement membrane of the epithelium, Bowman's layer, and anterior stroma.
*   **Causes:** Chronic uveitis (especially Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis in children), phthisis bulbi, absolute glaucoma, hypercalcemia (hyperparathyroidism, renal failure, sarcoidosis).
*   **Clinical Features:** Chalky-white, horizontal band traversing the interpalpebral cornea, separated from the limbus by a clear zone (lucid interval of Vogt); presents small Swiss-cheese clear holes where corneal nerves penetrate.
*   **Treatment:** **Chelation Therapy with EDTA (0.01–0.05 M disodium EDTA)** applied to denuded cornea after mechanical debridement of epithelium; or Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK) using excimer laser.

---

Answer the following: /uni25CF What is the probable diagnosis. /uni25CF Describe the clinical features /uni25CF What are the investigations you order. /uni25CF How do you treat the patient /uni25CF Enumerate the complications (1+3+2+2+2=10)

note.title: Case of Acute Orbital Cellulitis
note.content:
#### a) Probable Diagnosis
**Acute Right Orbital Cellulitis** (secondary to ethmoidal/paranasal sinusitis).

#### b) Clinical Features
*   **REFER TO** `[[KUHS-QUESTION:301001:Q11]]` (Paper 1): High fever, severe retrobulbar pain, brawny lid edema, chemosis, axial proptosis, global painful limitation of ocular movements (ophthalmoplegia), and RAPD with visual loss.

#### c) Investigations
1.  *Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT) of Orbit, PNS, and Brain:* Diagnostic modality of choice; evaluates subperiosteal abscess, ethmoid sinusitis, and rules out intracranial extension (cavernous sinus thrombosis, brain abscess).
2.  *Microbiological Tests:* Blood cultures, nasal swab, and conjunctival discharge cultures.
3.  *Complete Blood Count (CBC):* Marked polymorphonuclear leukocytosis, elevated ESR and CRP.

#### d) Treatment
*   **Emergency Hospitalization & High-Dose IV Antibiotic Therapy:**
    *   IV **Ceftriaxone** (1–2 g daily) + IV **Vancomycin** (1 g BD) + IV **Metronidazole** (500 mg TDS) for 7–10 days, followed by oral antibiotics for another 2 weeks.
*   *Supportive Therapy:* Oral analgesics/antipyretics, topical nasal decongestant drops (Oxymetazoline) to facilitate sinus drainage, ocular lubricant ointments.
*   *Surgical Drainage:* Indicated for localized subperiosteal or orbital abscess, foreign body, or progressive optic neuropathy non-responsive to 48 hours of IV antibiotics.

#### e) Complications
1.  *Ocular:* Exposure keratopathy, central retinal artery occlusion, optic neuritis/atrophy.
2.  *Orbital:* Subperiosteal abscess, orbital abscess.
3.  *Intracranial (Life-threatening):* **Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (CST)**, meningitis, epidural/subdural abscess, temporal/frontal lobe brain abscess.

note.title: Latanoprost
note.content:
*   **Class:** Synthetic prostaglandin $F_{2\alpha}$ isopropyl ester analogue.
*   **Mechanism of Action:** Highly selective FP receptor agonist that lowers IOP by remodeling the extracellular matrix within the ciliary muscle, thereby significantly **increasing uveoscleral outflow**.

*   **Ocular Adverse Effects:** Irreversible hyperpigmentation of the iris (increased melanin content in melanocytes), hypertrichosis (hypertrophy, thickening, and darkening of eyelashes), conjunctival hyperemia, punctate keratopathy, reactivation of herpes simplex keratitis, and cystoid macular edema (in aphakic/pseudophakic patients).

questions.officialText: 60 years old female patient with type II diabeti c mellitus since 12 years, presents to OPD with complaining of sudden painless loss of vision in one eye. Answer the following: ● What is your more probable diagnosis ● What are the differential diagnosis ● What are the clinical features of the condition ● How will you confirm the diagnosis ● How will you manage the case. (1+2+2+2+3=10)

note.title: Case of Sudden Painless Visual Loss in a Diabetic Patient
note.content:
#### a) Most Probable Diagnosis
**Right Eye Massive Vitreous Hemorrhage secondary to Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR)** (or Central Retinal Vein Occlusion).

#### b) Differential Diagnosis
1.  *Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO)* (ischemic type).
2.  *Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment involving Macula*.
3.  *Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)*.
4.  *Non-Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (NAION)*.

#### c) Clinical Features
*   *Symptoms:* Sudden, painless, profound drop in vision; perception of dark black floaters, red haze, or complete obscuration of vision.
*   *Signs:*
    *   Distant direct ophthalmoscopy: Loss of normal orange-red fundal reflex (absent red glow or black shadow).
    *   Slit-lamp biomicroscopy: Blood cells, clots, and debris floating in the anterior/mid vitreous cavity.
    *   Direct/Indirect ophthalmoscopy: Retinal details obscured by dense dark-red intra-vitreal collection.
    *   Fellow Eye: Demonstrates features of PDR (NVD, NVE, microaneurysms, hemorrhages, hard exudates).

#### d) Confirmation of Diagnosis
1.  **B-Scan Ultrasonography (Essential):** Evaluates vitreous cavity through opaque media; demonstrates mobile, point-like, low-to-medium amplitude internal acoustic echoes (vitreous hemorrhage) and rules out underlying tractional/rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
2.  **Blood Glucose Profiling:** Fasting, post-prandial blood sugar, and HbA1c.

#### e) Management Plan
*   *Conservative Management (Initial 4–12 Weeks):*
    *   Bed rest with head elevation (propped-up position at 45°) to facilitate gravitational settling of blood into the inferior fundus.
    *   Strict glycemic control and avoidance of strenuous physical exertion/heavy lifting.
    *   Serial B-scan ultrasonography every 2–4 weeks to monitor for tractional retinal detachment.
*   *Laser Photocoagulation:* Once the hemorrhage clears sufficiently to visualize the retina, perform urgent **Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP)** to induce regression of neovascularization.
*   *Intravitreal Anti-VEGF Agents:* Injection of **Bevacizumab (1.25 mg)** or **Ranibizumab (0.5 mg)** to accelerate hemorrhage clearance and cause rapid neovascular involution.
*   *Surgical Intervention:* **Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV):**
    *   *Indications:* Non-clearing dense vitreous hemorrhage persisting $>1–3\text{ months}$, associated tractional retinal detachment involving or threatening the macula, or ghost cell glaucoma.
    *   *Procedure:* 3-port PPV, core vitrectomy, membrane peeling, endolaser PRP, and fluid-gas/silicone oil exchange.

---

note.title: Hyphaema
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Presence of free blood within the anterior chamber of the eye.
*   **Causes:** Blunt contusion trauma (rupture of iris/ciliary body vessels at angle - commonest), intraoperative trauma, neovascularization (rubeosis iridis), intraocular tumors (juvenile xanthogranuloma, retinoblastoma).
*   **Grading:** Microhyphaema (suspended RBCs only), Grade I ($<1/3$ AC), Grade II ($1/3–1/2$ AC), Grade III ($>1/2$ AC), Grade IV (total/black-ball/eight-ball hyphaema).
*   **Complications:** Secondary glaucoma (trabecular clogging), **blood staining of the cornea** (due to hemosiderin imbibition across endothelium under high IOP), secondary re-bleeding (typically at 3–5 days).
*   **Management:** Bed rest with head elevation (30°–45°), eye shield, topical cycloplegics (Atropine 1%), topical corticosteroids, oral Tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic); surgical paracentesis/AC washout indicated if IOP $>35\text{ mm Hg}$ for 7 days or at early signs of corneal blood staining.

note.title: Case of Phacomorphic Glaucoma
note.content:
#### a) Most Probable Diagnosis
**Right Eye Phacomorphic Glaucoma (Secondary Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma induced by an Intumescent Senile Cataract).**
*Clinical scenario:* 60-year-old with acute eye pain, redness, hemicranial headache, pre-existing gradual visual loss for 6 months, and prior cataract surgery in the fellow eye.

#### b) Differential Diagnosis
1.  *Acute Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (PACG):* Fellow eye shows an occludable shallow angle (in phacomorphic glaucoma, the fellow eye is pseudophakic or has a normal open angle).
2.  *Phacolytic Glaucoma:* Lens is hypermature/Morgagnian with a deep anterior chamber and inflammatory pseudohypopyon.
3.  *Acute Anterior Uveitis (Hypertensive):* Keratic precipitates, miosed irregular pupil, posterior synechiae.
4.  *Neovascular Glaucoma:* Rubeosis iridis present; history of CRVO or PDR.

#### c) Clinical Features
*   **Symptoms:** Severe unilateral ocular pain radiating along the trigeminal distribution, hemicranial headache, nausea, vomiting, marked photophobia, lacrimation, and sudden drop in vision.
*   **Signs:**
    *   Lids: Edema and blepharospasm.
    *   Conjunctiva: Intense mixed ciliary and conjunctival congestion.
    *   Cornea: Steamy, hazy epithelial microcystic edema.
    *   Anterior Chamber: Very shallow anterior chamber due to forward displacement of the iris by the swollen lens.
    *   Pupil: Vertically oval, mid-dilated, fixed, unreactive to light.
    *   Lens: Swollen, opacified, milky-white intumescent cataract with visible water clefts pushing forward.
    *   Intraocular Pressure: Severely elevated (typically **40–70 mm Hg**; stony hard on palpation).

#### d) Confirmation of Diagnosis
1.  *Slit-Lamp Examination:* Demonstrates intumescent swollen cataractous lens causing mechanical axial shallowing of the anterior chamber.
2.  *Gonioscopy (of Fellow Eye & Affected Eye once cleared):* Affected eye shows complete $360^\circ$ appositional angle closure; fellow eye confirms pseudophakia or normal depth.
3.  *Applanation Tonometry:* Confirms acute high ocular tension.
4.  *B-Scan Ultrasonography:* Rules out posterior segment pathology (mass lesion, retinal detachment) behind the opaque lens.

#### e) Management Plan
*   **Phase 1: Emergency Medical Lowering of IOP:**
    *   **IV Mannitol 20%:** $1.5–2.0\text{ g/kg}$ IV over 30 minutes to dehydrate the vitreous.
    *   **IV Acetazolamide:** 500 mg stat, followed by 250 mg orally TDS.
    *   **Topical Beta-Blocker:** Timolol maleate 0.5% BD.
    *   **Topical Alpha-2 Agonist:** Brimonidine 0.2% BD.
    *   **Topical Corticosteroid:** Prednisolone acetate 1% QID to control secondary iridocyclitis.
    *   *(Avoid Pilocarpine initially, as it increases pupillary block and shifts the lens anteriorly).*
*   **Phase 2: Definitive Surgical Treatment:**
    *   **Cataract Extraction with Posterior Chamber IOL (PCIOL) Implantation:**
        *   Performed once IOP is normalized and the cornea is clear.
        *   *Surgical technique:* Manual SICS or Phacoemulsification.
        *   *Capsular decompression:* Anterior capsule is punctured with a fine 26G needle to aspirate liquefied cortex, releasing intralenticular pressure and preventing uncontrolled capsular tear ("Argentinean flag sign"). Followed by continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis (CCC), nuclear delivery, and in-the-bag PCIOL placement.

---

note.title: IOL Power Calculation
note.content:
*   **Principle:** Determining the precise dioptric power of an artificial intraocular lens to achieve the desired postoperative refractive target (usually emmetropia).
*   **Parameters Measured (Biometry):**
    1.  *Corneal Curvature / Power ($K$):* Measured by manual or automated **Keratometry** in horizontal ($K_1$) and vertical ($K_2$) meridia (average corneal power $\approx +43\text{ to }+44\text{ D}$).
    2.  *Axial Length ($L$):* Measured from anterior corneal vertex to foveal internal limiting membrane using **A-Scan Ultrasound** (immersion/applanation) or optical biometry (**IOLMaster / Lenstar** based on partial coherence interferometry). Normal $\approx 22–24\text{ mm}$.
    3.  *Anterior Chamber Depth (ACD):* Important for newer third- and fourth-generation formulas.
*   **Formulas:**
    *   **SRK-I Regression Formula:**
        $$\mathbf{P = A - 2.5(L) - 0.9(K)}$$
        *(where $P = \text{IOL Power in Dioptres}$, $A = \text{Manufacturer-specific A-constant}$ [typically 118.0–118.5 for PCIOL], $L = \text{Axial Length in mm}$, $K = \text{Average Keratometric power in Dioptres}$).*
    *   **SRK-II Formula:** Adjusts A-constant based on axial length ($A$ increased if $L < 22\text{ mm}$, decreased if $L > 24.5\text{ mm}$).
    *   **Modern Theoretical Formulas:**
        *   *SRK/T, Holladay-1, Hoffer-Q:* Standard for normal-to-long eyes.
        *   *Hoffer-Q:* Most accurate for short eyes ($L < 22\text{ mm}$).
        *   *Barrett Universal II, Olsen, Haigis:* Fourth/fifth-generation formulas predicting Effective Lens Position (ELP) with high refractive accuracy.

---

note.title: Legal Blindness
note.content:
*   **Definition:** Statutory definition established for legal, administrative, and compensatory entitlements (disability pensions, tax exemptions, vocational rehabilitation).
*   **Criteria:**
    *   *Western / USA Standard:* Best-corrected visual acuity of **$\le 20/200$ ($6/60$)** in the better eye, or a visual field constricted to **$\le 20^\circ$** around central fixation.
    *   *Indian Statutory Standard (Aligned with WHO 2017):* Best-corrected visual acuity of **$<3/60$** in the better eye or visual field constricted to **$<10^\circ$** around fixation [5].
