note.title: Treatment of Atrophic Rhinitis
note.content:
Atrophic rhinitis (ozaena) is a chronic debilitating inflammatory disorder characterized by progressive atrophy of the nasal mucosa, seromucinous glands, and turbinate bones, with prominent foul-smelling green crusting [172–173].

#### A. Medical Management (Symptomatic Relief and Hygiene) [173]
1. **Nasal Douche / Alkaline Irrigations**:
   * Washing the nasal cavity 2–3 times daily with a warm alkaline solution:
     * Sodium bicarbonate (1 part) — liquefies tenacious mucus.
     * Sodium biborate/borax (1 part) — antiseptic.
     * Sodium chloride (2 parts) — maintains physiological tonicity [173].
   * Loosens and evacuates dry crusts, reduces putrefaction, and eliminates foul odor [173].
2. **25% Glucose in Glycerine**:
   * Instilled into the nasal cavities following alkaline douching; inhibits the growth of proteolytic organisms (*Klebsiella ozaenae*) responsible for the characteristic foetor [173].
3. **Local Antibiotic Applications**:
   * Kemicetine™ solution (chloramphenicol, estradiol, and vitamin D2) or topical rifampicin drops to control secondary bacterial colonization [173].
4. **Systemic Antibiotics**:
   * Streptomycin (1 g/day IM for 10 days) or ciprofloxacin to eradicate *Klebsiella ozaenae* [173].
5. **Systemic Vasodilators & Vitamins**:
   * Vitamin A and D; oral potassium iodide to stimulate seromucinous secretions [173].

#### B. Surgical Management [173]
```
                    SURGICAL PROCEDURES IN ATROPHIC RHINITIS
                                       |
         +-----------------------------+-----------------------------+
         |                                                           |
CLOSURE OF NARES                                            NARROWING OF NASAL CAVITY
• Young’s Operation (Total bilateral)                       • Submucosal injection of Teflon
• Modified Young’s (Partial closure)                        • Submucoperichondrial implants
  (Provides rest, reduces drying currents)                    (Cartilage, bone, silastic)
                                                            • Medialization of lateral nasal wall
```

1. **Young’s Operation**: Complete bilateral surgical closure of the anterior nares using circular vestibulocutaneous flaps; reopened after 6 to 12 months; restores normal mucosal architecture and decreases crusting [173].
2. **Modified Young’s Operation**: Partial closure of the anterior nares, creating a narrow central aperture to maintain some nasal respiration while eliminating drying air currents [173].
3. **Operations to Narrow the Roomy Nasal Cavity**:
   * Submucosal implantation of autologous cartilage, bone, acrylic chips, or silastic along the nasal floor and septum to reduce air currents [173].
   * Medial displacement of the lateral nasal wall (Lautenschlager’s operation) [173].

---

questions.officialText: Hearing evaluation of a deaf child.

note.title: Hearing Evaluation of a Deaf Child
note.content:
Hearing evaluation in pediatric age groups requires subjective and objective diagnostic modalities tailored to developmental age [132–133].

```
                     PEDIATRIC AUDIOLOGICAL TESTING
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                         |                         |
ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL             BEHAVIORAL TESTS          CONDITIONED RESPONSE
(Birth onwards / Objective)      (0 to 6 months)           (6 months to 5 years)
• OAE (Outer hair cells)         • Moro's reflex           • Visual Reinforcement
• ABR / BERA (Nerve/Stem)        • Cochleopalpebral reflex   Audiometry (6m–2y)
• ASSR (>80 dB threshold)        • Cessation reflex        • Play Audiometry (2–5y)
• Impedance Audiometry                                     • Speech Audiometry
```

1. **Universal Newborn & Infant Screening (0 to 6 Months)** [132]:
   * **Otoacoustic Emissions (OAEs - TEOAE & DPOAE)**: Non-invasive, rapid assessment of cochlear outer hair cell integrity; absent in cochlear hearing loss >30 dB [29–30, 132].
   * **Automated Auditory Brainstem Response (AABR)**: Tests neural synchronization from CN VIII to the brainstem; passed if Wave V is identified at 35 dB nHL [29, 132].
2. **Objective Electrophysiological Tests (Any Age)** [133]:
   * **Diagnostic Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR / BERA)**: Identifies absolute latencies, Wave I-V interpeak latencies, and electrophysiological thresholds (clicks: 1–4 kHz, tone bursts: frequency-specific) [29, 133].
   * **Auditory Steady-State Response (ASSR)**: Quantifies frequency-specific hearing thresholds in severe-to-profound deafness (>80 dB loss) where ABR reaches limits [29].
   * **Impedance Audiometry & Acoustic Reflex**: Evaluates middle ear status (Type B indicates otitis media with effusion) [26–27, 133].
3. **Behavioral Observation Audiometry (BOA - Infants <6 Months)** [132]:
   * Observes unconditioned physiological responses to calibrated auditory stimuli (e.g., sound intensity 70–90 dB):
     * *Moro’s Reflex*: Sudden generalized startle response, limb extension, and crying [132].
     * *Cochleopalpebral Reflex*: Blinking of eyes in response to sudden loud sound [132].
     * *Cessation Reflex*: Sudden stopping of suckling or crying activity [132].
4. **Visual Reinforcement Audiometry (VRA - Age 6 Months to 2 Years)** [132]:
   * Child is conditioned to turn their head toward a sound source, reinforced by an illuminated animated mechanical toy or video screen [132].
5. **Play Audiometry (Age 2 to 5 Years)** [132]:
   * Child performs a playful motor task (dropping a marble into a box, putting rings on a peg) in response to pure tones delivered via headphones [132].

---

note.title: Discuss Treatment of Otogenic Facial Palsy
note.content:
Otogenic facial paralysis arises as an intratemporal complication of acute or chronic middle ear infections [88, 103t].

#### A. Facial Palsy Secondary to Acute Otitis Media (AOM) [88]
* **Pathophysiology**: Infection spreads through a pre-existing congenital dehiscence in the tympanic segment of the fallopian canal, producing inflammatory epineural edema and conduction block (neurapraxia) [88, 100].
* **Management**:
  1. **Immediate Wide Myringotomy**: Under local or general anesthesia; relieves pus under tension, drains the middle ear, and decompresses the nerve [68, 88]. Send aspirate for culture and sensitivity [88].
  2. **Intravenous Antibiotics**: Broad-spectrum agents (Ceftriaxone / Co-amoxiclav) continued for 10–14 days [68, 88].
  3. **Systemic Corticosteroids**: Oral Prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) to rapidly relieve intraneural edema [104].
  4. **Cortical Mastoidectomy**: Indicated if acute coalescent mastoiditis is present or if medical therapy fails after 48 hours [86, 88]. Bony canal is not decompressed unless directly traumatized [88].

#### B. Facial Palsy Secondary to Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) [88]
* **Pathophysiology**: Direct bone erosion and osteitis induced by **cholesteatoma** or invasive granulation tissue compressing the nerve [74, 88].
* **Management**:
  1. **Emergency Mastoid Exploration (Within 24 Hours)** [88]:
     * Perform a Canal Wall Down (Modified Radical / Radical) Mastoidectomy to eradicate the underlying cholesteatoma and granulation tissue [80, 88].
  2. **Facial Canal Decompression**:
     * Inspect the entire horizontal and vertical segments of the fallopian canal [88].
     * Clear cholesteatoma and granulations surrounding the sheath [88].
     * If granulation tissue penetrates the nerve sheath, do not avulse it [88]. Carefully uncap the bony canal 5 mm proximal and distal to the involved site to decompress the perineural tissue [88].
  3. **Nerve Repair (in cases of complete transection or loss of continuity)**:
     * End-to-end anastomosis or **cable nerve graft** (greater auricular nerve or sural nerve) if a segment of the nerve has been destroyed [108–109].
  4. **Adjunctive Therapy**: Broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics, eye protection, and electrical muscle stimulation/physiotherapy during rehabilitation [104, 108].

---

```
(CONE OF LIGHT at 7 o'clock)\                /

```

#### Key Anatomical Landmarks of the Left Eardrum [3, 4f]:
1. **Pars Tensa**: Forms the major vibrating lower portion of the drum [3].
2. **Pars Flaccida (Shrapnell’s Membrane)**: Upper triangular portion located in the notch of Rivinus [3].
3. **Lateral Process of Malleus**: Conspicuous, knob-like projection pointing toward the anterosuperior quadrant [3, 4f].
4. **Handle of Malleus**: Angled downward and backward, ending at the **umbo** [3, 4f].
5. **Cone of Light**: Radiates anteroinferiorly from the umbo toward the periphery at the **7 o'clock position** in the left ear (contrasted with 5 o'clock in the right ear) [3, 4f, 58f].
6. **Anterior and Posterior Malleal Folds**: Arching from the lateral process to the periphery [3, 4f].
7. **Annulus Tympanicus**: The outer fibrocartilaginous ring [3].

note.title: Diagram of Waldeyer’s Ring (Draw and Label)
note.content:
Waldeyer’s lymphatic ring is an interrupted annular arrangement of lymphoid tissue surrounding the confluence of the aerodigestive tracts [269, 270f].

```
                          WALDEYER'S LYMPHATIC RING
                                     
                           [ NASOPHARYNGEAL TONSIL ]
                                  (Adenoids)
                                      |
                      +---------------+---------------+
                      |                               |
             [ TUBAL TONSILS ]                [ TUBAL TONSILS ]
             (Eustachian tube)                (Eustachian tube)
                      |                               |
          [ LATERAL PHARYNGEAL ]            [ LATERAL PHARYNGEAL ]
                 BANDS                             BANDS
                      |                               |
           [ PALATINE TONSILS ]              [ PALATINE TONSILS ]
            (Faucial Tonsils)                 (Faucial Tonsils)
                      |                               |
                      +---------------+---------------+
                                      |
                           [ LINGUAL TONSILS ]
                            (Base of Tongue)
```

#### Components of the Ring [269, 270f]:
1. **Superior / Posterosuperior**: **Nasopharyngeal tonsil (Adenoids)** at the junction of the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx [269, 275].
2. **Lateral**:
   * **Tubal tonsils** (in the fossa of Rosenmüller surrounding the pharyngeal opening of the eustachian tube) [269, 271].
   * **Lateral pharyngeal bands** running down behind the posterior faucial pillars [269, 272f].
   * **Palatine (faucial) tonsils** situated bilaterally between the anterior and posterior pillars in the oropharynx [269, 271, 291].
3. **Inferior**: **Lingual tonsils** located subepithelially over the posterior one-third (base) of the tongue [269, 271].
4. **Posterior Wall**: Scattered subepithelial solitary **lymphoid follicles** on the posterior pharyngeal wall [269].

*Reference Link*: [Waldeyer's Tonsillar Ring](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Waldeyer%27s_Tonsillar_Ring.png)

note.title: Radical Mastoidectomy
note.content:
* **Definition**: A destructive, non-reconstructive surgical procedure that converts the mastoid air cells, tympanic antrum, aditus, epitympanum (attic), and mesotympanum into a single, exteriorized, smooth, common cavity widely open to the external auditory canal [459, 459f].
* **Indications** [459]:
  1. Extensive cholesteatoma invading the eustachian tube, perilabyrinthine cells, or hypotympanum where complete removal via reconstructive techniques is impossible.
  2. Carcinoma of the middle ear and mastoid (often as an approach preceding full-course radiotherapy).
  3. Unresponsive, complicated chronic ear disease in an only hearing ear or deaf ear.
  4. Surgical approach to the petrous apex.
* **Key Steps** [459]:
  1. Postaural or endaural approach; complete cortical exenteration [459].
  2. Removal of the "bridge" (posterior superior canal wall) and anterior/posterior buttresses, exteriorizing the attic and antrum [459].
  3. Lowering of the facial ridge down to the level of the vertical segment of the facial nerve [459].
  4. Radical toilet of the middle ear: Complete excision of all remnants of the tympanic membrane, annulus, malleus, incus, mucoperiosteum, and granulations (stapes footplate is left undisturbed) [459].
  5. Permanent obliteration/occlusion of the eustachian tube orifice using tensor tympani muscle, bone chips, or cartilage [459].
  6. Wide conchomeatoplasty to provide inspection and self-cleaning [459].

---

note.title: Fistula Test
note.content:
* **Principle**: Inducing pressure alterations in the external auditory canal and middle ear that transmit directly through an abnormal bony defect (fistula) in the otic capsule to stimulate the underlying vestibular labyrinth, evoking transient vertigo and nystagmus [43, 88].
* **Method**: Intermittent positive and negative pressure is applied to the external canal by pumping air using a Siegle’s pneumatic speculum or by intermittent inward tragal pressure [43, 88].
* **Interpretation**:
  * **Positive Fistula Test**:
    * Positive pressure induces nystagmus with its fast component toward the diseased ear (ampullopetal endolymph deflection) accompanied by vertigo [43, 88].
    * Negative pressure reverses endolymph flow (ampullofugal), producing nystagmus with its fast component toward the healthy contralateral ear [43, 88].
    * *Significance*: Indicates an erosion/fistula of the bony labyrinth, most commonly the horizontal (lateral) semicircular canal, caused by cholesteatoma or previous fenestration surgery, and confirms a **viable/functioning labyrinth** [43, 88].
  * **False Negative Test**: Can occur if cholesteatoma matrix or granulation tissue tightly seals the defect, preventing pressure transmission, or if the labyrinth is dead (non-functional) [43].
  * **False Positive Test (Hennebert’s Sign)**: Positive test with an intact eardrum; seen in congenital syphilis (hypermobile stapes footplate) and Ménière's disease (fibrous band between stapes and saccule) [43, 508].

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Pre malignant conditions of oral cavity

note.title: Premalignant Conditions of the Oral Cavity
note.content:
Premalignant lesions or conditions represent altered tissue morphology that carries a statistically higher risk of transforming into invasive squamous cell carcinoma [253–254].

1. **Leukoplakia**:
   * A predominantly white lesion/plaque of the oral mucosa that cannot be clinically or pathologically characterized as any other definitive disease [253].
   * Subtypes: Homogeneous (low risk) and Non-homogeneous (speckled/erythroleukoplakia, nodular, verrucous; high malignant potential up to 15–20%) [253].
2. **Erythroplakia**:
   * A fiery red patch or plaque that cannot be clinically or pathologically attributed to any other condition [253].
   * Highest malignant transformation rate (>85–90% show severe dysplasia, carcinoma-in-situ, or frank invasive carcinoma at presentation) [253–254].
3. **Oral Submucous Fibrosis (OSF)**:
   * Chronic, progressive disorder linked to areca nut/betel quid chewing; marked by subepithelial fibroelastic bands and epithelial atrophy, resulting in severe trismus; malignant transformation rate of 3–7.6% [248–249].
4. **Lichen Planus (Erosive / Atrophic Type)**:
   * Chronic cell-mediated mucocutaneous disorder; erosive and atrophic forms carry a 0.5–2% risk of malignant transformation [247].
5. **Syphilitic Glossitis (Tertiary Atrophic Syphilis)**:
   * Chronic interstitial glossitis predisposing to dorsal tongue carcinoma [254, 255].
6. **Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Brown-Kelly) Syndrome**:
   * Microcytic hypochromic anemia with mucosal atrophy and esophageal webs; associated with oral and postcricoid malignancies [254, 388].

---

note.title: Rhinolalia Clausa (Hyponasality)
note.content:
* **Definition**: A speech resonance disorder characterized by the lack of normal nasal resonance for nasal consonant sounds (M, N, and NG) during phonation [158, 357].
* **Speech Characteristics**: The nasal consonants are converted into their non-nasal, oral plosive counterparts:
  * **/M/** is replaced by **/B/** (e.g., "Mother" sounds like "Bother") [158].
  * **/N/** is replaced by **/D/** [158].
  * **/NG/** is replaced by **/G/** [158].
* **Etiology (Upper Airway Obstruction)** [357, 357t]:
  1. *Nasal Cavity*: Large bilateral nasal polyposis, severe deviated nasal septum, hypertrophic inferior turbinates, acute coryza, allergic/vasomotor rhinosinusitis [357t].
  2. *Nasopharynx*: Adenoid hypertrophy in children, juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, antrochoanal polyp, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, bilateral choanal atresia [275, 357t].

---

note.title: Weber’s Test
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q13]]` (under 2021_MAY) for method and detailed interpretation [24].

* **Core Summary**: Bone conduction test using a 512 Hz tuning fork on the midline of the skull. Lateralizes to the poorer ear in conductive deafness and to the better ear in sensorineural deafness [24, 24t].

---

note.title: Boundaries of Pyriform Fossa
note.content:
The pyriform sinus (fossa) is an inverted pyramidal recess of the hypopharynx situated on either side of the laryngeal inlet [272]:

```
                       PYRIFORM FOSSA BOUNDARIES
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                                                   |
    MEDIAL WALL                                         LATERAL WALL
• Aryepiglottic fold                             • Thyroid cartilage lamina
• Arytenoid cartilage                            • Thyrohyoid membrane
• Cricoid lamina (posteromedial)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
• SUPERIOR / ANTERIOR BOUNDARY: Pharyngoepiglottic fold
• INFERIOR APEX: Blends into the postcricoid hypopharynx / cricopharynx
```

* **Important Relations**: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve courses submucosally along its lateral wall (site for local topical anesthesia block and pathway for referred otalgia to the ear via Arnold's nerve) [143, 272].

---

note.title: Little’s Area
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q07]]` (under 2021_MAY) for anastomosing arterial architecture and labelled diagram [197, 198f].

* **Definition**: Area in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum just above the vestibule where Kiesselbach's plexus is formed by the anastomosis of 4 arteries: anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine, and superior labial (septal branch) [197, 198f]. It is the most common site of anterior epistaxis (90%) [197, 510].

---

note.title: Treacher Collins Syndrome (Mandibulofacial Dysostosis)
note.content:
* **Genetics**: Autosomal dominant inheritance with high penetrance and variable expressivity; mapped to mutations in the *TCOF1* gene (affecting 1st and 2nd branchial arch development) [130t].
* **Classical Phenotypic Features** [130t]:
  1. Antimongoloid (downward-slanting) palpebral fissures with coloboma of the outer third of the lower eyelids [130t].
  2. Malar and mandibular hypoplasia (micrognathia, retrognathia) resulting in a bird-like facies [130t].
  3. External ear malformations: Microtia, anotia, or atresia of the external auditory canal [130t].
  4. Middle ear abnormalities: Malformed, hypoplastic, or fused malleus and incus (stapes is usually spared), leading to bilateral congenital **conductive hearing loss** [130t].

---

note.title: Boundaries of Macewen’s Triangle (Suprameatal Triangle)
note.content:
Macewen’s triangle is a surgical surface landmark on the outer cortical surface of the mastoid bone, guiding the surgeon directly to the underlying **mastoid antrum** (which lies 12–15 mm deep to it in adults) [7, 7f, 457, 509]:

```
                     MACEWEN'S SUPRAMEATAL TRIANGLE
                                   
                    TEMPORAL LINE / SUPRAMASTOID CREST
                   ==================================== (Superior Border)
                                  /  \
                                 /    \
                                /      \
    TANGENT TO POSTERIOR       /        \   POSTEROSUPERIOR MARGIN
    CANAL WALL                /          \  OF EXTERNAL AUDITORY MEATUS
    (Posterior Border)       /            \ (Anterior Border)
                            +--------------+
                             SPINE OF HENLE
```

1. **Superior Boundary**: The supramastoid crest (posterior horizontal continuation of the temporal line of the zygomatic process) [7, 7f].
2. **Antero-inferior Boundary**: The posterosuperior margin of the bony external acoustic meatus (marked by the suprameatal spine of Henle) [7, 7f].
3. **Posterior Boundary**: A vertical line drawn tangential to the midpoint of the posterior curve of the external auditory meatus [7, 7f].

---

questions.officialText: Mention a bout the differential diagnosis of sudden onset stridor and discuss about the investigations & management. (4+3+3)

note.title: Differential Diagnosis, Investigations, and Management of Sudden-Onset Stridor
note.content:
#### A. Differential Diagnosis of Sudden-Onset Stridor
Sudden-onset stridor is an emergency caused by rapid mechanical occlusion of the larynx, trachea, or primary bronchi [333].

1. **Inhaled Foreign Body (Most Common in Toddlers/Children)**:
   * Foreign body lodged in the laryngeal inlet, glottis, or cervical trachea (e.g., peanuts, seeds, small plastic toy parts) [334t, 365].
2. **Acute Severe Infections (Rapid Inflammatory Edema)**:
   * **Acute Epiglottitis**: *Haemophilus influenzae* type B infection producing rapid supraglottic swelling [327, 328t].
   * **Acute Laryngotracheobronchitis (Viral Croup)**: Subglottic edema [328, 328t].
   * **Laryngeal Diphtheria**: Tough obstructive pseudomembrane [328–329, 334t].
   * **Retropharyngeal / Parapharyngeal Abscess**: Rapid enlargement compressing the airway [299–301, 334t].
3. **Trauma and Physical/Chemical Inhalation**:
   * Blunt or penetrating external laryngotracheal trauma with fracture, mucosal tear, and expanding hematoma [325, 334t].
   * Thermal burn (inhalation of steam or superheated gases) or chemical inhalation burns [327, 329].
4. **Allergic / Anaphylactic & Angioneurotic Edema**:
   * Severe Type I hypersensitivity reactions, ACE-inhibitor-induced angioedema, or hereditary C1-esterase deficiency causing rapid transudation into the supraglottic loose tissues [329, 507].
5. **Neurogenic**:
   * Acute bilateral abductor vocal cord paralysis (e.g., following thyroid surgery, bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve damage) [338, 340].
6. **Laryngospasm**:
   * Post-extubation laryngospasm, hypocalcemic tetany, or tetanus [334t].

---

#### B. Investigations in Sudden-Onset Stridor
* **Clinical Caution**: In impending respiratory failure, avoid invasive or distressing examinations (e.g., forceful tongue depression) as they may trigger complete obstruction and cardiac arrest [327].

1. **Radiological Studies (Performed only when the patient is stable)**:
   * **X-Ray Soft Tissue Neck (Lateral View, in Extension)**:
     * Epiglottic enlargement: Classical **"Thumb sign"** in acute epiglottitis [327, 328t].
     * Prevertebral soft tissue widening (>7 mm at C2; >14–22 mm at C6) or gas in retropharyngeal abscess [502f].
     * Radio-opaque foreign bodies in the laryngeal/tracheal lumen [366, 499f].
   * **X-Ray Neck and Chest (Anteroposterior View)**:
     * Subglottic tapering: Classical **"Steeple sign"** (inverted V) in laryngotracheobronchitis [328t].
     * Foreign bodies in the bronchial tree [366, 501f].
     * Inspiratory/expiratory films: Demonstrates unilateral obstructive emphysema (mediastinal shift) or atelectasis [366, 501f].
2. **Pulse Oximetry and Arterial Blood Gas (ABG)**:
   * Continuous monitoring of oxygen saturation (SpO2); ABG reveals hypoxemia (low PaO2), hypercapnia (rising PaCO2), and respiratory acidosis denoting respiratory failure [314, 362].
3. **Flexible Fiberoptic Laryngoscopy**:
   * Conducted with resuscitation equipment ready; provides direct visualization of the supraglottis, cords, webs, edema, or impacted foreign bodies [335, 438].
4. **Diagnostic Endoscopy under General Anesthesia (Direct Laryngoscopy & Bronchoscopy)**:
   * In a controlled operating room setting: Identifies and removes foreign bodies, defines strictures, and permits suctioning of crusts [335, 481, 483].

---

#### C. Management Protocol
```
                     MANAGEMENT OF SUDDEN STRIDOR
                                  |
         +------------------------+------------------------+
         |                                                 |
  AIRWAY EMERGENCIES                               CONSERVATIVE / MEDICAL
(Severe retractions, cyanosis)                     (Mild to moderate stridor)
• Awake Orotracheal Intubation                     • 100% Humidified Oxygen
• Cricothyrotomy (Immediate)                       • IV Dexamethasone / Hydrocortisone
• Emergency Tracheostomy (3rd/4th ring)            • Nebulized Racemic Epinephrine
• Endoscopic Foreign Body Removal                  • Specific IV Antibiotics
```

1. **Emergency Airway Stabilization (Highest Priority)** [359]:
   * Position patient upright; administer 100% humidified oxygen via face mask [328, 362].
   * Avoid sedatives.
   * If complete obstruction occurs:
     * Perform **Heimlich Maneuver** if choking on a foreign body is suspected [367, 367f].
     * **Endotracheal Intubation**: Rapid orotracheal intubation with a small-caliber tube or via awake flexible fiberoptic guidance [328, 363].
     * **Cricothyrotomy (Mini-Tracheostomy)**: Emergency transverse puncture through the cricothyroid membrane using a 12–14G cannula or scalpel to establish immediate oxygenation when intubation fails [363].
     * **Emergency Tracheostomy**: Vertical midline incision through the 2nd to 4th tracheal rings [360, 363].
2. **Medical Pharmacotherapy**:
   * **Parenteral Corticosteroids**: IV Dexamethasone (0.5 mg/kg) or Hydrocortisone (100 mg) to rapidly reduce laryngeal/subglottic inflammatory edema [326, 328].
   * **Nebulized Racemic Adrenaline (1:1000)**: Induces mucosal alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction, reducing subglottic swelling in croup [328].
   * **Parenteral Antibiotics**: High-dose 3rd-generation cephalosporins (Ceftriaxone 50–100 mg/kg/day) for acute epiglottitis and deep neck infections [328, 328t].
3. **Definitive Procedural Intervention**:
   * **Rigid Direct Laryngoscopy and Bronchoscopy**: Under general anesthesia in the operating room to extract foreign bodies using optical grasping forceps [367, 483].
   * Surgical drainage for deep neck space collections (retropharyngeal/parapharyngeal space abscess) [300, 303].

---

note.title: Allergic Fungal Sinusitis (AFS / AFRS)
note.content:
AFS is a non-invasive, IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction of the sinonasal mucosa against aerosolized environmental fungal antigens [194, 220].

```
                ALLERGIC FUNGAL RHINOSINUSITIS (AFRS)
                                 |
         +-----------------------+-----------------------+
         |                                               |
BENT-KUHN CRITERIA                              CT / MRI FINDINGS
• Type I hypersensitivity (Atopy)                • CT: Expansile hyperdense sinus
• Bilateral multiple nasal polyposis               mass with bone remodeling
• Characteristic eosinophilic mucin              • MRI: "Flow void-like" central
• Non-invasive fungal hyphae in mucin              signal void on T2 sequences
```

* **Bent-Kuhn Diagnostic Criteria (5 Cardinal Criteria)**:
  1. Documented Type I hypersensitivity (atopy confirmed by skin prick test or elevated serum specific IgE) [189].
  2. Bilateral diffuse nasal polyposis [194, 220].
  3. Characteristic CT findings: Heterogeneous expansile soft-tissue mass with central areas of high attenuation (hyperdensity) and bony remodeling/thinning [220, 504f].
  4. Presence of **eosinophilic mucin** (peanut-butter-like, thick, tenacious, sticky allergic mucin containing sloughed eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals) [220].
  5. Positive fungal stain (Grocott’s methenamine silver [GMS] or fungal culture) of the allergic mucin, with **absence of fungal tissue invasion** into the mucosa or bone [220, 220f].
* **Causative Fungi**: Dematiaceous fungi (*Bipolaris*, *Curvularia*, *Alternaria*) and *Aspergillus* species [220].
* **Management**:
  1. **Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS)**: Meticulous, complete evacuation of all polypoid tissues, complete exenteration of sinuses, and thorough clearance of all allergic fungal mucin while restoring wide aeration and drainage [196, 220].
  2. **Systemic Corticosteroids**: Oral Prednisolone (0.5–1 mg/kg/day) preoperatively to shrink polyps and continued postoperatively in a tapering schedule over several weeks to months to prevent relapse [219, 220].
  3. **Long-Term Topical Intranasal Corticosteroid Sprays**: Essential to prevent recurrence of mucosal hypersensitivity [219].
  4. **Antifungal Therapy**: Systemic antifungals are **not indicated** because the disease is non-invasive; post-surgical maintenance with fungal immunotherapy or topical nasal irrigations can be considered [220].

---

note.title: Internal Auditory Meatus (IAM)
note.content:
The internal auditory meatus is a bony canal situated within the petrous part of the temporal bone, running transversely from the posterior cranial fossa to the inner ear [99, 126f].

```
                 FUNDUS OF RIGHT INTERNAL AUDITORY MEATUS
                     (Transverse Crista Division)
                                      
                  ANTERIOR                          POSTERIOR
                    |                                   |
    SUPERIOR        |   FACIAL NERVE (VII)  :   SUPERIOR VESTIBULAR
                    |   (Fallopian aqueduct):       NERVE
                    |          [Bill's Bar separating]
    ----------------+-----------------------------------------------
                    |   TRANSVERSE CREST (Crista Falciformis)
                    |-----------------------------------------------
    INFERIOR        |   COCHLEAR NERVE      :   INFERIOR VESTIBULAR
                    |   (Tractus spiralis   :       NERVE
                    |     foraminosus)      : (Singular nerve post.)
```

* **Dimensions**: Approximately 1 cm long and 4–5 mm wide [99].
* **Fundus Anatomy (Lateral End)**:
  * Divided into an upper and lower half by a horizontal bony ridge called the **transverse crest (crista falciformis)** [126f].
  * The upper compartment is further partitioned into anterior and posterior segments by a vertical bony ridge called **Bill’s Bar** (surgical landmark) [126f].
* **Four Quadrants of the Fundus and Contents** [126f]:
  1. **Anterosuperior**: Transmits the **Facial Nerve (CN VII)** and Nervus Intermedius (Nerve of Wrisberg) [99, 126f].
  2. **Posterosuperior**: Transmits the **Superior Vestibular Nerve** (innervates utricle and superior & lateral semicircular ducts) [19, 126f].
  3. **Anteroinferior**: Transmits the **Cochlear Nerve** entering the tractus spiralis foraminosus to supply the organ of Corti [15, 126f].
  4. **Posteroinferior**: Transmits the **Inferior Vestibular Nerve** (innervates saccule) and the **Singular Nerve** (posterior ampullary nerve supplying the posterior semicircular duct) [19, 126f].
* **Vascular Contents**: Internal auditory (labyrinthine) artery and vein [12, 100].

---

note.title: Acoustic Neuroma (Vestibular Schwannoma)
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q04]]` (Chapter 18) for pathology and comprehensive staging [125–127].

* **Definition**: A benign, encapsulated, slow-growing tumor arising from the Schwann cell sheath of the **vestibular division of the 8th cranial nerve** (most commonly the inferior vestibular nerve) within the internal auditory meatus [125].
* **Clinical Features**:
  1. *Cochleovestibular (Earliest)*: Unilateral progressive sensorineural hearing loss, disproportionately poor **speech discrimination score (speech-tone disparity)**, high-pitched tinnitus, and vague unsteadiness [125, 126].
  2. *Trigeminal (CN V)*: Earliest non-auditory nerve affected; hypoesthesia of the cornea (depressed corneal reflex) and facial paresthesia [125].
  3. *Facial (CN VII)*: Sensory fibers involved first: **Hitzelberger’s sign** (hypoesthesia of the posterior-superior bony external meatal wall) [5, 125, 510].
  4. *Brainstem & Cerebellum*: Incoordination, intention tremors, dysdiadochokinesia, ataxia, and signs of raised intracranial pressure in large tumors (>4 cm) [125].
* **Diagnosis**:
  * **Contrast-Enhanced MRI (with Gadolinium)**: The **gold standard**; detects intrameatal tumors as small as 1–2 mm [126].
  * **Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA)**: Prolongation of Wave V latency or Interwave I–V latency delay >0.2 ms [29, 126].
  * **Caloric Test**: Reduced or absent response (canal paresis) in 95% of patients [45, 126].
* **Treatment**:
  * Surgical excision via **Translabyrinthine** (for non-serviceable hearing), **Retrosigmoid / Suboccipital**, or **Middle Cranial Fossa** approaches [127].
  * **Stereotactic Radiosurgery (Gamma Knife / CyberKnife)**: Preferred in elderly patients, tumors <3 cm, or medical comorbidities [127, 415].

---

note.title: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) and its Management
note.content:
BPPV is the most common cause of peripheral vestibular vertigo, characterized by brief episodes of rotational vertigo provoked by specific changes in head position relative to gravity [47].

* **Etiopathogenesis**:
  * **Canalithiasis Theory**: Otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) detach from the degenerating macula of the utricle and float freely in the endolymph of the **posterior semicircular canal** (most common canal involved) [47].
  * When the head tilts into the plane of the affected canal, the gravitational movement of this heavy otolith debris induces hydrodynamically abnormal ampullopetal/ampullofugal deflection of the cupula, triggering violent nystagmus and vertigo [19, 47].
* **Clinical Features**:
  * Paroxysms of sudden spinning vertigo lasting **less than 60 seconds**, provoked by rolling over in bed, looking upward, or bending forward [44t, 47].
  * No hearing loss, no tinnitus, and no other focal neurological deficits [47].
* **Diagnostic Test: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver** [44, 44f]:
  * Patient is rapidly brought from a seated position to a supine position with the head extended 30° below the horizontal plane and rotated 45° to the test side [44, 44f].
  * **Positive Findings (Diagnostic of Posterior Canal BPPV)** [44, 44t]:
    1. **Latency**: Vertigo and nystagmus appear after 2 to 20 seconds [44t].
    2. **Duration**: Brief paroxysm lasting <60 seconds [44t].
    3. **Direction of Nystagmus**: Torsional, geotropic nystagmus beating toward the undermost (affected) ear [44t].
    4. **Fatigability**: Repeated testing leads to progressive diminution and disappearance of the nystagmus and vertigo [44, 44t].
    5. **Reversibility**: On sitting upright, the direction of nystagmus reverses [44t].
* **Management**:
  1. **Particle Repositioning Maneuver (Epley’s Maneuver)**:
     * A sequential 5-position head maneuver that guides the free-floating otolith debris from the posterior canal back into the utricle under the influence of gravity [47, 48f]. Cures >80–90% of cases in a single session [47].
     * *Positions*:
       * Pos. 1: Dix-Hallpike position with the affected ear down [47, 48f].
       * Pos. 2: Head rotated 90° to the contralateral side [47, 48f].
       * Pos. 3: Body and head rolled another 90° onto the healthy shoulder (facing downward) [47, 48f].
       * Pos. 4: Patient brought upright to a seated position [47, 48f].
       * Pos. 5: Chin tilted 20° downward [47, 48f].
  2. **Semont’s Liberatory Maneuver**: Alternative dynamic repositioning technique [47].
  3. **Vestibular Rehabilitation Exercises**: Brandt-Daroff habituation exercises [47].

---

note.title: Cerumen (Ear Wax)
note.content:
* **Composition**: Cerumen is an emulsion formed by secretions of the **ceruminous glands** (modified apocrine sweat glands producing lipid/pigments) and **sebaceous glands** (fatty acids) blended with desquamated keratinocytes, hair, and dust particles in the outer cartilaginous meatus [3, 56, 56f].
* **Physiological Properties & Functions** [56]:
  1. **Protective & Lubricating**: Forms an oily coating that lubricates the meatal skin, preventing dryness, cracking, and maceration [56].
  2. **Bacteriostatic & Fungistatic**: Acidic pH (around 6.0) inhibits colonization by bacteria and fungal spores [56].
  3. **Mechanical Cleansing**: Traps foreign bodies and debris; expelled laterally by normal outward epithelial migration aided by jaw movements (chewing, talking) [56].
* **Impacted Wax**: Excess production, tortuous meatus, or improper cotton-tip usage causes compaction; presents with conductive deafness, tinnitus, ear fullness, or reflex coughing (mediated by Arnold’s nerve) [56, 507].
* **Removal**: Warm water syringing (37°C directed posterosuperiorly), micro-suction clearance, or ceruminolytic drops (5% sodium bicarbonate, paradichlorobenzene) [56, 57f].

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: OAE – What is it. What is its use.

note.title: OAE (Otoacoustic Emissions) — What is it and What is its Use?
note.content:
* **Definition**: Otoacoustic emissions are low-intensity acoustic signals generated by the healthy **outer hair cells (OHCs)** of the cochlea, which propagate in reverse through the basilar membrane, perilymph, oval window, ossicular chain, and tympanic membrane into the external meatus, where they can be measured by a sensitive probe microphone [29].
* **Types** [29]:
  1. **Spontaneous OAEs (SOAEs)**: Occur without acoustic stimulation (present in ~50% of normal ears) [29, 30].
  2. **Evoked OAEs**:
     * *Transient Evoked OAEs (TEOAEs)*: Elicited by brief broadband clicks [29].
     * *Distortion Product OAEs (DPOAEs)*: Elicited by two simultaneous pure tones (f1 and f2); measures cochlear response up to 8 kHz [29].
* **Clinical Uses** [29]:
  1. **Universal Newborn Hearing Screening**: Rapid, non-invasive, objective bedside evaluation of cochlear status in neonates and infants [29, 132].
  2. **Early Detection of Ototoxicity & Noise-Induced Hearing Loss**: OHC damage is detected by reduced OAE amplitudes before threshold shifts appear on pure tone audiometry [29, 37].
  3. **Site-of-Lesion Differentiation (Cochlear vs. Retrocochlear)**: OAEs are absent in cochlear lesions (>30 dB loss), but preserved in retrocochlear lesions [29].
  4. **Diagnosis of Auditory Neuropathy**: Characterized by **present/intact OAEs** with an **absent or abnormal ABR / BERA**, indicating normal outer hair cell function with neural dys-synchrony of CN VIII [29].
  5. Objective confirmation of hearing in malingerers and uncooperative children [29].

---

note.title: Fracture Nasal Bone — Diagnosis and Management
note.content:
Fracture of the nasal pyramid is the most common facial skeletal fracture [203].

* **Diagnosis** [204]:
  * *Clinical Features*: Epistaxis, periorbital ecchymosis, edema, tender nasal dorsum, palpable bony crepitus, step-deformities, and obvious lateral deviation or depression of the nasal bridge [204, 205f].
  * *Intranasal Examination*: Crucial to diagnose a **septal hematoma** (bilateral fluctuant boggy septal swelling) or mucosal lacerations [168, 204].
  * *Radiology*: X-ray nasal bones (lateral and occlusal views) demonstrates fracture lines, comminution, and displacement [204, 205f].
* **Management** [204]:
  * *Timing*: Optimal within **2–3 hours** (before edema develops) OR **5 to 7 days post-injury** (once inflammatory soft-tissue edema subsides) [204]. Fractures become united/fixed within 14 days [204].
  * *Closed Reduction*:
    * Performed under local or general anesthesia [204].
    * Depressed fragments: Elevated using a straight, flat instrument (Walsham’s forceps or Ash's forceps) inserted intranasally beneath the nasal bone while external digital pressure molds the fragment [204].
    * Deviated nasal bridge: Realinked with firm external manual thumb pressure [204].
    * Septum straightened with Ash's forceps [204].
  * *Splinting & Packing*:
    * Anterior nasal packing for 24–48 hours to prevent hematoma and support unstable fractures [204].
    * External nasal splint (plaster of Paris, aluminium, or thermoplastic) maintained for 7–10 days [204].
  * *Open Reduction / Septorhinoplasty*: Reserved for severe comminuted fractures or malunited old nasal deformities (>2 weeks old) [204].

---

note.title: Rhinosporidiosis — Diagnosis and Management
note.content:
Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic, non-contagious granulomatous infection of the mucocutaneous tissue caused by the aquatic protist/mesomycetozoan parasite *Rhinosporidium seeberi* [175, 177].

```
                          RHINOSPORIDIOSIS
                                 |
         +-----------------------+-----------------------+
         |                                               |
CLINICAL PRESENTATION                           DIAGNOSIS & MANAGEMENT
• History: Bathing in common ponds / tanks      • Biopsy: Sporangia filled with
• Morphology: Fragile, polypoid, leaf-like,       thousands of endospores
  friable, strawberry-like vascular mass        • Treatment: Complete wide-base
• Studded with white dots (sporangia)             diathermy excision + base cautery
• Frequent painless epistaxis / obstruction     • Medical adjunct: Oral Dapsone
```

* **Clinical Presentation**: Common in southern India (Tamil Nadu, Kerala) [177]. Transmitted via bathing in stagnant ponds frequented by cattle [177, 178]. Presents with a friable, painless, pedunculated or sessile, leaf-like, **"strawberry-like"** reddish vascular mass studded with distinct white surface dots (mature sporangia) on the nasal septum or inferior turbinate, causing epistaxis and nasal obstruction [177, 177f, 178].
* **Diagnosis** [177]:
  * **Histopathological Biopsy**: Unequivocal demonstration of large, thick-walled, round or oval **sporangia** (100–350 µm) embedded in fibrovascular stroma, packed with hundreds to thousands of mature and immature **endospores** (spores 6–8 µm) that burst through a germinal pore [177, 177f].
* **Management** [178]:
  1. **Complete Wide Surgical Excision with High-Frequency Diathermy / Laser**: The mass must be excised cleanly with an electrocautery knife at its base, followed by extensive electrocoagulation/cauterization of the healthy mucoperichondrial margins to prevent local recurrence [178].
  2. **Medical Therapy (Dapsone)**: Oral Dapsone (100 mg daily for 6–12 months) inhibits the maturation of sporangia, significantly reducing postoperative recurrence rates [178].

---

note.title: Vocal Nodule (Singer’s / Screamer’s Nodes)
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q02]]` (under 2019_JULY) for comprehensive etiology and features [343, 343f].

* **Definition**: Symmetrical, bilateral, non-inflammatory fibrous nodules arising at the **junction of the anterior 1/3rd and posterior 2/3rds** of the true vocal cords (the mid-membranous portion, representing the point of maximum mechanical impact and amplitude of vibration) [343, 343f, 511].
* **Etiology**: Chronic vocal abuse or misuse (teachers, singers, hawkers, assertive children) [343].
* **Pathology**: Submucosal microtrauma → localized hematoma and edema of Reinke's space → organization, hyalinization, and epithelial thickening [343].
* **Management**: Voice therapy (conservative cornerstone), strict vocal rest, and speech rehabilitation [343]. Persistent, mature fibrotic nodules are precisely excised via **microlaryngeal surgery (MLS)** using micro-scissors or CO2 laser, preserving the deep vocal ligament [343, 344f].

---

note.title: Rinne’s Test
note.content:
* **Definition**: A qualitative tuning fork test that compares the duration and loudness of sound perceived by **air conduction (AC)** through the outer/middle ear with that perceived by **bone conduction (BC)** through direct skull vibration [24].
* **Technique**: A 512 Hz vibrating fork is held alternate between the mastoid process (BC) and 2 cm lateral to the external auditory meatus (AC) [23–24, 24f].
* **Results**:
  * **Rinne Positive (AC > BC)**: Normal hearing or sensorineural hearing loss [24, 24t].
  * **Rinne Negative (BC > AC)**: Indicates conductive hearing loss (air-bone gap ≥15–20 dB) [24, 24t].
  * **False Negative Rinne**: Severe unilateral sensorineural hearing loss (BC sound is perceived by the opposite, normal ear via transcranial transmission) [24].

---

note.title: Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Brown-Kelly) Syndrome
note.content:
* **Triad**: **Microcytic hypochromic (iron deficiency) anemia**, postcricoid **esophageal web causing dysphagia**, and **glossitis/angular stomatitis** [388].
* **Other Features**: Spooning of nails (koilonychia), splenomegaly, and achlorhydria [388].
* **Significance**: Strongly premalignant; carries a ~10% risk of developing **postcricoid carcinoma** or squamous cell cancer of the oral cavity and hypopharynx in middle-aged females [272, 388].

note.title: Antrochoanal Polyp
note.content:
* **Definition**: A solitary, benign, pedunculated polypoid mass arising from the inflamed, edematous lining of the maxillary antrum, emerging through its natural or accessory ostium into the nasal cavity, and expanding posteriorly into the choana and nasopharynx [193, 194f].
* **Triad of Components**: Antral part, nasal stalk, and choanal/nasopharyngeal globular body [193, 195t].
* **Clinical Feature & Treatment**: Presents with unilateral progressive nasal obstruction in a child or young adult; definitively cured by functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) with complete clearance of the antral base [193, 195t].

---

note.title: Pott’s Puffy Tumor
note.content:
* **Definition**: A subperiosteal abscess of the frontal bone presenting as a circumscribed, doughy, pitting, fluctuant, tender swelling of the forehead overlying the frontal sinus [224, 224f].
* **Etiology**: Complication of acute or chronic frontal sinusitis spreading via diploic veins (osteothrombophlebitis) to cause osteomyelitis of the frontal bone [223–224].
* **Complications & Treatment**: High risk of extradural abscess, subdural empyema, and frontal lobe abscess; managed with prolonged high-dose IV antibiotics, frontal sinus trephination, and debridement of necrotic bone [224, 225].

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: A 30 years old female patient presents to the ENT OPD with complaints of gradually progressing hearing loss in both ears, for the past 5 years. She gives history of the hearing loss worsening during pregnancy. On examination, her tympanic membranes are normal. Tuning fork tests show negative rinne in both ears and Weber lateralized to right ear. Answer the following: (1+2+2+3+2)  What is the most likely diagnosis  Mention two relevant investigations and the expected findings in each  Mention four differential diagnosis  How will you treat this patient  Mention four complications of the surgical procedure used to treat this patient.

note.title: Young Female with Bilateral Conductive Hearing Loss Worsening in Pregnancy
note.content:
#### A. Most Likely Diagnosis
**Bilateral Stapedial Otosclerosis (Otospongiosis)** [95].

---

#### B. Two Relevant Investigations and Expected Findings
1. **Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA)** [25, 96]:
   * Symmetrical or asymmetrical bilateral **conductive hearing loss** with a significant Air-Bone (AB) gap, prominently in the lower frequencies (125 to 500 Hz) [96, 96f].
   * **Carhart’s Notch**: An elevation/dip in the bone-conduction threshold peaking at **2000 Hz (mean 15 dB)** [96, 96f, 507].
2. **Impedance Audiometry (Tympanometry and Acoustic Reflex)** [26–27, 97]:
   * **Tympanogram**: Shows a **Type As curve** (normal peak middle ear pressure, but diminished peak compliance due to ossicular stiffness from stapes fixation) [27, 27f].
   * **Acoustic Reflex**: Absent stapedial reflex bilaterally (in early stapes fixation, an "on-off" phenomenon or diphasic pattern may be observed) [27, 97].

---

#### C. Four Differential Diagnoses
1. **Secretory Otitis Media (Otitis Media with Effusion)**: Presents with conductive hearing loss and dull retracted eardrum (Type B tympanogram) [69, 70, 97].
2. **Adhesive Otitis Media**: Severe drum thinning, medialization onto the promontory, and previous middle ear infections [71, 97].
3. **Tympanosclerosis**: Dense hyalinized calcification of the tympanic membrane or ossicular chain (chalky white plaques visible otoscopically) [59, 97].
4. **Ossicular Discontinuity / Disruption**: History of trauma or chronic otitis; exhibits Type Ad hypercompliant tympanogram [27, 97].

---

#### D. Treatment
* **Definitive Treatment: Small Fenestra Stapedotomy** [97]:
  * Performed under local or general anesthesia using a transcanal approach (Rosen's flap) [97, 455].
  * Incudostapedial joint divided, stapedius tendon sectioned, and posterior crus fractured [97].
  * A 0.4–0.6 mm micro-fenestra is created in the footplate using a microdrill or laser (CO2/KTP) [97, 403].
  * A Teflon or titanium piston is crimped onto the long process of the incus, bridging sound vibrations into the vestibule [97, 97f].
* **Alternative / Non-Surgical Treatment**:
  * **Hearing Aid**: Air-conduction hearing aid (BTE/ITC) in patients refusing surgery or with an only-hearing ear [98, 135].
  * **Sodium Fluoride (20–40 mg/day)**: To arrest progression in active otospongiosis (positive Schwartze sign) [97].

---

#### E. Four Complications of the Surgical Procedure (Stapedotomy / Stapedectomy)
1. **Sensorineural Hearing Loss ("Dead Ear")**: Permanent profound inner ear damage due to surgical acoustic/mechanical trauma or perilymph serous labyrinthitis (occurs in ~1% of cases) [98].
2. **Vertigo and Disequilibrium**: Postoperative transient labyrinthine irritation, perilymph leak, or benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) [97].
3. **Persistent Perilymph Fistula**: Incomplete sealing around the fenestra, leading to fluctuating hearing loss and persistent vertigo on exertion [48, 97].
4. **Chorda Tympani Nerve Injury**: Stretching or division of the nerve causing temporary or permanent loss of taste over the anterior 2/3rds of the tongue and dry mouth [97, 99].

---

questions.officialText: Etiopathogenesis and clinical features of vocal nodule

note.title: Etiopathogenesis and Clinical Features of Vocal Nodule
note.content:
* **Etiopathogenesis** [343]:
  * Caused by chronic hyperfunctional voice production (vocal abuse, screaming, prolonged unnatural phonation) [343].
  * Repeated forceful impact at the point of maximum displacement/vibration—the **junction of the anterior 1/3rd and posterior 2/3rds of the vocal cord** [343, 343f].
  * Triggers vascular congestion and submucosal edema in Reinke’s space, which organizes through fibroblastic proliferation and hyalinization, accompanied by hyperkeratosis/acanthosis of the overlying squamous epithelium [343].
* **Clinical Features** [343]:
  * **Progressive Hoarseness**: Breathy, rough, strained voice that worsens with speaking [343].
  * **Vocal Fatigue (Phonasthenia)**: Inability to sustain speaking pitch, voice breaks during singing [343, 356].
  * Aching discomfort in the anterior neck muscles due to compensatory straining [343].
  * *Laryngoscopy*: Symmetrical, bilateral, small (pin-head to split-pea sized), smooth, pale or whitish-pink nodules at the junction of the anterior 1/3rd and posterior 2/3rds of both true vocal cords; vocal cord mobility is normal [343, 343f]. An hourglass gap is seen on phonation [343].

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Aetiopathology of chronic sinusitis with nasal polyposis

note.title: Aetiopathology of Chronic Sinusitis with Nasal Polyposis
note.content:
* **Etiological Factors** [193–194, 219]:
  1. Chronic local inflammation / eosinophilic inflammation (mediated by Th2 cytokines: IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) [187, 219].
  2. Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (Samter’s Triad: Asthma, Aspirin sensitivity, Nasal polyposis) [193–194, 219].
  3. Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AFRS) [194, 220].
  4. Mucociliary disorders: Cystic fibrosis (altered CFTR chloride transport, viscid secretions), Kartagener syndrome [194, 219].
* **Pathogenesis** [194]:
  * Persistent mechanical or immunologic inflammation increases vascular permeability in the lamina propria [194].
  * Extravasation of protein-rich fluid causes progressive, irreversible **edema of the subepithelial space** of the middle meatus, ethmoidal sinuses, and turbinates [194].
  * Protrusion of the edematous tissue produces polypoid mucosa, which elongates under the effects of gravity, negative inspiratory pressures, and venous/lymphatic stasis [194].
* **Histopathology**: Pseudostratified ciliated respiratory epithelium undergoing squamous metaplasia; marked stroma edematous expansion with numerous eosinophils, plasma cells, and mast cells, and thickened basement membrane [194].

---

note.title: Ludwig’s Angina
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q10]]` (under 2021_JANUARY / Chapter 52) for full structural relations [297–298].

* **Definition**: A rapidly spreading, bilateral cellulitis involving both the **sublingual and submaxillary compartments of the submandibular space**, usually originating from a dental infection without primary abscess formation [297].
* **Etiology**: 80% arise from the 2nd and 3rd lower molar roots extending below the mylohyoid ridge [297, 298f]. Polymicrobial (streptococci, staphylococci, and anaerobes) [297].
* **Clinical Features**: Severe odynophagia, trismus, "woody" brawny hard swelling of the submental and submandibular triangles; elevation and posterior displacement of the tongue into the hypopharynx, threatening airway obstruction with fatal stridor [297–298, 298f].
* **Management**: Immediate airway security (awake tracheostomy if needed); IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole); surgical decompression via a wide transverse submental incision dividing the mylohyoid muscle [298].

---

note.title: Type II Le Fort Fracture (Pyramidal Fracture)
note.content:
Le Fort II is a complex midfacial fracture that separates the central midface from the rest of the skull base in a pyramidal configuration [207, 207f].

```
                     LE FORT II (PYRAMIDAL) FRACTURE
                                   /\
                                  /  \  Fracture traverses:
     Root of Nasal Bone -------- /    \ • Nasofrontal suture
                                /      \• Lacrimal bone
     Infraorbital Rim ---------*        *• Inferior orbital rim & floor
                              /          \• Anterior maxillary antral wall
     Pterygomaxillary        /            \• Pterygoid plates (middle 1/3rd)
     Junction ------------- *--------------*
```

* **Fracture Line Course** [207]:
  * Traverses the root of the nasal bones through the nasofrontal suture [207].
  * Passes laterally across the nasal process of the maxilla and lacrimal bone [207].
  * Traverses the inferior orbital rim and floor of the orbit (involving the infraorbital canal) [207].
  * Crosses the anterolateral wall of the maxillary sinus beneath the zygomaticomaxillary buttress [207].
  * Extends posteriorly through the pterygomaxillary fissure to fracture the middle third of the pterygoid plates [207].
* **Clinical Features** [207]:
  * Pyramidal mobility of the central midface while the zygomatic arches remain stable [207].
  * "Panda facies" / bilateral periorbital ecchymosis and subconjunctival hemorrhage [204, 207].
  * Paresthesia or anesthesia of the cheek and upper lip (infraorbital nerve injury) [206, 207].
  * Malocclusion with an anterior open bite [207].
  * CSF rhinorrhea if the fracture line involves the cribriform plate [183, 207].
* **Management**: Closed reduction with intermaxillary fixation, or open reduction and internal rigid fixation (ORIF) with microplates along the infraorbital rim and zygomaticomaxillary buttresses [207].

---

note.title: Membranous Labyrinth (Draw and Label)
note.content:
The membranous labyrinth lies within the bony labyrinth and is filled with **endolymph** [10, 11].

```
                        MEMBRANOUS LABYRINTH
                                               
           Superior Semicircular Duct
                  /          \
                 /    CRUS    \
                |   COMMUNE    |----- Posterior Semicircular Duct
  Lateral Duct -+        |     |
                 \       |     /
                  \      v    /
                 [  UTRICLE  ]
                     |      \
    Utriculosaccular |       +---> Endolymphatic Duct -> Endolymphatic Sac
         Duct        |
                     v
                [ SACCULE ]
                     |
              Ductus Reuniens
                     |
                     v
             [ COCHLEAR DUCT ]
               (Scala Media)
```

#### Key Anatomical Components [10f, 11]:
1. **Cochlear Duct (Scala Media)**: Blind-ending, spiral canal making 2.5 to 2.75 turns; contains the organ of Corti [10, 11, 11f].
2. **Ductus Reuniens**: Tiny connecting duct uniting the saccule with the cochlear duct [11, 11f].
3. **Saccule**: Lies in the spherical recess of the vestibule; contains the macula (vertical plane) [10, 11].
4. **Utricle**: Lies in the elliptical recess; receives the 5 openings of the 3 semicircular ducts; contains the macula (horizontal plane) [10, 11].
5. **Utriculosaccular Duct**: Y-shaped connecting channel whose prolongation forms the **endolymphatic duct** [11, 11f].
6. **Endolymphatic Duct and Sac**: Traverses the vestibular aqueduct; the sac expands extradurally on the posterior petrous surface to absorb endolymph [11].
7. **Semicircular Ducts**: Superior, posterior, and lateral ducts with dilated **ampullae** containing **crista ampullaris** [11].
8. **Crus Commune**: Formed by the union of non-ampullated ends of superior and posterior ducts [10].

*Reference Link*: [Membranous Labyrinth Illustration](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gray924.png)

questions.officialText: Pure tone audiogram and speech audiogram findings in Meniere’s disease.

note.title: Pure Tone Audiogram and Speech Audiogram Findings in Ménière’s Disease
note.content:
1. **Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA)** [112, 112f]:
   * Early stage: Low-frequency **sensorineural hearing loss** presenting as a characteristic **rising curve** (250–500 Hz primarily involved due to apical cochlear hydropic distention) [112, 112f].
   * Advancing stage: Progression to involve mid and high frequencies, producing a **flat audiometric curve** or gently down-sloping curve (40–70 dB loss) [112, 112f].
   * Fluctuating nature: Documented threshold shifts between symptomatic attacks and periods of remission [111, 112].
2. **Speech Audiometry** [25, 113]:
   * Speech Reception Threshold (SRT) is elevated commensurate with the pure tone average [25].
   * **Speech Discrimination Score (SDS)**: Impaired (typically 55–85%), markedly worsening during and immediately after acute attacks [113].
   * Shows a **plateau configuration** on the Performance-Intensity (PI) function curve; absence of significant roll-over differentiates it from retrocochlear lesions [26, 113t].
   * Loudness recruitment is positive (demonstrated by Alternate Binaural Loudness Balance [ABLB] test and SISI score >70%) [28, 113].

---

note.title: Functions of the Larynx
note.content:
1. **Protection of Lower Airway (Phylogenetically Most Primitive & Essential)** [323]:
   * Three-tiered sphincteric closure: Laryngeal inlet (aryepiglottic folds), false cords (vestibular folds), and true vocal cords close in sequence [323].
   * Reflex cessation of breathing during deglutition [323].
   * Powerful **cough reflex** to dislodge foreign particles [323].
2. **Phonation (Voice Production)** [323]:
   * Subglottic air pressure forces approximated vocal cords to vibrate, converting expired air into sound (aerodynamic-myoelastic theory) modulated into speech by resonance cavities and articulators [323].
3. **Respiration**:
   * Active abductor widening of the vocal cords during inspiration regulates airflow [321, 323].
4. **Fixation of the Thoracic Cage**:
   * Complete adduction of cords locks intrathoracic air; crucial for straining actions requiring abdominal muscular compression (coughing, micturition, defecation, childbirth, and heavy lifting) [323].

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Cardinal signs of acute coalescent mastoiditis

note.title: Cardinal Signs of Acute Coalescent Mastoiditis
note.content:
1. **Mastoid Tenderness**: Exquisite localized tenderness elicited on deep pressure over the suprameatal triangle (antrum), middle of the mastoid process, or mastoid tip [85].
2. **Swelling over the Mastoid with Forward Displacement of Pinna**: Periosteal thickening gives a velvety, "ironed-out" feel, obliterating the retroauricular sulcus and pushing the pinna **forwards, outwards, and downwards** [85, 85f].
3. **Sagging of the Posterosuperior Meatal Wall**: Caused by periostitis of the bony party wall separating the mastoid antrum from the external osseous meatus [85].
4. **Pulsatile Otorrhoea with "Reservoir Sign"**: Profuse, thick, purulent discharge through a central perforation that rapidly re-accumulates in the external canal immediately after being mopped dry [85, 86].

---

note.title: Management of Post-Tonsillectomy Reactionary Hemorrhage
note.content:
Reactionary hemorrhage occurs within the **first 24 hours postoperatively**, triggered by slipping of a ligature, recovery from hypotensive anesthesia, or coughing [489].

1. **Immediate Resuscitation**: Keep patient in the recovery (coma) position; clear the airway; monitor pulse, blood pressure, and respiration; establish an IV line with crystalloids [488, 489].
2. **Bedside Intervention**:
   * Seat the patient upright; reassure them [489].
   * Remove obstructing blood clots from the tonsillar fossa with suction or Luc’s forceps to allow the superior constrictor muscle fibers to contract and constrict severed arterioles [489].
   * Apply firm pressure to the bleeding fossa for 5–10 minutes using a gauze swab held in a sponge-holding forceps, moistened with 1:1000 adrenaline or 4% lignocaine [489].
3. **Operating Room Intervention under General Anesthesia**:
   * If bleeding continues despite pressure: Transfer to the operating room [489].
   * Re-intubate with a cuffed endotracheal tube with rapid-sequence induction [487].
   * Insert Boyle-Davis mouth gag [487].
   * Identify bleeding points; secure with bipolar electrocautery or tie with 2-0 silk sutures [488, 489].
   * If tissue is friable, sew the anterior and posterior tonsillar pillars together over a gauze roll [489].

---

questions.officialText: Causes of referred otalgia Give precise answers: (4x1=4)

note.title: Causes of Referred Otalgia
note.content:
Referred otalgia is earache with normal ear findings, mediated by shared sensory nerves [143]:

```
                       NERVES MEDIATING REFERRED OTALGIA
                                       |
       +-----------------+-------------+-----------------+---------------+
       |                 |                               |               |
   CN V (V3)           CN IX                           CN X           C2, C3
 (Auriculotemporal) (Tympanic / Jacobson's)     (Auricular / Arnold's) (Lesser Occipital
       |                 |                               |              Greater Auricular)
• Dental caries      • Acute tonsillitis             • Carcinoma of      • Cervical spondylosis
• TMJ dysfunction    • Peritonsillar abscess           pyriform sinus    • Caries spine
• Lingual cancer     • Base of tongue cancer         • Laryngeal cancer  • Whiplash injury
• Impacted molars    • Elongated styloid process     • Vallecular ulcers
```

1. **Via Cranial Nerve V (Auriculotemporal Nerve)** [143, 143f]:
   * Dental causes: Carious teeth, impacted lower 3rd molar, periapical abscess [143].
   * Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) dysfunction / Costen’s syndrome [143, 508].
   * Ulcers/carcinoma of the oral tongue, floor of mouth, and buccal mucosa [143].
2. **Via Cranial Nerve IX (Jacobson’s Tympanic Branch)** [143, 143f]:
   * Acute tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), post-tonsillectomy bed pain [143].
   * Carcinoma of the base of tongue, vallecula, or palatine tonsil [143].
   * Elongated styloid process (Eagle’s syndrome) [143, 308].
3. **Via Cranial Nerve X (Arnold’s Auricular Branch)** [143, 143f]:
   * Ulcerative/malignant lesions of the larynx (vocal cords, supraglottis) [143].
   * Carcinoma of the hypopharynx (pyriform sinus) [143].
4. **Via Cervical Nerves C2 and C3 (Greater Auricular & Lesser Occipital Nerves)** [143, 143f]:
   * Cervical spondylosis, neck muscle spasms, and tuberculosis of cervical spine [143].

---

note.title: Laryngeal Crepitus
note.content:
* **Definition**: A physiological rough, palpable and audible grating or clicking sensation elicited by gently grasping the thyroid cartilage between the thumb and fingers and shifting it side-to-side across the anterior aspect of the cervical spine [319, 437].
* **Clinical Significance**:
  * **Present in Health**: Confirms a free, non-infiltrated retrovisceral/retrolaryngeal space [319, 437].
  * **Loss of Laryngeal Crepitus (Le Noir’s Sign)**: Diagnostic sign of **postcricoid carcinoma** or large retrolaryngeal masses/abscesses that push the larynx forward and infiltrate the prevertebral space [310, 437].

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Classify and enumerate the causes of stridor in a child. Discuss the etiology, clinical features and management of acute retropharyngeal abscess. (1+2+1+3+3)

note.title: Stridor in a Child and Acute Retropharyngeal Abscess
note.content:
#### A. Classification and Causes of Stridor in a Child
Stridor is classified based on the respiratory phase into **Inspiratory**, **Expiratory**, and **Biphasic** [333, 334f]:

```
                         CLASSIFICATION OF STRIDOR
                                     |
         +---------------------------+---------------------------+
         |                                                       |
   INSPIRATORY STRIDOR               BIPHASIC STRIDOR            EXPIRATORY STRIDOR
(Supraglottic Obstruction)         (Glottic/Subglottic Level)    (Tracheobronchial Level)
• Laryngomalacia (commonest)       • Subglottic stenosis         • Tracheal foreign body
• Acute epiglottitis               • Laryngeal web               • Tracheobronchitis
• Retropharyngeal abscess          • Juvenile papillomatosis     • Bronchial foreign body
• Micrognathia / Pierre-Robin      • Vocal cord paralysis        • Vascular rings
```

1. **Inspiratory Stridor (Supraglottic / Pharyngeal lesions)** [333, 334t]:
   * *Congenital*: Laryngomalacia (most common cause in infants), micrognathia (Pierre-Robin syndrome), thyroglossal/vallecular cysts [333, 334t].
   * *Inflammatory*: Acute epiglottitis, retropharyngeal abscess, peritonsillar abscess, hypertrophic adenotonsillitis [327, 334t].
2. **Biphasic Stridor (Glottic, Subglottic, and Cervical Trachea)** [333, 334t]:
   * *Congenital*: Congenital subglottic stenosis, glottic webs, subglottic hemangioma [333, 334t].
   * *Inflammatory*: Acute laryngotracheobronchitis (viral croup), laryngeal diphtheria [328, 334t].
   * *Neoplastic*: Juvenile recurrent respiratory papillomatosis [334t, 345].
   * *Neurogenic*: Bilateral vocal cord paralysis (birth trauma, Arnold-Chiari malformation) [333, 334t].
3. **Expiratory Stridor (Lower Tracheobronchial Tree)** [333, 334t]:
   * Tracheal and bronchial foreign bodies [334t, 365].
   * Compression by vascular rings (double aortic arch) [334t, 335].
   * Tracheomalacia, bronchial stenosis [334t].

---

#### B. Etiology of Acute Retropharyngeal Abscess
1. **Suppuration of Retropharyngeal Lymph Nodes (Nodes of Rouviere)** [300, 440]:
   * Prominent in infants and children <3–4 years of age; these nodes drain the nasopharynx, adenoids, paranasal sinuses, and middle ear cleft [300, 440]. They atrophy by age 4–5 [299].
   * Pyogenic organisms: Group A beta-hemolytic *Streptococci*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and oral anaerobes [298, 300].
2. **Traumatic Penetration**: Trauma to the posterior pharyngeal wall from hard/sharp foreign bodies, lolly sticks, or instrumentation [300].

---

#### C. Clinical Features of Acute Retropharyngeal Abscess [300]
* High-grade remittent fever, irritability, toxemia [300].
* **Severe Dysphagia and Odynophagia**: Child refuses all feeds, drools saliva [300].
* **Upper Respiratory Distress & Stridor**: Muffled, "quacking" or "duck-like" cry [300].
* **Neck Rigidity and Torticollis**: Head maintained in hyperextension [300].
* *Oropharyngeal Inspection*: Unilateral, smooth, rounded bulging of the posterior pharyngeal wall pushing the palatopharyngeal arch forward (limited to one side of the midline by the median fibrous raphe) [300].

---

#### D. Management of Acute Retropharyngeal Abscess
1. **Emergency Airway Maintenance**: Immediate intubation (cuffed, with suction ready) or tracheostomy if severe respiratory obstruction threatens asphyxia [300–301].
2. **Surgical Incision and Drainage (Transoral Approach)** [300]:
   * Performed with the child in **Rose’s or steep Trendelenburg (head-low) position** to prevent aspiration of pus [181, 300].
   * Operating under general anesthesia with an endotracheal tube in situ (or without anesthesia in emergencies) [300].
   * A vertical incision is made through the mucosa over the most fluctuant bulge, followed by immediate insertion of a wide-bore suction tip to evacuate pus completely [300].
3. **Parenteral Antimicrobial Therapy**: Intravenous Ceftriaxone / Co-amoxiclav + Metronidazole for 10–14 days [300].
4. **IV Hydration and Analgesics** [300].

note.title: Etio-Pathology of Cholesteatoma
note.content:
Cholesteatoma is a non-neoplastic, destructive mass of keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium in the middle ear cleft or mastoid ("skin in the wrong place") [73].

```
                    THEORIES OF CHOLESTEATOMA GENESIS
                                     |
       +-----------------+-----------+-----------+-----------------+
       |                 |                       |                 |
  INVAGINATION      EPITHELIAL              BASAL CELL        SQUAMOUS
(Wittmaack's Pocket) INVASION              HYPERPLASIA       METAPLASIA
       |            (Habermann's)           (Ruedi's)         (Sade's)
• Negative middle   • Ingrowth through     • Basal cells of  • Chronic infection
  ear pressure        marginal drum          pars flaccida     converts normal
• Deep attic pocket   perforation            proliferate       mucosa to skin
• Keratin collects  • Migrating skin         downward
```

#### Etiological Theories [73, 74f]:
1. **Invagination Theory (Wittmaack)**:
   * Chronic eustachian tube dysfunction produces persistent negative middle ear pressure [64, 73].
   * Retracts the flexible pars flaccida into the attic, creating a **retraction pocket** [73].
   * Desquamated keratin debris fails to clear, accumulates, becomes infected, and expands into a primary acquired cholesteatoma [73].
2. **Epithelial Migration / Invasion Theory (Habermann)**:
   * Keratinizing epithelium from the external canal or drum surface migrates into the middle ear through a pre-existing posterosuperior marginal or total perforation (secondary acquired) [73, 74].
3. **Basal Cell Hyperplasia Theory (Ruedi)**:
   * Subclinical childhood infections stimulate the basal cells of the pars flaccida to proliferate and form papillary cords that grow downward into the middle ear spaces [73, 74].
4. **Metaplasia Theory (Sade)**:
   * Chronic middle ear mucosal inflammation induces non-keratinizing cuboidal/columnar cells to undergo squamous metaplasia [73, 74].
5. **Congenital Cell Rests**: Embryonic epithelial rests trapped in the temporal bone during development [73, 74].

#### Mechanism of Bone Destruction [74]:
* Cholesteatoma destroys bone enzymatically: Osteoclasts and inflammatory mononuclear cells liberate osteolytic enzymes—**collagenase**, **acid phosphatase**, and **proteolytic enzymes** (not simply pressure necrosis) [74].

---

note.title: Framework of Nasal Septum (Draw and Label)
note.content:
The nasal septum consists of an osteocartilaginous framework covered by mucoperichondrium and mucoperiosteum [165].

```
                     FRAMEWORK OF NASAL SEPTUM
                                                 
                 FRONTONASAL SPINE
                      |
                      v     PERPENDICULAR PLATE
     NASAL BONES ---> /\   OF ETHMOID (Superior)
                     /  \===========================+
                    /    \                          |  ROSTRUM OF
                   /      \                         |  SPHENOID
                  /        \                        |
  SEPTAL CARTILAGE          \                       |
  (Quadrilateral Cartilage)  \                      |
               \              \                     |
                \              \     VOMER          |
                 \              \ (Posteroinferior) |
                  \              \                  |
                   \              \=================+
                    v              v
            ANTERIOR NASAL    MAXILLARY CREST &
                SPINE         PALATINE CREST
```

#### Components [165, 166f]:
1. **Quadrilateral (Septal) Cartilage**: Forms the anterior/cartilaginous two-thirds; articulates with nasal bones, ethmoid plate, vomer, and maxillary crest [165].
2. **Perpendicular Plate of Ethmoid**: Forms the thin posterosuperior bony septum [165].
3. **Vomer**: Forms the posteroinferior bony framework [165].
4. **Minor Peripheral Contributions**: Crest of the maxilla, crest of the palatine bone, nasal spine of frontal bone, and anterior nasal spine of maxilla [165].
5. **Membranous and Columellar Septum**: Mobile anterior portions containing medial crura of alar cartilages [165].

*Reference Link*: [Nasal Septum Skeletal Components](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gray854.png)

note.title: False Negative Rinne
note.content:
* **Definition**: A clinical scenario during the Rinne tuning fork test where a patient with severe or profound unilateral sensorineural hearing loss perceives bone conduction (BC) to be louder/longer than air conduction (AC), falsely imitating a conductive loss (negative Rinne) [24].
* **Mechanism**: When the fork is placed on the mastoid of the deaf test ear, vibrations transmit **transcranially through skull bone** to stimulate the contralateral, healthy cochlea [24]. The patient perceives this sound, reporting BC > AC [24].
* **Confirmation / Differentiation**:
  * Mask the contralateral (good) ear with a Barany noise box or narrow-band noise; repeat testing demonstrates complete absence of both AC and BC in the deaf ear [21, 24].
  * Weber test strongly **lateralizes to the contralateral (good) ear** (distinguishing it from true conductive hearing loss, where Weber lateralizes to the worse ear) [24, 24t].

---

note.title: Air-Conditioning Function of Nasal Cavity
note.content:
The nose warms, humidifies, and purifies inspired air before it enters the lungs [157].

1. **Temperature Control (Heating / Warming)** [157]:
   * The subepithelial vascular network of the inferior and middle turbinates possesses rich cavernous venous sinusoids acting as an efficient **radiator** [157].
   * Inspired air, regardless of outside temperature (from sub-zero to 40°C), is brought to body temperature (**37°C**) by the time it reaches the nasopharynx (traversal time: 0.25 seconds) [157].
2. **Humidification (Moisture Adjustment)** [157]:
   * Nasal seromucinous glands, goblet cells, and mucosal transudate saturate inspired air, adjusting relative humidity to **≥75–95%** [157].
   * The nose evaporates approximately **1 liter of water every 24 hours** to humidify inspired air, protecting delicate bronchial ciliated epithelium from desiccation [157].
3. **Filtration and Cleansing**:
   * Coarse anterior vibrissae filter particles >3 µm; the overlying moving **mucus blanket** ("conveyor belt") traps finer particles (0.5–3 µm) and clears them to the pharynx via ciliary action [157, 158f].

note.title: Cardinal Signs of Chronic Tonsillitis
note.content:
1. **Enlargement of Jugulodigastric Lymph Nodes**: Persistent, non-tender or mildly tender palpable enlargement of the tonsillar nodes below the angle of the mandible [291, 295].
2. **Persistent Congestion of Anterior Pillars**: Distinct crescent of erythema along the anterior faucial pillars compared to the rest of the oropharynx [295].
3. **Expression of Cheesy Debris or Pus from Crypts**: Firm pressure over the base of the anterior pillar using a tongue depressor expresses purulent exudate or cheesy plugs from the crypta magna [291, 295].
4. **Tonsillar Morphology**: Bilateral parenchymatous hypertrophy meeting in the midline, or small, shrunken, fibrotic tonsils embedded within scarred pillars [294–295, 295f].

note.title: Laryngopharyngeal Reflux (LPR)
note.content:
* **Definition**: The retrograde flow of gastric contents (acid, pepsin) above the upper esophageal sphincter into the larynx and hypopharynx [330, 389–390].
* **Clinical Features**: Persistent throat clearing, globus pharyngeus (sensation of a lump), chronic dry cough, vocal fatigue, and hoarseness [330, 390].
* **Laryngoscopic Signs**: Interarytenoid and postcricoid erythema and edema, contact granulomas over vocal processes, and thick mucus pooling in the posterior commissure [330, 344, 389].
* **Treatment**: High-dose Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs, e.g., Omeprazole 20–40 mg twice daily for 3–6 months) and antireflux dietary modifications [344, 389].

---

note.title: Griesinger’s Sign
note.content:
* **Definition**: Edema and tenderness over the posterior part of the mastoid bone (over the mastoid emissary vein) [93, 508].
* **Significance**: Pathognomonic sign of **Lateral (Sigmoid) Sinus Thrombophlebitis**, caused by retrograde thrombosis spreading into the mastoid emissary vein [93, 508].

---

note.title: Ventricle of the Larynx (Sinus of Morgagni)
note.content:
* **Definition**: A fusiform lateral outpouching/recess of the laryngeal cavity situated between the false vocal cord (vestibular fold) above and the true vocal cord below [321, 511].
* **Significance**: Anteriorly, it leads into a blind ascending pouch—the **laryngeal saccule** ("oil-can of the larynx"), whose secretions lubricate the true vocal cords; abnormal dilatation of the saccule produces a **laryngocele** [321, 345].
