note.title: Cause of Rhinitis Medicamentosa
note.content:
* **Etiology**: Prolonged, excessive, uninterrupted topical use (typically **>5 to 7 days**) of over-the-counter **topical sympathomimetic nasal decongestants** (e.g., oxymetazoline, xylometazoline, ephedrine) [172, 191].
* **Mechanism**: Chronic alpha-adrenergic stimulation causes receptor downregulation, refractory vasodilation, rebound mucosal hyperemia, and persistent nasal blockage [191].

---

note.title: Keratosis Pharyngis
note.content:
* **Definition**: A benign, asymptomatic, non-inflammatory condition of the pharynx characterized by the presence of hard, yellowish-white, horny excrescences projecting from the crypts of the palatine/lingual tonsils and pharyngeal wall [289, 289f].
* **Etiology & Nature**: Caused by localized epithelial hyperkeratosis and hypertrophy of mucosal epithelium; **firmly adherent** and cannot be wiped off without tearing (unlike follicular tonsillitis) [289]. Self-limiting; requires reassurance [289].

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Enumerate the causes of epistaxis. Discuss the management of sudden, profuse nasal bleed in an adolescent male. (3 +7)

note.title: Causes of Epistaxis & Management of Profuse Bleeding in an Adolescent Male
note.content:
#### A. Causes of Epistaxis (Classified) [197–198]
```
                           CAUSES OF EPISTAXIS
                                    |
         +--------------------------+--------------------------+
         |                                                     |
    LOCAL CAUSES                                         GENERAL CAUSES
• Trauma (nose-picking, fractures)                  • Cardiovascular (Hypertension)
• Infections (vestibulitis, rhinosinusitis)         • Hematologic (Hemophilia, ITP,
• Neoplasms (JNA, Carcinoma)                          Leukemia, Aplastic Anemia)
• Structural (DNS, Septal spur/perforation)         • Hepatic & Renal failure
• Foreign bodies (rhinolith, living maggots)        • Drugs (NSAIDs, Anticoagulants)
```

1. **Local Causes** [197]:
   * *Trauma*: Digital trauma (nose-picking), facial fractures, nasal bone fractures, septal injuries, iatrogenic surgical trauma (FESS, septoplasty) [197, 203].
   * *Infections*: Acute viral rhinitis, acute sinusitis, atrophic rhinitis, tuberculous/syphilitic ulceration, rhinosporidiosis [175–177, 197].
   * *Neoplasms*: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA), inverted papilloma, capillary hemangioma (bleeding polypus of septum), squamous cell carcinoma [197, 227–229, 279].
   * *Structural*: Deviated nasal septum with mucosal stretching/drying over a spur [167, 197].
   * *Foreign Bodies*: Retained organic bodies, rhinoliths, nasal myiasis [181, 197].
2. **General / Systemic Causes** [198]:
   * *Cardiovascular*: Systemic arterial hypertension, arteriosclerosis, mitral stenosis [198].
   * *Hematological*: Thrombocytopenic purpura, hemophilia, leukemia, aplastic anemia, von Willebrand's disease [198, 487].
   * *Hepatic Disorders*: Cirrhosis (coagulation factor II, VII, IX, X deficiencies) [198].
   * *Vascular*: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease) [198, 201].
   * *Drugs*: High-dose aspirin, NSAIDs, anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin) [198].
3. **Idiopathic**: Unidentified underlying cause in a significant proportion [198].

---

#### B. Management of Sudden Profuse Bleeding in an Adolescent Male
* **Clinical Suspicion**: In an adolescent male presenting with sudden, unprovoked, profuse epistaxis, **Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA)** must be suspected until proven otherwise [49, 197].

1. **Immediate Resuscitation & First Aid** [199–200]:
   * Place patient upright, leaning forward over a basin (Trotter’s method) to avoid swallowing blood; instruct them to breathe quietly through the mouth [199].
   * Secure two large-bore IV cannulae; draw blood for grouping, cross-matching, complete blood count, and coagulation profile [200, 281].
   * Infuse IV crystalloids (Ringer’s lactate/Normal Saline); prepare packed red blood cells for emergency transfusion [200].
2. **Local Hemostasis (Nasal Packing)**:
   * **Anterior Nasal Packing**: Ribbon gauze lubricated with liquid paraffin/antibiotic ointment layered horizontally into both nasal cavities [200, 200f].
   * **Posterior Nasal Packing / Balloon Tamponade**:
     * Essential in profuse postnasal bleeding [200].
     * Insert a 12–14 Fr Foley catheter or epistaxis balloon into the nasopharynx, inflate the bulb with 10 mL saline, pull forward snug against the choana, and secure [201, 201f].
     * Alternatively, place a traditional 3-tie gauze postnasal pack under sedation [200, 200f].
3. **Avoid Blind Manipulation / Contraindicated Biopsy**:
   * Strict avoidance of outpatient biopsy or instrumentation of any visible nasopharyngeal mass due to the danger of fatal hemorrhage [50, 122].
4. **Radiological Work-up & Embolization**:
   * Perform emergency Contrast-Enhanced CT/MRI to assess the tumor and evaluate for the Holman-Miller sign [50, 503f].
   * Perform urgent Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) and **preoperative trans-arterial embolization** of internal maxillary branches to arrest ongoing bleeding and prepare for definitive surgery [50, 281f].
5. **Definitive Treatment**: Surgical excision via transnasal endoscopic or open approaches once hemodynamically stable [50, 282t].

---

questions.officialText: Clinical features of attico-antral type of chronic suppurative otitis media

note.title: Clinical Features of Attico-Antral Type of Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media
note.content:
Attico-antral CSOM ("unsafe" or "dangerous" type) is a chronic destructive infection of the posterosuperior middle ear cleft associated with cholesteatoma and osteitis [75, 78].

* **Ear Discharge** [75t, 79]:
  * Scanty, persistent or intermittent, purulent, and **characteristically foul-smelling** due to underlying bone destruction and anaerobic infection [75t, 79].
  * May be blood-stained due to friable granulation tissue or aural polyps [79].
* **Hearing Loss** [75t, 79]:
  * Conductive or mixed hearing loss; typically more severe than tubotympanic disease due to early ossicular necrosis (long process of incus and stapes superstructure) [75t, 79].
  * "Cholesteatoma hearer": Hearing may remain deceptively good if the cholesteatoma mass bridges the defect between the drum and stapes footplate [79].
* **Otoscopic Signs** [75t, 79, 79f]:
  * **Attic Perforation**: Perforation in the pars flaccida [75t, 79f].
  * **Posterosuperior Marginal Perforation**: Perforation in the posterosuperior quadrant of the pars tensa involving the bony annulus [75t, 76f, 79f].
  * Presence of visible pearly-white flakes of **cholesteatoma matrix** within a deep retraction pocket [79–80].
  * Red, fleshy, vascular **aural polyps or granulations** protruding through the perforation into the meatus [75t, 76f, 78].
* **Danger Signs of Impending Complications** [80]:
  * Deep-seated earache, headache, vertigo (positive fistula test), facial asymmetry, projectile vomiting, and high fever with chills [80, 85].

---

note.title: Complications of Tracheostomy
note.content:
Complications are classified by the time of occurrence into **Immediate**, **Intermediate**, and **Late** [362]:

```
                     COMPLICATIONS OF TRACHEOSTOMY
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                         |                         |
     IMMEDIATE                   INTERMEDIATE                   LATE
 (During Procedure)           (First Few Days)             (Weeks to Months)
• Hemorrhage (veins/thyroid) • Displacement of tube        • Tracheal stenosis
• Apnea (CO2 washout)        • Accidental decannulation    • Tracheoesophageal fistula
• Pneumothorax /             • Subcutaneous emphysema      • Tracheoinnominate erosion
  Pneumomediastinum          • Tube blockage by crusts       (fatal hemorrhage)
• Recurrent nerve injury     • Atelectasis / Lung abscess  • Difficult decannulation
```

1. **Immediate Complications (During Operation)** [362]:
   * *Hemorrhage*: Laceration of thyroid isthmus, anterior jugular veins, or thyroidea ima artery [360, 362].
   * *Apnea*: Sudden removal of chronic hypoxic respiratory drive in severe COPD/hypercapnia (CO2 washout effect) [362].
   * *Pneumothorax and Pneumomediastinum*: Direct injury to the apical pleural dome in children [361, 362].
   * *Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Damage* [361, 362].
   * *Esophageal Perforation*: Knife passes through the posterior tracheal wall, forming a tracheoesophageal fistula [361, 362].
2. **Intermediate Complications (First Few Hours / Days)** [362]:
   * *Tube Displacement or Accidental Decannulation*: Tube slips into the pretracheal space [362].
   * *Tube Blockage*: Impaction by thick crusts, blood clots, or dried mucus [361, 362].
   * *Subcutaneous Emphysema*: Due to tight skin suturing or extensive tissue dissection [361, 362].
   * *Secondary Hemorrhage and Tracheitis Sicca* [361, 362].
3. **Late Complications (Weeks to Months)** [362]:
   * *Tracheal Stenosis*: Granulation tissue and circumferential cicatricial ring formation at the cuff or stoma site [361, 362].
   * *Tracheoesophageal Fistula*: Pressure necrosis between a rigid tracheostomy tube/cuff and a rigid nasogastric tube [362].
   * *Tracheoinnominate Artery Fistula*: Erosion into the innominate artery by a low tracheostomy tube, resulting in fatal hemorrhage [359, 362].
   * *Difficult Decannulation*: Due to stomal granulations, subglottic stenosis, or tracheomalacia [361–362].

---

note.title: Management of Parapharyngeal Abscess
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q02]]` (under 2016_SEPTEMBER / Chapter 52) for comprehensive anatomy and surgical steps [301–303].

* **Management Summary**:
  * Protect the airway (awake tracheostomy if trismus and laryngeal edema are severe) [303].
  * High-dose IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole + vancomycin) [303].
  * Surgical drainage via an **external transcervical approach** (incision 2–3 cm below the angle of the mandible; blunt dissection medial to the medial pterygoid and submandibular gland into the space) [303]. *Transoral drainage is strictly contraindicated* due to the risk of internal carotid laceration [303].

note.title: Osteomeatal Complex (Draw and Label)
note.content:
The osteomeatal complex (OMC) is the functional channel located in the middle meatus that drains and aerates the anterior group of paranasal sinuses (frontal, anterior ethmoid, and maxillary) [150–151].

```
                 CORONAL SECTION: OSTIOMEATAL COMPLEX
                                                 
             Cribriform Plate         Crista Galli
             ===============+=========+===============
                     Fovea Ethmoidalis
                   +-------------------+
                   |  ANTERIOR ETHMOID |
                   |     AIR CELLS     |
     Orbit --------|                   |----------- Middle Turbinate
    (Lamina        |  BULLA ETHMOIDALIS|
   Papyracea)      +----+         +----+
     |                  | Hiatus  |
     |                  | Semi-   |
     |                  | lunaris |
     |    INFUNDIBULUM -+    |    +---> UNCINATE PROCESS
     |         |             v
     |         v       MIDDLE MEATUS
     |    MAXILLARY
     |      OSTIUM
     |         |
     +---------+-----------------------+
               |                       |
               |    MAXILLARY ANTRUM   |
```

#### Key Anatomical Structures [150–152, 152f]:
1. **Uncinate Process**: Hook-like mucosal-covered bony lamella forming the medial boundary of the ethmoidal infundibulum [150, 152f].
2. **Ethmoid Bulla (Bulla Ethmoidalis)**: Large, hemispherical anterior ethmoid air cell forming the posterior boundary of the hiatus semilunaris [151, 152f].
3. **Hiatus Semilunaris**: Cleft-like opening between the posterior margin of the uncinate process and the anterior surface of the bulla [150, 151].
4. **Ethmoidal Infundibulum**: Funnel-shaped channel bounded laterally by the lamina papyracea and medially by the uncinate process [151, 152f].
5. **Maxillary Sinus Ostium**: Natural opening draining into the floor of the ethmoidal infundibulum [151].
6. **Middle Turbinate**: Medial boundary separating the middle meatus from the nasal septum proper [150].

*Reference Link*: [Ostiomeatal Complex Diagram](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Paranasal_sinuses_coronal.png)

---

note.title: Medial Wall of the Tympanic Cavity (Draw and Label)
note.content:
The medial wall of the middle ear separates the tympanic cavity from the internal ear (labyrinth) [6, 7f].

```
              MEDIAL WALL OF RIGHT TYMPANIC CAVITY
                                              
               PROCESSUS COCHLEARIFORMIS
                   (Tensor Tympani)
                        |
                        v    PROMINENCE OF HORIZONTAL CANAL
        +---------------*---------------+
        |                                \
        |              [ CANAL FOR  ]     \
        |              [FACIAL NERVE]      \
        |                    |              \
        |                    v               \
        |               OVAL WINDOW           \
        |           (Fenestra Vestibuli)       \
        |                                       v
 ANTERIOR                                  PYRAMIDAL EMINENCE
 (Eustachian)                               (Stapedius tendon)
        |                                       |
        |              PROMONTORY               v
        |           (Basal Cochlear        SINUS TYMPANI
        |                Turn)                  |
        |                                       |
        |              ROUND WINDOW             /
        |          (Fenestra Cochleae)         /
        +-------------------------------------+
```

#### Key Structures on the Medial Wall [6, 7f]:
1. **Promontory**: Rounded bony bulge in the center, formed by the underlying basal turn of the cochlea; covered by the **tympanic plexus** [6, 7f].
2. **Oval Window (Fenestra Vestibuli)**: Posterosuperior to the promontory; receives the stapes footplate and annular ligament [6, 7f].
3. **Round Window (Fenestra Cochleae)**: Posteroinferior to the promontory; sealed by the secondary tympanic membrane [6, 7f].
4. **Bony Canal for the Facial Nerve**: Runs horizontally along the medial wall above the oval window [6, 7f].
5. **Processus Cochleariformis**: Curved, hook-like bony projection situated anterior to the oval window; the tendon of tensor tympani turns around it laterally toward the malleus handle [6, 7f].
6. **Prominence of the Lateral (Horizontal) Semicircular Canal**: Bulges posterosuperior to the facial canal [6, 7f].
7. **Sinus Tympani**: Deep recess in the posterior part of the medial wall lying medial to the pyramid and facial nerve [6, 7f].

*Reference Link*: [Medial Wall of the Middle Ear](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gray910.png)

note.title: Functions of the Middle Ear
note.content:
The primary function of the middle ear is to overcome the acoustic impedance mismatch between the air of the external canal and the fluid of the cochlear labyrinth (impedance matching mechanism / transformer action) [16].

1. **Areal (Hydraulic) Ratio of Drum to Footplate**:
   * Total surface area of the tympanic membrane is 90 mm², but its effective vibrating area is **55 mm²** [16, 17, 507].
   * The area of the stapes footplate is **3.2 mm²** [17, 507].
   * This yields an **areal advantage of 17:1** (or 14:1 by alternative measurements) [16, 17]. Sound force concentrated over this smaller footplate increases acoustic pressure proportionally [16].
2. **Ossicular Lever Ratio**:
   * The handle of the malleus is 1.3 times longer than the long process of the incus, providing a **mechanical lever advantage of 1.3:1** [16, 509].
   * Total transformer ratio = 17 × 1.3 = **22.1 to 1** (recovers ~25–30 dB of sound energy) [17].
3. **Catenary / Curved Membrane Lever Effect**:
   * The radial fibers of the tympanic membrane displace more at the periphery than at the umbo, focusing energy at the malleus attachment [17].
4. **Phase Differential Between the Two Windows**:
   * Intact drum and ossicular coupling preferentially direct sound waves to the oval window [17]. Sound arrives at the oval window in the phase of compression, while a cushion of middle ear air shields the round window (phase of rarefaction), allowing perilymph to circulate [17].
5. **Acoustic Reflex Protection**:
   * Contraction of the stapedius and tensor tympani muscles attenuates sound transmission above 70–80 dB, protecting the inner ear from low-frequency acoustic trauma [9, 17, 27].

---

note.title: Cardinal Signs of Tuberculous Laryngitis
note.content:
Laryngeal tuberculosis is usually secondary to advanced open cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis [331].

1. **Posterior Laryngeal Predilection**: Marked predilection for the posterior half of the larynx (interarytenoid space, arytenoids, and posterior vocal cords) bathed by infected sputum [331].
2. **Mammillated Interarytenoid Swelling**: Granulomatous thickening and papillary heaping up of mucosa in the interarytenoid space [331].
3. **"Mouse-Nibbled" Vocal Cords**: Superficial, multiple, ragged ulcerative erosions along the edges of the vocal cords [331, 510].
4. **"Turban" Epiglottis**: Pale, boggy, uniform pseudo-edematous enlargement of the epiglottis [331, 511].
5. **Marked Pallor of Surrounding Mucosa**: Contrasts with the intense hyperemia of pyogenic acute laryngitis [327, 331].

---

note.title: Hennebert’s Sign
note.content:
* **Definition**: A positive fistula sign (nystagmus and vertigo elicited by applying positive/negative pressure in the external canal) **in the presence of an intact, completely normal tympanic membrane** without an actual bony fistula of the horizontal semicircular canal [43, 508].
* **Etiology** [43]:
  1. **Congenital Syphilis** (most classic cause; due to osteitis creating an abnormally hypermobile stapes footplate) [43, 49].
  2. **Ménière’s Disease** (in ~25% of cases; fibrous adhesions form between the footplate and the distended saccular wall) [43].

note.title: Function of Turbinates
note.content:
1. **Surface Area Amplification**: Significantly expands the mucosal surface area of the nasal cavities to facilitate air filtration, heat exchange, and humidification [149, 157].
2. **Nasal Cycle Regulation**: Periodic alternating congestion and decongestion of the erectile venous sinusoids directs the airstream between the nasal cavities [157].
3. **Airflow Dynamics**: Deflects straight laminar airflow into controlled turbulence, slowing inspired air to maximize contact with the mucus blanket [157].
4. **Sinus Drainage**: Protects and overlies the ostia in the inferior, middle, and superior meatuses [150, 153].

questions.officialText: Enumerate the causes of sleep apnoea. Describe the etiology ,clinical features, investigations and treatment of of the most common cause of sleep apnoea in children. (2+1+2+2+3=10)

note.title: Causes of Sleep Apnea & Adenoid Hypertrophy in Children
note.content:
#### A. Causes of Sleep Apnea (Classified) [313–314]
```
                          CAUSES OF SLEEP APNEA
                                    |
         +--------------------------+--------------------------+
         |                                                     |
    OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNEA                               CENTRAL SLEEP APNEA
• Nasal: Septal deviation, polyps, atresia           • Brainstem stroke / Infarct
• Oral / Pharyngeal: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy,     • Central nervous system tumors
  Macroglossia, Micrognathia, Retrognathia           • Bulbar encephalitis
• Laryngeal: Laryngeal web, subglottic stenosis      • Chronic narcotic ingestion
• Systemic: Morbid obesity (thick neck >42 cm)       • Idiopathic central hypoventilation
```

1. **Obstructive Sleep Apnea (Airway Collapse / Obstruction)** [313–314]:
   * *Nose / Nasopharynx*: Hypertrophied adenoids, choanal atresia, polyposis, severe septal deviations [313, 314].
   * *Oral Cavity & Oropharynx*: **Hypertrophied palatine tonsils**, macroglossia (Down syndrome, hypothyroidism), elongated flaccid soft palate/uvula, micrognathia/retrognathia (Pierre-Robin sequence) [313, 315].
   * *Larynx & Hypopharynx*: Laryngomalacia, subglottic stenosis, cysts [313, 333].
   * *General*: Morbid obesity (BMI >30), collar size >42 cm in males, myxedema [313, 315].
2. **Central Sleep Apnea (Absence of Respiratory Effort)** [314]:
   * Brainstem strokes, central nervous system infections, congestive heart failure (Cheyne-Stokes breathing), and narcotic use [314].
3. **Mixed Sleep Apnea**: Coexistence of initial central pause followed by obstructive efforts [314].

---

#### B. Most Common Cause in Children: Adenotonsillar Hypertrophy
#### Etiology [275]:
* Recurrent viral or bacterial upper respiratory tract infections stimulating lymphoid hyperplasia in Waldeyer’s ring [275].
* Underlying atopy and inhalant allergies causing chronic inflammatory hyperplasia [187, 275].

#### Clinical Features [275]:
1. **Nasal**: Persistent mouth breathing, stertorous breathing, daytime snoring, chronic mucopurulent rhinorrhoea, denasal voice (rhinolalia clausa) [158, 275].
2. **Obstructive Sleep Features**: Restless sleep, witnessed apneas, choking episodes, enuresis, daytime somnolence, and poor scholastic concentration (aprosexia) [275, 313].
3. **Aural**: Conductive hearing loss due to eustachian tube obstruction, recurrent acute otitis media, or persistent otitis media with effusion [64, 275].
4. **Adenoid Facies**: Pinched nostrils, open mouth, elongated dull expressionless face, high-arched palate, and crowded, retro-positioned upper incisors [275, 276f, 507].

#### Investigations [275–276]:
1. **X-Ray Soft Tissue Nasopharynx (Lateral View)**: Delineates the soft-tissue adenoid mass narrowing the nasopharyngeal air column [276, 276f].
2. **Diagnostic Flexible Nasopharyngoscopy**: Direct visualization of the enlarged adenoid pad obstructing the posterior choanae and compressing the torus tubarius [276].
3. **Overnight Polysomnography (Sleep Study)**: Identifies an Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) >1 to 5 events/hr and documents nocturnal desaturations [315].

#### Treatment [276, 491]:
* **Medical**: A trial of intranasal steroid spray (Mometasone / Fluticasone for 6–8 weeks) ± oral montelukast for mild hypertrophy [189, 219].
* **Definitive Surgical Management**: **Adenoidectomy** (often combined with bilateral tonsillectomy if tonsillar hypertrophy contributes to obstruction) [276, 491].
  * *Methods*: Curettage using St. Clair Thomson curette with guard, microdebrider endoscopic-assisted adenoidectomy, or coblation adenoidectomy [491, 520].

---

note.title: Tracheostomy Tubes
note.content:
Tracheostomy tubes maintain an artificial stomal airway [524].

```
                     TYPES OF TRACHEOSTOMY TUBES
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                         |                         |
   METALLIC TUBES            SYNTHETIC (PVC/SILICONE)       SPECIAL TYPES
• Jackson's (3-piece)      • Portex (Cuffed/Uncuffed)     • Fenestrated (Phonation)
• Fuller's (Bivalved outer)• Thermolabile (softens)       • Suction-aid (Evacuation)
• Long-term use without IPV • Cuffs prevent aspiration    • Adjustable flange (Deep necks)
```

1. **Classification by Material** [524]:
   * **Metallic Tubes (Silver / Stainless Steel)**:
     * *Jackson’s Tube*: 3-piece assembly: outer cannula, inner cannula, and solid introducer (obturator); durable, easy to clean; used in permanent stomas [524, 525].
     * *Fuller’s Bivalved Tube*: Outer cannula has split blades that compress together for easy insertion; inner cannula maintains the lumen [524].
   * **Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) & Silicone (Portex / Silastic)**:
     * Thermolabile; softens at body temperature to conform to tracheal curvature; disposable and causes less mucosal crusting [524].
2. **Cuffed vs. Uncuffed Tubes** [524]:
   * *Cuffed Tubes*: An inflatable balloon seals the space between the tube and tracheal wall; prevents aspiration of saliva and permits positive-pressure ventilation [524, 525]. Periodic deflation is required to prevent pressure-induced tracheal necrosis [525].
   * *Uncuffed Tubes*: Used in children (due to the narrow cricoid ring) and long-term tracheostomies without aspiration risk [361, 524].
3. **Specialized Tubes** [524]:
   * *Fenestrated Tubes*: Have an opening on the posterior curvature of the outer cannula, allowing airflow over the vocal cords for phonation during decannulation weaning [524].
   * *Suction-Aid Tubes*: Include an integrated dorsal subglottic suction port to evacuate pooled secretions above the cuff [524, 525].

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Draw a diagram of ossicular chain

note.title: Diagram of Ossicular Chain (Draw and Label)
note.content:
The middle ear contains three interconnected ossicles bridging the tympanic membrane to the oval window [9, 9f].

```
                         OSSICULAR CHAIN
                               
            [ HEAD OF MALLEUS ] ========= [ BODY OF INCUS ]
                  |                                 |
               NECK OF                              | SHORT PROCESS
               MALLEUS                              |
                  |                                 v LONG PROCESS
            LATERAL PROCESS                         |
                  |                                 v LENTICULAR PROCESS
                  |                                 |
              MANUBRIUM                             +-- (Incudostapedial Joint)
             (HANDLE OF                             |
              MALLEUS)                      [ HEAD OF STAPES ]
                  |                                 |
                  v                            NECK OF STAPES
                UMBO                             /      \
                                           ANT. CRUS   POST. CRUS
                                                \        /
                                            [ FOOTPLATE OF ]
                                            [    STAPES    ]
                                                   ||
                                             (OVAL WINDOW)
```

#### Detailed Anatomy [9, 9f]:
1. **Malleus (Hammer)**: Head (lies in the attic; articulates with the body of the incus at an incudomalleolar synovial joint), neck, anterior process, lateral process, and manubrium (handle) attached to the fibrous layer of the eardrum, ending at the umbo [9].
2. **Incus (Anvil)**: Body (lies in the epitympanum), short process (rests in the fossa incudis of the aditus), and long process (descends vertically, terminating in the lenticular process) [9].
3. **Stapes (Stirrup)**: Smallest bone in the body; head (articulates with the lenticular process at an incudostapedial synovial joint), neck (insertion of stapedius tendon), anterior and posterior crura, and footplate (held in the oval window by the annular ligament) [9].

*Reference Link*: [Auditory Ossicles Diagram](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1405_Auditory_Ossicles.jpg)

questions.officialText: Draw the diagram showing structures in tonsillar bed Answer briefly: (5x2=10)

note.title: Structures in Tonsillar Bed (Draw and Label)
note.content:
The tonsillar bed (fossa) supports the lateral encapsulated surface of the palatine tonsil [291, 292f].

```
                     STRUCTURES IN THE TONSILLAR BED
                               (Coronal View)
                               
          [ PALATINE TONSIL ]
                   |
     Fibrous Capsule of Tonsil
                   |
     Loose Areolar Tissue + Paratonsillar Vein
                   |
     Pharyngobasilar Fascia
                   |
=====================================================  <-- SUPERIOR CONSTRICTOR
                                                           & STYLOGLOSSUS MUSCLE
=====================================================
                   |
     Buccopharyngeal Fascia
                   |
     +-------------+-------------+
     |                           |
Glossopharyngeal Nerve (IX)    Facial Artery (Cervical Loop)
& Styloid Process              Submandibular Gland
```

#### Layer-by-Layer Components from Inside Out [291, 292f]:
1. **Capsule of the Tonsil**: A specialized layer of deep pharyngeal fascia covering the lateral surface [291].
2. **Loose Areolar Tissue Space**: Separates the capsule from the muscular wall; site of collection of quinsy pus, containing the **paratonsillar vein** [291, 298].
3. **Pharyngobasilar Fascia**: Fibrous inner lining of the pharyngeal constrictor muscles [269, 291].
4. **Muscular Bed**:
   * **Superior Constrictor Muscle** (forms the upper two-thirds) [291].
   * **Styloglossus Muscle** (forms the lower third, accompanied by fibers of palatopharyngeus) [291].
5. **Buccopharyngeal Fascia**: External covering of the pharyngeal wall [269, 291].
6. **Key External Relations (Neurovascular)** [291, 292f]:
   * **Glossopharyngeal Nerve (CN IX)**: Courses close to the lower pole [291].
   * **Facial Artery**: Ascending cervical loop of the facial artery [291].
   * Submandibular salivary gland and medial pterygoid muscle [291].

---

note.title: Management of Bezold’s Abscess
note.content:
* **Definition**: A complication of acute coalescent mastoiditis where pus erodes through the thin medial cortex of the mastoid tip into the digastric groove and tracks down along the sheath of the sternocleidomastoid muscle into the upper neck [86f, 87].
* **Management Protocol** [87]:
  1. **Hospitalization and Preoperative IV Antibiotics**: Broad-spectrum parenteral regimen targeting *S. pneumoniae*, *S. pyogenes*, and anaerobes (Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole) [87].
  2. **Cortical (Schwartz) Mastoidectomy**: Thorough exenteration of all mastoid air cells; eradication of the infected tip cells; identification and curettage of the fistulous tract on the medial aspect of the mastoid tip [87, 457].
  3. **Drainage of the Cervical Abscess**: Independent horizontal incision in the neck over the fluctuant swelling; blunt dissection deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle to evacuate deep collections, placing a dependent corrugated drain [87].

---

note.title: Cottle’s Test
note.content:
* **Purpose**: To evaluate nasal obstruction originating from abnormalities of the **nasal valve area** (the narrowest segment of the nasal airway, bounded by the caudal septum, upper lateral cartilage, and anterior end of the inferior turbinate) [149, 167].
* **Technique**: The examiner places fingertips on the patient's cheek lateral to the nasal ala and draws the cheek laterally away from the midline, pulling the lateral nasal wall and widening the nasal valve angle while the patient breathes quietly through the nose [167, 167f].
* **Interpretation**:
  * **Positive Cottle Test**: The patient experiences distinct improvement in nasal airflow; confirms vestibular/nasal valve collapse, stenosis, or caudal septal deflection amenable to valve repair or septoplasty [167, 167f].
  * **Negative Cottle Test**: No improvement in airflow; indicates deeper nasal cavity obstruction (posterior septal deviations, turbinate hypertrophy, choanal atresia) [167].

---

note.title: Pre-Auricular Sinus
note.content:
* **Embryology**: Results from incomplete or faulty fusion of the **six auditory hillocks of His** (mesodermal tubercles from the 1st mandibular and 2nd hyoid arches) during embryonic formation of the pinna [51–52, 117].
* **Anatomy & Presentation**: A tiny, blind-ending, epithelial-lined pit situated just anterior to the ascending crus of the helix or above the tragus [51, 52f, 117]. The subcutaneous branching tract is lined by squamous epithelium [117].
* **Clinical Course**: Usually asymptomatic; can present with recurrent secondary infection, cheesy foul discharge, cellulitis, or preauricular abscess [52, 52f, 117].
* **Management**: If recurrently infected, perform **complete surgical excision of the sinus tract and its ramifications** down to the perichondrium under magnification (often using an elliptical incision around the pit with methylene blue staining) to prevent recurrence [52, 117].

---

note.title: Rhinolalia Aperta (Hypernasality)
note.content:
* **Definition**: A speech resonance disorder where excessive nasal resonance accompanies oral vowels and consonants due to failure of the velopharyngeal sphincter to separate the oropharynx from the nasopharynx during phonation [158, 357].
* **Speech Characteristics**: The voice has a "talking through the nose" quality; intraoral air pressure for plosives (P, B) and fricatives (S, Z) leaks into the nose, producing nasal emission [158, 357].
* **Etiology** [357, 357t]:
  1. *Structural / Palatal Defects*: Cleft palate, submucous cleft palate, congenitally short soft palate, post-tonsillectomy/post-adenoidectomy velopharyngeal scarring, and oronasal fistula [357, 357t].
  2. *Neurological (Velopharyngeal Paralysis)*: Diphtheritic paralysis, bulbar/pseudobulbar palsy, or stroke involving CN IX and X [357t].

---

note.title: Schwabach’s Test
note.content:
* **Definition**: A qualitative tuning fork test that compares the patient's bone conduction (BC) duration with that of an examiner presumed to have normal hearing [24].
* **Technique**: A vibrating 512 Hz tuning fork is held alternate between the patient's and examiner's unoccluded mastoid bones until it is no longer heard [24].
* **Interpretation** [24, 24t]:
  * **Schwabach Equal**: Normal hearing [24t].
  * **Schwabach Lengthened / Prolonged**: Conductive hearing loss (patient hears longer than the examiner due to lack of ambient room noise masking) [24, 24t].
  * **Schwabach Shortened / Reduced**: Sensorineural hearing loss (patient stops hearing before the examiner due to cochlear/neural reserve damage) [24, 24t].

---

note.title: Woodruff’s Plexus
note.content:
* **Anatomical Location**: A confluence of thin-walled submucosal veins situated on the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, **inferior and posterior to the posterior end of the inferior turbinate** [197, 511].
* **Clinical Significance**: The major anatomical source of **posterior epistaxis** in elderly hypertensive or arteriosclerotic patients; bleeding is profuse, drains directly into the hypopharynx, and often requires posterior nasal packing or endoscopic arterial ligation [197, 199, 511].

---

note.title: Gradenigo’s Syndrome
note.content:
Gradenigo’s syndrome is a triad of clinical features indicative of **petrositis (infection of the petrous temporal apex)** complicating otitis media [88, 508]:

1. **Persistent Otorrhoea**: Ongoing purulent middle ear discharge [88, 508].
2. **Deep-Seated Retro-Orbital / Facial Pain**: Irritation of the ophthalmic branch of the **Trigeminal Nerve (CN V)** and Gasserian ganglion at Dorello’s canal [88, 508].
3. **Lateral Rectus Muscle Palsy (Diplopia)**: Paralysis of the **Abducens Nerve (CN VI)** as it crosses Dorello’s canal adjacent to the inflamed petrous apex [88, 508].

---

note.title: Schwartz Sign (Schwartze Sign)
note.content:
* **Definition**: A reddish, flamingo-pink vascular hue visualized through an intact, translucent tympanic membrane over the promontory of the middle ear [96, 510].
* **Clinical Importance**: Indicates **active, rapidly progressive otospongiosis (florid phase)** with increased vascularity of the promontory; indicates an increased risk of sensorineural deterioration and serves as an indication for medical therapy with **Sodium Fluoride** [96, 97, 510].

---

note.title: Adolescent Boy with Recurrent Epistaxis and Progressive Nasal Obstruction
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q01]]` (under 2021_JANUARY) for full notes on JNA [49–50].

* **Diagnosis**: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) [49].
* **Etiology**: Androgen-dependent hamartomatous proliferation arising from the margins of the sphenopalatine foramen [49].
* **Clinical Features**: Unilateral or bilateral progressive nasal obstruction, recurrent spontaneous epistaxis, cheek fullness, conductive hearing loss, and "frog-face" deformity in advanced stages [49].
* **Investigations**: CECT (demonstrates the pathognomonic **Holman-Miller sign** and bony erosion), MRI (evaluates skull base/intracranial extension), and 4-vessel DSA with embolization [49, 50, 503f]. Biopsy is strictly contraindicated [50].
* **Treatment**: Preoperative trans-arterial embolization followed by surgical resection via transnasal endoscopic, transpalatal, or lateral rhinotomy approaches [50, 282t].

note.title: Septoplasty
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q02]]` (Chapter 88) for detailed operative steps [473–474].

* **Definition**: A conservative reconstructive surgical procedure on the nasal septum where the deviated components of the cartilaginous and bony framework are repositioned, morselized, scored, or excised, preserving as much of the framework and mucoperichondrium as possible [168, 473].
* **Advantages over SMR** [474t]:
  1. Minimal cartilage removal, preventing supratip depression or columellar retraction [472f, 474t].
  2. Safe in children and adolescents without retarding midfacial growth [474t].
  3. Elevation of mucoperichondrial flap on only one side preserves contralateral blood supply [473, 474t].
  4. Allows simultaneous correction of caudal septal dislocations [473].

note.title: Otogenic Brain Abscess
note.content:
Otogenic brain abscess constitutes a life-threatening intracranial complication of chronic suppurative otitis media with cholesteatoma (or rarely acute otitis media) [90].

```
                     OTOGENIC BRAIN ABSCESS
                               |
         +---------------------+---------------------+
         |                                           |
TEMPORAL LOBE ABSCESS                       CEREBELLAR ABSCESS
• Spread via tegmen erosion                 • Spread via Trautmann's triangle
• Signs: Nominal aphasia,                   • Signs: Rombergism, past-pointing,
  homonymous hemianopia, motor palsy          dysdiadochokinesia, nystagmus
```

* **Sites**: Temporal lobe (twice as common as cerebellar) and Cerebellar hemisphere [90].
* **Pathways of Infection**: Direct bone erosion through the tegmen tympani/antri (temporal) or Trautmann’s triangle (cerebellar); or retrograde thrombophlebitis through emissary veins [83, 90].
* **Four Pathological Stages** [90–91]:
  1. *Stage of Invasion (Initial Encephalitis)*: Headache, low-grade fever, malaise [90].
  2. *Stage of Localization (Latent)*: Encapsulation of pus; minimal symptoms [90–91].
  3. *Stage of Enlargement (Manifest)*: Expanding mass effect and cerebral edema [91].
  4. *Stage of Termination*: Fatal rupture into ventricles or subarachnoid space [91].
* **Clinical Features** [91]:
  * *Raised Intracranial Pressure*: Severe headache (worse in mornings), projectile vomiting, drowsiness, papilledema, bradycardia [91].
  * *Temporal Lobe Abscess*: Nominal aphasia (inability to name common objects), contralateral upper quadrant homonymous hemianopia, and contralateral motor weakness/fits [91].
  * *Cerebellar Abscess*: Ataxia (falling to the side of the lesion), intention tremor, past-pointing, dysdiadochokinesia, and coarse multidirectional nystagmus [44, 91].
* **Diagnosis**: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI shows a single or multiloculated ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding vasogenic edema [91, 91f, 92f].
* **Management** [92]:
  1. *Neurosurgical*: High-dose IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole + vancomycin); IV dexamethasone/mannitol to reduce intracranial pressure; burr-hole aspiration or surgical excision of the abscess [92].
  2. *Otological*: Once intracranial pressure is stabilized, perform a canal-wall-down modified radical mastoidectomy to eradicate the primary cholesteatoma source [80, 92].

note.title: Complications of Adenoidectomy
note.content:
Complications can occur during or following surgical curettage of adenoids [491–492]:

1. **Hemorrhage (Most Common)**:
   * *Primary*: Persistent bleeding during surgery; managed by nasopharyngeal packing or direct suction diathermy [491].
   * *Reactionary / Secondary*: Occurs in the immediate postoperative period; presents with epistaxis, blood spitting, or vomiting dark blood [491].
2. **Injury to Surrounding Structures**:
   * *Eustachian Tube Orifice*: Laceration of the torus tubarius produces scarring and permanent tubal stenosis, causing chronic middle ear effusion [64, 492].
   * *Pharyngeal Musculature & Cervical Spine*: Excessive pressure can lacerate the superior constrictor or damage the anterior arch of the atlas [492].
3. **Velopharyngeal Insufficiency (Hypernasality / Rhinolalia Aperta)**:
   * Escape of air and food fluids into the nose during deglutition and speech [357, 492]. Pre-existing submucous cleft palate is a strict contraindication to adenoidectomy [491, 492].
4. **Grisel’s Syndrome**:
   * Spasm of prevertebral muscles leading to subluxation of the atlanto-axial joint; presents as painful torticollis (high risk in Down syndrome) [131t, 492].
5. **Nasopharyngeal Stenosis**: Cicatricial adhesions between the soft palate and posterior pharyngeal wall [492].
6. **Recurrence of Symptoms**: Due to incomplete curettage of residual lymphoid tissue [492].

note.title: Reinke’s Edema
note.content:
* **Definition**: A chronic, diffuse, symmetrical, bilateral swelling of the true vocal cords caused by the accumulation of gelatinous, watery edema fluid within the subepithelial space of Reinke (superficial layer of the lamina propria) [322, 330, 344].
* **Etiology**: Strongly associated with **heavy cigarette smoking**, vocal abuse, and gastroesophageal/laryngopharyngeal reflux; more common in middle-aged women [330, 344].
* **Clinical Features**: Low-pitched, husky, coarse voice; voice breaks; in women, voice becomes masculine [330, 344].
* **Laryngoscopy**: Translucent, flabby, bag-like, polypoid fusiform mucosal swellings along the entire length of both true vocal cords that flutter with respiration [330, 344].
* **Treatment**: Smoking cessation; antireflux medications; speech therapy; surgical decortication (micro-flap incision with evacuation of gelatinous fluid using micro-suction, operating on one cord at a time to prevent anterior commissure webbing) [330, 344].

---

note.title: Noise-Induced Hearing Loss (NIHL)
note.content:
* **Definition**: Permanent sensorineural hearing impairment caused by prolonged, chronic exposure to occupational or recreational noise exceeding safe limits (≥85 dB A-weighted SPL for 8 hours/day) [36, 37, 37t].
* **Pathophysiology**: Chronic acoustic overstimulation damages the stereocilia and causes metabolic exhaustion, apoptosis, and loss of outer hair cells, initially affecting the **basal turn of the cochlea** [15, 37].
* **Audiometric Hallmark**: Pure Tone Audiometry demonstrates a characteristic, bilateral, symmetrical **notch at 4000 Hz ("acoustic notch")** involving both air and bone conduction thresholds, with recovery at 8000 Hz [37, 37f, 510].
* **Clinical Symptoms**: Insidious hearing difficulty in noisy backgrounds, accompanied by high-pitched sensorineural tinnitus [37].
* **Prevention**: Hearing conservation programs: pre-employment and serial audiograms; use of hearing protective devices (earplugs: 15–30 dB attenuation; earmuffs: 30–40 dB attenuation) [37, 37t].

---

note.title: Modified Radical Mastoidectomy
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q01]]` (Chapter 82) for complete operative details [461, 461f].

* **Definition**: A canal-wall-down surgical procedure that eradicates disease confined to the attic, aditus, and mastoid antrum while preserving functioning ossicular remnants, tympanic membrane remnants, and middle ear mucosal function to retain or reconstruct hearing [455, 461].
* **Indications**: Cholesteatoma limited to the epitympanum and antrum with an intact, functional pars tensa and mobile stapes footplate [461].

---

note.title: Boundaries of Trautmann’s Triangle
note.content:
Trautmann’s triangle is a surgical surface area located on the inner cortical surface of the mastoid, through which infections can track from the mastoid to the posterior cranial fossa, and serves as an operative route to the cerebellopontine angle [88, 90, 511]:

```
                     TRAUTMANN'S TRIANGLE
                               
                    SUPERIOR PETROSAL SINUS
                   ========================= (Superior Boundary)
                                / \
                               /   \
                              /     \
    BONY LABYRINTH /         /       \   SIGMOID SINUS PLATE
    POSTERIOR CANAL         /         \  (Posterior Boundary)
    (Anterior Boundary)    /           \
                          +-------------+
```

1. **Anterior Boundary**: Bony otic capsule (posterior semicircular canal) [458f, 511].
2. **Posterior Boundary**: Sigmoid (lateral) venous sinus plate [458f, 511].
3. **Superior Boundary**: Superior petrosal sinus or middle cranial fossa dural plate [458f, 511].

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: A 45 years old male, presented with chronic inte rmittent scanty purulent foul smelling ear discharge in right ear for past 15 years and progre ssive hardness of hearing for 5 years. On examination of the right ear, tympanic membrane revealed an attic perforation- presently with right sided facial nerve palsy. Answer the following: /uni25CF What is the most probable diagnosis /uni25CF Describe the aetiopathology /uni25CF Describe the clinical features /uni25CF What investigations will you do /uni25CF How will you treat this patient (1+2+2+2+3=10)

note.title: Chronic Foul-Smelling Ear Discharge with Attic Perforation and Facial Nerve Palsy
note.content:
#### A. Most Probable Diagnosis
**Right-Sided Attico-Antral Type of Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) with Cholesteatoma**, complicated by **Right Lower Motor Neuron Facial Nerve Paralysis (Intratemporal Complication)** [78, 83, 88].

---

#### B. Aetiopathology
* **Origin**: Persistent negative middle ear pressure or inflammatory stimulus leads to a deep retraction pocket in the pars flaccida (primary acquired) or squamous epithelial migration through an attic defect (secondary acquired) [73–74].
* **Mechanism of Facial Palsy**:
  * Cholesteatoma matrix produces osteolytic enzymes (**collagenase, acid phosphatase, proteolytic enzymes**) that erode the thin bony fallopian canal, commonly at the **tympanic (horizontal) segment** above the oval window [6, 74, 88].
  * The nerve is directly compressed by the expanding cholesteatoma and surrounding granulation tissue, and secondary bacterial inflammation induces intraneural edema, ischemia, and conduction block (neurapraxia progressing to axonotmesis) [88, 101].

---

#### C. Clinical Features
1. **Ear Discharge**: Chronic, scanty, purulent, characteristically **foul-smelling** (bone destruction), sometimes blood-stained [75t, 79].
2. **Hearing Loss**: Marked conductive or mixed hearing loss [75t, 79].
3. **Facial Nerve Paralysis Signs (Right Lower Motor Neuron Type)** [104, 107]:
   * Asymmetry of the face; loss of forehead wrinkles on the right [104, 104f].
   * Inability to close the right eye (lagophthalmos); globe rolls upward and outward on attempted closure (**Bell’s phenomenon**) [104, 104f, 507].
   * Deviation of the mouth to the healthy left side; drooling from the right angle [104, 104f].
   * Obliteration of the right nasolabial fold; food collection in the right cheek [104].
4. **Otoscopic Findings**:
   * Defect/perforation in the pars flaccida (attic) [79, 79f].
   * Visible pearly-white flakes of cholesteatoma and/or a vascular, red granulation polyp [75t, 79].

---

#### D. Investigations
1. **High-Resolution CT (HRCT) of Temporal Bone (Axial and Coronal Views)** [80, 85]:
   * Demonstrates the soft-tissue mass filling the attic, aditus, and antrum with bony erosion [80].
   * Identifies the exact site of **erosion of the bony fallopian canal** (tympanic or vertical segment) [6, 88].
   * Evaluates the tegmen tympani and lateral semicircular canal for associated fistulae [6, 88].
2. **Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA)**: Quantifies the degree of conductive/sensorineural loss and reserves bone conduction thresholds [25, 80].
3. **Electrodiagnostic Facial Nerve Testing**:
   * *Electroneuronography (ENoG)*: Identifies the percentage of degenerated nerve fibers [103].
   * *Electromyography (EMG)*: Detects fibrillation potentials or intact motor unit action potentials [103].
4. **Pus Culture and Sensitivity**: Swab of discharge for aerobic/anaerobic bacteria [76, 80].

---

#### E. Treatment Protocol
```
                     MANAGEMENT OF COMPLICATED CSOM
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                                                   |
MEDICAL PREPARATION                                 EMERGENCY MASTOID SURGERY
• IV Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole                    • Modified Radical Mastoidectomy
• IV Dexamethasone (Anti-edema)                     • Clear Cholesteatoma from nerve
• Eye protection (Artificial tears, pad)            • Facial Canal Decompression
```

1. **Immediate Medical Stabilization**:
   * High-dose parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole) to treat active middle ear infection [80, 88].
   * Short course of intravenous steroids (Dexamethasone) to reduce acute intraneural inflammatory edema [104].
   * **Meticulous Eye Care**: Artificial tear drops, lubricating ointment, and nighttime eye protection to prevent exposure keratitis [108].
2. **Emergency Surgical Intervention (Within 24 Hours)** [88]:
   * **Canal Wall Down (Modified Radical) Mastoidectomy**:
     * Complete exenteration of the mastoid air cells, removal of the posterior meatal wall, and exteriorization of the attic and antrum [80, 461].
     * Thorough clearance of the cholesteatoma matrix and granulations from around the facial nerve [88].
   * **Facial Nerve Decompression**:
     * Expose the facial canal 5 mm proximal and distal to the site of erosion [88].
     * Carefully slit the epineural sheath longitudinally with a fine nerve knife to relieve intraneural pressure [108].
     * If granulations directly infiltrate the nerve tissue, they should not be avulsed [88].
   * **Nerve Repair (if transected)**: Cable nerve grafting (using the greater auricular or sural nerve) if nerve continuity has been destroyed [108–109].
3. **Postoperative Rehabilitation**:
   * Facial muscle physical therapy, electrical stimulation, and long-term surveillance for cholesteatoma recurrence [80, 104].

---

note.title: Management of Epistaxis
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q01]]` (under 2018_FEBRUARY) for classification and detailed medical/surgical protocols [199–201].

* **Stepwise Protocol**:
  1. Trotter's first-aid positioning with bilateral digital pressure over Little's area for 5–10 minutes [199].
  2. Topical vasoconstrictor-soaked packs (4% lignocaine + adrenaline) [200].
  3. Chemical cautery (silver nitrate) or bipolar electrocautery of localized bleeding points [200].
  4. Anterior nasal packing with lubricated ribbon gauze [200, 200f].
  5. Posterior nasal packing or Foley’s balloon catheter tamponade for intractable posterior bleeds [200–201, 201f].
  6. Surgical ligation: Transnasal Endoscopic Sphenopalatine Artery Ligation (TESPAL), anterior ethmoidal artery ligation, or interventional embolization [201].

note.title: Surgical Treatment of Ménière’s Disease
note.content:
Surgical options are indicated in patients with disabling episodic vertigo refractory to comprehensive medical therapy (~10–20% of cases) [115].

```
                     SURGICAL MANAGEMENT OF MÉNIÈRE’S
                                    |
         +--------------------------+--------------------------+
         |                                                     |
CONSERVATIVE (HEARING-PRESERVING)                     DESTRUCTIVE (NON-PRESERVING)
• Endolymphatic sac decompression                     • Surgical Labyrinthectomy
  or shunt (to subarachnoid / mastoid)                  (Transmastoid / Transcanal)
• Vestibular Nerve Section                            • Chemical Labyrinthectomy
  (Retrosigmoid / Middle fossa)                         (Intratympanic Gentamicin)
```

1. **Conservative Procedures (Hearing Preserved)** [115]:
   * **Endolymphatic Sac Decompression and Shunt Surgery**:
     * Decompression of the sac by removing overlying bone on the posterior fossa dura medial to the sigmoid sinus; insertion of a Silastic shunt tube draining endolymph into the mastoid cavity or subarachnoid space [115].
   * **Vestibular Neurectomy**:
     * Selective transection of the vestibular nerve via a retrosigmoid or middle cranial fossa approach; eliminates vertigo while preserving residual cochlear hearing [115].
   * **Intermittent Low-Pressure Pulse Therapy (Meniett Device)**:
     * Transmits micro-pressure pulses to the round window via a ventilation tube, promoting endolymph drainage [115–116, 116f].
2. **Destructive Procedures (Hearing Sacrificed / Non-Serviceable Hearing)** [115]:
   * **Chemical Labyrinthectomy (Intratympanic Gentamicin)**:
     * Serial instillation of vestibulotoxic gentamicin through the tympanic membrane; selectively ablates vestibular neuroepithelium (Type I hair cells) [35, 115].
   * **Surgical Labyrinthectomy**:
     * Transmastoid or transcanal drill-out and avulsion of the membranous neuroepithelium of the semicircular canals and vestibule; permanently cures vertigo in a non-serviceable, deaf ear [115].

---

note.title: Puberphonia (Mutational Falsetto Voice)
note.content:
* **Definition**: The persistence of a high-pitched, childish falsetto voice in a physically and biologically mature post-pubertal male [356].
* **Etiopathogenesis**: Laryngeal development and vocal cord lengthening occur normally at puberty under testosterone influence, but the boy subconsciously resists this transformation due to emotional immaturity, over-attachment to the mother, or fear of assuming adult responsibilities [323, 356]. The vocal cords remain excessively tensed by the cricothyroid muscle during phonation [320, 356].
* **Diagnosis**: Normal laryngeal anatomy; pressing the thyroid prominence posteriorly and downward relaxes the cords, instantly producing a normal low-pitched voice (**Gutzmann’s Pressure Test positive**) [356, 508].
* **Management**: Voice therapy (counseling, humming exercises while applying laryngeal pressure); refractory cases managed by Type III thyroplasty (relaxation thyroplasty) [341, 356].

---

note.title: Rhinoscleroma
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q12]]` (Chapter 28) for detailed pathology [175, 176f].

* **Definition**: A chronic, progressive granulomatous disease of the respiratory tract caused by the Gram-negative bacillus *Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis* (Frisch bacillus) [175].
* **Pathological Stages** [175]:
  1. *Catarrhal/Atrophic*: Purulent discharge and crusting mimicking atrophic rhinitis [175].
  2. *Granulomatous (Nodular)*: Non-ulcerative, bluish-red granulomatous nodules on the septum and inferior turbinate, causing woody induration of the upper lip and tip of the nose ("Hebra nose") [175, 176f].
  3. *Cicatricial*: Severe fibrous scarring causing stenosis of the nares and subglottis [175].
* **Microscopy**: Pathognomonic **Mikulicz cells** (large foamy macrophages containing Frisch bacilli) and **Russell bodies** (eosinophilic hyaline inclusions in plasma cells) [175, 176f, 510].
* **Treatment**: Streptomycin (1 g/day IM) + Tetracycline/Rifampicin for 6 weeks; steroids to prevent subglottic stenosis [175].

---

note.title: Treatment of Keratosis Obturans
note.content:
* **Definition**: The accumulation of a pearly-white, desquamated cholesteatoma-like plug of keratin in the deep osseous external auditory canal, causing bony erosion and widening [58].
* **Treatment** [58]:
  1. Softening the hard impacted keratin mass using 5% sodium bicarbonate or 2% salicylic acid in alcohol drops for 3–5 days [57, 58].
  2. Complete evacuation of the mass via micro-suction clearance or warm water syringing under direct surgical microscopic visualization [56, 58].
  3. Debridement of secondary granulations in the bony meatus floor [58].
  4. Regular follow-up every 6 months to evacuate recurrent epithelial accumulations [58].

---

note.title: Four Causes for Referred Otalgia
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q12]]` (under 2019_JULY) for cranial nerve mapping [143, 143f].
1. Carious lower molar tooth / Periapical dental abscess (via CN V3) [143].
2. Acute tonsillitis / Peritonsillar abscess (via CN IX) [143].
3. Ulcer/carcinoma of the pyriform sinus or larynx (via CN X) [143].
4. Cervical spondylosis (via C2, C3 greater auricular/lesser occipital nerves) [143].

note.title: Two Indications for Cochlear Implant
note.content:
1. Bilateral severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss in children (≥12 months of age) or adults, receiving little or no auditory benefit from appropriately fitted digital hearing aids [138, 139].
2. Postlingually deafened adolescents or adults who lose hearing bilaterally following trauma, meningitis, or ototoxicity, with intact auditory neural pathways [139, 140].

note.title: Four Complications of SMR Operation
note.content:
1. Septal perforation (due to bilateral opposing lacerations of the mucoperichondrial flaps) [169, 472].
2. Supratip depression / Saddle nose deformity (due to over-resection of the dorsal cartilaginous strut) [161, 471, 472f].
3. Retraction of the columella (due to excessive excision of the caudal cartilaginous strut) [471, 472, 472f].
4. Septal hematoma and septal abscess [168, 471].

note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q01]]` (under 2019_JULY) for comprehensive stapedial otosclerosis notes [95–98].

* **Diagnosis**: Bilateral Stapedial Otosclerosis [95].
* **Clinical Features**: Insidious, bilateral, painless, progressive conductive hearing loss worsening in pregnancy; paracusis Willisii; soft modulated speech; normal drum with positive Schwartze sign in 10% [95–96].
* **Audiometric Findings**: Low-frequency conductive hearing loss with an AB gap; Carhart's notch (dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz by 15 dB); Type As tympanogram; absent acoustic reflex [27, 96, 96f].
* **Non-Surgical Treatment**: Behind-the-ear digital hearing aids; oral Sodium Fluoride (20–40 mg/day) to arrest active otospongiosis [97, 98].
* **Surgical Treatment**: Small Fenestra Stapedotomy with Teflon piston prosthesis [97].
* **Four Surgical Complications**: Sensorineural hearing loss (dead ear), post-stapedectomy vertigo, perilymph fistula, chorda tympani taste loss [97–98].

note.title: Parapharyngeal Space
note.content:
The parapharyngeal space is an inverted pyramidal potential space situated on the lateral aspect of the neck [301].

```
                     PARAPHARYNGEAL SPACE
                                              
               BASE: Skull Base (Sphenoid & Temporal)
               ======================================
                                |
             +------------------+------------------+
             |                                     |
   PRESTYLOID COMPARTMENT               RETROSTYLOID COMPARTMENT
   (Anterior)                           (Posterior)
   • Internal Maxillary Artery          • Internal Carotid Artery
   • Lingual & Auriculotemporal Nerves  • Internal Jugular Vein
   • Deep lobe of Parotid Gland         • Cranial Nerves: IX, X, XI, XII
   • Fat & Lymph nodes                  • Cervical Sympathetic Trunk
                                |
               ======================================
               APEX: Greater cornu of Hyoid Bone
```

* **Boundaries** [301]:
  * *Superior (Base)*: Undersurface of the skull base (petrous and sphenoid bones) [301].
  * *Inferior (Apex)*: Greater cornu of the hyoid bone [301].
  * *Medial*: Buccopharyngeal fascia covering the superior constrictor muscle [269, 301, 302f].
  * *Lateral*: Medial pterygoid muscle, ascending ramus of mandible, and deep lobe of the parotid gland [301, 302f].
  * *Posterior*: Prevertebral fascia [301, 302f].
* **Division & Contents** (Divided by the styloid process and attached muscles into prestyloid and retrostyloid compartments) [301]:
  * **Prestyloid (Anterior) Compartment**: Contains the internal maxillary artery, inferior alveolar, lingual, and auriculotemporal nerves, deep lobe of parotid gland, and fat [301].
  * **Retrostyloid (Posterior) Compartment**: Contains the **Internal Carotid Artery**, **Internal Jugular Vein**, **Cranial Nerves IX, X, XI, and XII**, and the **Cervical Sympathetic Chain** [301].

---

note.title: Aural Polyp
note.content:
An aural polyp is a pedunculated mass of edematous, inflamed, hyperplastic tissue originating within the middle ear cleft or external meatus and projecting into the canal [75, 76f].

* **Etiology** [75]:
  1. *Tubotympanic CSOM*: Pale, edematous, smooth, non-ulcerated polyp arising from inflamed promontory mucosa [75, 75t, 76f].
  2. *Attico-antral CSOM*: Red, fleshy, vascular, friable granulation polyp associated with underlying cholesteatoma and osteitis [75, 75t, 78].
  3. *Malignancy*: Squamous cell carcinoma of the middle ear/meatus [119, 123].
* **Clinical Significance**: Indicates chronic middle ear disease; can obstruct drainage, triggering complications [78, 80].
* **Management & Clinical Rule**:
  * *Never avulse an aural polyp blindly*: It may arise from the facial nerve sheath, stapes footplate, or lateral semicircular canal, and avulsion can cause immediate facial paralysis, total deafness, or severe labyrinthitis [78].
  * Cautious snare excision or micro-debridement under the operating microscope, followed by histopathological examination to rule out malignancy [78, 80].

---

note.title: Complications of Tonsillectomy
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q04]]` (under 2018_FEBRUARY) for full temporal classification [489–490].

* **Immediate**: Primary hemorrhage, anesthetic complications, trauma to teeth/pillars/uvula, aspiration of blood [489].
* **Reactionary (First 24 Hours)**: Slipped ligatures, rise in BP causing bleeding from the paratonsillar vein [489].
* **Secondary (5th–10th Day)**: Infection of the tonsillar bed and premature slough detachment [490].
* **Late**: Scarring of soft palate, persistent tonsillar remnants, hypernasality, compensatory hypertrophy of lingual tonsil [490].

note.title: Allergic Rhinitis
note.content:
Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity disorder of the nasal mucosa triggered by airborne allergens [187].

* **Pathophysiology** [187, 188f]:
  * Inhaled allergens bind to specific IgE antibodies bound to high-affinity Fc-receptors on tissue mast cells [187, 188f].
  * Cross-linking triggers mast cell degranulation, releasing preformed mediators (**histamine**) and synthesized mediators (**leukotrienes, prostaglandins**) [187, 188f].
  * Produces acute vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, and sensory nerve stimulation (early phase), followed 4–8 hours later by eosinophil and T-lymphocyte infiltration (late phase) [187].
* **ARIA Classification** [188, 189t]:
  * *Intermittent*: Symptoms <4 days/week OR <4 consecutive weeks [189t].
  * *Persistent*: Symptoms >4 days/week AND >4 consecutive weeks [189t].
  * *Mild*: Normal sleep, no impairment of daily activities/work [189t].
  * *Moderate-Severe*: One or more items abnormal (sleep disturbance, impairment of daily activities, troublesome symptoms) [189t].
* **Clinical Symptoms**: Paroxysms of sneezing (10–20 sneezes in succession), watery rhinorrhoea, nasal obstruction, and itching of the nose, eyes, and palate [187].
* **Signs**: Pale, edematous, bluish nasal mucosa with swollen turbinates; transverse nasal crease ("allergic salute"); and infraorbital dark circles ("allergic shiners") [187].

note.title: Vocal Cord Polyp
note.content:
* **Definition**: A benign, usually unilateral, gelatinous or vascular pedunculated/sessile mass arising from the subepithelial space of Reinke on the free edge of the true vocal cord [330, 343–344].
* **Site**: Junction of the anterior 1/3rd and posterior 2/3rds of the true vocal cord [343, 344f].
* **Etiology**: Sudden, acute, violent vocal trauma (shouting, screaming), chronic smoking, and reflux [343, 344].
* **Clinical Features**: Constant hoarseness, diplophonia (double-toned voice caused by differing vibratory frequencies of the cords), and inspiratory stridor if the polyp is large and mobile [344].
* **Treatment**: Microlaryngeal surgical excision (MLS) using cold instruments or CO2 laser, followed by voice therapy [344, 404].

note.title: Laryngomalacia
note.content:
* **Definition**: The most common congenital anomaly of the larynx, characterized by excessive flaccidity and softness of the supraglottic cartilages, which collapse inward into the laryngeal inlet during inspiration [333, 334f].
* **Clinical Features**: High-pitched **inspiratory stridor** appearing at birth or within the first few weeks of life; worse when supine or crying; improves when prone; normal cry [333].
* **Endoscopic Findings**:
  1. Elongated, tubular, curled-up epiglottis (**omega-shaped Ω epiglottis**) [333, 334f].
  2. Short aryepiglottic folds that approximate during inspiration [333].
  3. Prominent, flaccid arytenoids with redundant mucosal folds tumbling forward into the glottis [333].
* **Management**: Self-limiting condition that resolves spontaneously by 18–24 months as cartilages mature; severe airway obstruction with failure to thrive is managed by **supraglottoplasty** (division of short aryepiglottic folds and excision of redundant arytenoid mucosa) [333].

---

note.title: Malleus
note.content:
* **Anatomy**: The largest and most lateral of the three auditory ossicles (hammer-shaped) [9, 9f].
* **Parts** [9, 9f]:
  1. *Head*: Rounded portion located in the epitympanic recess; articulates with the body of the incus [9].
  2. *Neck*: Slender portion below the head; crossed medially by the chorda tympani nerve [9, 99].
  3. *Handle (Manubrium)*: Descends vertically, embedded within the middle fibrous layer of the tympanic membrane; terminates inferiorly at the umbo [4, 9].
  4. *Lateral Process*: Conspicuous projection at the root of the handle, producing a landmark bulge on the drum from which the malleal folds arise [4, 9].
  5. *Anterior Process*: Slender spicule connected to the petrotympanic fissure by an anterior ligament [9].
* **Muscle Attachment**: Tensor tympani tendon inserts onto the medial aspect of the root of the handle [9, 320].

---

4. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea (due to avulsion of the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid tearing the cribriform plate) [183, 474].

questions.officialText: A 38 years old female patient coming with progre ssive hearing loss and occasional tinnitus with no history of ear discharge. Tuning f ork tests reveal a bilateral similar conductive hearing loss. There is family history of hardness of hearing. Answer the following: ● What is the probable diagnosis ● Describe the clinical features of this condition ● Enumerate non-suppurative causes of conductive hearing loss. ● What investigations are to be done ● Discuss the treatment. (1+2+2+2+3=10)

note.title: Middle-Aged Female with Bilateral Conductive Hearing Loss and Family History
note.content:
#### A. Probable Diagnosis
**Otosclerosis (Stapedial Otospongiosis)** [95].

---

#### B. Clinical Features of Otosclerosis
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q05]]` (under 2021_JANUARY) for full signs [96].
* Characterized by bilateral, progressive, painless conductive hearing loss; Paracusis Willisii; soft, monotonous speech; normal drum with occasional Schwartze sign; negative Rinne test and normal ABC [96].

---

#### C. Non-Suppurative Causes of Conductive Hearing Loss
1. **External Canal**: Impacted cerumen, keratosis obturans, exostoses, osteoma, and congenital meatal atresia [32t, 53, 56, 58, 118].
2. **Tympanic Membrane**: Tympanosclerosis, atrophic monomeric eardrum, traumatic rupture/perforation [32t, 58, 59].
3. **Middle Ear / Ossicular Chain**:
   * Otosclerosis (stapedial fixation) [32t, 95].
   * Otitis media with effusion (secretory/serous otitis media) [32t, 69].
   * Adhesive otitis media [32t, 71].
   * Ossicular disruption / dislocation (incudostapedial disconnect from head trauma) [32t, 458].
   * Congenital ossicular fixation (malleus/stapes) [32t].
   * Hemotympanum [32t, 507].
4. **Eustachian Tube**: Eustachian tube dysfunction/blockage and barotrauma (aero-otitis media) [32t, 64, 71].

---

#### D. Investigations
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q05]]` (under 2021_MAY) for audiometric trace features [96–97].
* Pure Tone Audiometry: Air-bone gap, Carhart’s notch at 2000 Hz [96, 96f].
* Impedance Audiometry: Type As tympanogram; absent stapedial acoustic reflexes [27, 27f, 97].
* HRCT Temporal Bone: Confirms otospongiotic demineralization around the fissula ante fenestram [95, 96f].

---

#### E. Treatment
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q05]]` (under 2021_JANUARY) for full operative technique [97–98].
* Small fenestra stapedotomy with Teflon piston insertion [97].
* Hearing aids for patients with contraindications or who decline surgery [98, 135].
* Oral Sodium Fluoride for florid active phases [97].

---

note.title: Cartilages of Larynx
note.content:
The larynx consists of **nine cartilages**: three unpaired and three paired [319].

```
                         CARTILAGES OF THE LARYNX
                                    |
         +--------------------------+--------------------------+
         |                                                     |
  UNPAIRED CARTILAGES                                   PAIRED CARTILAGES
(Larger, Framework)                                  (Smaller, Fine Control)
• THYROID (Hyaline, shield-like)                     • ARYTENOID (Pyramidal, vocal proc.)
• CRICOID (Hyaline, complete ring)                   • CORNICULATE (Santorini, horn-like)
• EPIGLOTTIS (Elastic, non-ossifying)                • CUNEIFORM (Wrisberg, rod-shaped)
```

1. **Unpaired Cartilages** [319]:
   * *Thyroid Cartilage*: Largest; hyaline; two alae meet at 90° (males) / 120° (females); forms Adam's apple [319].
   * *Cricoid Cartilage*: Hyaline; signet-ring shape; only complete cartilaginous ring of the airway; at C6 level [319].
   * *Epiglottis*: Yellow elastic fibrocartilage; leaf-shaped; does not ossify; guards the laryngeal inlet [319].
2. **Paired Cartilages** [319]:
   * *Arytenoid Cartilages (2)*: Pyramidal; hyaline; articulate with the cricoid lamina; have a vocal process (attaches vocal ligament) and muscular process (attaches lateral and posterior cricoarytenoid muscles) [319, 320f].
   * *Corniculate Cartilages (of Santorini) (2)*: Elastic; horn-like nodules surmounting the apex of each arytenoid [319].
   * *Cuneiform Cartilages (of Wrisberg) (2)*: Small rod-shaped elastic cartilages embedded within the aryepiglottic folds [319].

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Draw a diagram of the auditory pathway

note.title: Diagram of the Auditory Pathway (Draw and Label)
note.content:
The ascending central auditory pathway transmits nerve impulses from the cochlea to the auditory cortex [15, 16f]. Mnemonic: **E. COLI MA** [15].

```
                     ASCENDING AUDITORY PATHWAY
                                 
                       AUDITORY CORTEX (A)
                (Brodmann's Area 41, 42 - Temporal Lobe)
                                 ^
                                 |
                    MEDIAL GENICULATE BODY (M)
                            (Thalamus)
                                 ^
                                 |  Brachium of Inf. Colliculus
                                 |
                       INFERIOR COLLICULUS (I)
                             (Midbrain)
                                 ^
                                 |  LATERAL LEMNISCUS (L)
                                 |
                    SUPERIOR OLIVARY COMPLEX (O)
                           (Pons / Medulla)
                            /         \  (Trapezoid Body Decussation)
                           ^           ^
             DORSAL & VENTRAL COCHLEAR NUCLEI (C)
                                 ^
                                 |
                       EIGHTH CRANIAL NERVE (E)
                           (Cochlear Division)
                                 ^
                                 |
                       SPIRAL GANGLION CELLS
                                 ^
                                 |
                       [ ORGAN OF CORTI ]
```

#### Order of Relay Centers [15, 16f]:
1. **E**ighth Nerve (Auditory Nerve): From bipolar spiral ganglion cells [15].
2. **C**ochlear Nuclei (Dorsal and Ventral): In the pontomedullary junction [15].
3. **O**livary Complex (Superior): Bilateral relay in the pons (sound localization) [15].
4. **L**ateral Lemniscus: Ascending tract in the brainstem [15].
5. **I**nferior Colliculus: Midbrain auditory reflex center [15].
6. **M**edial Geniculate Body: Thalamic auditory relay station [15].
7. **A**uditory Cortex: Brodmann’s areas 41 & 42 in the superior temporal gyrus [15].

*Reference Link*: [Central Auditory Pathways Diagram](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Auditory_Pathways.png)

note.title: Myringotomy
note.content:
REFER TO Chapter 78 for procedural details [453, 453f].

* **Definition**: A surgical incision made through the tympanic membrane to evacuate suppurative or non-suppurative fluid from the middle ear and relieve middle ear pressure [453].
* **Indications** [453]:
  1. Acute suppurative otitis media with severe earache, bulging drum, or impending complications (facial palsy, mastoiditis) [68, 453].
  2. Otitis media with effusion (serous otitis media) with fluid persisting >12 weeks [68, 70, 453].
  3. Severe aero-otitis media (barotrauma) [71, 453].
* **Incision Technique** [453, 453f]:
  * *Acute Suppurative Otitis Media*: **Curvilinear / Circumferential incision** in the **posteroinferior quadrant** (parallel to the annulus; avoids injury to the incudostapedial joint and chorda tympani) [453, 453f].
  * *Serous Otitis Media (with Grommet Insertion)*: **Radial incision** in the **anteroinferior quadrant** (less bleeding, lower extrusion rate) [453, 453f].

---

note.title: Bat Ear (Prominent / Protruding Ear)
note.content:
* **Definition**: A congenital deformity of the pinna characterized by an abnormally protruding, cup-like auricle that stands out from the side of the head at an angle **>30°** (or auriculocephalic distance >20 mm) [51].
* **Embryological Defect**: Caused by failure of normal folding of the **antihelix** (concha is excessively deep and large while the antihelical fold is poorly developed or absent) [51].
* **Treatment: Otoplasty (Pinnaplasty)** [51]:
  * Electively performed after **6 years of age** (when the auricle has attained ~90% of adult dimensions and cartilage is firm enough to hold sutures) [51].
  * Performed through a posterior elliptical skin excision, thinning the cartilage, and placing permanent mattress sutures (Mustarde sutures) to reconstruct the antihelical fold, combined with conchal cartilage setback (Furnas sutures) [51].

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Four surgical treatments for atrophic rhinitis.

note.title: Four Surgical Treatments for Atrophic Rhinitis
note.content:
1. **Young’s Operation**: Complete bilateral closure of the anterior nares with circular vestibulocutaneous flaps for 6–12 months [173].
2. **Modified Young’s Operation**: Partial closure of the anterior nares to narrow the airway while maintaining partial nasal breathing [173].
3. **Submucosal Implantation Operations**: Submucoperichondrial or submucoperiosteal implantation of autologous cartilage, cancellous bone chips, or Teflon/silastic strips along the septum and nasal floor to narrow the roomy cavity [173].
4. **Lautenschlager’s Operation**: Medial displacement of the lateral nasal wall following medial mobilization of the maxillary antral wall [173].
