questions.officialText: A two years old child brought to the outpatient department with complaints of nasal obstruction, foul smelling unilateral nasal dischar ge for past one month. Answer the following: /uni25CF What is the probable diagnosis /uni25CF What are the causes for unilateral nasal obstruction /uni25CF What is the etiology of choanal atresia /uni25CF What are the investigations to be done /uni25CF Discuss the treatment of this child. (1+2+2+ 2+3=10)

note.title: Two-Year-Old Child with Unilateral Foul-Smelling Nasal Discharge
note.content:
#### A. Probable Diagnosis
**Impacted Foreign Body in the Nasal Cavity** (Right/Left) [181].
* *Clinical Maxim*: "Unilateral, purulent, foul-smelling, or blood-stained nasal discharge in a child is considered an impacted foreign body until proven otherwise" [181].

---

#### B. Causes of Unilateral Nasal Obstruction
```
                 CAUSES OF UNILATERAL NASAL OBSTRUCTION
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                                                   |
     CHILDREN                                             ADULTS
• Impacted foreign body                             • Deviated Nasal Septum (DNS)
• Unilateral choanal atresia                        • Antrochoanal polyp
• Nasal dermoid / Encephalocele                     • Inverted Papilloma
• Rhinolith                                         • Rhinosporidiosis
• Unilateral purulent sinusitis                     • Sinonasal Carcinoma
```

1. **In Children** [181, 194t]:
   * Neglected/impacted foreign body (organic seed, plastic toy) [181].
   * Unilateral congenital choanal atresia [183].
   * Rhinolith (calcified foreign body) [181].
   * Congenital masses: Intranasal glioma, meningoencephalocele, nasal dermoid [161, 228–229].
   * Acute/chronic unilateral sinusitis [181, 194t].
2. **In Adults** [194t]:
   * Deviated nasal septum (DNS) with or without hypertrophied turbinate [166–167, 194t].
   * Antrochoanal polyp [193, 194t].
   * Sinonasal neoplasms: Inverted papilloma, bleeding polypus of septum, carcinoma of maxillary/ethmoid sinus [194t, 227–229, 232].
   * Rhinosporidiosis [177, 194t].

---

#### C. Etiology of Choanal Atresia
* **Embryological Basis**:
  * Failure of breakdown/reabsorption of the **buccopharyngeal membrane** (persistent bucconasal membrane of Hochstetter) between the 5th and 6th weeks of intrauterine development [183].
  * Misdirected mesodermal flow resulting in abnormal persistence and thickening of the vertical and horizontal processes of the palatine bone [183].
* **Nature**: 90% bony or mixed bony-membranous, 10% purely membranous [183, 507].
* **Associations**: 50% are associated with other congenital anomalies, notably the **CHARGE syndrome** (Coloboma, Heart defects, Atresia choanae, Retarded growth, Genital hypoplasia, Ear anomalies) [183, 507].

---

#### D. Investigations to be Done
1. **Diagnostic Rigid / Flexible Nasal Endoscopy**:
   * Performed following topical suction and decongestion; directly visualizes the foreign body, surrounding mucosal edema, or granulation tissue [181, 475].
2. **Radiograph of the Paranasal Sinuses / Nose (Lateral & Waters' Views)**:
   * Identifies radio-opaque foreign bodies (batteries, metal pins, stones) [181, 366].
   * Disc battery reveals a pathognomonic **"halo sign" / double contour ring** on AP view [396].
3. **Gentle Instrumental Probe Test**:
   * Careful probing under direct vision to determine whether the object is hard, gritty (rhinolith), firm, or yielding [181, 432].

---

#### E. Treatment of this Child
1. **Immediate Pre-Procedure Caution**:
   * Do not attempt blind grasping of smooth, round foreign bodies with ordinary forceps; it can push the object posteriorly into the nasopharynx, risking fatal aspiration into the bronchial tree [57, 181].
2. **Instrumental Removal**:
   * **In a Cooperative Child**: Restrain securely in the parent's lap; introduce a blunt right-angled hook, Eustachian catheter, or Jobson-Horne probe beyond the superior margin of the foreign body, rotate down, and roll the object along the floor of the nose out through the anterior nares [57, 181].
   * **In an Uncooperative Child / Impacted Foreign Body**:
     * Performed in the operating room under **General Anesthesia with a Cuffed Endotracheal Tube and Pharyngeal Pack** [181].
     * Direct visualization using a 0° rigid nasal endoscope; extract the foreign body atraumatically with Luc’s forceps or a blunt hook [181, 475].
3. **Special Alert: Button / Disc Battery**:
   * Requires **emergency removal within hours** [397]. Alkaline electrolytes cause liquefactive necrosis, septal perforation, and saddle nose deformity [397].
4. **Post-Removal Care**:
   * Suction purulent discharge; administer oral antibiotics (Amoxicillin) for 5 days [68, 181].
   * Saline nasal drops to clear crusts [181].

---

note.title: Management of Ménière’s Disease
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q09]]` (under 2016_FEBRUARY) and Chapter 15 for complete protocols [114–116].

* **Management Summary**:
  1. *Acute Attack*: Bed rest; IV fluids; labyrinthine vestibular sedatives (Prochlorperazine, Promethazine, Diazepam); carbogen inhalation [114–115].
  2. *Maintenance (Chronic Phase)*: Low-salt diet (<1.5–2 g/day); avoidance of caffeine, smoking, and alcohol; vasodilators (Betahistine 16–24 mg TDS); maintenance diuretics (Hydrochlorothiazide) [114, 115].
  3. *Chemical Labyrinthectomy*: Intratympanic Gentamicin [115].
  4. *Surgical Options*: Endolymphatic sac decompression/shunt; vestibular nerve section; surgical labyrinthectomy [115].

note.title: Discuss Treatment of Lateral Sinus Thrombosis
note.content:
Lateral (sigmoid) sinus thrombosis is an intracranial thrombophlebitic complication of middle ear suppuration [92].

```
                MANAGEMENT OF LATERAL SINUS THROMBOSIS
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                                                   |
MEDICAL THERAPY                                     SURGICAL INTERVENTION
• High-dose IV Antibiotics                          • Modified Radical Mastoidectomy
  (Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole +                     • Bony sinus plate decompression
   Vancomycin x 3–4 weeks)                          • Incision of sinus wall & clot removal
• Anticoagulation (LMWH)                            • Ligation of Internal Jugular Vein
  (Reserved for retrograde sinus extension)           (If septic embolization continues)
```

1. **Intravenous Antimicrobial Therapy (Immediate)** [93]:
   * High-dose parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotic regimen covering *Proteus*, *Pseudomonas*, *Streptococci*, and anaerobes (*Bacteroides*) [92]:
   * **Ceftriaxone (2 g IV 12-hourly) + Metronidazole (500 mg IV 8-hourly) + Vancomycin**; continued for 3 to 4 weeks [92, 93].
2. **Surgical Exploration (Canal-Wall-Down Mastoidectomy)** [93]:
   * Perform a cortical or modified radical mastoidectomy to eradicate the primary cholesteatoma and coalescent mastoid infection [93].
   * The bony sinus plate is thinned and removed, exposing the outer dural wall of the sigmoid sinus and draining any **perisinus abscess** [92, 93].
3. **Incision and Evacuation of the Sinus (Thrombectomy)** [93]:
   * The sinus is palpated and aspirated with a fine needle; failure to aspirate blood indicates an intrasinus thrombus [93].
   * Pack the sinus lumen extralumenally with Surgicel/ribbon gauze superiorly (near the torcula) and inferiorly (near the jugular bulb) to control hemorrhage [93].
   * The sinus wall is incised longitudinally, the infected, necrotic mural thrombus evacuated with suction and forceps until free fresh bleeding appears from both ends, and the packs are left in situ for 5–6 days [93].
4. **Internal Jugular Vein Ligation**:
   * Indicated if recurrent septic pulmonary emboli, persistent high spiking fever with rigors, or spreading tender neck induration continue despite complete mastoid drainage [93].
5. **Anticoagulation**:
   * Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH) is reserved for cases showing retrograde thrombus extension into the cavernous sinus or sagittal sinus on serial contrast MRI/MRV [93].

---

note.title: Diagram of Taste Bud (Draw and Label)
note.content:
Taste buds are barrel-shaped sensory neuroepithelial structures embedded within the stratified squamous epithelium of the tongue papillae (circumvallate, foliate, fungiform), soft palate, and pharynx [272].

```
                         STRUCTURE OF A TASTE BUD
                                                 
                               TASTE PORE
                                 |  |
                                 v  v
      +-----------------------\      /-----------------------+
      |  STRATIFIED SQUAMOUS   \    /  STRATIFIED SQUAMOUS   |
      |       EPITHELIUM        \  /        EPITHELIUM       |
      |                          ||                          |
      |                   +------++------+                   |
      |                  /  |    ||    |  \                  |
      |                 /   |    ||    |   \                 |
      |                /    |   Micro- |    \                |
      |               |     |   villi  |     |               |
      |               |     |    ||    |     |               |
      |               |  G  |    ||    |  S  |               |
      |               |  U  |    ||    |  U  |               |
      |               |  S  |    ||    |  P  |               |
      |               |  T  |    ||    |  P  |               |
      |               |  A  |    ||    |  O  |               |
      |               |  T  |    ||    |  R  |               |
      |               |  O  |    ||    |  T  |               |
      |               |  R  |    ||    |  I  |               |
      |               |  Y  |    ||    |  N  |               |
      |               |     |    ||    |  G  |               |
      |               |CELL |    ||    |CELL |               |
      |                \    |    ||    |    /                |
      |                 \   +----+-----+   /                 |
      |                  \  BASAL CELLS   /                  |
      +-------------------\==============/-------------------+
                           BASEMENT MEMBRANE
                                  ||
                        GUSTATORY NERVE FIBERS
                   (Synapsing at base of Hair Cells)
```

#### Cellular Elements:
1. **Taste Pore**: Apical micro-opening onto the mucosal surface [153].
2. **Gustatory (Taste / Hair) Cells (Type I and II)**: Spindle-shaped neuroepithelial receptor cells; possess apical microvilli protruding through the pore to bind tastants [18].
3. **Supporting (Sustentacular) Cells**: Provide structural and metabolic support to receptor cells [15].
4. **Basal Cells (Stem Cells)**: Lie at the basement membrane; proliferate and differentiate into mature taste cells (turnover: 10–14 days).
5. **Nerve Endings**: Afferent sensory nerve fibers (CN VII chorda tympani for anterior 2/3rds; CN IX for posterior 1/3rd) invaginate and synapse at the base of the taste cells [9, 99, 272].

*Reference Link*: [Taste Bud Histology Diagram](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1402_The_Taste_Bud.jpg)

note.title: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL)
note.content:
* **Definition**: A sensorineural hearing loss of **≥30 dB across at least three contiguous audiometric frequencies**, developing rapidly within **72 hours or less** [38].
* **Etiology (Mnemonic: "In The Very Ear Too No Major Pathology")** [38]:
  1. *Infectious*: Viral labyrinthitis (mumps, measles, herpes simplex, CMV) [35, 38].
  2. *Vascular*: Labyrinthine arterial spasm, thrombosis, or hemorrhage [38].
  3. *Trauma / Membrane Rupture*: Spontaneous rupture of the round/oval window membrane (perilymph fistula following vigorous sneezing, weightlifting, diving) [38, 48].
  4. *Otologic*: Early Ménière’s disease [38, 111].
  5. *Neoplastic*: Acoustic neuroma (presents as sudden loss in 10–15%) [38, 125].
* **Management Protocol** [38–39]:
  1. Bed rest, avoid straining [38].
  2. **Oral Systemic Corticosteroids (First-Line)**: Prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day, typically 60 mg/day) for 7–14 days, followed by a taper [38].
  3. **Intratympanic Dexamethasone Injections**: Delivers high local inner ear drug concentrations; used as salvage or initial therapy [39, 115].
  4. **Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT)**: Administered within 14 days of onset (2.0–2.5 ATA for 90 min daily) [38, 405–406].
  5. Vasodilators (Carbogen inhalation: 95% O2 + 5% CO2) [38].
* **Prognosis**: ~50–60% recover spontaneously within 2 weeks; poor prognosis if associated with vertigo, severe high-frequency loss, or age >60 years [39, 39t].

---

* **Indications**: Acute coalescent mastoiditis, masked mastoiditis, and as the initial approach for cochlear implantation, endolymphatic sac surgery, or facial nerve decompression [457].

note.title: Theories of Hearing
note.content:
Theories explaining how the cochlea analyzes sound frequency and transmits it to the brain:

1. **Traveling Wave Theory (von Békésy - Accepted Theory)** [17]:
   * Sound vibrations transmitted by the stapes footplate generate fluid waves in the perilymph that displace the basilar membrane [17].
   * The wave travels along the basilar membrane from the base to the apex, reaching **maximum amplitude at a specific, frequency-dependent site**:
     * **High-frequency sounds**: Peak near the narrow, stiff **base of the cochlea** [11, 17, 17f].
     * **Low-frequency sounds**: Peak near the broad, compliant **apex (helicotrema)** [11, 17, 17f].
   * Hair cells at the point of maximum displacement undergo shearing against the tectorial membrane, initiating sensory transduction [15, 17].
2. **Place (Resonance) Theory (Helmholtz)**: Postulated that the basilar membrane behaves like a set of tuned piano strings, with individual transverse fibers resonating to specific sound frequencies.
3. **Telephone (Frequency) Theory (Rutherford)**: Proposed that the cochlea acts like a telephone transmitter, converting sound waves into electrical pulses of identical frequency transmitted along the acoustic nerve.
4. **Volley Principle (Wever)**: States that groups of auditory nerve fibers fire in synchronized volleys to encode frequencies up to 4000–5000 Hz, surpassing the firing rate limit of individual neurons.

---

note.title: Boundaries of Facial Recess (Posterior Sinus)
note.content:
The facial recess is a triangular surgical space on the posterior middle ear wall that allows trans-mastoid access into the mesotympanum (posterior tympanotomy) [6, 7f, 455]:

```
                       FACIAL RECESS BOUNDARIES
                                   
                              FOSSA INCUDIS
                           (Short Process of Incus)
                           ======================== (Superior Boundary)
                                    /    \
                                   /      \
      VERTICAL SEGMENT            /        \  CHORDA TYMPANI NERVE
      OF FACIAL NERVE (CN VII)   /          \ (Lateral Boundary)
      (Medial Boundary)         /            \
                               +--------------+
                                APEX: Junction of VIIth Nerve
                                      & Chorda Tympani
```

1. **Medial Boundary**: The vertical (mastoid) segment of the **Facial Nerve (CN VII)** [6, 7f].
2. **Lateral Boundary**: The **Chorda Tympani Nerve** and tympanic annulus [6, 7f].
3. **Superior Boundary (Base)**: Bony fossa incudis (lodging the short process of the incus) [6, 7f].

* **Diagnosis**: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) [49].
* **Clinical Features**: Recurrent unprovoked torrential epistaxis, progressive nasal obstruction, cheek fullness, conductive hearing loss, and "frog-face" deformity [49].
* **Investigations**: CECT Head/PNS (demonstrates **Holman-Miller sign** / anterior bowing of posterior antral wall), MRI (delineates intracranial/dural involvement), and 4-vessel DSA (maps maxillary artery feeders) [49, 50, 503f]. Biopsy is strictly contraindicated [50].

* **Treatment**: Preoperative trans-arterial embolization followed by complete surgical resection via endoscopic transnasal, transpalatal, or facial translocation/infratemporal approaches [50, 282t].

note.title: Vincent’s Angina
note.content:
* **Definition**: An acute, ulcerative-membranous, necrotizing infection of the tonsil and pharynx [245, 293].
* **Etiology**: Synergistic anaerobic polymicrobial infection by two symbiotic organisms: **Borrelia vincentii** (a spirochete) and **Fusobacterium fusiforme** (a Gram-negative fusiform bacillus) [245, 293]. Predisposed by poor oral hygiene, smoking, nutritional deficiency, and physical exhaustion [245, 293].
* **Clinical Features**:
  * Unilateral sore throat, odynophagia, fetid halitosis, and low-grade pyrexia [245, 293].
  * *Oropharynx*: A deep, ragged, punched-out ulcer on one palatine tonsil covered by a loose, dirty-grey, friable pseudomembrane that sloughs easily, leaving an indurated bleeding base [245, 293].
  * Tender ipsilateral jugulodigastric lymphadenopathy [293].
* **Diagnosis**: Deep swab smear stained with Gram stain / Giemsa demonstrating abundant fusiform bacilli and spirilla [245, 293].
* **Treatment**:
  * Systemic Penicillin (or oral Amoxicillin / Erythromycin for 7–10 days) [245].
  * Oral Metronidazole (400 mg 8-hourly) to eradicate anaerobic spirochetes [245].
  * Warm hydrogen peroxide / sodium bicarbonate oral mouthwashes [245].

---

note.title: Septal Abscess
note.content:
REFER TO Chapter 26 for full etiology and clinical features [168–169].

* **Etiology** [168]:
  * Secondary bacterial suppuration of a neglected **septal hematoma** following nasal trauma (most common) [168].
  * Extension from a furuncle of the upper lip or nasal vestibule [168].
  * Causative organism: *Staphylococcus aureus* [168].
* **Clinical Features** [168]:
  * Severe bilateral nasal obstruction, throbbing local pain, frontal headache, and high fever with chills [168].
  * Marked swelling, redness, and edema of the external nasal dorsum [168].
  * *Anterior Rhinoscopy*: Smooth, bilateral, soft, boggy, exquisitely tender fluctuant swelling of the nasal septum obstructing both nasal cavities [168, 168f].
* **Complications** [168, 169]:
  * Rapid ischemic avascular necrosis of the quadrilateral cartilage within 24–48 hours, causing **supratip saddle nose deformity** [168, 169].
  * Cavernous sinus thrombosis and meningitis (via valveless facial/ophthalmic veins) [169].
* **Treatment** [169]:
  * Emergency incision and drainage: Incision placed in the dependent part of the septal mucosa; pus and necrotic cartilage cleared via suction [168, 169].
  * Bilateral anterior nasal packing to prevent reaccumulation [168].
  * High-dose systemic IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics for 10–14 days [169].

---

note.title: Labyrinthitis
note.content:
Labyrinthitis is an inflammation of the sensory end-organs of the inner ear (vestibule, semicircular canals, and cochlea) [48, 88].

```
                          TYPES OF LABYRINTHITIS
                                     |
         +---------------------------+---------------------------+
         |                                                       |
   CIRCUMSCRIBED                       DIFFUSE SEROUS             DIFFUSE SUPPURATIVE
• Bony erosion of otic capsule      • Non-purulent inflammation • Purulent bacterial invasion
• Lateral semicircular canal        • Secondary to toxins / AOM • Labyrinth destroyed completely
• Fistula test POSITIVE             • Reversible SNHL / vertigo • Irreversible dead ear
• Transient positional vertigo      • Fast component to lesion  • Fast component to good ear
```

1. **Circumscribed Labyrinthitis (Labyrinthine Fistula)** [48, 88]:
   * Thinning or complete erosion of the bony labyrinth (most commonly the horizontal semicircular canal) caused by cholesteatoma [48, 88].
   * Bony wall is breached, but the underlying endosteum and membranous labyrinth remain intact [48, 88].
   * *Features*: Transient positional vertigo on sudden head movements; **positive fistula test** [48, 88].
2. **Diffuse Serous Labyrinthitis** [48, 88–89]:
   * Diffuse non-purulent, sterile inflammation of the inner ear caused by bacterial toxins entering through the oval/round windows or a pre-existing fistula [48, 88–89].
   * *Features*: Severe spinning vertigo, nausea, vomiting, spontaneous nystagmus (fast component toward the diseased ear), and mild-to-moderate sensorineural hearing loss [89].
   * *Significance*: **Potentially reversible** with early IV antibiotics and mastoidectomy [48, 89].
3. **Diffuse Suppurative Labyrinthitis** [48, 89]:
   * Direct pyogenic bacterial invasion of the labyrinth, filling the perilymphatic and endolymphatic spaces with pus [48, 89].
   * *Features*: Violent vertigo, intractable nausea/vomiting, spontaneous nystagmus (fast component directed away toward the healthy ear due to unilateral vestibular paralysis) [89].
   * *Significance*: Causes **permanent, irreversible total destruction of the cochlea and vestibular labyrinth ("dead ear")**, with permanent sensorineural deafness and subsequent labyrinthitis ossificans [89]. High risk of tracking into the subarachnoid space causing meningitis [89].

---

note.title: Ototoxicity
note.content:
REFER TO Chapter 5 for drug classifications and toxic mechanisms [35–36, 36t].

* **Definition**: Damage to the cochlear and/or vestibular neuroepithelium caused by exposure to therapeutic pharmaceuticals or chemicals, resulting in sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and equilibrium disturbances [35].
* **Classification of Common Ototoxic Agents** [35, 36t]:
  1. *Aminoglycoside Antibiotics*:
     * **Cochleotoxic** (destroys outer hair cells starting at the basal turn): Amikacin, Kanamycin, Neomycin, Dihydrostreptomycin [35, 36t].
     * **Vestibulotoxic** (destroys type I sensory hair cells of the cristae): Streptomycin, Gentamicin, Tobramycin [35, 36t].
  2. *Loop Diuretics*: Furosemide, Bumetanide, Ethacrynic acid (inhibit stria vascularis Na+/K+-ATPase, causing edema and fluid shifts) [36, 36t].
  3. *Antineoplastic Agents*: Cisplatin and Carboplatin (cause bilateral high-frequency OHC apoptosis) [36, 36t, 420t].
  4. *Salicylates & NSAIDs*: High-dose aspirin (causes reversible high-frequency sensorineural loss and tinnitus by altering outer hair cell electromotility) [36, 36t].
  5. *Antimalarials*: Quinine, Chloroquine (microvascular vasoconstriction) [36, 36t].
  6. *Iron Chelators*: Deferoxamine [36, 36t].
* **Clinical Monitoring**: Serial pure tone audiometry (high frequencies up to 8–16 kHz) and Otoacoustic Emissions (DPOAEs show reduced amplitudes before clinical hearing loss develops) [29, 35].

---

note.title: Stapes (Draw and Label)
note.content:
The stapes (stirrup) is the smallest bone in the human body, measuring 3.5 mm in height and weighing approximately 3 mg [9, 9f].

```
                          STAPES (RIGHT EAR)
                                              
                        [ HEAD OF STAPES ]
                                |
                          NECK OF STAPES <--- (Insertion of Stapedius Tendon)
                           /          \
                          /            \
              ANTERIOR CRUS            POSTERIOR CRUS
             (Straight, Thin)         (More Curved, Thicker)
                        \                /
                         \              /
                       ====================
                       [  FOOTPLATE OF    ]
                       [     STAPES       ]
                       ====================
                         (Held in the Oval
                        Window by Annular
                            Ligament)
```

#### Anatomical Parts [9, 9f]:
1. **Head (Capitulum)**: Small hemispherical articular surface; articulates with the lenticular process of the incus (incudostapedial synovial joint) [9].
2. **Neck**: Narrow constricted portion immediately below the head; gives insertion posteriorly to the **tendon of the stapedius muscle** (innervated by CN VII) [9].
3. **Anterior Crus**: Slender, relatively straight bony limb [9].
4. **Posterior Crus**: More curved and thicker bony limb [9].
5. **Footplate (Base)**: Thin, flat oval plate of bone closing the fenestra vestibuli (oval window); held in place by the elastic **annular ligament** [9]. Its vestibular surface is bathed in perilymph [11].

*Reference Link*: [Stapes Bone Anatomy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gray908.png)

note.title: Presbyacusis
note.content:
* **Definition**: Symmetrical, bilateral, progressive, sensorineural hearing loss associated with the physiological aging process, typically manifesting after 60–65 years of age [39].
* **Four Pathological Types (Schuknecht’s Classification)** [39]:
  1. *Sensory*: Atrophy of the organ of Corti and hair cells at the basal coil; steep high-frequency hearing loss with preserved speech discrimination [39].
  2. *Neural*: Degeneration of spiral ganglion cells; marked loss of speech discrimination disproportionate to pure-tone thresholds ("phonemic regression") [39].
  3. *Strial (Metabolic)*: Patchy atrophy of the stria vascularis affecting endolymph production; flat audiometric configuration with good speech discrimination [39].
  4. *Cochlear Conductive*: Stiffening/calcification of the basilar membrane; straight, downward-sloping audiometric curve [39].
* **Management**: Binaural digital hearing aids with compression circuits; auditory rehabilitation; speech reading training [39, 135].

---

note.title: Grommet (Tympanostomy Tube)
note.content:
REFER TO Chapter 78 for technical specifications and complications [454].

* **Definition**: A tiny, hour-glass or spool-shaped biocompatible ventilation tube (Teflon, silicone, or titanium) inserted across a radial myringotomy incision in the tympanic membrane [70, 454, 454f].
* **Indications**: Otitis media with effusion refractory to medical therapy for >12 weeks; recurrent acute otitis media; severe eustachian tube dysfunction with atelectasis [70, 453].
* **Mechanism & Function**: Equilibrates middle ear pressure with ambient atmospheric pressure, aerates the middle ear cleft, facilitates mucosal recovery, and provides drainage [61, 70, 454]. Extrudes spontaneously in 6–12 months [70].
* **Complications**: Secondary purulent otorrhea, persistent dry perforation after extrusion, localized tympanosclerosis, and premature extrusion [454].

note.title: Korner’s Septum and its Importance
note.content:
* **Anatomy**: A persistent petrosquamous bony lamina/suture that separates the superficial squamosal mastoid air cells from the deeper petrosal air cells [8, 8f, 509].
* **Surgical Importance** [8, 457, 509]:
  * At mastoidectomy, the surgeon may mistake this false bony plate for the true medial cortical boundary or floor of the antrum [8, 457].
  * Failure to recognize and drill through Korner’s septum leads to **failure to enter the true mastoid antrum**, leaving deep infected petrosal air cells and cholesteatoma unaddressed [8, 457].

questions.officialText: A 55 years old man presented with progressive hoarsness and neck swelling since two months with stridor since one day. Answer the following: /uni25CFWhat is the most probable diagnosis /uni25CFDescribe the clinical features of this condition /uni25CFHow will you investigate the condition /uni25CFHow does the lesion spread /uni25CFWhat is the treatment of this condition (1+2+2+2+3=10)

note.title: 55-Year-Old Male with Progressive Hoarseness, Neck Swelling, and Acute Stridor
note.content:
#### A. Most Probable Diagnosis
**Carcinoma Larynx (Glottic/Transglottic T4a N+)** with thyroid cartilage/soft-tissue invasion and cervical lymph node metastasis, presenting in **acute upper airway obstruction (stridor)** [348t, 349, 350].

---

#### B. Clinical Features of this Condition [349–350]
1. **Progressive Hoarseness**: Earliest, hallmark symptom of glottic cancer; progresses from rough, coarse dysphonia to aphonia [349, 355].
2. **Acute Stridor & Dyspnoea**: Inspiratory and biphasic stridor with suprasternal/intercostal indrawing denoting critical airway narrowing [333, 350].
3. **Neck Mass**: Hard, painless, fixed or mobile metastatic lymph node swelling (typically Level II/III jugulodigastric or jugulo-omohyoid chain) [349, 441, 441t].
4. **Local Spread Symptoms**: Throbbing throat pain radiating to the ipsilateral ear (referred otalgia via CN X), odynophagia, dysphagia, and hemoptysis [143, 349].
5. **Loss of Laryngeal Crepitus**: Thyroid expansion and prevertebral soft-tissue fixation abolishes the normal grating sensation [310, 437].

---

#### C. How to Investigate the Condition
1. **Airway Security First**: Immediate priority; invasive testing is postponed until the compromised airway is secured [350, 481].
2. **Flexible Fiberoptic Video-Laryngoscopy**:
   * Evaluates the exophytic, ulcerative cordal mass, anterior commissure involvement, extension into the ventricle and subglottis, and confirms **fixation/immobility of the true vocal cords** [349, 350, 438].
3. **Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT) of Neck and Larynx**:
   * Delineates **thyroid/cricoid cartilage invasion** and extra-laryngeal spread into strap muscles, pre-epiglottic space, paraglottic space, and thyroid gland [322, 350].
   * Identifies metastatic cervical lymph nodes (Level II to VI) [350, 441].
4. **Direct Laryngoscopy under General Anesthesia with Deep Biopsy**:
   * Inspects hidden areas (subglottis, laryngeal ventricle, apex of pyriform sinus) and confirms histological diagnosis (**Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma**) [347, 351, 481, 508].
5. **Chest Radiograph / CT Chest**: Excludes pulmonary metastases and synchronous second primary lung carcinoma [350].

---

#### D. How the Lesion Spreads
```
                        ROUTES OF LARYNGEAL CANCER SPREAD
                                        |
         +------------------------------+------------------------------+
         |                              |                              |
    DIRECT SPREAD                LYMPHATIC SPREAD               HEMATOGENOUS
• Pre-epiglottic space         • Glottis: Poor lymphatics     • Lungs (most common)
• Paraglottic space              (early lesions rarely spread) • Bone
• Cartilage invasion           • Supraglottic/Subglottic:     • Liver
  (ossified thyroid/cricoid)     Rich lymphatics ->
• Strap muscles & thyroid        Level II, III, IV, VI
```

1. **Direct (Local) Extension** [349–350]:
   * *Anteriorly*: Crosses the anterior commissure (Broyles’ ligament) to invade the contralateral true cord and anterior thyroid angle [349, 507].
   * *Laterally*: Breaches the internal perichondrium to infiltrate the vocalis and thyroarytenoid muscles, entering the **paraglottic space** and eroding through the ossified thyroid lamina into strap muscles and the thyroid gland [322, 349, 350].
   * *Inferiorly*: Spreads into the subglottis and upper trachea, penetrating through the cricothyroid membrane [349, 350].
   * *Superiorly*: Infiltrates the laryngeal ventricle, false cords, and **pre-epiglottic space** [322, 349].
2. **Lymphatic Metastasis** [322, 349–350]:
   * While true vocal cords have minimal lymphatics, extension into the supraglottis or subglottis allows drainage into **upper and middle deep jugular lymph nodes (Levels II, III, IV)** and anterior compartment nodes (pretracheal, prelaryngeal Delphian nodes — Level VI) [322, 350, 440].
3. **Distant (Hematogenous) Metastasis**: Late spread via systemic circulation to lungs (most common), liver, and bones [350].

---

#### E. Treatment of this Condition
1. **Immediate Airway Relief**:
   * Patient presents with acute stridor: Perform an immediate **Awake Tracheostomy under Local Anesthesia** (placed low through the 3rd or 4th tracheal ring, preserving surgical margins for subsequent laryngectomy) [350, 360, 360f].
2. **Definitive Treatment: Combined Radical Surgery with Postoperative Adjuvant Radiotherapy** [351]:
   * **Total Laryngectomy**:
     * En bloc resection of the entire larynx from the tongue base to upper tracheal rings, including the hyoid bone, pre-epiglottic space, and attached strap muscles [351].
     * The pharynx is repaired primarily; the distal tracheal stump is sutured to the lower cervical skin to create a permanent end-tracheostome [351].
   * **Neck Dissection**:
     * Comprehensive neck dissection (ipsilateral or bilateral modified radical/radical neck dissection) clearing Levels II through V, along with central compartment (Level VI) lymphadenectomy [351, 442–443].
   * **Postoperative Adjuvant Chemoradiotherapy**:
     * Indicated for cartilage invasion, positive/close margins, and extracapsular nodal spread: External beam radiation (60–66 Gy) + concurrent Cisplatin [413, 416].
3. **Postoperative Vocal and Physical Rehabilitation**:
   * Speech restoration via **Tracheoesophageal Puncture (TEP)** with a Blom-Singer/Provox voice prosthesis, esophageal speech training, or electrolarynx [352–353, 352t, 353f].

---

note.title: Mastoid Air Cells (Draw and Label)
note.content:
The temporal bone mastoid air cell system functions as a pneumatic reservoir connected to the middle ear [7–8].

```
                     MASTOID AIR CELL TRACTS
                                              
               ZYGOMATIC CELLS (Root of Zygoma)
                     \
                      \     TEGMEN CELLS (Tegmen Tympani)
                       \         |
                        v         v
     [ RETROFACIAL ] <--- [ MASTOID ANTRUM ] ---> [ PERISINUS CELLS ]
         CELLS                    |                (Overlying Sinus Plate)
      (Around CN VII)             v
                          CENTRAL MASTOID TRACT
                                  |
                                  v
                            [ TIP CELLS ]
                         (Medial & Lateral to
                           Digastric Ridge)
                                  |
                        MARGINAL CELLS / SQUAMOSAL CELLS
```

#### Anatomical Groups of Mastoid Air Cells [7–8, 8f]:
1. **Central Cells (Antral & Periantral)**: Surrounding the mastoid antrum [7, 8f].
2. **Tegmen Cells**: Extend superiorly into the tegmen tympani toward the middle fossa dura [7, 8f].
3. **Perisinus Cells**: Directly overlie the sigmoid venous sinus plate [7, 8f].
4. **Zygomatic Cells**: Extend anteriorly into the posterior root of the zygomatic arch [7, 8f].
5. **Retrofacial Cells**: Cluster along the vertical segment of the fallopian canal [7, 8f].
6. **Perilabyrinthine Cells**: Surround the semicircular canals and cochlea (track to petrous apex) [8, 8f].
7. **Tip Cells**: Large cells in the mastoid tip, situated medial and lateral to the digastric ridge [8, 8f].
8. **8. **Marginal Cells**: Lie posterior to the sigmoid sinus plate; can extend posteriorly into the occipital bone [8].
9. **Squamosal Cells**: Extend superiorly into the squamous portion of the temporal bone [8].

*Reference Link*: [Mastoid Air Cells and Middle Ear Cavity](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gray139.png)

note.title: Audiometric Findings in Otosclerosis
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q05]]` (under 2021_MAY) and `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q08]]` (under 2019_JULY) for comprehensive audiological findings [27, 96].

#### Summary of Classical Findings:
1. **Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA)** [96, 96f]:
   * Low-frequency conductive hearing loss with an **Air-Bone (AB) gap** (typically 30–50 dB) [31, 96, 96f].
   * Air conduction thresholds are worst at lower frequencies (125–500 Hz), producing an upward-sloping or horizontal curve [96, 96f].
   * **Carhart’s Notch**: An artificial elevation of bone-conduction thresholds maximum at **2000 Hz (mean 15 dB)** (5 dB at 500 Hz, 10 dB at 1000 Hz, 15 dB at 2000 Hz, and 5 dB at 4000 Hz) due to loss of the normal ossicular inertia component of bone conduction [96, 507]. It completely resolves following successful stapedotomy [96].
2. **Speech Audiometry** [25, 96]:
   * Speech Reception Threshold (SRT) is elevated commensurate with the pure tone average [25].
   * **Speech Discrimination Score (SDS)** remains normal (**90% to 100%**) because cochlear sensorineural reserve is preserved in stapedial fixation [25, 96].
3. **Impedance Audiometry** [27, 97]:
   * **Tympanogram**: Shows a **Type As curve** (normal peak middle ear pressure with reduced compliance amplitude due to increased ossicular stiffness) [27, 27f].
   * **Acoustic (Stapedial) Reflex**: Completely absent (early fixation may exhibit an "on-off" diphasic pattern) [27, 97].

---

note.title: Allergic Fungal Rhino-Sinusitis (AFRS)
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q02]]` (under 2019_JANUARY) for full Bent-Kuhn diagnostic criteria and management [194, 220].

* **Salient Summary**:
  * An IgE-mediated non-invasive fungal hypersensitivity disease of the sinonasal tract (*Dematiaceous fungi*, *Aspergillus*) [220].
  * Characterized by the **Bent-Kuhn criteria**: Type I hypersensitivity (atopy), diffuse bilateral nasal polyposis, expansile hyperdense sinus masses with bone remodeling on CT, thick peanut-butter-like **eosinophilic mucin with Charcot-Leyden crystals**, and non-invasive fungal hyphae identified on GMS staining [194, 220, 504f].
  * Managed by complete functional endoscopic clearance (FESS), postoperative systemic oral corticosteroid taper, and long-term topical intranasal steroid sprays [219, 220].

---

note.title: Grommet (Tympanostomy Tube)
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q11]]` (under 2014_MARCH) and Chapter 78 for technical specifications and complications [70, 454].

* **Definition**: A miniature spool- or collar-button-shaped biocompatible ventilation tube (Teflon, silicone, or titanium) inserted across a myringotomy incision to aerate the middle ear cavity [70, 454, 454f].
* **Indications**:
  1. Otitis media with effusion (glue ear) persistent for >12 weeks refractory to medical treatment [68, 70, 453].
  2. Recurrent acute otitis media (≥3–4 episodes in 6 months) [71, 453].
  3. Severe eustachian tube dysfunction with adhesive atelectasis or persistent negative middle ear pressure [64, 71, 453].
* **Placement**: Inserted through a small radial myringotomy incision in the **anteroinferior quadrant** of the pars tensa under operating microscope visualization [453, 453f].
* **Duration**: Spontaneously extrudes within **6 to 12 months** as the tympanic membrane epithelium migrates laterally [70].

---

note.title: Portex Tracheostomy Tube
note.content:
The Portex tracheostomy tube is a widely used modern synthetic airway cannula [524].

```
                     PORTEX TRACHEOSTOMY TUBE
                                                 
             FLANGE (NECK PLATE)         15 mm CONNECTOR (Ventilator)
              +----------------+             |
              |                |             v
              |    PORTEX      |===========+===+
              |                |           |   |
              +----------------+           |   |
                       \                   |   |
                        \                  |   |
                         \   SHAFT (PVC)   |   |
                          \                |   |
                           \               |   |
                            \              |   |
      INFLATION LINE --------\-------------+   |
            |                 \                |
            v                  \    LOW-PRESSURE/
       PILOT BALLOON            \   HIGH-VOLUME CUFF
     & ONE-WAY VALVE             \     +-------+
                                  \    | (Air) |
                                   \===+=======+=== (BEVELLED DISTAL TIP)
```

* **Material and Properties** [524]:
  * Constructed from **medical-grade Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC)** or silicone [524].
  * **Thermolabile**: Rigid at room temperature to facilitate insertion, but softens at core body temperature (37°C), conforming to the anatomical curvature of the patient's trachea and minimizing mucosal pressure necrosis [524].
  * Impregnated with a longitudinal **radiopaque line** for radiographic verification of tube position [361, 524].
* **Structural Components** [524, 525]:
  1. **Standard 15 mm Machine Connector**: Allows connection to mechanical ventilator tubing, Ambu bags, or closed-circuit anesthesia circuits [524].
  2. **Neck Flange**: Anchors the tube securely to the neck with twill tape ties [360, 524].
  3. **Low-Pressure, High-Volume Inflatable Cuff**: Distends symmetrically within the tracheal lumen, providing an airtight seal for positive-pressure ventilation while preventing aspiration of pharyngeal secretions and blood [524, 525].
  4. **Pilot Balloon with Spring-Loaded One-Way Valve**: Indicates cuff inflation status and pressure [525].
* **Clinical Advantages Over Metal Tubes** [524]:
  * Disposable (reduces cross-infection risk) [524].
  * Flexible and atraumatic to delicate tracheal rings [361, 524].
  * The low-pressure cuff allows safe artificial mechanical ventilation in ICU settings [524].

---

note.title: Objective Tinnitus
note.content:
* **Definition**: An abnormal sound perceived by the patient that can also be detected and heard by an examiner using a stethoscope or auscultation tube placed over the ear, mastoid, or neck [145, 145t].

```
                          OBJECTIVE TINNITUS
                                  |
         +------------------------+------------------------+
         |                        |                        |
  VASCULAR ORIGIN          PALATAL MYOCLONUS         PATULOUS TUBE
• Pulsatile sound          • Clicking noise          • Blowing / Rushing sound
• Synchronous with pulse   • Rhythmic contractions   • Synchronous with
• Glomus tumors, AV        • Tensor veli palatini      respiration
  fistulae, Carotid bruits   muscle twitching        • Autophony of own voice
```

* **Causes and Classifications** [145, 145t]:
  1. **Pulsatile Vascular Tinnitus (Synchronous with Arterial Pulse)** [145, 145t]:
     * *Vascular Neoplasms*: Glomus jugulare and glomus tympanicum tumors (pulsatile swishing sound temporarily abolished by ipsilateral carotid compression) [121, 145].
     * *Arteriovenous Malformations (AVMs) and Carotid-Cavernous Fistulae* [145t, 238].
     * *Arterial Stenosis or Carotid Aneurysms*: Generates an audible turbulent bruit [145t].
     * *Benign Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri)*: Venous hum over the lateral sinus [145t].
     * *Anatomical Dehiscences*: High-riding dehiscent jugular bulb, persistent stapedial artery [145t].
  2. **Neuromuscular / Myoclonic Tinnitus (Clicking Tinnitus)** [145, 145t]:
     * **Palatal Myoclonus**: Rapid, involuntary, rhythmic clonic twitching of the tensor veli palatini or levator veli palatini muscles (producing a rhythmic clicking sound, 60–120 beats/min) [145, 145t].
     * **Middle Ear Myoclonus**: Spasmodic clonic contractions of the stapedius or tensor tympani muscles [145, 145t].
  3. **Respiratory Synchronous Tinnitus**:
     * **Patulous Eustachian Tube**: Abnormally patent eustachian tube allows direct transmission of nasopharyngeal airflow, producing a roaring, rushing sound synchronous with respiration, accompanied by autophony [65, 145t].
  4. **Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ) Clicking**: Clicking sound produced on chewing or jaw opening due to meniscus subluxation [143, 145t].

---

note.title: Tympanic Plexus
note.content:
The tympanic plexus is an autonomic and sensory neural meshwork situated in shallow grooves over the **promontory** of the medial wall of the middle ear [9, 145, 509].

```
                     COMPOSITION OF TYMPANIC PLEXUS
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                                                   |
TYMPANIC BRANCH OF CN IX                             CAROTICOTYMPANIC NERVES
 (Jacobson's Nerve)                                  (Sympathetic Fibers from
• Sensory to middle ear mucosa,                       Internal Carotid Plexus)
  Eustachian tube & mastoid                          • Vasomotor to mucosa
• Preganglionic Parasympathetic
  secretomotor fibers to parotid
                                   |
                                   v
                         [ TYMPANIC PLEXUS ]
                            (Promontory)
                                   |
                                   v
                         LESSER PETROSAL NERVE
                                   |
                                   v
                             OTIC GANGLION
                                   |  (Relay)
                                   v
                        AURICULOTEMPORAL NERVE
                                   |
                                   v
                            PAROTID GLAND
                         (Secretomotor Flow)
```

* **Contributors to the Plexus** [9, 509]:
  1. **Jacobson’s Nerve (Tympanic branch of Glossopharyngeal Nerve, CN IX)**: Enters the middle ear through the inferior tympanic canaliculus between the jugular fossa and carotid canal [9, 509].
  2. **Caroticotympanic Nerves (Superior and Inferior)**: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers derived from the plexus around the internal carotid artery [9, 507].
  3. Communicating branch from the greater superficial petrosal nerve (variable) [9].
* **Branches and Distribution** [9]:
  * *Sensory Innervation*: Supplies sensation to the mucosal lining of the middle ear, mastoid air cells, tympanic antrum, and bony portion of the eustachian tube [9].
  * *Secretomotor Pathway to Parotid*: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers coalesce and exit the middle ear as the **Lesser Petrosal Nerve**, traversing the foramen ovale to synapse in the **Otic Ganglion** [9]. Postganglionic fibers travel via the **auriculotemporal nerve** to supply secretomotor function to the **parotid salivary gland** [9].
* **Clinical Significance**:
  * **Tympanic Neurectomy**: Surgical sectioning of the tympanic plexus across the promontory can be performed to treat **Frey’s syndrome (gustatory sweating)** and chronic intractable sialorrhea [9, 108, 508].

*Reference Link*: [Tympanic Plexus on Promontory of Middle Ear](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gray911.png)

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology

note.title: Four Major Complications of FESS (Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery)
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q14]]` (Chapter 90) for full complications table [479, 479t].

1. **Intraorbital Hemorrhage / Retrobulbar Hematoma**:
   * Caused by injury to the anterior ethmoidal artery or penetration through the lamina papyracea, producing rapid intraorbital hypertension, optic nerve ischemia, and **permanent blindness** within 60–90 minutes unless decompressed by urgent lateral canthotomy [478, 479, 479t].
2. **Direct Optic Nerve Injury**:
   * Direct mechanical trauma from micro-instruments or debriders, particularly in the posterior ethmoid area or within an **Onodi cell** (sphenoethmoid air cell lateral to the sphenoid sinus) [153, 478, 479t].
3. **Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Leak and Meningitis**:
   * Perforation of the fovea ethmoidalis, lateral lamella of the cribriform plate (Keros classification area of weakness), or roof of the sphenoid, causing dural tears, CSF rhinorrhea, pneumocephalus, meningitis, or frontal lobe trauma [184, 478, 479t].
4. **Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) Laceration / Massive Hemorrhage**:
   * Penetration through a dehiscent lateral wall of the sphenoid sinus causing catastrophic arterial hemorrhage that can be fatal [210, 479, 479t].

---

note.title: What is Schwartze’s Sign and its Clinical Importance?
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q16]]` (under 2017_AUGUST) for clinical description [96, 510].

* **Definition**: A pinkish or reddish-orange vascular blush (flamingo-pink sign) seen through an intact, translucent tympanic membrane over the promontory of the middle ear [96, 510].
* **Clinical Importance** [96–97, 510]:
  1. Indicates an **active, florid, hypervascular otospongiotic focus** in the underlying bony otic capsule [96, 510].
  2. Identifies patients at high risk of rapid progression and sensorineural hearing loss (cochlear otosclerosis) [95, 96].
  3. Acts as an indication for medical therapy with **Sodium Fluoride (20–40 mg daily)** to promote remineralization and maturation of the active spongy bone [97].
  4. Alerts the surgeon to proceed with caution or postpone stapedectomy, as surgical intervention in this vascular phase carries a higher risk of troublesome bleeding, postoperative granuloma formation, and sensorineural hearing loss [97].

---

note.title: Name Four Arteries Supplying Little’s Area
note.content:
REFER TO `[[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q07]]` (under 2021_MAY) for labeled arterial confluence diagram and clinical role [197, 198f].

1. **Anterior Ethmoidal Artery**: Branch of the ophthalmic artery (from the **Internal Carotid Artery** system) [197].
2. **Sphenopalatine Artery (Septal Branch)**: Terminal branch of the maxillary artery (from the **External Carotid Artery** system) [197].
3. **Greater Palatine Artery (Septal Branch)**: Branch of the maxillary artery entering via the incisive canal (from the **External Carotid Artery** system) [197].
4. **Superior Labial Artery (Septal Branch)**: Branch of the facial artery (from the **External Carotid Artery** system) [197].

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: A 25 year old male patient complaints of left sided throat pain since 3 days associated with chills and rigors and left ear pain. On examination palatine tonsil, pillars and soft palate on left side are congested and swollen, with uvula pushed to right side and trismus. Left jugulodigastric lymph nodes are enlarged and tender. a) What is the most likely diagnosis b) What are the aetiopathogenesis c) Write the investigations with expected findings and complications of this condition d) What are the treatment modalities of this patient (1+3+3+3)

note.title: Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy)
note.content:
#### a) Most Likely Diagnosis
* **Left Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy)** with secondary referred otalgia and ipsilateral acute jugulodigastric lymphadenitis.

```
       Normal Palate             Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy)
    +-------------------+             +-------------------+
    |    [ ] Uvula [ ]  |             |      \  Uvula     |  <-- Pushed to
    |   /           \   |             |   **  \       [ ] |      contralateral
    | [T]           [T] |             |  ****      |      |      side
    |  L             R  |             | (BULGE)   [T]     |  <-- Left palate &
    +-------------------+             +-------------------+      tonsil swollen
```

#### b) Aetiopathogenesis
1. **Anatomical Basis:** 
   * The peritonsillar space lies between the fibrous capsule of the palatine tonsil medially and the superior constrictor muscle laterally. It is filled with loose, vascular areolar tissue.
   * Superiorly, this space communicates with the supratonsillar fossa and the glands of Weber (salivary glands in the supratonsillar fossa).
2. **Mechanism of Infection:**
   * It usually arises as a complication of acute follicular tonsillitis.
   * Infection in the deep tonsillar crypts (especially the **crypta magna**) leads to cryptitis and localized microabscess formation.
   * The microabscess penetrates the thin capsule of the tonsil into the surrounding loose areolar tissue of the peritonsillar space.
   * This leads first to **peritonsillar cellulitis (peritonsillitis)**, followed by tissue liquefaction and pus accumulation forming a **quinsy (abscess)**.
   * Suppuration in the supratonsillar salivary glands of Weber also contributes to abscess formation in the upper pole.
3. **Bacteriology:**
   * Usually polymicrobial:
     * **Aerobes:** *Streptococcus pyogenes* (Group A beta-haemolytic), *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*.
     * **Anaerobes:** *Fusobacterium necrophorum*, *Bacteroides fragilis*, *Peptostreptococcus*.
4. **Clinical Manifestations Explained:**
   * **Trismus:** Caused by irritation and reflex spasm of the internal (medial) pterygoid muscle, which lies immediately lateral to the superior constrictor.
   * **Referred Otalgia:** Mediated by the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (**Jacobson's nerve**) via the tympanic plexus, as cranial nerve IX supplies sensory fibers to both the tonsillar bed and middle ear.
   * **Hot Potato Voice:** Due to oedema of the soft palate and impaired mobility of the palate, leading to a muffled, thick speech.
   * **Contralateral Uvular Deviation:** Asymmetrical swelling of the anterior pillar and soft palate pushes the oedematous uvula towards the healthy side.

#### c) Investigations and Expected Findings & Complications
##### Investigations
* **Diagnostic Needle Aspiration:** 
  * A 16–18 G needle mounted on a 10 mL syringe is inserted into the point of maximum bulge (after topical spray). Aspiration of frank, thick, foul-smelling pus confirms the abscess and differentiates it from simple cellulitis. The pus is sent for Gram stain, aerobic, and anaerobic culture and sensitivity.
* **Complete Blood Count (CBC):** 
  * Marked polymorphonuclear leukocytosis (>12,000–15,000/cu mm) with an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP).
* **Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT) of Neck:** 
  * Indicated if trismus prevents direct view or if deep neck extension is suspected.
  * *Expected Finding:* A hypodense, non-enhancing fluid collection surrounded by an irregular, brightly enhancing peripheral rim in the left peritonsillar bed with medial displacement of the left tonsil.

##### Complications
* **Intratemporal & Local Extension:**
  * Parapharyngeal space abscess (quinsy is a direct portal into the prestyloid compartment).
  * Retropharyngeal space abscess.
  * Laryngeal oedema leading to life-threatening acute airway obstruction.
* **Vascular Complications:**
  * Thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with septic emboli (**Lemierre syndrome**).
  * Erosion or pseudoaneurysm of the internal carotid artery, resulting in fatal rupture ("carotid blowout").
* **Pulmonary Complications:**
  * Spontaneous rupture of quinsy during sleep or anesthesia resulting in pulmonary aspiration, asphyxia, or lung abscess.
* **Systemic Complications:**
  * Septicaemia, toxic shock syndrome, metastatic abscesses.

#### d) Treatment Modalities
```
                      MANAGEMENT OF QUINSY
                               |
       +-----------------------+-----------------------+
       |                                               |
Medical Therapy                               Surgical Intervention
  - Hospitalization & IV access                 - Needle Aspiration
  - IV Fluids (hydration)                       - Incision & Drainage (I&D)
  - IV Antibiotics (Amox-Clav + Metronidazole)   - Abscess / Hot Tonsillectomy
  - Analgesics (Paracetamol / NSAIDs)           - Interval Tonsillectomy (at 4-6 wk)
  - Antiseptic Mouthwash
```
1. **Immediate Supportive & Medical Care:**
   * **Hospitalization & IV Hydration:** Correct dehydration resulting from severe odynophagia.
   * **Intravenous Antibiotics:** Broad-spectrum empirical therapy covering aerobes and anaerobes:
     * IV Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (1.2 g IV 8-hourly) **OR** Cefotaxime/Ceftriaxone (1 g IV 12-hourly) **PLUS** IV Metronidazole (500 mg IV 8-hourly).
   * **Analgesics & Antipyretics:** Paracetamol infusion or IV Diclofenac; avoids oral drugs initially due to severe pain.
   * **Oral Hygiene:** Warm saline gargles or 1.5% hydrogen peroxide mouth rinses.
2. **Incision and Drainage (I&D):**
   * Definitive surgical evacuation under local anesthesia (10% lignocaine spray).
   * **Site of Drainage:** 
     1. Point of maximum fluctuance/bulge, **OR**
     2. The intersection of an imaginary horizontal line through the base of the uvula and a vertical line along the anterior faucial pillar.
   * **Procedure:** A guarded knife (blade wrapped in adhesive plaster leaving only the distal 0.5–1 cm exposed) makes a stab incision. A sinus forceps or quinsy forceps is introduced into the cavity and spread open widely to break down loculi. Pus is evacuated by continuous suction.
3. **Tonsillectomy Options:**
   * **Interval Tonsillectomy:** Performed **4 to 6 weeks** after complete resolution of the acute episode. Indicated in young children, patients with a prior history of chronic recurrent tonsillitis, or second attacks of quinsy.
   * **Abscess ("Hot") Tonsillectomy:** Tonsillectomy performed concurrently under general anesthesia during the acute phase. Indicated when quinsy occurs in uncooperative young children, failed drainage with worsening airway distress, or suspected underlying neoplasm.

---

note.title: Fibrous Dysplasia of Maxilla
note.content:
* **Definition:** A non-neoplastic, benign fibro-osseous bone condition characterized by progressive replacement of normal bony architecture and marrow by cellular fibrous connective tissue interspersed with irregular, poorly formed woven bone trabeculae.
* **Etiology & Genetics:** Caused by a postzygotic activating somatic mutation in the *GNAS1* gene (encoding the alpha subunit of Gs stimulatory protein), resulting in autonomous osteoblast proliferation and abnormal bone deposition.
* **Forms:**
  1. *Monostotic:* Involves a single bone (maxilla is most common in the head and neck; ~70%).
  2. *Polyostotic:* Involves multiple bones (~30%).
  3. *McCune-Albright Syndrome:* Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia + endocrine dysfunction (precocious puberty) + café-au-lait skin pigmentation.
* **Clinical Features:**
  * Predominantly presents in children and young adults (first to second decade of life).
  * Painless, slow-growing, unilateral, smooth bony swelling of the maxilla.
  * Causes facial asymmetry, elevation of the orbital floor (proptosis, diplopia), obliteration of the canine fossa, nasal obstruction, and dental malocclusion.
* **Radiological Findings:**
  * **CT Scan (Gold Standard):** Characteristic **"ground-glass"** appearance with expansion of the cortical envelope, ill-defined blending margins with surrounding normal bone, and maintenance of a thin, intact outer cortex.
* **Management:**
  * **Watchful Waiting:** Most lesions stabilize ("burn out") after puberty when skeletal maturation is attained.
  * **Surgical Re-contouring / Shaving:** Indicated for severe facial disfigurement or functional impairment (nasal airway compromise, visual distortion due to optic canal narrowing). Total resection is rarely necessary and often morbid.
  * **Contraindication:** **Radiotherapy is strictly contraindicated** as it carries a high risk (0.5–1%) of malignant transformation into osteosarcoma or fibrosarcoma.

note.title: Management of Chronic Maxillary Sinusitis
note.content:
* **Definition:** Persistent inflammation of the mucosal lining of the maxillary sinus lasting longer than 12 consecutive weeks, characterized by mucociliary clearance failure and ostial blockage.

#### 1. Medical Management (First-Line Therapy)
* **Saline Nasal Irrigations:** High-volume, low-pressure isotonic or hypertonic alkaline nasal washes to clear crusts, dilute viscid mucus, and disrupt bacterial biofilms.
* **Intranasal Corticosteroid Sprays:** Fluticasone propionate (2 sprays/nostril OD) or Mometasone furoate to reduce ostiomeatal complex mucosal oedema.
* **Prolonged Antibacterial Therapy:** Guided by endoscopically directed middle meatal swab culture:
  * Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (625 mg TID) or Cefuroxime axetil (500 mg BD) along with Clindamycin or Metronidazole (for anaerobes) for 3–4 weeks.
  * In refractory cases, low-dose, long-term macrolides (e.g., Clarithromycin 250 mg OD for 12 weeks) are used for their immunomodulatory and anti-biofilm properties.
* **Systemic Decongestants & Mucolytics:** Pseudoephedrine and oral guaifenesin/N-acetylcysteine.

#### 2. Surgical Management (Indicated on Failure of Medical Therapy)
1. **Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS) with Middle Meatal Antrostomy (MMA) — Standard of Care:**
   * Restores physiological mucociliary clearance via the natural ostium.
   * *Steps:* Uncinectomy $\rightarrow$ identification of the natural maxillary ostium in the infundibulum $\rightarrow$ enlargement of the ostium posteriorly and inferiorly into the fontanelle $\rightarrow$ clearance of intrasinus diseased mucosa/polyps preserving healthy respiratory epithelium.
2. **Historic & Open Procedures:**
   * **Antral Puncture and Lavage (Proof Puncture):** Puncture of inferior meatus with a Lichtwitz trocar to aspirate and flush the sinus.
   * **Intranasal Inferior Meatal Antrostomy:** Creation of a non-physiological dependent window in the inferior meatus.
   * **Caldwell–Luc Operation:** Sublabial approach through the canine fossa; used when FESS is impossible, in severe trauma, or for removal of foreign bodies/tumours.

---

note.title: Singer’s Nodule (Vocal Nodule)
note.content:
* **Definition:** Bilateral, symmetrical, localized, inflammatory, benign fibroepithelial lesions located at the free margin of the vocal folds.
* **Site of Predilection:** Exactly at the **junction of the anterior one-third and posterior two-thirds** of the true vocal cords (the mid-point of the membranous vocal fold). This is the point of maximum mechanical amplitude of vibration and maximal shearing impact during phonation.
* **Aetiopathogenesis:**
  * Caused by chronic voice abuse, misuse, or hyperfunctional phonation (frequently seen in school teachers, singers, actors, vendors, and hyperactive children — "screamer's nodes").
  * Mechanical trauma $\rightarrow$ submucosal capillary haemorrhage and oedema in the superficial layer of lamina propria (**Reinke's space**) $\rightarrow$ hyalinization $\rightarrow$ organization with fibroblastic proliferation $\rightarrow$ overlying stratified squamous epithelial hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis.
* **Clinical Stages & Features:**
  * **Symptoms:** Persistent, painless hoarseness (rough, breathy voice), vocal fatigue, pitch instability, inability to sing higher registers.
  * **Signs (Indirect Laryngoscopy / Videostroboscopy):**
    * *Early nodules:* Soft, red, oedematous, pin-point swellings.
    * *Mature/Late nodules:* Pale, white, firm, fibrotic, symmetrical, cornified nodules. An hourglass glottic chink is noted on phonation.
* **Management:**
  1. **Conservative (Primary & Mandatory First Step):**
     * Absolute voice rest (short term) followed by **vocal hygiene and speech therapy** (voice therapy directed by a speech-language pathologist). Corrects hyperfunctional vocal behavior; cures >80% of early nodules.
     * Treatment of concurrent GERD/LPR (proton pump inhibitors) and allergy.
  2. **Phonomicrosurgery:**
     * Indicated only for mature, fibrous, longstanding nodules that fail structured voice therapy.
     * Excision using cold microlaryngeal instruments or pulse-mode $\text{CO}_2$ laser with strict preservation of the underlying intermediate/deep vocal ligament layers to avoid scarring and permanent dysphonia.
     * Postoperative voice therapy is mandatory to prevent recurrence.

---

  2. **Choanae (Posterior Nasal Apertures):** Paired oval apertures communicating with nasal cavities.

  8. **Roof and Posterior Wall:** Showing lymphoid adenoid tissue (in children) or smooth mucosa.
  9. **Upper Surface of Soft Palate and Uvula:** Lies inferiorly.

note.title: Nasal Myiasis (Maggots in Nose)
note.content:
* **Definition & Aetiology:** Infestation of the nasal cavities and paranasal sinuses by the living larvae (maggots) of flies, most commonly *Chrysomyia bezziana* (screwworm fly).
* **Precipitating Factors:** Endemic in tropical regions; strongly associated with poor personal hygiene, low socioeconomic status, advanced atrophic rhinitis (ozaena), syphilis, leprosy, open wounds, and unconscious or debilitated patients. The fly is attracted by the fetid odour of nasal discharge and deposits hundreds of eggs in the nostrils.
* **Clinical Features:**
  * **Stage 1 (Initial 3–4 days):** Severe tickling, sneezing, lacrimation, headache, serosanguinous discharge, and facial puffiness.
  * **Stage 2 (Larval activity):** Maggots burrow deeply, feeding on living and necrotic tissue, bone, and cartilage. Profuse epistaxis, intensely foul-smelling purulent discharge, necrosis of the nasal septum (perforation), hard palate perforation, orbital cellulitis, and loss of the eyeball can occur.
  * **Stage 3:** Meningitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, and fatal intracranial complications.
* **Treatment:**
  1. **Asphyxiation & Mobilization:** Instillation of **chloroform water and light liquid paraffin or turpentine oil (1:4 ratio)** into the nasal cavity. This paralyzes and asphyxiates the larvae, forcing them to loosen their hooks.
  2. **Mechanical Extraction:** Dead or paralyzed maggots are manually picked under direct endoscopic guidance using Tilley's or Hartmann's forceps.
  3. **Saline Irrigation:** Frequent warm alkaline nasal douching to wash out dead larvae, slough, and crusts.
  4. **Systemic Management:** Broad-spectrum antibiotics to control secondary pyogenic infection; single-dose oral Ivermectin (200 $\mu\text{g/kg}$) is effective in extensive infestations. Treat the underlying atrophic rhinitis.

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Technique and interpretation of absolute bone conduction test

note.title: Technique and Interpretation of Absolute Bone Conduction (ABC) Test
note.content:
* **Principle:** Bone conduction is a direct measure of sensorineural (cochlear) function. The ABC test measures the patient's bone conduction threshold while eliminating ambient room noise (occlusion of external acoustic meatus), comparing it with the examiner's hearing (presumed to be normal).

#### Technique
1. A **512 Hz tuning fork** is struck against the examiner's thenar eminence/elbow.
2. The vibrating fork's footplate is placed firmly on the patient's mastoid process.
3. The examiner immediately occludes the patient's external auditory meatus by tragal compression using a finger.
4. When the patient signals that the sound is no longer heard, the fork is transferred immediately to the examiner's own mastoid while the examiner's own tragus is occluded.
5. The duration of tone perception is compared between the patient and the examiner.

#### Interpretation
| Condition | Finding | Pathophysiological Interpretation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Normal Hearing** | Patient hears the sound for the same duration as the examiner. | Intact cochlear and retrocochlear pathway. |
| **Conductive Hearing Loss** | Patient hears the sound for the same duration as the examiner (Normal ABC). | Cochlear function is completely normal; defect lies only in the sound-conducting apparatus. |
| **Sensorineural Hearing Loss** | Patient stops hearing earlier than the examiner (**Reduced / Shortened ABC**). | Damage to the hair cells of the organ of Corti or the cochlear nerve. |

---

note.title: Little’s Area
note.content:
* **Location:** Located on the anteroinferior part of the cartilaginous nasal septum, approximately 1.5 cm behind the anterior naris and just above the vestibular skin.
* **Clinical Significance:** 
  * It is the site of **Kiesselbach’s arterial plexus**.
  * It is responsible for over **90% of cases of epistaxis** (anterior epistaxis), especially in children and young adults, due to its exposed position to inspiratory drying currents and digital fingernail trauma.
* **Constituents of Kiesselbach's Plexus (Anastomosis of 4 Arteries):**
  1. **Anterior Ethmoidal Artery** (Septal branch) — *Internal Carotid Artery system* (via Ophthalmic artery).
  2. **Sphenopalatine Artery** (Nasopalatine branch) — *External Carotid Artery system* (via Maxillary artery).
  3. **Greater Palatine Artery** (Septal branch) — *External Carotid Artery system* (via Maxillary artery).
  4. **Superior Labial Artery** (Septal branch) — *External Carotid Artery system* (via Facial artery).
* **Associated Venous Plexus:** The **retrocolumellar vein** runs vertically behind the columella just anterior to Little's area, frequently causing venous bleeding in young adults.

---

note.title: Theories of Hearing
note.content:
The conversion of airborne sound waves into perceived neural impulses is explained by classical physiological theories:

1. **Travelling Wave Theory of Georg von Békésy (Most Accepted Theory):**
   * Stapes footplate vibrations generate travelling waves in the incompressible perilymph of the scala vestibuli.
   * This displaces the basilar membrane. The wave travels from base to apex, gradually building up amplitude to reach a specific maximum at a localized point, and then dies out rapidly.
   * **Tonotopic Frequency Organization:**
     * The basilar membrane at the **cochlear base** is narrow, stiff, and taut $\rightarrow$ responds maximally to **high-frequency sounds**.
     * The basilar membrane at the **cochlear apex** is wide, flaccid, and loose $\rightarrow$ responds maximally to **low-frequency sounds**.
2. **Helmholtz's Resonance (Place) Theory:**
   * Postulated that the transverse fibers of the basilar membrane act like vibrating strings of a piano or harp, each segment resonating selectively to a specific frequency.
3. **Rutherford’s Telephone Theory:**
   * Postulated that the basilar membrane vibrates as a whole, mimicking a telephone transmitter, and the frequency analysis is performed centrally in the cerebral cortex.
4. **Wever’s Volley Principle:**
   * For sound frequencies above 1000 Hz (up to 4000–5000 Hz), where single nerve fibers cannot fire at corresponding rates due to refractory periods, groups of auditory nerve fibers fire in sequential "volleys", phase-locked to the sound cycle.

---

note.title: Presbycusis
note.content:
* **Definition:** Bilateral, symmetrical, progressive sensorineural hearing loss associated with physiological aging, typically manifesting past 60–65 years of age.
* **Schuknecht’s Clinicopathological Classification:**
  1. **Sensory Presbycusis:**
     * *Pathology:* Epithelial atrophy with loss of sensory hair cells and supporting cells in the basal turn of the organ of Corti.
     * *Audiogram:* Abrupt, steeply down-sloping high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss; speech discrimination remains well-preserved.
  2. **Neural Presbycusis:**
     * *Pathology:* Loss of neurons in the spiral ganglion and central auditory pathways (>50% neuron loss occurs with age).
     * *Audiogram:* Flat or gently sloping curve; marked, disproportionate loss of speech discrimination (**phonemic regression** — "hears sound but cannot understand words").
  3. **Strial / Metabolic Presbycusis:**
     * *Pathology:* Patchy atrophy and vascular degeneration throughout the stria vascularis, impairing endolymph production and endocochlear DC potential (+80 mV "battery").
     * *Audiogram:* Characteristically flat audiogram across all frequencies with excellent speech discrimination.
  4. **Cochlear Conductive (Mechanical) Presbycusis:**
     * *Pathology:* Stiffening and calcification of the basilar membrane and spiral ligament hyalinization.
     * *Audiogram:* Smooth, linear, gently down-sloping audiometric curve.
* **Clinical Characteristics:** Difficulty hearing in background noise (cocktail party effect), recruitment positive, bilateral high-pitched tinnitus.
* **Rehabilitation:** Binaural behind-the-ear (BTE) or in-the-canal (ITC) digital hearing aids with wide dynamic range compression (WDRC), assistive listening devices, speech reading, and cochlear implants in profound cases.

---

note.title: Causes of Referred Otalgia
note.content:
Referred otalgia occurs because sensory nerves supplying the ear (cranial nerves V, IX, X, and cervical nerves C2, C3) share central neural pathways with distant head and neck sites:

```
                  PATHWAYS OF REFERRED OTALGIA
                               |
   +------------+--------------+--------------+------------+
   |            |                             |            |
  CN V         CN IX                         CN X        C2, C3
(Auriculo-   (Jacobson's                   (Arnold's    (Greater Auricular,
 temporal)      Nerve)                        Nerve)      Lesser Occipital)
   |            |                             |            |
Dental caries  Acute tonsillitis            Laryngeal    Cervical spondylosis
Impacted molar Quinsy, Tonsil cancer        malignancy   Cervical spine injury
TMJ arthritis  Base of tongue cancer        Pyriform CA  Cervical lymphadenitis
Mouth ulcers   Elongated styloid (Eagle)    Vallecula CA
```

1. **Via Mandibular Division of Trigeminal Nerve (CN $V_3$) through Auriculotemporal Nerve:**
   * Carious lower molars, impacted third molars, apical dental abscesses.
   * Temporomandibular joint dysfunction (Costen syndrome).
   * Carcinoma or ulcerative lesions of the oral tongue, floor of mouth, or buccal mucosa.
2. **Via Glossopharyngeal Nerve (CN IX) through Tympanic Branch (Jacobson’s Nerve):**
   * Acute tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), post-tonsillectomy slough.
   * Malignancy of the palatine tonsil, anterior pillar, or base of the tongue.
   * Elongated styloid process (**Eagle syndrome**).
3. **Via Vagus Nerve (CN X) through Auricular Branch (Arnold’s Nerve):**
   * Carcinoma of the pyriform sinus, postcricoid area, vallecula, or supraglottic larynx.
   * Ulcerative conditions and foreign bodies of the hypopharynx and upper cervical oesophagus.
4. **Via Cervical Nerves (C2, C3) through Greater Auricular and Lesser Occipital Nerves:**
   * Cervical spondylosis, whiplash injury, caries of cervical vertebrae, and tender upper cervical lymphadenitis.

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Topodiagnostic tests for lesions in intratemporal part of facial nerve

note.title: Topodiagnostic Tests for Intratemporal Lesions of Facial Nerve
note.content:
These tests localize the site of facial nerve compromise along its bony intratemporal path:

1. **Schirmer’s Test (Tests Greater Superficial Petrosal Nerve / Lacrimation):**
   * *Site:* Geniculate ganglion or proximal (labyrinthine segment).
   * *Method:* Strips of filter paper folded into lower conjunctival fornices for 5 minutes. >50% reduction in unilateral wetting indicates a lesion at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion.
2. **Acoustic Stapedial Reflex (Tests Nerve to Stapedius):**
   * *Site:* Tympanic or vertical mastoid segment proximal to the pyramidal eminence.
   * *Method:* Impedance tympanometry with loud acoustic stimulation (70–100 dB SL). Absence of stapedial reflex with normal hearing confirms a lesion proximal to the nerve to stapedius.
3. **Electrogustometry / Chemical Taste Test (Tests Chorda Tympani):**
   * *Site:* Mastoid segment proximal to the takeoff of chorda tympani.
   * *Method:* Application of sugar, salt, citric acid, and quinine solutions to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Impaired or absent taste perception localizes the lesion above the exit of chorda tympani.
4. **Submandibular Salivary Flow Test (Blatt’s Test — Tests Chorda Tympani Secretomotor Fibres):**
   * *Method:* Cannulation of both Wharton’s ducts with polyethylene tubes; saliva drop output is stimulated with 6% citric acid on the tongue. A reduction in salivary flow >25% on the affected side indicates chorda tympani denervation.

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Aetiology of perforation of nasal septum

note.title: Aetiology of Perforation of Nasal Septum
note.content:
1. **Traumatic / Iatrogenic (Most Common):**
   * Complication of submucous resection (SMR) or septoplasty due to opposing tears of bilateral mucoperichondrial flaps.
   * Habitual digital nose picking (**ulcus septi perforans** of Hajek).
   * Chemical cautery (silver nitrate/trichloroacetic acid) or galvanocautery for epistaxis applied symmetrically to opposing septal sides.
   * Neglected septal haematoma or septal abscess leading to ischemic chondronecrosis.
   * Longstanding retained unilateral nasal foreign body or rhinolith.
2. **Infective & Chronic Granulomatous Diseases:**
   * *Cartilaginous Septum:* Lupus vulgaris, tuberculosis, leprosy.
   * *Bony Septum:* Tertiary syphilis (gumma of the vomer/perpendicular plate).
   * *Midline Destructive Lesions:* Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener’s), sinonasal NK/T-cell lymphoma.
3. **Chemicals & Drugs:**
   * Chronic illicit intranasal cocaine snorting (causes intense local vasospasm and ischemic necrosis).
   * Chronic exposure to industrial dust/vapours: Chromium plating, arsenic, mercury, sodium carbonate.
   * Prolonged, improper topical nasal corticosteroid spray directed straight onto the anterior nasal septum.
4. **Neoplastic:** Squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, malignant melanoma of the nasal septum.

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Pathology of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo

note.title: Pathology of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
note.content:
* **Definition:** A peripheral vestibular end-organ disorder presenting as brief, episodic, violent vertigo and rotatory nystagmus provoked by specific changes in head position relative to gravity.
* **Underlying Pathophysiological Mechanisms:**
  1. **Source of Pathology:** Degeneration, fragmentation, and shedding of dense calcium carbonate ($CaCO_3$) crystals (**otoconia / statoconia**) from the otolithic gelatinous membrane of the **utricular macula** (due to head trauma, labyrinthitis, vestibular neuronitis, ischemia, or aging).
  2. **Canalithiasis Theory (Hall et al. — Most Accepted):**
     * Dislodged otoconial debris migrates and floats freely within the endolymph of the most dependent semicircular canal (usually the **posterior semicircular canal** in 85–90% of cases, due to its gravitationally inferior position).
     * When the head is moved into the provoking plane (e.g., Dix–Hallpike position), gravity causes the heavier otoconial mass to move along the canal.
     * This fluid movement acts like a piston, producing an abnormal hydrodynamic suction/pressure that displaces the **cupula**, sending a false discharge of intense excitation to the vestibular nuclei, causing rotatory vertigo and nystagmus.
     * *Latency (2–20 seconds):* Represents the time taken for the detached otolith mass to overcome inertia and move within the viscous endolymph.
     * *Fatigability:* Repeated provocation disperses the particles along the canal, reducing their ability to deflect the cupula.
  3. **Cupulolithiasis Theory (Schuknecht):**
     * The detached otoconia settle and become physically adhered directly to the gelatinous cupula of the posterior canal ampulla.
     * This transforms the normally neutrally buoyant cupula into a heavy, gravity-sensitive organ that deflects whenever the head changes spatial orientation.
