questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: A 35-year-old female patient presents with hearing loss in both ears since past 5 years. She also gives past history of exacerbation of hearing loss during pregnancy. On otoscopic examination both the tympanic membranes appear normal. a) What is your diagnosis b) What are the other clinical features of this condition c) Discuss the audiological investigations of this patient d) Discuss the treatment options for this patient. (1+2+3+4)

note.title: Otosclerosis
note.content:
#### a) Diagnosis
* **Clinical Otosclerosis (Stapedial Otosclerosis)**.

#### b) Other Clinical Features
* **Progressive Hearing Loss:** Painless, insidious, bilateral conductive hearing loss starting in the 2nd–3rd decades; aggravated by pregnancy, lactation, or menopause.
* **Paracusis Willisii (Pathognomonic):** The patient paradoxically hears better in noisy environments than in quiet surroundings (because normal speakers subconsciously raise their voice in noise, which the otosclerotic patient perceives clearly through unmasked bone conduction).
* **Tinnitus:** Constant, low-pitched roaring or buzzing tinnitus.
* **Speech Character:** Soft, well-modulated, quiet speech (because their own voice sounds abnormally loud to them via bone conduction).
* **Schwartze Sign (Flamingo Pink Sign):** Pinkish or reddish glow seen through an intact drum over the promontory, indicating active hypervascularity of an active focus.

#### c) Audiological Investigations
1. **Tuning Fork Tests:** Rinne test negative bilaterally (BC > AC); Weber test central or lateralized to the worse ear; Absolute Bone Conduction (ABC) test normal.
2. **Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA):**
   * Shows a conductive hearing loss with a significant Air-Bone Gap (A-B gap), predominantly affecting lower frequencies.
   * **Carhart’s Notch:** Characteristic dip in the **bone conduction curve** maximal at **2000 Hz (15 dB at 2 kHz)**, caused by disruption of normal ossicular inertial resonance; disappears following successful stapedectomy.
3. **Impedance Audiometry:**
   * **Type As Tympanogram:** Normal peak pressure ($0\text{ daPa}$), but significantly reduced static compliance ($<0.3$ mL) due to stapedial ankylosis.
   * **Absent Stapedial Reflex:** Reflex is absent because the fixed stapes footplate cannot be moved by the stapedius muscle.
4. **Speech Audiometry:** Speech Discrimination Score is characteristically excellent ($>90–100\%$) unless cochlear otosclerosis supervenes.

#### d) Treatment Options
```
                     MANAGEMENT OF OTOSCLEROSIS
                                  |
         +------------------------+------------------------+
         |                                                 |
Medical / Conservative                               Surgical Therapy
  1. Hearing Aids (BTE/ITE)                            - Small-Fenestra Stapedotomy
  2. Sodium Fluoride Therapy                             (Standard of Care)
     (20-40 mg/day; arrests active focus)              - Total / Partial Stapedectomy
  3. Bisphosphonates                                     (Piston: Teflon / Platinum)
```
1. **Surgical Treatment (Stapedotomy / Stapedectomy — Treatment of Choice):**
   * *Selection Criteria:* Conductive loss $\ge 30$ dB, A-B gap $\ge 20–25$ dB, speech discrimination $\ge 60\%$. Always operate on the poorer hearing ear first.
   * *Procedure (Small-Fenestra Stapedotomy):* Under local anesthesia $\rightarrow$ transcanal approach via Rosen’s incision $\rightarrow$ elevate tympanomeatal flap $\rightarrow$ verify stapedial fixation $\rightarrow$ divide stapedius tendon $\rightarrow$ disarticulate incudostapedial joint $\rightarrow$ fracture and remove stapes superstructure $\rightarrow$ create a 0.6 mm micro-fenestra in the center of the footplate using a micro-drill, pick, or laser $\rightarrow$ insert a 0.4–0.6 mm Teflon piston hooked over the incus long process.
2. **Hearing Aids:** Air-conduction digital hearing aids provide an effective non-surgical alternative for patients refusing surgery, unfit for anesthesia, or with an only-hearing ear.
3. **Medical Therapy (Sodium Fluoride):** Indicated only in **active otosclerosis** (positive Schwartze sign) or rapidly progressing cochlear otosclerosis to accelerate bone remineralization and arrest sensorineural decline.

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: A 14-year-old male patient is brought to the ENT Out Patient Department with history of repeated nasal bleed for 2 months. There is no history of trauma. On anterior rhinoscopy a reddish mass is seen in the left nasal cavity. a) What is your probable diagnosis b) What is the etiopathogenesis c) What are the other clinical symptoms and signs of this condition d) Radiological signs of this condition e) Discuss its surgical management. (1+2+2+2+3)

note.title: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA)
note.content:
* **Clinical Scenario:** 14yo male, repeated unprovoked epistaxis, left nasal mass, no trauma history.

#### a) Probable Diagnosis
* **Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA)**.

#### b) Etiopathogenesis
* **Demographics:** Occurs almost exclusively in **adolescent males** (second decade of life, 10–20 years).
* **Hormonal Dependence:** Highly sensitive to androgenic stimulation; growth is driven by testosterone receptor activation within vascular tissue.
* **Site of Origin:** Arises from a vascular nidus ofembryonic tissue located in the posterolateral wall of the nasal cavity, specifically at the superior margin of the **sphenopalatine foramen**.
* **Histopathology:** Non-encapsulated, benign lesion composed of two components:
  1. *Vascular network:* Thin-walled, irregular endothelial channels lacking a complete muscularis layer (tunica media) and elastic lamina. Because the vessels cannot contract or vasconstrict, manipulation or biopsy causes massive, uncontrollable hemorrhage.
  2. *Fibrous stroma:* Dense to loose collagenous connective tissue background.

#### c) Other Clinical Symptoms and Signs
* **Symptoms:**
  * Unilateral, progressive nasal obstruction leading to bilateral blockage as the mass grows into the nasopharynx.
  * Hyponasal speech (*rhinolalia clausa*).
  * Unilateral conductive hearing loss, autophony, and recurrent otitis media with effusion due to mechanical obstruction of the Eustachian tube cushion.
  * Anosmia/hyposmia.
  * Facial deformity, headache, diplopia, and cheek numbness (CN $V_2$ compression).
* **Signs:**
  * *Anterior Rhinoscopy / Endoscopy:* Lobulated, firm, pinkish-to-dark-red or purplish mass filling the posterior nasal cavity and nasopharynx.
  * *External Deformity:*
    * Protrusion of the cheek due to extension into the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae.
    * Proptosis, lateral displacement of the eyeball, and broadening of the nasal root (**"frog-face deformity"**).
  * **Clinical Caveat:** **Biopsy is strictly contraindicated in the outpatient department** due to the catastrophic risk of torrential, life-threatening hemorrhage.

#### d) Radiological Signs
1. **Holman–Miller Sign (Antral Sign):**
   * Seen on axial CT/MRI and lateral radiographs: Pathognomonic **anterior bowing and forward push of the posterior wall of the maxillary antrum** caused by tumour expansion within the pterygomaxillary/pterygopalatine fossa.
2. **Widening of Sphenopalatine Foramen & Pterygomaxillary Fissure:** Expansion and bony remodeling without osteoclastic infiltration.
3. **Contrast-Enhanced CT / MRI:** Demonstrates intense, vivid, heterogeneous contrast enhancement and delineates extension into the orbit, infratemporal fossa, middle cranial fossa, and sphenoid sinus.

#### e) Surgical Management
```
                     MANAGEMENT WORKFLOW FOR JNA
                                  |
              Preoperative Digital Subtraction Angiography
                                  |
                                  v
           Superselective Embolization (24–48 hours prior)
                                  |
                                  v
                  Definitive Surgical Resection
                                  |
      +---------------------------+---------------------------+
      |                                                       |
Endoscopic / Transnasal Approach                     Open External Approaches
  - Radkowski Stage I & II                             - Transpalatal
  - Powered microdebriders, coblation                  - Lateral Rhinotomy / Weber-Ferguson
  - Strict preservation of ICA                         - Sublabial Midfacial Degloving
                                                       - Infratemporal Fossa Approach (Fisch)
```
1. **Preoperative Angiography & Embolization (Mandatory):**
   * Superselective catheterization of the internal maxillary artery branches.
   * Transarterial embolization using polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) particles or Gelfoam performed **24 to 48 hours prior to surgery** to reduce intraoperative blood loss by up to 70–80%.
2. **Surgical Approaches (Selected by Stage):**
   * **Transnasal Endoscopic Resection:** Currently the standard of care for Radkowski Stages I and II (tumours confined to the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, ethmoids, sphenoid, and medial pterygopalatine fossa).
   * **Transpalatal Approach:** Provides direct midline exposure of the nasopharynx for localized posterior choanal tumours.
   * **Lateral Rhinotomy / Weber–Fergusson Approach:** For large tumours involving the maxilla, orbit, and anterior ethmoids.
   * **Sublabial Midfacial Degloving:** Provides bilateral, wide exposure of the midface without visible external facial incisions.
   * **Infratemporal Fossa Approach (Fisch Type C/D):** For massive lesions invading the infratemporal fossa, parasellar region, or cavernous sinus.

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Clinical features and management of acute retropharyngeal abscess.

note.title: Acute Retropharyngeal Abscess: Clinical Features and Management
note.content:
* **Definition:** Suppuration within the potential retropharyngeal space of Gillette, situated between the buccopharyngeal fascia anteriorly and the alar/prevertebral fascia posteriorly.

#### Clinical Features
* **Demographics:** Most commonly seen in infants and children under 3–4 years of age due to suppuration of the lymph nodes of Rouviere (which atrophy after age 4–5).
* **Symptoms:**
  * Sudden onset high fever with toxaemia and irritability.
  * Inability or refusal to suckle/swallow (**odynophagia/dysphagia**), with persistent drooling of saliva.
  * Inspiratory stridor, dyspnea, and a muffled, croupy, **"quacking duck"** cry.
  * Torticollis: Child holds the neck extended and tilted to one side; passive neck flexion produces severe pain.
* **Signs:**
  * *Oropharyngeal Inspection:* Unilateral, smooth, rounded bulging of the posterior pharyngeal wall (confined to one side of the midline due to the median raphe).
  * Tender, enlarged upper deep cervical lymph nodes.

#### Management
1. **Airway Security (Primary Concern):** Maintain the child in a propped-up or Trendelenburg position. Emergency endotracheal intubation or tracheostomy if stridor is severe.
2. **Parenteral Antibiotic Therapy:** Broad-spectrum IV coverage against *Staph. aureus*, *Streptococcus*, and anaerobes:
   * IV Amoxicillin-Clavulanic acid + IV Metronidazole **OR** IV Ceftriaxone + Clindamycin.
3. **Incision and Drainage (Transoral I&D — Treatment of Choice):**
   * Performed in the operation theatre under general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation, or in the conscious child secured in a **steep Trendelenburg (head-low) position** to prevent aspiration.
   * A vertical incision is made over the most prominent fluctuant area of the posterior pharyngeal wall using a guarded knife.
   * An assistant applies continuous, powerful suction to evacuate pus immediately upon entering the cavity.

---

note.title: Bell’s Palsy: Etiology and Management
note.content:
* **Definition:** Acute, isolated, idiopathic, lower motor neuron paralysis or paresis of the facial nerve, presenting over a period of $<72$ hours.

#### Etiology
1. **Viral Reactivation (Primary Cause):** Latent **Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1 (HSV-1)** or Varicella-Zoster Virus reactivation within the geniculate ganglion.
2. **Microvascular Ischaemia & Entrapment Neuropathy:** Primary neural ischemia $\rightarrow$ capillary breakdown $\rightarrow$ endoneurial oedema within the rigid, unyielding **labyrinthine segment** of the fallopian canal $\rightarrow$ secondary venous compression and conduction block (**neurapraxia**).
3. **Autoimmune Reactions:** Cell-mediated demyelination following acute viral prodromes.
4. **Hereditary Susceptibility:** Narrowed bony fallopian canal in a subset of patients.

#### Management
```
                     MANAGEMENT OF BELL'S PALSY
                                 |
         +-----------------------+-----------------------+
         |                                               |
Medical Pharmacotherapy                     Supportive & Eye Care
  1. Systemic Corticosteroids                 1. Lubricating Drops (Daytime)
     - Oral Prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day x 10d)  2. Ointment & Eye Taping (Night)
  2. Antiviral Therapy (Severe cases:         3. Dark Sunglasses
     House-Brackmann Grade IV-VI)             4. Facial Physiotherapy
     - Oral Valacyclovir / Acyclovir
```
1. **Medical Pharmacotherapy (Standard of Care):**
   * **Systemic Oral Corticosteroids:** Most critical drug. Must be initiated within 72 hours of onset:
     * **Oral Prednisolone: 1 mg/kg/day (typically 60 mg daily)** for 5–7 days, followed by a 5-day taper (total 10–12 days). Reduces endoneurial oedema within the fallopian canal.
   * **Antiviral Therapy:** 
     * Indicated in severe cases (House-Brackmann Grade IV–VI): Oral **Valacyclovir (1000 mg TID)** or **Acyclovir (400 mg 5 times daily)** for 7 days in combination with steroids.
2. **Eye Protection (Crucial to Prevent Exposure Keratitis):**
   * Due to lagophthalmos (inability to close the eye) and loss of corneal blink reflex:
     * Preservative-free artificial tear drops (0.5% carboxymethylcellulose) instilled hourly during waking hours.
     * High-viscosity eye lubricating ointment and nocturnal eye taping/pad.
     * Sunglasses to protect against dust and wind trauma.
3. **Surgical Decompression:**
   * Indicated only if Electroneuronography (ENoG) reveals **$>90\%$ nerve degeneration within 14 days** of complete paralysis and EMG shows no voluntary motor unit potentials.
   * Involves transmastoid/middle cranial fossa decompression of the labyrinthine and tympanic segments.

---

questions.officialText: Enumerate the causes of peripheral vertigo. Discuss the management of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo.

note.title: Peripheral Vertigo: Causes and Management of BPPV
note.content:
* **Causes of Peripheral Vertigo:**
  1. Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV — most common).
  2. Meniere’s Disease (Endolymphatic hydrops).
  3. Vestibular Neuronitis.
  4. Labyrinthitis (Circumscribed, Serous, Suppurative).
  5. Perilymph Fistula.
  6. Labyrinthine concussion / Temporal bone trauma.
  7. Ototoxicity (Aminoglycosides).
* **Management of BPPV:**
  * **Diagnostic Confirmation:** **Dix–Hallpike Manoeuvre:** Diagnostic test of choice; demonstrates latency (2–20s), geotropic torsional/rotatory nystagmus lasting $<60$ seconds, fatigability, and vertigo when the affected ear is dependent.
  * **Particle Repositioning Maneuvers (Definitive Treatment):**
    * **Epley’s Canalith Repositioning Manoeuvre (for Posterior Canal BPPV):**
      * Sequentially rotates the head through 5 spatial orientations to guide free-floating otolith particles (canaliths) out of the posterior semicircular canal back into the utricle by gravity.
      * *Success Rate:* $>85–90\%$ complete resolution with a single manoeuvre.
    * **Semont’s Liberatory Manoeuvre:** Rapid side-to-side body-swinging repositioning.
    * **Barbeque Roll Manoeuvre (Lempert):** Indicated for lateral (horizontal) canal BPPV.
  * **Vestibular Rehabilitation:** Brandt–Daroff home exercises for persistent mild symptoms.

note.title: Thyroglossal Duct Cyst
note.content:
* **Embryological Basis:** Results from failure of complete obliteration of the embryonic thyroglossal duct, which descends from the **foramen caecum** at the base of the tongue through the midline neck, crossing the hyoid bone, to form the mature thyroid gland.
* **Clinical Features:**
  * Most common congenital neck anomaly; commonly presents in children and young adults ($<20$ years).
  * Painless, smooth, cystic, fluctuant, non-tender midline neck mass, most commonly located **subhyoid** (60%).
  * **Pathognomonic Clinical Sign:** Moves upward with **both deglutition and active tongue protrusion** (due to fibrous tethering of the tract to the foramen caecum via the hyoid bone).
  * May undergo secondary infection following upper respiratory infection, causing rapid enlargement, redness, or rupture forming a **thyroglossal fistula**.
* **Management:**
  * Preoperative ultrasound or CT neck is mandatory to confirm the presence of a normally located orthotopic thyroid gland.
  * **Sistrunk’s Operation (Treatment of Choice):**
    * Complete en bloc surgical excision of the cyst, the entire fibrous tract, the **central one-third (body) of the hyoid bone**, and a core of muscle tissue around the tract extending to the foramen caecum.
    * Simple enucleation carries a recurrence rate $>50\%$; Sistrunk's procedure reduces recurrence to $<3\%$.

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: A 24 -year-old male presents to the OPD with fever, otalgia and swelling over the right mastoid. He also gives history of foul smelling scanty right ear discharge for the last three years. On examination there is a retraction pocket in the right tympanic me mbrane with whitish flakes and a boggy swelling in the right postaural region. a) What is your provisional diagnosis b) What is the immediate intervention to be planned c) What are the other clinical features of this condition d) What are the investigations to be done in this patient e) Discuss the treatment options for this patient (1+1+2+3+3)

note.title: Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media with Postaural Mastoid Abscess
note.content:
* **Clinical Scenario:** 24yo male, fever, right otalgia, mastoid swelling, scanty foul-smelling otorrhoea for 3 years, attic retraction pocket with white flakes, boggy postaural swelling.

#### a) Provisional Diagnosis
* **Right Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) — Atticoantral (Squamosal / Unsafe) Type, with Cholesteatoma, complicated by Acute Coalescent Mastoiditis and Postaural Subperiosteal Abscess**.

#### b) Immediate Intervention to be Planned
1. **Immediate Hospitalization & Resuscitation:** Secure IV access, initiate broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics, and administer analgesics.
2. **Subperiosteal Abscess Aspiration:** Urgent needle aspiration of the fluctuant postaural abscess using an 18G needle under aseptic conditions to decompress tissues, reduce pain, and obtain pus for aerobic/anaerobic culture and sensitivity.
3. **Emergency Mastoid Surgery:** Urgent surgical exploration (**Modified Radical Mastoidectomy**) within 24–48 hours once initial stabilization is achieved.

#### c) Other Clinical Features of this Condition
* **Ear Discharge:** Scanty, thick, creamy-yellow, and characteristically **foul-smelling (fetid)** due to bone destruction and anaerobic infection.
* **Otoscopy / Micro-otoscopy:** Attic or posterosuperior marginal perforation; retraction pocket packed with white, desquamated, keratotic cholesteatoma flakes; red, fleshy granulation tissue or an aural polyp presenting in the external auditory canal.
* **Conductive / Mixed Hearing Loss:** Significant hearing impairment due to necrosis of the ossicular chain (especially the long process of incus and stapes superstructure).
* **Warning Signs of Impending Complications:** Vertigo with a positive fistula sign, severe persistent hemicranial headache, projectile vomiting, facial nerve weakness, chills, rigors, and neck stiffness.

#### d) Investigations to be Done
1. **High-Resolution CT (HRCT) of Temporal Bone (Mandatory):**
   * *Findings:* Soft-tissue mass in the attic, aditus, and antrum; erosion of the scutum (early sign of attic cholesteatoma); demineralization of mastoid trabeculae with coalescence; breach of the outer mastoid cortex (confirming subperiosteal abscess); integrity of tegmen tympani, sigmoid sinus plate, and lateral semicircular canal.
2. **Pus Culture and Sensitivity:** Identifies *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, *Proteus*, *Staph. aureus*, and *Bacteroides fragilis*.
3. **Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA):** Quantifies conductive or mixed hearing loss and assesses cochlear reserve before surgery.
4. **Contrast MRI Brain:** Indicated if headache, vomiting, or neurological signs suggest intracranial extension.

#### e) Treatment Options
```
                MANAGEMENT OF ATTICOANTRAL CSOM
                               |
         +---------------------+---------------------+
         |                                           |
Phase 1: Emergency Stabilization            Phase 2: Definitive Surgery
  - IV Antibiotics (Ceftriaxone +             - Modified Radical Mastoidectomy
    Metronidazole / Piperacillin-Tazobactam)    (Exteriorizes attic & antrum)
  - Postaural Abscess Needle Aspiration       - Concomitant Meatoplasty
  - Pain control & supportive care            - Tympanoplasty / Ossiculoplasty
```
* **Definitive Surgical Intervention (Canal Wall Down — Modified Radical Mastoidectomy):**
  * Approached via a postaural incision.
  * Subperiosteal abscess is drained and granulation tissue cleared.
  * The mastoid cortex is drilled to open the antrum and exteriorize the attic, aditus, and mastoid cells into a single, smooth cavity.
  * The posterior bony meatal wall is lowered to the level of the facial ridge.
  * All cholesteatoma matrix, diseased bone, and granulations are removed.
  * A wide **meatoplasty** is fashioned to ensure adequate aeration and lifelong access for cavity cleaning.
  * Hearing reconstruction (tympanoplasty/ossiculoplasty) is performed primarily or staged.

note.title: Adenoidectomy Operation
note.content:
* **Indications:** Obstructive sleep apnoea / loud snoring in children; recurrent acute otitis media / persistent otitis media with effusion; chronic rhinosinusitis refractory to medical therapy; dental malocclusion and adenoid facies.
* **Contraindications:** Cleft palate or submucous cleft palate (causes severe velopharyngeal insufficiency and hypernasal speech); active acute upper respiratory infection; uncorrected bleeding disorders.
* **Anesthesia & Position:** General anesthesia with oral endotracheal intubation. **Rose’s position** (supine with a shoulder roll extending the neck, head stabilized on a doughnut ring).
* **Steps of Curettage Method:**
  1. A **Boyle–Davis mouth gag** is inserted and suspended with Draffin bipods.
  2. Palpation of the nasopharynx to assess size and rule out choanal atresia or pulsating vessels.
  3. A guarded **St. Clair Thomson adenoid curette** is introduced into the nasopharynx until it engages the superior border of the adenoid mass at the roof.
  4. With a gentle, shaving, curved downward sweep conforming to the posterior pharyngeal wall, the adenoid mass is resected in a single piece. Neck is slightly flexed to avoid injury to the atlas anterior tubercle.
  5. Immediate hemostasis achieved by firm packing of the nasopharynx with dry gauze swabs for 5 minutes.
  6. Persistent bleeding points are cauterized under direct vision using suction diathermy or endoscopic coblation.
* **Modern Alternative:** **Endoscopic Coblation / Microdebrider-assisted Adenoidectomy** under transoral 70° telescope vision.

note.title: Objective Tinnitus
note.content:
* **Definition:** A rare form of tinnitus where the sound perceived by the patient is an actual physical sound generated within the body that can also be heard by the examining clinician (via auscultation with a stethoscope over the skull, neck, or external ear).
* **Causes:**
  1. **Vascular Causes (Pulsatile Tinnitus):**
     * Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) and dural AV fistulae.
     * Glomus jugulare and glomus tympanicum tumours.
     * Atherosclerotic internal carotid artery stenosis, aneurysm, or aberrant carotid artery.
     * Benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumour cerebri; produces venous hum).
  2. **Muscular Causes (Clicking / Fluttering Tinnitus):**
     * **Palatal Myoclonus:** Rhythmic, involuntary contractions of the tensor veli palatini or levator veli palatini muscles.
     * Middle ear myoclonus: Clonic spasms of the stapedius or tensor tympani muscle.
  3. **Respiratory / Mechanical Causes:**
     * **Patulous Eustachian Tube:** Tube remains abnormally open; patient hears roaring sounds synchronous with nasal respiration, accompanied by autophony.
     * Temporomandibular joint clicking during mastication.

note.title: Odynophagia
note.content:
* **Definition:** Severe, sharp, burning, or aching pain triggered specifically by the act of swallowing.
* **Distinction:** Differs from dysphagia (which represents mechanical difficulty or food arrest during transit); odynophagia and dysphagia frequently coexist.
* **Common Causes:**
  1. *Infective / Inflammatory:* Acute follicular tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), acute epiglottitis, retropharyngeal/parapharyngeal abscess, candidal/herpetic oesophagitis, Vincent’s angina.
  2. *Ulcerative:* Severe aphthous ulcers, Behçet syndrome, pemphigus vulgaris.
  3. *Traumatic:* Ingested sharp foreign bodies (fish bone in tonsil/vallecula), corrosive acid/alkali ingestion, post-tonsillectomy slough.
  4. *Neoplastic:* Advanced infiltrating ulcerated carcinomas of the hypopharynx, base of tongue, and tonsil.

note.title: Inverted Papilloma (Ringertz Tumour)
note.content:
* **Definition:** A unique, locally aggressive benign epithelial neoplasm of the sinonasal tract characterized histologically by the **inversion of surface respiratory epithelium into the underlying connective tissue stroma**, rather than outward exophytic growth.
* **Aetiology & Features:** Associated with Human Papilloma Virus (HPV types 11 and 16). Typically seen in men aged 40–70 years. Arises from the **lateral nasal wall** (middle meatus/ethmoids).
* **Clinical Features:** Unilateral progressive nasal obstruction, recurrent epistaxis, purulent rhinorrhoea, and hyposmia. On rhinoscopy/endoscopy, presents as a firm, lobulated, fleshy, pale-pink or dark red mulberry-like mass that bleeds on probing.
* **Clinical Significance:** 
  1. High propensity for local bone destruction and invasion into the orbit/skull base.
  2. High rate of local recurrence ($30–40\%$) if incompletely resected.
  3. Associated with **synchronous or metachronous Squamous Cell Carcinoma in 10% to 15% of cases**.
* **Treatment:** **Complete wide surgical excision with negative margins**. Modern standard is **Transnasal Endoscopic Medial Maxillectomy (TEMM)**; historically performed via lateral rhinotomy or midfacial degloving.

---

note.title: Tripod Fracture
note.content:
* **Definition:** Fracture of the zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) resulting from a direct blunt blow to the malar prominence, separating the zygoma from its three primary anatomical attachments:
  1. Frontozygomatic suture (lateral orbital wall).
  2. Zygomaticomaxillary buttress and infraorbital rim (anterior maxillary wall/orbital floor).
  3. Zygomaticotemporal suture (zygomatic arch).
* **Triad of Clinical Signs:** Flattening of the malar prominence + step deformity of the infraorbital margin + anesthesia of the cheek/upper lip (injury to the infraorbital nerve).

---

* **x. Muscles supplied by recurrent laryngeal nerve:**
  * Statements: 1) Posterior crico-arytenoid (True), 2) Thyroarytenoid (True), 3) Cricothyroid (False), 4) Lateral crico-arytenoid (True).
  * **Answer:** **b) 1, 2 and 4 are correct**

#### Questions xi to xv: Assertion (A) & Reason (R)
* **xi. Assertion:** Stimulation of external auditory canal can cause cough in patient.  
  **Reason:** External auditory canal is also supplied by nervus intermedius, which is a branch of VIIth cranial nerve.  
  * **Answer:** **b) A and R correct, and R does not explain A**  
  * *Reasoning:* Arnold's nerve reflex cough is mediated by the **auricular branch of the vagus nerve (CN X)** supplying the posterior and inferior meatal wall, triggering vagal afferents to the cough center. The sensory innervation of CN VII is true but does not explain the cough reflex.
* **xii. Assertion:** Acute membranous tonsillitis caused by group A beta hemolytic streptococci can lead to rheumatic heart disease.  
  **Reason:** Rheumatic heart disease is because of antigen-antibody reaction due to antigenic similarity between cardiac valves and bacterial antigen.  
  * **Answer:** **a) A and R correct, and R explains A** (Molecular mimicry).
* **xiii. Assertion:** Injury to subglottic region is the commonly seen post extubation injury in pediatric age group.  
  **Reason:** Subglottis is the narrowest part of pediatric airway.  
  * **Answer:** **a) A and R correct, and R explains A**
* **xiv. Assertion:** There is false positive fistula sign in congenital syphilis.  
  **Reason:** There is superior semicircular canal dehiscence in congenital syphilis.  
  * **Answer:** **c) A is correct, R is incorrect** (False-positive sign / Hennebert's sign is due to an abnormally mobile stapes footplate, not SSCD).
* **xv. Assertion:** Pinna of the ear is elastic in nature.  
  **Reason:** Hyaline cartilage is present in pinna.  
  * **Answer:** **c) A is correct, R is incorrect** (Pinna is formed of yellow **elastic fibrocartilage**, not hyaline cartilage).

#### Questions xvi to xx: Case Scenario (Croup)
* **xvi. Most probable diagnosis:** **b) Croup (Acute Laryngotracheobronchitis)**

Otoscopic examination revealed a posterosuperior marginal perforation with whitish flakes in the ear. a) What is your diagnosis. b) Etiopathogenesis of this condition. c) Enumerate the complications associated with this disease. d) Describe the surgical management of this disease. note.title: Unsafe CSOM with Cholesteatoma
note.content:
* **Clinical Scenario:** 35yo female, chronic scanty foul-smelling left ear discharge, posterosuperior marginal perforation with whitish flakes.

#### a) Diagnosis
* **Left Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) — Atticoantral (Squamosal / Unsafe) Type, Active Stage with Cholesteatoma**.

#### b) Etiopathogenesis of Cholesteatoma
REFER TO [[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q01]] (2025_MARCH) AND Standard Theories:
1. **Wittmaack’s Invagination Theory:** Negative middle ear pressure pulls pars flaccida or posterosuperior pars tensa inward, creating a deep retraction pocket that accumulates trapped keratin.
2. **Habermann’s Epithelial Invasion Theory:** Canal squamous epithelium migrates through a marginal perforation where the annulus is destroyed.
3. **Ruedi’s Basal Cell Hyperplasia Theory:** Basal layers of Shrapnell’s membrane proliferate downward into subepithelial layers in response to infection.
4. **Sade’s Metaplasia Theory:** Middle ear columnar/cuboidal mucosa undergoes squamous metaplasia secondary to chronic infection.

#### c) Complications Associated with this Disease
REFER TO [[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q03]] (2026_MARCH)

#### d) Surgical Management

note.title: Ramsay Hunt Syndrome (Herpes Zoster Oticus)
note.content:
* **Aetiology:** Reactivation of latent **Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV)** within the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve.
* **Clinical Triad:**
  1. Severe, burning, excruciating otalgia.
  2. Eruption of painful, erythematous vesicular skin rash on the concha, posterior meatal wall, tragus, and external auditory drum (sensory distribution of CN VII).
  3. Acute, complete lower motor neuron **facial nerve paralysis** (Bell's palsy pattern).
* **Eighth Nerve Involvement:** Often associated with sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and severe rotatory vertigo due to spread of the virus to the adjacent vestibulocochlear nerve within the internal auditory meatus.
* **Treatment:** High-dose oral/IV **Acyclovir** (800 mg 5 times daily for 7–10 days) or Valacyclovir (1000 mg TID) + **Systemic Corticosteroids** (Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day tapered over 2 weeks) + Eye protection. Prognosis for complete facial nerve recovery is poorer than in idiopathic Bell's palsy.

questions.officialText: How do you counsel a patient posted for Tonsillectomy.

note.title: Counselling a Patient Posted for Tonsillectomy
note.content:
* **Introduction & Explanation:** Explain the diagnosis (e.g., chronic recurrent tonsillitis meeting Paradise criteria, obstructive sleep apnea) and why medical therapy is no longer sufficient.
* **Nature of Operation:** Complete surgical dissection and excision of both palatine tonsils with their capsules from the tonsillar fossae under general endotracheal anesthesia.
* **Postoperative Course & Expectations:**
  * **Severe Throat Pain & Referred Earache:** Common for the first 7–10 days, particularly during swallowing. Emphasize compliance with prescribed analgesics 30 minutes before meals.
  * **Dietary Instructions:** Cold liquid/semisolid diet (ice cream, cold milk) on Day 1; progress to soft, bland foods. Avoid hot, spicy, rough, or acidic foods.
  * **White Slough in Tonsillar Bed:** Reassure the patient that the white coating in the throat is normal healing granulation tissue, not infection or residual tonsil.
* **Risks & Warning Signs (Haemorrhage):**
  * *Primary/Reactionary Bleeding (First 24 Hours).*
  * *Secondary Bleeding (Days 5 to 10):* Can occur when the white slough separates. Instruct the patient to spit out and not swallow blood, and to report to the emergency room immediately if bleeding occurs.

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: A 25-year-old male presented with history of headache, fever, projectile vomiting since two days. Past history of foul smelling, blood stained left ear discharge since 10 years. No history of diabetes mellitus. On examination: L eft ear: scanty purulent discharge present, neck rigidity present. a) What is provisional diagnosis. Substantiate your diagnosis. b) How do you confirm the diagnosis. c) Enumerate FOUR causes of purulent foul smelling ear discharge. d) How do you manage this patient. (2+2+2+4)

note.title: Otogenic Intracranial Complication (Meningitis / Brain Abscess)
note.content:
* **Clinical Scenario:** 25yo male, foul-smelling blood-stained left otorrhoea for 10 years, headache, fever, projectile vomiting for 2 days, scanty purulent discharge, neck rigidity.

#### a) Provisional Diagnosis and Substantiation
* **Left Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) — Atticoantral (Squamosal) Type with Cholesteatoma, complicated by Otogenic Meningitis and Suspicion of Temporal Lobe / Cerebellar Abscess**.
* *Substantiation:* Long-standing foul-smelling, blood-stained otorrhoea indicates bone-eroding cholesteatoma/granulations; acute fever with neck rigidity confirms **meningism/meningitis**; projectile vomiting and severe headache indicate **raised intracranial tension** and space-occupying brain abscess.

#### b) How to Confirm Diagnosis
1. **Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT) of Brain and HRCT Temporal Bone (Emergency):**
   * *Temporal bone:* Demonstrates attic-antral bone erosion, destruction of tegmen tympani or Trautmann’s triangle.
   * *Brain:* Delineates cerebral oedema, leptomeningeal enhancement (meningitis), or a smooth, ring-enhancing hypodense mass with surrounding vasogenic oedema (temporal or cerebellar brain abscess).
2. **Lumbar Puncture and CSF Analysis:**
   * **Caution:** Perform **only after CT confirms absence of midline shift or impending cerebellar herniation**.
   * *Findings in Meningitis:* Turbid CSF, opening pressure $>200\text{ mm }H_2O$, marked pleocytosis with polymorphonuclear predominance, elevated protein ($>100$ mg/dL), reduced glucose ($<40$ mg/dL or $<50\%$ of blood glucose), and positive Gram stain/culture.

#### c) Four Causes of Purulent, Foul-Smelling Ear Discharge
1. Atticoantral (squamosal) CSOM with cholesteatoma.
2. Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa.
3. Carcinoma of the middle ear / external acoustic canal.
4. Tuberculous otitis media with extensive secondary infection and bone sequestrum.

#### d) Management
```
                     EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT
                              |
       +----------------------+----------------------+
       |                                             |
Phase 1: Medical Stabilization              Phase 2: Surgical Clearance
  - Immediate ICU admission                   - Neurosurgical: Burr-hole
  - IV Ceftriaxone (2 g q12h) +                 aspiration or excision of
    IV Metronidazole (500 mg q8h) +             brain abscess (if present)
    IV Vancomycin                             - Otological: Radical / Modified
  - Anticonvulsants & Analgesics                Radical Mastoidectomy once
  - IV Mannitol / Dexamethasone for ICP         intracranial sepsis stabilizes
```
1. **Immediate Medical Stabilization (Highest Priority):**
   * Urgent admission to intensive care; elevate head-end by 30°.
   * **Empirical High-Dose Parenteral Antibiotics:** Must penetrate the blood-brain barrier:
     * IV Ceftriaxone (2 g 12-hourly) **PLUS** IV Metronidazole (500 mg 8-hourly) **PLUS** IV Vancomycin (1 g 12-hourly) for 14–21 days.
   * **Antiedema Therapy:** IV Mannitol 20% (0.5–1 g/kg IV infusion) and IV Dexamethasone to lower raised intracranial pressure.
2. **Neurosurgical Intervention:** If a brain abscess $>2.5$ cm is present with mass effect, perform immediate burr-hole aspiration or craniotomy with abscess evacuation.
3. **Definitive Otological Surgery:** Once the patient is stabilized neurologically (usually within 24–48 hours), perform a **Radical or Modified Radical Mastoidectomy** to exteriorize the disease, remove the cholesteatoma, and seal the bony defect in the tegmen/dura.

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Enumerate congenital causes of stridor and its management.

note.title: Congenital Causes of Stridor and Management
note.content:
* **Congenital Causes:**
  1. **Laryngomalacia:** Most common congenital cause (60%); flaccid supraglottis collapses during inspiration.
  2. **Congenital Subglottic Stenosis:** Incomplete canalization of the cricoid ring ($<4$ mm diameter).
  3. **Congenital Vocal Fold Paralysis:** Unilateral or bilateral; secondary to birth trauma or central Arnold-Chiari malformation.
  4. **Laryngeal Web:** Incomplete recanalization at anterior commissure.
  5. **Subglottic Haemangioma:** Vascular proliferation causing progressive biphasic stridor by 3–6 months.
  6. **Laryngocele / Congenital Laryngeal Cysts.**
  7. **Vascular Ring / Slings:** Double aortic arch compressing the trachea.
* **Principles of Management:**
  * Secure the airway: Supplemental humidified oxygen; prone positioning for laryngomalacia; intubation or tracheostomy for critical subglottic stenosis/bilateral vocal cord paralysis.
  * Direct endoscopy under general anesthesia for definitive anatomical diagnosis.
  * Endoscopic surgical interventions: Supraglottoplasty (for severe laryngomalacia), $\text{CO}_2$ laser excision of webs/cysts, oral Propranolol for subglottic haemangioma, or open laryngotracheal reconstruction (LTR) with cartilage grafting for severe subglottic stenosis.

---

note.title: Cardinal Signs of Chronic Tonsillitis
note.content:
1. **Enlargement / Embedding of Tonsils:** Hypertrophic parenchymatous tonsils meeting in the midline, or small, shrunken, fibrotic tonsils embedded deep within the pillars.
2. **Expression of Cheesy Material or Pus:** Applying digital pressure on the anterior pillar with a tongue depressor expresses thick, white-yellow, foul-smelling cheesy debris or frank pus from the crypta magna.
3. **Flushing of Anterior Pillars:** Distinct, persistent hyperaemia and congestion of the anterior tonsillar pillars compared to the rest of the pharyngeal mucosa.
4. **Enlargement of Jugulodigastric Lymph Nodes:** Non-tender, persistent, firm enlargement of the tonsillar (jugulodigastric) lymph nodes behind the angle of the mandible.

note.title: Rinne Test
note.content:
* **Technique:** A 512 Hz vibrating tuning fork is placed on the mastoid process until the patient signals sound cessation, then immediately held 2 cm from the external acoustic meatus to assess air conduction (AC) versus bone conduction (BC).
* **Interpretation:**
  * **Positive Rinne (AC > BC):** Normal hearing OR Sensorineural hearing loss.
  * **Negative Rinne (BC > AC):** Conductive hearing loss (indicates an Air-Bone Gap of at least 15–20 dB).
  * **False Negative Rinne:** In severe unilateral SNHL, the sound from the mastoid is transmitted via the skull base to the contralateral normal ear, leading to false perception of BC > AC. Prevented by masking the non-test ear with a Barany noise box.

---

note.title: Rhinoscleroma – Clinical Features and Management
note.content:
* **Definition:** Chronic granulomatous infection of the upper respiratory tract caused by *Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis* (Frisch bacillus).
* **Clinical Stages:**
  1. *Catarrhal / Atrophic Stage:* Foul-smelling purulent rhinorrhoea, mucosal crusting resembling atrophic rhinitis.
  2. *Granulomatous / Nodular Stage:* Non-ulcerative, bluish-red granulomatous nodules filling the nasal cavity, causing nasal widening and induration of the tip and upper lip (**"woody nose" / Hebra nose**).
  3. *Cicatricial Stage:* Severe subepithelial fibrosis leading to stenosis of anterior nares, choanae, and subglottic stenosis.
* **Histopathology:** Diagnostic **Mikulicz cells** (large foamy histiocytes containing bacilli) and **Russell bodies** (eosinophilic plasma cell inclusion bodies).
* **Management:** Oral Rifampicin (450 mg OD) + Ciprofloxacin (500 mg BD) or Streptomycin + Tetracycline for 6–12 weeks until two consecutive negative biopsy cultures are obtained; surgical excision or laser dilation for cicatricial stenosis.

---

questions.officialText: Types of tracheostomy tubes. Give precise answers: (4x1=4)

note.title: Types of Tracheostomy Tubes
note.content:
1. **Metallic Tubes (Jackson’s / Fuller’s Bivalved):** Reusable, non-irritating, consist of outer cannula, inner cannula, and introducer/obturator; un-cuffed, used for long-term airway maintenance.
2. **Cuffed Synthetic (Portex / Siliconized PVC):** Disposable; inflatable low-pressure high-volume cuff prevents aspiration and allows positive-pressure mechanical ventilation.
3. **Uncuffed Plastic Tubes:** Used in children to avoid pressure-induced subglottic necrosis.
4. **Fenestrated Tubes:** Contain a window in the superior curvature; allows phonation when plugged while the patient breathes around the tube.
5. **Adjustable Flange Tubes:** Movable neck flange accommodates thick or obese necks.

note.content:

3. **Dennie-Morgan Lines:** Prominent infraorbital skin folds.
4. **Pale, Oedematous, Bluish Nasal Mucosa:** Swollen, boggy inferior turbinates coated with thin watery secretions.

note.title: Eagle's Syndrome

note.title: Preauricular Sinus
note.content:
* **Embryological Basis:** Incomplete fusion of the six embryonic hillocks of His during the development of the pinna from the first and second branchial arches.
* **Clinical Features:**
  * Small pinpoint pit or opening located typically at the anterior margin of the ascending crus of the helix.
  * Extends as a tortuous, branching epithelial-lined tract terminating in the perichondrium of auricular cartilage.
  * Asymptomatic unless blocked; recurrent retention can lead to foul cheese-like discharge, cellulitis, or recurrent preauricular abscesses.
* **Management:**
  * *Acute Infection / Abscess:* Antibiotics and incision and drainage.
  * *Definitive Treatment:* **Complete surgical excision of the sinus tract and its arborizations**, including a cuff of cartilage at its base. Incomplete removal results in recurrence.

questions.officialText: Clinical signs and tests of lateral sinus thrombophlebitis.

note.title: Lateral Sinus Thrombophlebitis: Clinical Signs and Tests
note.content:
1. **Picket-Fence Fever:** Spiking septic temperatures with chills and rigors coinciding with the release of septic thrombi.
2. **Griesinger’s Sign:** Oedema over the posterior part of the mastoid due to thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein.
3. **Tobey–Ayer (Queckenstedt) Test:** Manometric measurement of CSF pressure during lumbar puncture. Compression of the internal jugular vein on the healthy side causes a rapid rise in CSF pressure, whereas compression of the thrombosed side produces no rise.
4. **Crowe–Beck Test:** Compression of the healthy internal jugular vein produces engorgement of retinal and supraorbital veins on ophthalmoscopy.
5. **Tender Neck Cord:** Palpable, tender induration along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle if thrombosis extends into the internal jugular vein.

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: a) Enumerate the causes of vertigo b) Describe the etiopathogenesis and clinical features of Meniere’s disease c) Write a note on management of Meniere’s disease (4+5+6)

note.title: Vertigo & Meniere’s Disease
note.content:
#### a) Causes of Vertigo
* **Peripheral Vestibular Causes (85%):**
  * Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV).
  * Meniere’s Disease.
  * Vestibular Neuronitis.
  * Labyrinthitis (Circumscribed, Serous, Suppurative).
  * Perilymph Fistula.
  * Ototoxicity (Aminoglycosides).
* **Central Vestibular Causes (15%):**
  * Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency (VBI).
  * Vestibular Migraine (Basilar Migraine).
  * Acoustic Neuroma (CPA Tumours).
  * Multiple Sclerosis.
  * Wallenberg Syndrome (PICA Thrombosis / Lateral Medullary Syndrome).
  * Cerebellar stroke, infarction, or abscess.

#### b) Etiopathogenesis and Clinical Features of Meniere’s Disease
* **Etiopathogenesis:**
  * Hallmark pathology is **Endolymphatic Hydrops** (marked ballooning and dilatation of the scala media and saccule due to increased endolymph volume).
  * Caused by:
    1. *Defective endolymph resorption:* Fibrosis, ischemia, or hypoplasia of the endolymphatic duct and sac.
    2. *Hypersecretion:* Overactivity of the stria vascularis.
    3. *Allergy, Autoimmunity, or Vasospasm* of the internal auditory artery.
  * Episodic attacks are triggered by micro-ruptures of the distended Reissner's membrane, mixing potassium-rich endolymph with perilymph, paralyzing vestibular and auditory nerve fibers.
* **Classic Symptom Tetrad:**
  1. **Episodic True Rotatory Vertigo:** Sudden attacks lasting 20 minutes to several hours, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, sweating, and ataxia.
  2. **Fluctuating Sensorineural Hearing Loss:** Initially involves **low frequencies** (up-sloping audiogram) and improves between attacks; becomes progressive and flat in late stages.
  3. **Tinnitus:** Low-pitched, roaring, continuous or episodic tinnitus, worsening prior to an attack.
  4. **Aural Fullness:** Sensation of pressure or fullness in the affected ear.

#### c) Management of Meniere’s Disease
```
                    MANAGEMENT OF MENIERE'S DISEASE
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                                                   |
Acute Attack Management                             Prophylactic / Maintenance
  - Bed rest in quiet room                            - Lifestyle: Low salt (<2 g/d),
  - Vestibular Sedatives:                               caffeine/smoking cessation
    (IM Dimenhydrinate / Promethazine)                - Betahistine (16-48 mg/d)
  - IV Labyrinthine Sedative:                         - Diuretics (Hydrochlorothiazide)
    (IV Diazepam 5-10 mg)                             - Intratympanic Gentamicin (chemical)
  - Anti-emetics (IV Ondansetron)                     - Surgery (Sac decompression / VNS)
```
1. **Acute Attack Management:**
   * Absolute bed rest with head supported.
   * *Vestibular Sedatives:* IM Promethazine (Avomine) or IV Diazepam (5–10 mg) to suppress vestibular nuclei.
   * *Antiemetics:* IV Ondansetron (4 mg) or Prochlorperazine (Stemetil).
2. **Maintenance / Prophylactic Therapy:**
   * *Dietary / Lifestyle:* Strict low-salt diet ($<1.5–2$ g/day), avoid caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol.
   * *Vasodilators:* **Betahistine dihydrochloride (16–24 mg TID)** to increase cochlear and stria vascularis microcirculation.
   * *Diuretics:* Hydrochlorothiazide or Acetazolamide to reduce endolymph volume.
3. **Minimally Invasive Interventions:**
   * **Intratympanic Dexamethasone Injections:** For refractory fluctuating loss.
   * **Intratympanic Gentamicin (Chemical Labyrinthectomy):** Selective vestibulotoxic ablation of dark cells; controls vertigo in $>85\%$ of cases.
   * **Meniett Device:** Delivers micropressure pulses via a ventilation tube.
4. **Surgical Procedures:**
   * *Conservative:* Endolymphatic sac decompression/shunt, vestibular nerve section.
   * *Destructive (for non-serviceable hearing):* Surgical labyrinthectomy.

---

note.title: Anatomy of Olfactory Pathway
note.content:
* **1. Olfactory Neuroepithelium:** Specialized pseudostratified neuroepithelium located in the olfactory cleft (roof of nasal cavity, superior turbinate, and upper 1/3 of the nasal septum).
* **2. Primary Sensory Neurons (Bipolar Olfactory Cells):** Receptors detect odorants; their unmyelinated central axonal processes assemble into 18–20 bundles forming the **first cranial nerve (Olfactory Nerve)**.
* **3. Cribriform Plate:** Filaments traverse the cribriform plate of the ethmoid, entering the anterior cranial fossa.
* **4. Olfactory Bulb:** Axons synapse with dendrites of **Mitral cells and Tufted cells**, forming complex spherical synapses (**olfactory glomeruli**).
* **5. Olfactory Tract:** Axons of mitral and tufted cells travel posteriorly in the olfactory groove.
* **6. Central Cortical Terminations:** Divides into medial and lateral olfactory striae. Fibers terminate directly in the primary olfactory cortex (pyriform cortex, entorhinal area, and amygdaloid nucleus) **without an obligatory thalamic relay**.

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Etiology and management of vocal cord polyp

note.title: Vocal Cord Polyp: Etiology and Management
note.content:
* **Definition:** A unilateral, benign, pedunculated or sessile, gelatinous or vascular mass arising from the free edge of the true vocal fold.
* **Etiology:** Acute, violent phonotrauma (screaming, shouting, coughing attack) causing focal rupture of capillaries in **Reinke’s space**, followed by transudation, thrombosis, and organized localized oedema. Aggravated by cigarette smoking, chronic laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR), and vocal abuse.
* **Clinical Features:** Persistent hoarseness, breathy voice, vocal fatigue; large pedunculated polyps flop between the vocal cords, producing **diplophonia** (double pitch) or sudden choking spells.
* **Management:**
  * *Surgical Excision (Treatment of Choice):* **Phonomicrosurgery / Microlaryngeal Surgery (MLS):** The polyp is excised at its base under operating microscope visualization using cold micro-scissors or pulsed $\text{CO}_2$ laser, with preservation of the underlying vocal ligament.
  * *Postoperative Vocal Hygiene & Speech Therapy:* Mandatory voice therapy to correct vocal technique, along with PPI therapy for LPR to prevent recurrence.

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Tests to evaluate Eustachian Tube Dysfunction

note.title: Tests to Evaluate Eustachian Tube Dysfunction
note.content:
1. **Valsalva Manoeuvre:** Forced expiration against a closed nose and mouth builds nasopharyngeal pressure; outward drum excursion confirms patency.
2. **Toynbee’s Test:** Swallowing with the nostrils pinched; creates negative pressure in the middle ear causing inward movement of the drum (more physiological).
3. **Politzerization:** Insufflation of air into one nostril using a Politzer rubber bag while the patient swallows or says "K-K-K".
4. **Eustachian Tube Catheterization:** Transnasal insertion of a curved metal catheter into the tubal orifice with air insufflation; verified with a Toynbee auscultation tube.
5. **Impedance Tympanometry (Inflation-Deflation Test):** Measures middle ear pressure equilibration across the drum.
6. **Methylene Blue / Saccharin Clearance Test:** Trans-tympanic clearance into the pharynx.

note.title: Tuberculosis of the Larynx
note.content:
* **Etiology:** Secondary to active, cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis via bronchogenic spread of bacillus-laden sputum (*Mycobacterium tuberculosis*).
* **Clinical Features:**
  * Severe **weakness of voice and progressive hoarseness**.
  * Severe **odynophagia and pain radiating to ears**, worse on swallowing liquids.
  * Classical Laryngeal Findings:
    * Asymmetric hyperaemia and ulceration of the true vocal cords (**"mouse-nibbled" appearance**).
    * Mammillated, pale granulation tissue in the **interarytenoid space** and posterior glottis.
    * Infiltration and pale oedema of the epiglottis (**"turban epiglottis"**).
* **Diagnosis & Treatment:** Sputum CBNAAT/culture, chest radiograph, direct laryngoscopic biopsy; full standard course of Anti-Tubercular Therapy (ATT).

note.title: Frey’s Syndrome
note.content:
* **Pathophysiology:** Complication of parotidectomy caused by aberrant regeneration of cut parasympathetic secretomotor fibers of the **auriculotemporal nerve** (originally supplying the parotid gland), which misdirect and re-innervate the cutaneous sweat glands and subcutaneous blood vessels of the preauricular skin.
* **Clinical Feature:** Flushing, warmth, and profuse perspiration over the parotid skin provoked specifically by mastication or gustatory stimulation with sour/spicy food (**gustatory sweating**).
* **Treatment:** Minor starch-iodine test confirms area; treat with topical antiperspirants (aluminum chloride), intradermal **Botulinum toxin A** injections, or tympanic neurectomy (Jacobson's nerve section).

---

note.title: Importance of Carhart’s Notch
note.content:
* **Definition:** A reversible dip in the **bone conduction threshold** seen on pure tone audiometry in patients with stapedial otosclerosis, maximum at **2000 Hz (15 dB at 2 kHz)**.
* **Mechanism:** Not due to true sensorineural cochlear damage, but rather loss of the inertial bone-conduction component mediated by normal ossicular resonance when the stapes footplate is fixed.
* **Clinical Importance:** It confirms stapedial fixation; the dip **recovers and disappears postoperatively** after successful stapedotomy/stapedectomy, restoring true cochlear reserve.

---

note.title: Le Fort Fractures: Types
note.content:
1. **Le Fort I (Guerin / Transverse Fracture):** Horizontal fracture running above the alveolar ridge, passing through the lower nasal septum, pyriform aperture, and pterygoid plates; separates the palate from the upper facial skeleton.
2. **Le Fort II (Pyramidal Fracture):** Triangular fracture passing through the nasal bones, frontal process of the maxilla, lacrimal bones, orbital floor, and pterygoid plates; detaches the midface pyramid.
3. **Le Fort III (Craniofacial Dysjunction):** Complete separation of the facial skeleton from the cranial base, passing through the nasofrontal suture, ethmofrontal suture, orbital walls, and zygomatic arches.

---

questions.officialText: (a) Enumerate four causes for unilateral nasal obstruction (b) Discuss the aetiopathology of deviated nasal septum (c) Describe the clinical features of deviated nasal septum (d) Describe the treatment of deviated nasal septum. Add a note on complications of submucosal resection of septum (2+4+4+5)

note.title: Deviated Nasal Septum (DNS)
note.content:
#### a) Four Causes for Unilateral Nasal Obstruction
1. Deviated Nasal Septum (anterior dislocation or prominent spur).
2. Unilateral Antrochoanal Polyp.
3. Retained unilateral foreign body or rhinolith.
4. Unilateral sinonasal tumour (e.g., Inverted papilloma or Squamous cell carcinoma).

#### b) Aetiopathology of Deviated Nasal Septum
1. **Trauma (Most Common Cause):**
   * *Birth Trauma:* Moulding pressure during passage through the birth canal (forceps delivery or breech extraction).
   * *Accidental Trauma:* Direct blows to the nose during childhood or adulthood; lateral forces produce C-shaped deformities, while crushing frontal blows cause vertical/horizontal buckling, fractures, and telescoping.
2. **Developmental Error:** Disproportionate unequal growth rates between the facial bones/palate and the cranial base. High-arched palate (in mouth breathers with adenoids) leaves insufficient vertical height for the septum, forcing it to buckle.
3. **Hereditary & Racial Factors:** Common in Caucasians; familial clustering observed.

#### c) Clinical Features of Deviated Nasal Septum
* **Nasal Obstruction:** Cardinal symptom; unilateral or bilateral (S-shaped deviation); anterior/high septal deviations produce more severe obstruction as they compromise the internal nasal valve.
* **Cottle’s Test:** Drawing the cheek laterally on the affected side opens the internal nasal valve; improvement in nasal airflow confirms valve-level septal obstruction.
* **Headache:** Impinging septal spurs contact the sensitive middle turbinate/lateral wall, stimulating trigeminal sensory fibers (**Sluder’s contact point headache**).
* **Recurrent Sinusitis:** Mechanical occlusion of the ostiomeatal complex impairs sinus ventilation.
* **Epistaxis:** Thin, stretched mucosa over the convex summit of a spur dries and crusts easily; detachment of crusts causes bleeding.
* **Anosmia / Hyposmia:** Inability of the inspiratory air stream to reach the olfactory cleft.
* **External Deformity:** Crooked or deviated nasal dorsum, caudal subluxation into the nostril.

#### d) Treatment and Complications of Submucous Resection (SMR)
* **Treatment:**
  * **Septoplasty (Procedure of Choice):** Conservative approach; mucoperichondrial flap elevated on one side only; preserves the dorsal and caudal cartilaginous struts; realigns and repositions the septum while retaining structural support.
  * **Submucous Resection (SMR):** Classic operation in adults $>17$ years; bilateral flaps elevated and all deviated cartilage/bone excised.
* **Complications of SMR:**
  1. Supratip saddle nose deformity (due to loss of dorsal cartilaginous support).
  2. Retraction of the columella (due to excision of caudal cartilage strut).
  3. Permanent septal perforation.
  4. Septal haematoma and secondary septal abscess.
  5. Flapping of the membranous septum during respiration.
  6. Postoperative epistaxis.
  7. Synechiae formation between the septum and turbinates.

---

note.title: Physiology of Swallowing
note.content:
Swallowing is divided into three coordinated phases:

```
                            DEGLUTITION
                                 |
         +-----------------------+-----------------------+
         |                       |                       |
1. Oral Phase (Voluntary)    2. Pharyngeal Phase     3. Oesophageal Phase
   - Mastication & bolus        (Involuntary, Reflex)   (Involuntary Peristalsis)
     formation                  - Velopharyngeal closure- Cricopharyngeal relaxation
   - Tongue drives bolus into   - Laryngeal protection  - Primary & secondary
     oropharynx                   (3 sphincter tiers)     peristaltic waves
                                - Pharyngeal peristalsis- LES relaxation
```
1. **Oral Phase (Voluntary):** Food is masticated and lubricated with saliva to form a coherent bolus. The anterior tongue elevates against the hard palate, and a sequential backward rolling wave of the tongue pushes the bolus through the faucial isthmus into the oropharynx.
2. **Pharyngeal Phase (Involuntary, Reflex — $<1$ Second):** Initiated when the bolus contacts mucosal receptors on the anterior pillars and base of the tongue:
   * *Nasopharyngeal Closure:* Soft palate elevates against Passavant’s ridge to prevent nasopharyngeal regurgitation.
   * *Laryngeal Protection (Three Sphincteric Tiers):* Respiration ceases; epiglottis tilts backward over the inlet; false vocal cords approximate; true vocal cords adduct tightly; larynx is pulled upward and forward under the tongue base.
   * *Pharyngeal Propulsion:* Contraction of superior, middle, and inferior pharyngeal constrictors drives the bolus downward.
   * *Cricopharyngeal Relaxation:* The upper oesophageal sphincter relaxes to allow the bolus to enter the oesophagus.
3. **Oesophageal Phase (Involuntary — 4–8 Seconds):** Primary peristaltic wave initiated by swallowing propels the bolus down the oesophagus. Lower oesophageal sphincter (LES) relaxes ahead of the bolus, allowing entry into the stomach.

---

note.title: Left Vocal Cord Paralysis: Aetiology, Clinical Features, and Management
note.content:
* **Anatomical Basis:** The left recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) has an extended intrathoracic course; it loops around the arch of the aorta lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum and ascends in the tracheo-oesophageal groove, making it **twice as susceptible to injury or pathology** as the right RLN.

#### Aetiology
1. **Intrathoracic Malignancies:** Carcinoma of the left bronchus / lung apex (Pancoast tumour), carcinoma of the thoracic oesophagus.
2. **Cardiovascular:** Aortic aneurysm, left atrial dilatation in mitral stenosis (**Ortner’s syndrome**).
3. **Neck Pathology:** Thyroid malignancy, thyroidectomy, cervical lymphadenopathy.
4. **Surgical Trauma:** Thoracic surgeries (PDA ligation, lobectomy, esophagectomy) and carotid endarterectomy.
5. **Idiopathic (30%):** Post-viral neuropathy.

#### Clinical Features
* **Symptoms:** Hoarseness of voice (breathy, weak voice), vocal fatigue, loss of singing pitch; aspiration and coughing while drinking thin liquids; ineffective, weak cough (inability to generate explosive subglottic pressure).
* **Laryngeal Examination:** The left vocal fold rests immobilized in the **paramedian or median position** (Wagner and Grossman hypothesis: unopposed cricothyroid adductor tone). Over time, the contralateral right vocal cord hyper-adducts across the midline to compensate, improving voice quality.

#### Management
1. **Investigation of Underlying Cause (Mandatory):** Contrast CT from skull base to aortopulmonary window (to rule out mediastinal/pulmonary malignancy), chest radiograph, and upper GI endoscopy.
2. **Conservative / Speech Therapy:** Wait 6 to 12 months for idiopathic or post-surgical neuropraxia to allow spontaneous recovery or contralateral compensation. Structured voice therapy improves compensatory adduction.
3. **Temporary Vocal Cord Augmentation:** Injection of Gelfoam, hyaluronic acid, or carboxymethylcellulose into the paralyzed cord to medialize it during the observation period.
4. **Permanent Medialization Procedures (if no recovery after 12 months):**
   * **Type I Isshiki Thyroplasty (Medialization Thyroplasty):** Under local anesthesia, a window is created in the thyroid cartilage lamina and a Silastic/titanium implant is placed deep to the inner perichondrium to push the vocal cord medially.
   * **Arytenoid Adduction:** Added to thyroplasty if there is a large posterior glottic gap.

questions.officialText: What are the types of tracheostomy. Discuss the indications, steps, and complications of tracheostomy

note.title: Tracheostomy: Types, Indications, Steps, and Complications
note.content:
* **Types of Tracheostomy:**
  1. *Emergency Tracheostomy:* Rapid, lifesaving bedside procedure for acute upper airway obstruction.
  2. *Elective (Tranquil) Tracheostomy:* Planned, unhurried procedure in the operation theatre under controlled conditions.
  3. *Permanent Tracheostomy:* Permanent stoma created following total laryngectomy.
  4. *Percutaneous Dilatational Tracheostomy (PDT):* Bedside Seldinger technique performed in ICU settings.
  5. *Cricothyroidotomy (Mini-Tracheostomy):* Emergency temporary access via the cricothyroid membrane.
* **Indications:** REFER TO [[KUHS-QUESTION:315001:Q21]] (2026_JANUARY).

#### Surgical Steps of Elective Tracheostomy
1. **Position:** Supine with a sandbag under the shoulders to extend the neck; head stabilized in the midline.
2. **Anesthesia:** Local infiltration with 1–2% lignocaine with 1:100,000 adrenaline, or general anesthesia.
3. **Incision:** Transverse collar incision (two finger-breadths above the suprasternal notch) or vertical midline incision from the cricoid to just above the sternal notch.
4. **Dissection:** Deepened through the platysma; strap muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid) retracted laterally in the midline avascular plane.
5. **Thyroid Isthmus:** Identified crossing the 2nd to 4th tracheal rings; retracted superiorly, or divided between hemostats and suture-ligated.
6. **Tracheal Opening:** 2 mL of 4% lignocaine is injected into the tracheal lumen to suppress violent cough. Trachea is opened via a **vertical incision across the 2nd and 3rd (or 3rd and 4th) tracheal rings**. (First tracheal ring must never be cut to avoid perichondritis and subglottic stenosis).
7. **Tube Insertion:** Tracheal dilator introduced; appropriate-sized cuffed tracheostomy tube inserted; cuff inflated and position confirmed by symmetrical chest rise and auscultation.
8. **Fixation:** Tapes secured firmly around the neck with the neck flexed.

#### Complications of Tracheostomy
```
                    COMPLICATIONS OF TRACHEOSTOMY
                                  |
     +----------------------------+----------------------------+
     |                            |                            |
Immediate (Intraoperative)   Intermediate (Days 1–7)     Late (Weeks/Months)
  - Severe Haemorrhage         - Tube displacement/block   - Tracheal Stenosis
  - Apnoea (loss of $CO_2$     - Subcutaneous emphysema    - Tracheo-oesophageal fistula
    respiratory drive)         - Pneumothorax              - Tracheoinnominate fistula
  - Tracheal wall / oesophagus - Secondary wound infection - Decannulation difficulty
    perforation                - Tracheobronchial crusting - Persistent stoma
```

---

note.title: Jacobson’s Nerve
note.content:
* **Anatomy:** Tympanic branch of the **Glossopharyngeal Nerve (CN IX)**.
* **Course & Function:** Enters the middle ear through the inferior tympanic canaliculus on the promontory, where it forms the **tympanic plexus**.
* **Clinical Significance:** 
  1. Carries preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland (via lesser petrosal nerve and otic ganglion).
  2. Provides sensory innervation to the middle ear mucosa; responsible for **referred otalgia** from tonsillitis, quinsy, and tongue base carcinomas.
  3. Sectioned in **tympanic neurectomy** to manage Frey’s syndrome.

note.title: Reinke’s Oedema
note.content:
* **Pathology:** Diffuse, bilateral, symmetrical polypoid degeneration of the true vocal cords characterized by fluid accumulation in **Reinke’s space** (superficial lamina propria).
* **Etiology:** Strongly linked to chronic cigarette smoking, vocal abuse, and laryngopharyngeal reflux. Common in middle-aged women.
* **Features & Treatment:** Low-pitched, husky, "manly" voice; vocal fatigue. Treatment is smoking cessation and speech therapy; refractory cases undergo microlaryngeal decortication / suctioning of viscous fluid.

note.title: Boundaries of Macewen’s Triangle (Suprameatal Triangle)
note.content:
* **Significance:** Surgical surface landmark on the mastoid cortex for locating the **mastoid antrum**, which lies 12–15 mm deep to it in adults.
* **Boundaries:**
  1. *Superiorly:* Supramastoid crest (temporal line; posterior root of the zygoma).
  2. *Anteroinferiorly:* Posterosuperior margin of the bony external acoustic meatus.
  3. *Posteriorly:* A vertical tangent drawn along the posterior wall of the external acoustic meatus.

note.title: Bezold’s Abscess
note.content:
* **Pathophysiology:** A deep neck complication of acute coalescent mastoiditis where pus erodes through the thin **medial wall of the mastoid tip** into the digastric groove.
* **Clinical Course:** Pus tracks deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, presenting as a painful, tender, brawny swelling in the upper lateral neck, accompanied by torticollis and fever.
* **Treatment:** Cortical mastoidectomy with clearance of tip cells + separate external incision and drainage of the neck abscess.

---

note.title: Bleeding Septal Polyp (Capillary Haemangioma)
note.content:
* **Definition:** A benign, vascular, inflammatory lesion (lobular capillary haemangioma) arising typically from **Little’s area** on the anterior nasal septum.
* **Features & Treatment:** Presents with recurrent unprovoked epistaxis and unilateral nasal blockage. Appears as a red, pedunculated or sessile mass. Treatment is complete endoscopic local surgical excision with a cuff of surrounding perichondrium.

note.title: Dysphagia Lusoria
note.content:
* **Pathophysiology:** Dysphagia caused by extrinsic vascular compression of the oesophagus by an **aberrant right subclavian artery** (arteria lusoria) arising anomalously from the left descending aorta and traversing across the midline behind the oesophagus.
* **Diagnosis & Management:** Barium swallow shows an oblique posterior indentation; CT angiography confirms the anatomy. Treated conservatively with diet modification or vascular surgical transposition in severe cases.

questions.officialText: a) Draw and label neat diagram of osteomeatal complex. b) Clinical signs and investigations of chronic rhinosinusitis c) What are the principles of Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS). Enumerate the steps of FESS d) What are the complications of FESS (2+3+3+2)

note.title: Chronic Rhinosinusitis and FESS
note.content:
#### a) Osteomeatal Complex (Draw and Label)
REFER TO [[KUHS-QUESTION:315001:Q25]] (2026_APRIL)

#### b) Clinical Signs and Investigations of Chronic Rhinosinusitis
* **Signs (Anterior Rhinoscopy & Nasal Endoscopy):**
  * Congested, oedematous nasal mucosa with purulent or mucopurulent discharge in the middle meatus (anterior group) or sphenoethmoidal recess (posterior group).
  * Hypertrophy or polypoid changes over the uncinate process and middle turbinate.
  * Secondary mucosal crusting or true polyps prolapsing from ostia.
* **Investigations:**
  1. **Non-Contrast CT (NCCT) of Paranasal Sinuses (Coronal & Axial, Bone Window — Gold Standard):** Assesses mucosal thickening, sinus opacification, ostial obstruction, anatomical variants (concha bullosa, septal spurs, Haller cells), and evaluates the skull base (Keros classification) and lamina papyracea prior to surgery.
  2. **Diagnostic Nasal Endoscopy (DNE):** Allows direct examination and directed swab cultures.
  3. **Endoscopically Directed Middle Meatal Swab:** Aerobic/anaerobic cultures.

#### c) Principles and Steps of Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS)
* **Principles (Messerklinger & Stammberger):**
  1. Sinus ventilation and mucociliary clearance can be restored by clearing mechanical obstruction focused specifically at the **ostiomeatal complex**.
  2. Mucosal changes are largely reversible once ventilation and drainage are re-established.
  3. Preservation of normal, non-polypoid respiratory mucosa is prioritized over radical stripping.
* **Surgical Steps (Anteroposterior / Stammberger Technique):**
  1. Medialization of the middle turbinate to expose the middle meatus.
  2. **Uncinectomy:** Incision of the uncinate process with a sickle knife and excision with a backbiter or microdebrider.
  3. **Middle Meatal Antrostomy:** Identification and enlargement of the natural maxillary sinus ostium posteriorly and inferiorly.
  4. **Anterior Ethmoidectomy (Bullectomy):** Penetration and clearance of the bulla ethmoidalis.
  5. **Posterior Ethmoidectomy:** Traversal of the basal lamella to clear posterior ethmoidal cells.
  6. **Sphenoidotomy:** Enlargement of the sphenoid ostium if the sphenoid sinus is diseased.
  7. **Frontal Sinusotomy:** Clearance of the frontal recess and agger nasi cells if frontal sinus is involved.

#### d) Complications of FESS
REFER TO [[KUHS-QUESTION:318001:Q17]] (2025_MAY)

---

note.title: Subglottic Stenosis
note.content:
* **Definition:** Narrowing of the subglottic airway lumen between the vocal cords and the lower border of the cricoid cartilage ($<4$ mm in full-term neonate, $<11$ mm in an adult).
* **Aetiology:**
  1. *Congenital:* Developmental failure of laryngeal recanalization; abnormally thickened cricoid ring.
  2. *Acquired (90%):* Secondary to prolonged endotracheal intubation (cuff pressure-induced mucosal necrosis and scarring), high tracheostomy (cutting 1st ring/cricoid), external laryngeal trauma, or Wegener’s granulomatosis.
* **Clinical Grading (Cotton-Myer System):**
  * Grade I: $<50\%$ luminal obstruction.
  * Grade II: 51–70% obstruction.
  * Grade III: 71–99% obstruction.
  * Grade IV: No detectable lumen (complete atresia).
* **Treatment:**
  * Endoscopic balloon dilation, radial $\text{CO}_2$ laser incision with topical mitomycin-C for Grades I & II.
  * Open surgical reconstruction: **Laryngotracheal Reconstruction (LTR)** with anterior/posterior costal cartilage grafting, or **Cricotracheal Resection and Anastomosis (CTR)** for Grades III & IV.

---

note.title: Congenital Cholesteatoma
note.content:
* **Definition (Levenson’s Diagnostic Criteria):**
  1. White, pearly epithelial mass presenting medial to an intact, normal tympanic membrane.
  2. Normal pars tensa and pars flaccida (no retraction pockets).
  3. No prior history of ear discharge or tympanic perforation.
  4. No prior history of otological surgery.
* **Embryological Origin:** Persistence of an epidermoid cell rest in the embryonic middle ear cleft near the neck of the malleus.
* **Clinical Features & Treatment:** Presents as asymptomatic progressive conductive hearing loss in early childhood; identified as an incidental white mass during otoscopy. Treatment is surgical excision via tympanoplasty/mastoidectomy.

---

note.title: Stridor and Laryngomalacia
note.content:
REFER TO [[KUHS-QUESTION:318001:Q10]] `b` (2025_MAY) AND [[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q03]] (2024_AUGUST)

* **Note on Laryngomalacia:**
  * Most common congenital laryngeal anomaly (60–70% of neonatal stridor).
  * Caused by delayed neuromaturational development resulting in excessive hypotonia and flaccidity of the supraglottic cartilaginous structures.
  * During inspiration, negative intrathoracic pressure sucks the floppy aryepiglottic folds, large cuneiforms, and elongated, tubular **omega-shaped ($\Omega$) epiglottis** into the glottic aperture, creating **inspiratory stridor**.
  * Stridor is exacerbated by supine positioning, crying, agitation, and feeding; diminishes when the child is placed **prone**. Cry is typically normal.
  * Diagnosis confirmed by flexible fibreoptic laryngoscopy.
  * Self-limiting in $>90\%$ by 18–24 months; severe cases (hypoxia, feeding failure, cor pulmonale) undergo endoscopic **supraglottoplasty** (division of tight aryepiglottic folds and trimming redundant mucosa).

questions.officialText: Anatomy and course of Facial Nerve

note.title: Facial Nerve: Anatomy and Course
note.content:
REFER TO [[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q14]] (2026_MARCH) AND standard anatomical descriptions:
* **Segments of Facial Nerve:**
  1. *Intracranial (CP Angle):* Exits brainstem at pontomedullary junction $\rightarrow$ traverses subarachnoid space (15–17 mm) entering internal acoustic meatus.
  2. *Intratemporal / Fallopian Canal:*
     * Meatal segment (8–10 mm).
     * Labyrinthine segment (3–4 mm): Shortest and narrowest; ends at the **first genu / geniculate ganglion**.
     * Tympanic / Horizontal segment (11 mm): Runs along the medial wall of the middle ear above the oval window.
     * Mastoid / Vertical segment (13 mm): Starts at the second genu near the pyramid and descends to the **stylomastoid foramen**.
  3. *Extracranial:* Exits stylomastoid foramen $\rightarrow$ enters parotid gland $\rightarrow$ branches at *pes anserinus* into 5 terminal motor branches (Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal Mandibular, Cervical).

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Pathological features and management of Acoustic Neuroma

note.title: Acoustic Neuroma: Pathological Features and Management
note.content:
REFER TO [[KUHS-QUESTION:318001:Q02]] (2025_MAY) AND standard descriptions:
* **Pathology:** Benign, slow-growing, encapsulated Schwann cell tumour arising typically from the inferior or superior division of the vestibular nerve inside the internal auditory canal.
  * Histologically displays alternating areas: **Antoni A** (densely packed spindle cells with palisading nuclei forming **Verocay bodies**) and **Antoni B** (loose, myxoid tissue).
* **Management:**
  1. *Observation ("Wait and Scan"):* Serial contrast-enhanced MRIs every 6–12 months for elderly patients, small asymptomatic intracanalicular tumours ($<1$ cm), or in an only-hearing ear.
  2. *Stereotactic Radiosurgery (Gamma Knife / CyberKnife):* For tumours $<3$ cm without brainstem compression, elderly patients, or medical comorbidities. Arrests tumour growth in $>90\%$.
  3. *Microsurgical Resection:*
     * *Translabyrinthine Approach:* Best for non-serviceable hearing; gives direct access with minimal brain retraction and early facial nerve identification.
     * *Retrosigmoid / Suboccipital Approach:* Allows hearing preservation for small-to-medium tumours with good pre-existing auditory function.
     * *Middle Cranial Fossa Approach:* For small intracanalicular tumours with intact hearing.

---

note.title: Thornwaldt’s Cyst

* **Pathology:** A benign, congenital midline mucosal bursa/cyst located in the posterior wall of the nasopharynx, representing a persistent remnant of the embryonic **notochord attachment** to the pharyngeal endoderm.
* **Features:** Asymptomatic until obstructed by infection; presents with persistent, foul-smelling postnasal discharge, occipital headache, and Eustachian tube dysfunction.
