questions.officialText: Anatomy of Middle ear with diagram

note.title: Anatomy of Middle Ear (with Diagram)
note.content:
```
                            ROOF (Tegmen Tympani)
                                     ^
  ANTERIOR WALL                      |                 POSTERIOR WALL
  ------------------                 |                 ------------------
  Canal for Tensor  |          EPITYMPANUM            | Aditus ad Antrum
   Tympani          |    (Head of Malleus/Incus)      | Fossa Incudis
  Opening of        |                                 | Pyramid (Stapedius)
   Eustachian Tube  |          MESOTYMPANUM           | Facial Nerve Canal
  Canal for Internal|   (Vocal Ossicles, Promontory)  | (Mastoid Segment)
   Carotid Artery   |                                 | Chorda Tympani
  ------------------|          HYPOTYMPANUM           |------------------
                                     |
                                     v
                       FLOOR (Jugular Bulb Wall)
```
* **Walls of the Middle Ear (Tympanic Cavity):**
  1. *Roof (Tegmental Wall):* Thin bony plate of **tegmen tympani** separating the middle ear from the middle cranial fossa.
  2. *Floor (Jugular Wall):* Thin bone separating the hypotympanum from the **internal jugular bulb**.
  3. *Anterior Wall (Carotid Wall):* Thin bone separating the cavity from the internal carotid artery; contains openings for the **Eustachian tube** and the canal for the **tensor tympani muscle**.
  4. *Posterior Wall (Mastoid Wall):* Communicates superiorly with the mastoid antrum via the **aditus ad antrum**; contains the **pyramid** (transmits stapedius tendon), **fossa incudis**, and the canal for the vertical segment of the facial nerve.
  5. *Lateral Wall (Membranous Wall):* Formed by the **tympanic membrane** and bony scutum.
  6. *Medial Wall (Labyrinthine Wall):* REFER TO [[KUHS-QUESTION:318001:Q21]] (2025_OCTOBER) — features the **promontory, oval window, round window, horizontal facial canal prominence, and processus cochleariformis**.

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Etiopathogenesis and management of Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma

note.title: Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma: Etiopathogenesis and Management
note.content:
* **Etiopathogenesis:** Strongly associated with **Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)** infection (elevated anti-EBV IgA antibodies to Viral Capsid Antigen [VCA] and Early Antigen [EA]); genetic predisposition in Mongoloid/Chinese races (HLA-A2, B17); dietary consumption of salted dried fish containing volatile nitrosamines.
* **Histopathological Types (WHO Classification):**
  1. *Type 1:* Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma (25%; weakly linked to EBV).
  2. *Type 2:* Non-keratinizing differentiated carcinoma (12%).
  3. *Type 3:* Non-keratinizing undifferentiated carcinoma / lymphoepithelioma (63%; strongly linked to EBV, highly radiosensitive).
* **Management:**
  * **Primary Treatment is Non-Surgical:** Due to its deep anatomical location and high radiosensitivity:
    * *Stage I:* **Definitive External Beam Radiotherapy (EBRT / IMRT)** to the nasopharynx and bilateral neck nodes (66–70 Gy).
    * *Stages II, III, IVA/B (Locally Advanced):* **Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy (CCRT)**: High-dose cisplatin administered during radiation therapy, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy (Cisplatin + 5-Fluorouracil).
  * *Surgical Role:* Limited strictly to salvage: **Radical Neck Dissection** for persistent/recurrent neck nodes after complete primary radiotherapy clearance, or endoscopic/transpalatal nasopharyngectomy for isolated local recurrences.

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Classification and mechanism of Ototoxic drugs

note.title: Ototoxic Drugs: Classification and Mechanism
note.content:
* **Classification and Mechanisms:**
  1. **Aminoglycoside Antibiotics:**
     * *Vestibulotoxic (selective damage to Type I sensory hair cells of crista ampullaris):* Streptomycin, Gentamicin, Tobramycin.
     * *Cochleotoxic (damage to outer hair cells of the organ of Corti starting at the basal turn):* Amikacin, Kanamycin, Neomycin.
     * *Mechanism:* Produce reactive oxygen species (ROS), inhibit mitochondrial protein synthesis, and trigger hair cell apoptosis.
  2. **Loop Diuretics (Furosemide, Ethacrynic Acid):**
     * Disrupt active ion transport in the **stria vascularis**, eliminating the endocochlear potential (+80 mV); typically reversible.
  3. **Antineoplastic Agents (Cisplatin, Carboplatin):**
     * Form DNA cross-links and generate toxic ROS, destroying outer hair cells irreversibly in the basal turn (causing bilateral high-frequency SNHL).
  4. **Salicylates (Aspirin) & NSAIDs:**
     * Inhibit prestin electromotility in outer hair cells; cause reversible bilateral sensorineural loss and high-pitched tinnitus.
  5. **Antimalarials (Quinine, Chloroquine):**
     * Induce severe cochlear microvascular vasoconstriction and ischemia; usually reversible.

---

```
                            MEDIAL
                              ^
                    [ Palatine Tonsil ]
                              |
                    [ Tonsillar Capsule ]
                              |
              +---------------+---------------+
              | Loose Areolar Peritonsillar   |
              | Tissue & Paratonsillar Vein   |
              +---------------+---------------+
                              |
                 PHARYNGOBASILAR FASCIA
                              |
              +---------------+---------------+
              | SUPERIOR CONSTRICTOR MUSCLE   |
              | (Upper 2/3 of Bed)            |
              +---------------+---------------+

              | (Lower 1/3 of Bed)            |
              +---------------+---------------+
```

* **Structures Forming the Tonsillar Bed (from inside out):**
  1. *Loose areolar peritonsillar tissue* containing the paratonsillar vein (source of reactionary bleeding).

  3. *Superior constrictor muscle* (forms the upper two-thirds).
  4. *Styloglossus muscle* (forms the lower one-third).
  5. *Buccopharyngeal fascia.*
  6. *Immediate Lateral Relations:* Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), styloid process, loop of the facial artery, and submandibular gland.

note.title: Physiology of Hearing
note.content:
REFER TO [[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q11]] (2026_MARCH) AND standard principles:
* **Mechanism of Sound Transmission:**
  1. *Acoustic Collection:* Pinna collects and focuses sound waves into the external acoustic meatus (natural canal resonance at 3000 Hz).
  2. *Impedance Matching (Transformer Action of Middle Ear):* Matches low-impedance airborne sound to high-impedance liquid perilymph:
     * **Areal Ratio (Hydraulic Lever):** Effective vibrating area of tympanic membrane ($55\text{ mm}^2$) to stapes footplate area ($3.2\text{ mm}^2$) = **17:1**.
     * **Ossicular Lever Ratio:** Handle of malleus is 1.3 times longer than the long process of the incus = **1.3:1**.
     * **Total Transformer Ratio:** $17 \times 1.3 = \mathbf{22:1}$ (compensates for the 99.9% / 30 dB sound energy reflection at the air-fluid interface).
     * **Catenary / Curved Membrane Lever:** More movement at the periphery than the center adds leverage.
  3. *Phase Differential:* Sound reaches the oval window preferentially, preserving reciprocal round window displacement.
  4. *Cochlear Transduction:* Békésy's travelling wave deflects stereocilia against the tectorial membrane $\rightarrow$ mechanically gated $K^+$ channels open $\rightarrow$ depolarization $\rightarrow$ release of glutamate $\rightarrow$ auditory nerve action potential propagation.

---

note.title: Otolith Organs (Utricle and Saccule)
note.content:
* **Structure:** Specialized vestibular end-organs of the membranous labyrinth located within the vestibule. Contain sensory neuroepithelium called the **macula**.
* **Macular Architecture:** Hair cells (Type I and II) with stereocilia embedded in a gelatinous matrix topped by a layer of dense calcium carbonate crystals (**otoconia / statoconia**).
* **Physiological Function:**
  * *Utricle (horizontal macula):* Detects **linear horizontal acceleration** and head tilt.
  * *Saccule (vertical macula):* Detects **linear vertical acceleration** (gravity).

---

note.title: Uses of Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA)
note.content:
1. Determines quantitative hearing thresholds for air and bone conduction across frequencies (125 Hz to 8000 Hz).
2. Differentiates between Conductive, Sensorineural, and Mixed hearing loss based on the presence and magnitude of the Air-Bone Gap.
3. Essential for selection, programming, and fitting of hearing aids.
4. Baseline testing and serial monitoring for noise-induced hearing loss or ototoxicity.
5. Medicolegal documentation of hearing impairment and disability percentage calculation.

note.title: Kartagener Syndrome
note.content:
* **Pathology:** An autosomal recessive genetic disorder causing **primary ciliary dyskinesia** due to congenital absence or defect of the **dynein arms** in ciliary axonemes.
* **Classic Clinical Triad:**
  1. **Situs Inversus Totalis** (dextrocardia with inverted viscera).
  2. **Chronic Bronchiectasis**.
  3. **Chronic Rhinosinusitis** with nasal polyposis.
* Male infertility (due to immotile sperm flagella) and Eustachian tube dysfunction (chronic OME) are common.

---

note.title: Fuller’s Tracheostomy Tube
note.content:
* **Features:** A metallic, bivalved tracheostomy tube made of sterling silver.
* **Mechanism:** The outer cannula consists of two split blades that can be compressed together like forceps for easy insertion into the tracheal stoma without an introducer. It contains an inner cannula for cleaning.

---

note.title: Saddle Nose Deformity
note.content:
* **Definition:** Depression or collapse of the nasal dorsum, involving the cartilaginous dorsum (supratip depression) or both bony and cartilaginous components.
* **Aetiology:** Over-resection of the septum during SMR/septoplasty; destructive chondronecrosis from neglected septal haematoma/abscess; trauma; leprosy, syphilis, or Wegener’s granulomatosis.
* **Treatment:** Augmentation rhinoplasty using autologous cartilage (septal, conchal, or costal cartilage) or cancellous bone grafting from the iliac crest.

---

note.title: Mastoidectomy Surgery
note.content:
* **Types:** Cortical (simple/Schwartz), Modified Radical, and Radical Mastoidectomy.
* **Cortical Mastoidectomy Steps:**
  1. Postaural incision $\rightarrow$ expose Macewen’s triangle.
  2. Drill into Macewen’s triangle to enter the mastoid antrum.
  3. Identify the horizontal semicircular canal and aditus ad antrum.
  4. Exenterate all peripheral mastoid air cell tracts (zygomatic, retrofacial, perisinus, tip cells).
  5. Thin the tegmen tympani and sinus plate without breach; maintain an intact posterior meatal wall.
* **Complications:** Facial nerve paralysis, dural tear/CSF leak, sigmoid sinus laceration and profuse bleeding, horizontal canal fistulization with vertigo, hearing loss.

questions.officialText: Gastroesophageal reflux disease –clinical features and treatment

note.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD / LPR): Clinical Features and Treatment
note.content:
* **Clinical Features (Laryngopharyngeal Reflux — LPR):**
  * Persistent globus pharyngeus ("lump in throat"), chronic throat clearing, morning hoarseness, chronic cough, throat burn, postnasal drip sensation.
  * *Laryngoscopy:* Interarytenoid pachydermia, erythema and oedema of the posterior glottis and arytenoid mucosa (**posterior laryngitis**), vocal process contact ulcers/granulomas.
* **Treatment:**
  1. *Lifestyle & Dietary:* Elevate head of the bed (15 cm); avoid eating within 3 hours of sleep; eliminate coffee, chocolate, alcohol, peppermint, citrus, fatty/fried foods, and smoking; weight loss.
  2. *Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs):* Omeprazole (20 mg BD) or Pantoprazole (40 mg BD) for at least 8–12 weeks.
  3. *Prokinetics & Alginates:* Provide additional barrier and promote gastric emptying.
  4. *Antireflux Surgery (Nissen Fundoplication):* For medically refractory cases.

note.title: Treatment of Septal Haematoma
note.content:
1. **Urgent Surgical Evacuation:** Immediate aspiration with a wide-bore needle (small collection) or formal incision and drainage (large haematoma).
2. **Incision & Drainage:** Anteroposterior horizontal incision over the most fluctuant area along the floor of the nasal septum under local/topical anesthesia; remove blood clots and necrotic cartilage fragments.
3. **Bilateral Anterior Nasal Packing:** Firm, layered packing on **both sides of the septum** for 48 hours to coapt the mucoperichondrial flaps against the cartilage and prevent re-accumulation of blood.
4. **Parenteral Antibiotics:** Broad-spectrum systemic coverage to prevent secondary infection converting the haematoma into a **septal abscess**.

questions.officialText: A 60 years old man, who is a smoker and alcoholic for the past 40 years, presented to the ENT OPD with complaints of progressive, unremitting dysphonia of three months duration and noisy breathing for the past 5 days. Answer the following:  What is your provisional diagnosis  What is the immediate intervention to be planned  What are the other clinical features of this condition  What are the investigations to be done in this patient and mention the expected findings in each  Discuss the treatment options for this patient (1+1+2+3+3)

note.title: Laryngeal Carcinoma in an Elderly Smoker
note.content:
* **Clinical Scenario:** 60yo male, 40-year smoking and alcohol history, 3-month progressive unremitting dysphonia, 5-day noisy breathing (stridor).

#### a) Provisional Diagnosis
* **Carcinoma of the Larynx (Likely Glottic Carcinoma with Supraglottic / Subglottic Extension, Stage T3/T4) with Impending Upper Airway Obstruction**.

#### b) Immediate Intervention to be Planned
1. **Emergency Airway Security:** Administer humidified oxygen. If stridor and respiratory distress are severe:
   * Perform an **Emergency Awake Tracheostomy under local infiltration anesthesia** (low tracheostomy, dividing 3rd and 4th rings; strictly avoid cricoid cartilage and tumor margins).
   * Alternatively, perform gentle awake fibreoptic intubation.
2. Avoid emergency direct laryngoscopy or blind manipulation in the ward as it can precipitate complete laryngeal spasm and asphyxia.

#### c) Other Clinical Features
* **Progressive Hoarseness:** Gradually worsens from breathiness to complete aphonia.
* **Biphasic Stridor & Dyspnoea:** Due to tumor growth narrowing the glottic aperture.
* **Pain & Odynophagia:** Deep throat pain radiating to the ipsilateral ear (**referred otalgia** via CN X).
* **Haemoptysis & Foul Breath (Fetor Oris):** Blood-tinged sputum due to central tumor ulceration and necrotic slough.
* **Hard, Fixed Cervical Lymphadenopathy:** Painless upper/middle deep jugular nodal metastases.
* **Loss of Laryngeal Crepitus:** Resistance and absence of normal clicking when moving the thyroid cartilage across the cervical spine, indicating retro-laryngeal invasion.

#### d) Investigations and Expected Findings
1. **Flexible Fibreoptic Nasolaryngoscopy:** Visualizes the proliferative, fungating, or ulcerative vegetative mass on the vocal cord(s); assesses vocal cord fixation, anterior commissure involvement, and ventricular/subglottic extension.
2. **Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT) of Larynx & Neck (with Thin Slices):**
   * *Expected Findings:* Demonstrates deep soft tissue infiltration, invasion of the paraglottic and pre-epiglottic spaces, destruction or sclerosis of the thyroid/cricoid cartilage, and occult cervical nodal metastases (Level II, III, IV).
3. **Direct Laryngoscopy and Biopsy (Microlaryngoscopy under GA):**
   * *Findings:* Direct inspection of hidden areas (ventricle, subglottis, anterior commissure); biopsy confirms **invasive squamous cell carcinoma** and grade of differentiation.
4. **Chest Radiograph / CECT Thorax:** Evaluates for pulmonary metastases or a synchronous primary bronchogenic carcinoma.

#### e) Treatment Options
```
                     MANAGEMENT OF CANCER LARYNX
                                  |
         +------------------------+------------------------+
         |                                                 |
Early Disease (T1–T2, N0)                   Locally Advanced (T3–T4, N+)
  - Transoral Laser Microsurgery (TLM)        - Total Laryngectomy with Neck Dissection
    (Endoscopic CO2 laser cordectomy)           + Postoperative Radiotherapy (PORT)
  - OR Definitive EBRT                        - OR Organ Preservation Protocol:
    (66-70 Gy with voice preservation)          Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy (CCRT)
```
* **Locally Advanced Disease (T3 / T4a):**
  * **Option 1: Total Laryngectomy with Bilateral Selective Neck Dissection (Levels II–IV) + Postoperative Adjuvant Radiotherapy:**
    * Resection of the entire larynx, hyoid bone, pre-epiglottic space, strap muscles, and upper tracheal rings, creating a permanent end-tracheostome.
  * **Option 2: Organ Preservation Protocol (Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy — CCRT):**
    * High-dose Cisplatin combined with intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT - 70 Gy). Reserved for patients motivated to preserve their larynx with good pre-treatment laryngeal function. Total laryngectomy is reserved for salvage if disease recurs.
* **Alaryngeal Voice Rehabilitation Post-Laryngectomy:** Placement of a primary or secondary **Tracheo-Esophageal Voice Prosthesis (TEP — Blom-Singer / Provox)**.

---

questions.officialText: Malignant otitis externa - etiology, clinical features and treatment

note.title: Malignant Otitis Externa: Etiology, Clinical Features, and Treatment
note.content:
* **Definition:** A severe, necrotizing, osteomyelitic pseudomonal infection of the external acoustic canal and temporal bone, characteristically occurring in elderly diabetic or immunocompromised patients.
* **Etiology:** Causative organism is almost always ***Pseudomonas aeruginosa*** ($>95\%$). Infection starts in the cartilaginous canal and spreads via the **fissures of Santorini** and tympanomastoid suture into the skull base.
* **Clinical Features:**
  * Excruciating, deep-seated, boring otalgia that is characteristically **worse at night**.
  * Purulent, foul-smelling ear discharge.
  * **Pathognomonic Finding:** Persistent, bleeding **granulation tissue at the junction of the bony and cartilaginous canal** (floor of EAC) with an intact drum initially.
  * *Complications:* Skull base osteomyelitis with multiple cranial neuropathies (**Facial nerve CN VII is involved first** in 30–50%; followed by CN IX, X, XI, and XII at the jugular foramen).
  * Markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR typically $>100$ mm/hr).
* **Treatment:**
  1. *Strict Diabetic Glycemic Control.*
  2. *Prolonged Systemic Antipseudomonal Antibiotics:* Oral/IV **Ciprofloxacin** (750 mg BD) or IV **Ceftazidime / Piperacillin-Tazobactam** for a minimum of **6 to 8 weeks**.
  3. *Radionucleotide Monitoring:* **Technetium-99 bone scan** (sensitive for osteomyelitis diagnosis) and **Gallium-67 citrate scan** (correlates with active soft tissue infection; repeated every 4–6 weeks to assess treatment response and determine cure).
  4. *Local Care:* Regular micro-suction debridement and topical ciprofloxacin drops.

---

questions.subject: Otorhinolaryngology
questions.officialText: Cerebrospinal Fluid rhinorrhea - diagnosis and treatment

note.title: Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Rhinorrhoea: Diagnosis and Treatment
note.content:
* **Pathophysiology:** Abnormal communication between the subarachnoid space and the nasal cavity due to a breach in the arachnoid, dura mater, and skull base bone (cribriform plate, fovea ethmoidalis, sphenoid sinus). Most commonly caused by accidental or surgical head trauma (FESS, skull base surgery).
* **Diagnosis:**
  * *Clinical:* Unilateral, clear, watery nasal discharge that increases on bending forward or straining (**Reservoir Sign**); cannot be sniffed back; does not stiffen a handkerchief.
  * *Double Ring / Halo Sign:* Filter paper test shows central blood surrounded by a clear ring of CSF.
  * *Biochemical:* Detection of **Beta-2 Transferrin** (pathognomonic; absent in tears/mucus).
  * *Radiology:* High-Resolution Coronal CT (HRCT) of paranasal sinuses identifies bony defects; intrathecal fluorescein with nasal endoscopy localizes active leaks.
* **Treatment:**
  1. *Conservative (First-Line for Traumatic Leaks):* Strict bed rest with head elevated 30°, avoid nose blowing/straining, stool softeners, lumbar drain placement. Most resolve in 7–10 days.
  2. *Endoscopic Transnasal Skull Base Repair (Treatment of Choice):*
     * Multilayer underlay/overlay closure using fascia lata, temporalis fascia, middle turbinate mucosal graft, or pedicled **hadad-bassagasteguy nasoseptal flap**, secured with fibrin glue and Gelfoam.

---

note.title: Caldwell–Luc Operation
note.content:
* **Definition:** A surgical procedure to open the maxillary antrum through the **canine fossa** via a sublabial approach, providing wide access to the sinus cavity.
* **Indications:**
  1. Removal of foreign bodies or displaced dental roots from the maxillary sinus.
  2. Biopsy and staging of suspected maxillary antral tumours.
  3. Management of comminuted midfacial fractures (orbital floor reconstruction).
  4. Chronic maxillary sinusitis with irreversible hyperplastic mucosal changes (historic; largely replaced by FESS).
  5. Closure of persistent oroantral fistula.
* **Steps:**
  1. Sublabial gingivobuccal sulcus incision from lateral incisor to second molar.
  2. Periosteum elevated from the anterior maxillary wall up to the infraorbital nerve.
  3. Trephining of the thin bone of the canine fossa with a burr/gouge to enter the antrum.
  4. Diseased tissue, polyps, or foreign bodies removed.
  5. A counter-opening (**inferior meatal antrostomy**) created into the nasal cavity.
  6. Sublabial mucosal incision closed with absorbable sutures.
* **Complications:** Facial swelling/ecchymosis, numbness of the cheek and upper teeth (injury to infraorbital/superior alveolar nerves), and oroantral fistula.

---

note.title: Organ of Corti (Draw and Label)
note.content:
```
                            [ TECTORIAL MEMBRANE ]
                                 /          \
                                /            \
                      Outer Hair Cells    Inner Hair Cells
                         (3-4 Rows)           (1 Row)
                             |                   |
                             |  Tunnel of Corti  |
                             |   (Cortilymph)    |
                             v         ^         v
                      [Deiters'Cells]  |  [Inner Pillar]
                             |   [Outer Pillar]  |
                             v                   v
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------
                        [ BASILAR MEMBRANE ]
                                  ^
                                  |
                       Spiral Lamina & Fibers
```

* **Structures to Label:**
  1. *Basilar Membrane:* Supports the organ of Corti.
  2. *Inner Hair Cells:* Single row of flask-shaped sensory transducers; receive 95% of afferent auditory nerve fibers.
  3. *Outer Hair Cells:* 3 to 4 rows of cylindrical electromotile cells; amplify sound.
  4. *Tunnel of Corti:* Formed by the inner and outer pillar cells; contains cortilymph.
  5. *Supporting Cells:* Deiters’ cells, Hensen’s cells, Claudius' cells.
  6. *Tectorial Membrane:* Gelatinous acellular flap overlying the hair cell stereocilia.

note.content:
REFER TO [[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q09]] (2026_MARCH) AND [[KUHS-QUESTION:302001:Q08]] (2024_AUGUST)
* **Summary Table of Tests (512 Hz):**
  * *Rinne Test:* Normal / SNHL = Positive ($AC > BC$); Conductive loss = Negative ($BC > AC$).
  * *Weber Test:* Normal = Central; Conductive loss = Lateralizes to the *poorer* ear; SNHL = Lateralizes to the *better* ear.
  * *Absolute Bone Conduction (ABC):* Normal / Conductive loss = Normal; SNHL = Reduced.
  * *Schwabach’s Test:* Normal = Equal; Conductive loss = Lengthened; SNHL = Shortened.

note.title: Rhinolith
note.content:
* **Pathology:** A calcareous nasal calculus formed by the slow, progressive deposition of mineral salts (calcium and magnesium phosphate and carbonate) around an unrecognized exogenous foreign body (seed, cotton wool, bead) or endogenous nidus (blood clot, dried mucus).
* **Clinical Features:** Typically seen in adults; presents with **unilateral, foul-smelling, purulent, blood-stained nasal discharge** and unilateral obstruction. On probing, it feels **stony hard, rough, and gritty**, surrounded by friable granulation tissue.
* **Treatment:** Transnasal endoscopic extraction under local or general anesthesia; large or impacted calculi are crushed with forceps before removal.

note.title: Functions of the Nose
note.content:
1. **Respiration:** Natural physiological conduit for quiet tidal breathing.
2. **Air-Conditioning of Inspired Air:**
   * *Filtration:* Vibrissae trap coarse particles ($>3\ \mu\text{m}$); the sticky mucus blanket traps microscopic dust and bacteria.
   * *Humidification:* Saturates inspired air to $>75–90\%$ relative humidity via glandular secretions.
   * *Temperature Regulation:* Highly vascular erectile turbinate tissue acts as a radiator, warming or cooling inspired air to core body temperature ($37^\circ\text{C}$).
3. **Protection of Lower Airway:** Mucociliary clearance escalator clears trapped particles toward the pharynx; nasal secretions contain lysozyme, secretory IgA, and interferon.
4. **Olfaction:** Sensory detection of airborne volatile odorants by olfactory neuroepithelium in the olfactory cleft.
5. **Vocal Resonance:** Acts as an acoustic resonator for nasal consonants (/m/, /n/, /ng/).
